events.title: Russia plans to launch hundreds more satellites for its Starlink alternative in 2027, Ukraine says
events.summary: Russia plans to launch hundreds of satellites into orbit for its Rassvet system. Roscosmos/via REUTERS Ukrainian intel says Russia plans to launch hundreds of satellites for its Starlink alternative this year and next. Kyiv said on Friday that Russia is pressing ahead with its Rassvet constellation despite setbacks. Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to face disruption to its Starlink services. Russia plans to launch nearly 20 additional satellites this year and hundreds more next year as it accelerates the deployment of its Starlink alternative, Rassvet, Ukraine's military intelligence agency said Friday. The new assessment comes as Ukraine continues to face restrictions on its Starlink services , which it says are disrupting its drone operations. Russia has already launched 30 satellites this year for Rassvet, a low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation that it has billed as comparable to SpaceX's Starlink, which is widely used by Ukrainian forces. Rassvet's deployment has faced setbacks , including difficulties with launch and dependencies on foreign components, Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency said in a statement. Two of the 30 Russian satellites launched this year have already "deorbited," and while 26 have reached a stable position at an altitude of roughly 320 miles, none have reached the planned 500-mile altitude — though they are maneuvering toward it, the GUR said. Russia plans to expand the constellation to up to 48 satellites by the end of the year and launch another 240 next year to cover 94% of Russian territory with speeds of up to 150 Mbps, the GUR said. Moscow plans to bring the constellation up to 408 satellites by 2031 and 924 by 2035. The Rassvet satellites, each weighing little more than 600 pounds, rely on laser communication instead of ground stations to transfer data. Russia uses the Soyuz-2.1b three-stage rocket to launch its satellites into orbit. Ukraine has attacked production facilities that manufacture this family of rockets in an attempt to disrupt Moscow's space industry. Ukrainian forces are facing another round of Starlink service disruptions this week. Stringer/REUTERS Rassvet's main control center is in Moscow, but the GUR said Russia plans to build a network of ground stations across the country. Neither Russia's defense ministry nor its US embassy responded to a request for comment on the GUR's assessment. Rassvet is considered to be Russia's alternative to Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service that has been crucial for Ukrainian battlefield operations . Kyiv's forces also use Starshield, the military-grade variant. Russia was able to use Starlink in Ukraine until earlier this year, when Kyiv pressed SpaceX to disable its terminals . Starlink became a particularly significant asset for Ukraine in the months that followed, supporting a mix of combat operations by providing reliable communications for its drones. Last month, however, Ukraine was hit with  sudden restrictions on its Starshield services . Its forces endured speed limits for more than a week that severely affected its front-line operations. The shocking disruption came amid high tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure . Starlink services are available in Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory, but not inside Russia. Ukraine appears to be in the middle of another Starlink outage. On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had once again detected speed limits of 100 miles per hour. On Friday, Ukrainian defense ministry sources told Business Insider that these speed limits were being recorded across all Russian-occupied territory, but not on Ukrainian-controlled land. Zelenskyy said the disruption is affecting Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attack drones. Ukraine's defense ministry is in talks with SpaceX to resolve the issue and is seeking more information from the US Defense Department, the sources said. Ukraine's attack in August on Russia's Progress Rocket Space Center, the Rassvet satellite deployments, and the impacts of repeated Starlink outages underscore how space has emerged as a key focus of the war. events.title: Bessent: Treasury has wanted Megaspeed restrictions for months, but Commerce is in charge
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that his department and others have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, but Commerce is in charge. Jensen Huang, who just resigned as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal related to Megaspeed, had pushed to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months," Bessent told "Squawk Box." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal. But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box." The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed. Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported. Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room. Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s." "And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales. This is breaking news. events.title: Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years
events.summary: The producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, slightly less than the 0.4% forecast. On an annual basis, PPI surged 6.5%, the biggest increase since November 2022. Markets continued to full price in an interest rate hike of at least a quarter percentage point when the Fed meets in December. Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon. The producer price index , which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations. On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022. The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike. Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed. Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected. The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI. However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal. "Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched. "We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way." Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October. Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022. Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight. "We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks." Other items in the PPI report also showed multi-year gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

events.title: Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here
events.summary: Nvidia is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia's interim CEO. The implications of Huang's affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity. That's because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies. The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times . That was a "turbulent" period for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time. Nvidia was in the midst of redesigning some chips to comply with the first in a series of strict export controls imposed by the U.S. government that restricted sales to China. "The regulation is going to be just fine. We're going to be able to work through it," Huang told CNBC from Nvidia's headquarters in February 2023. The interview was for a documentary about how Huang created Nvidia and built it into the backbone of the AI boom. That same day, CNBC also interviewed Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair. It's not the first time Nvidia has faced an uncertain future. The company nearly went bankrupt in the early years after it was founded in 1993. "Every company makes mistakes and I make a lot of them," Huang said in the 2023 interview. "And some of them put the company in peril." In the early months of the AI boom, after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia was on the precipice of historic growth. Jensen Huang told CNBC he'd like to keep running the company for "three or four decades," as long as "I feel that I'm making a real contribution to the company." Less than four years later, Jensen Huang is out, and we're taking a look back at our interviews with the Nvidia co-founder and other company executives as the chipmaker enters this next critical chapter. events.title: ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans
events.summary: Canada gave Stellantis 30 days to address alleged breaches of a federal funding agreement or face potential legal action. The dispute escalated after Stellantis signed an agreement to sell its idled Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defense manufacturer Roshel. A Stellantis executive said the company would return $24 million in federal support, while Ottawa says the automaker could owe hundreds of millions of dollars. Canada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump 's trade war. Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action. "We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto. Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now "on the hook" for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as "unacceptable" and a "betrayal" of its workers. The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute , with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border. Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures. Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said in a statement shared with CNBC that the company would return $24 million it received in government support for the Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan. This amount, however, falls significantly short of the Canadian government's own estimate of what the company owes. "We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said. "As Canada's largest automotive employer, this decision also allows Stellantis to focus its resources on sustaining competitive manufacturing operations in Canada in the face of challenging market realities," he added. Stellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount. It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees. Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far. — CNBC's Michael Wayland contributed to this report.

events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow. The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled “Stand with Jensen,” and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company. The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him . Notable Several names have been floated for who could replace Huang, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, or even, on President Donald Trump’s suggestion , former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

events.title: Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey. Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam , respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge , a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows. However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook , November 2026 We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011. events.title: Nvidia lost its founding CEO. Can it keep its momentum?
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction. Nvidia’s founder Jensen Huang resigned after a scandal, but analysts say the chipmaker’s AI business should stay strong in the near term. The article says tech companies often do best when founders are replaced by leaders with deep technical and product skills, not mainly finance or sales experience. Apple, Microsoft and Intel show that successor choice can shape long-term success, while Nvidia now needs a leader to plan for rivals and the next AI shift. Advice to Nvidia’s board: choose a techie. As the chip giant’s directors seek a replacement to Jensen Huang , the history of successions at Silicon Valley companies suggests that the odds of long-term success are better with a person steeped in technology and product development rather than finance, sales or marketing. Replacing a founder is a defining moment for any company, whether it has been planned for years or is a sudden departure, whether the company is thriving or faltering. For Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and former CEO, the fall came remarkably quickly. He resigned on N ov 12 after the disclosure of affairs with a woman identified by US intelligence as a Chinese spy and with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia’s business as the leading chip supplier to artificial intelligence data centres is flourishing. Huang’s hasty exit, analysts say, will have little near-term effect on the company’s business, despite a big stock-market reaction – the company’s shares have fallen 14% in the past five days. But the best tech leaders steer their companies toward opportunity. At Nvidia, founded in 1993, Huang recognised more than a decade ago that chips used mainly for image-processing in computer games could be repurposed as the hardware engines for AI software. It was a huge bet for the small company – and paid off. “You can coast on the founder’s work for years with good execution,” said Steve Blank, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and investor, who is an adjunct professor at Stanford University. “But you can lack the founder’s vision to see over the horizon and identify what’s next. That’s why the best successors have a lot of technical acumen as well as business acumen.” Over the years, the results for tech companies replacing founding executives have been decidedly mixed. In 1985, Apple co-founder Steve Jobs was forced out after clashing with his CEO, John Sculley, who had come from Pepsico. Under Sculley, Apple enjoyed years of rising profits. But the company eventually struggled to compete against lower-cost personal computers based on Microsoft’s Windows software and Intel’s microprocessors. Scully left Apple in 1993. Three years later, with Apple’s survival uncertain, Jobs returned and became CEO. A renowned product team leader, he led a corporate renaissance, introducing new digital devices including the iPod and the iPhone that transformed the product categories of music players and cellphones. In 2011, shortly before he died, Jobs named Tim Cook as his successor. Cook has a degree in industrial engineering as well as a master’s in business administration. While some analysts said Apple lost some of its innovative spark, today the company is valued at US$5.16 trillion (S$6.65 trillion), the most valuable in the world. In September, Cook became executive chair and John Ternus, a mechanical engineer and product development executive, became the company’s CEO. Intel did not fare so well. While Andrew Grove did not found the chipmaker, he was among its first employees and led the company for nearly two decades. Grove emigrated from Hungary, learnt English and earned an undergraduate degree and a doctorate in chemical engineering. Grove led Intel’s drive to dominate the market for microprocessor chips, the electronic brains of personal computers. He became the face of Intel and one of the architects of the personal computer industry, named Time magazine’s Man Of The Year in 1997. Grove’s immediate successor in 1998, Craig Barrett, was also a technologist. But later successors less so – and Intel’s fortunes declined precipitously. As part of efforts to help revive American chip manufacturing, the US government said in 2025 that it would invest nearly US$9 billion in Intel for a stake of just under 10%. Some of the biggest tech companies have learnt that technical expertise at the top is indispensable. Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, stepped aside as CEO in 2000 and handed the job to his longtime business partner, Steve Ballmer. Ballmer was known as a brilliant sales and business development executive, and a tireless, hands-on manager. During his years as CEO, from 2000 to 2014, Microsoft’s sales and profits rose steadily. But Ballmer’s lack of tech expertise contributed to an erosion of Microsoft’s reputation as an industry leader.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said . The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change." Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it. Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms." Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put. The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027. Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite. Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well . events.title: ‘So lovely’: Stevie Wonder surprises Stalybridge restaurant with late-night visit and £1,000 tip
events.summary: Singer, 76, was in Manchester with his band for penultimate UK show of his Songs in the Key of Life anniversary tour When Stevie Wonder’s team just called to say: “Can we all come to your restaurant in Stalybridge at 11pm on a Sunday?” Ryan Robinson, of course, said yes. First the band turned up, and then – at 12.30am – the man himself arrived. Hours later, staff at the Cafe Continental were sharing a £1,000 tip. It was, the co-owner admitted, “all a bit mad”, as he praised Wonder as someone who was happy to chat to everybody, and the team around him as down to earth and extremely polite. Wonder, 76, was in Manchester with his band for the Sunday night gig at Co-op Live on his Songs in the Key of Life 50th anniversary tour. It was the penultimate night of a 13-date European leg of the tour in which Wonder performed all 21 songs from his most celebrated album, which includes Have a Talk With God, Sir Duke, Joy Inside My Tears and Isn’t She Lovely. Robinson told the Manchester Evening News that some of the musicians on the tour had already been in a few times, “as they often tour with other artists”. “Every time they’ve visited, they’ve been like: ‘Stevie might come’, and we were always just thinking that it would be amazing but we never expected anything from it. “His band visited again on Saturday and then we got the call to say they wanted to come again with Stevie’s youngest daughter after their show in Manchester, and they said again that Stevie might come. We stayed open late for them, and then he turned up – it was all a bit mad! “We normally just do a roast service on Sunday, so it was a bit of a scramble to make it all happen and ensure we had the full menu ready for them, but everybody was so lovely. Stevie is actually a really nice guy and was happy to pose for photographs and have a chat.” Among the late-night diners was Wonder’s daughter Aisha, for whom he wrote Isn’t She Lovely when she was a newborn. Robinson said: “His daughter, his family, and his entire team are just all down to earth and very polite. You wouldn’t think they were these massive global superstars. I just kept looking over being like: ‘Is this actually happening?’ We’ve still not come to terms with it now!” Cafe Continental describes itself as a neighbourhood restaurant in the heart of Stalybridge, “offering a modern, day to night dining experience”. The superstar and his musicians dined on steak and seafood and before leaving they gave a £1,000 tip, which was shared among staff, Robinson said. After the visit the restaurant posted on Facebook: “Surreal things happen now and again. This is one of them! Pleasure to welcome Mr Stevie Wonder to the restaurant to close off his tour!” Robinson said he thought the band had found the restaurant on social media. “If it wasn’t for social media, they more than likely may have Googled something nearby and it might have led them to the city centre,” he told the BBC. “But it’s brought them out here into the suburbs and it’s really nice to see. “It’s good for the area. For a small independent business like us to receive so much traction from this … getting a major celebrity to this town itself, it does a lot.”

events.title: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
events.summary: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said. Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment. State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official. Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible. "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period." The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel. His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so. In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds. On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran. A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think the current situation demands immediate military action against Iran.

events.title: Nvidia stock inches higher as investors continue to weigh Jensen Huang’s departure
events.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after coming under scrutiny for two extramarital affairs. Nvidia shares hovered near the flatline in premarket trading on Friday. Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs. It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower. Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Huang was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month. A lot of the company's success has been built around Huang, said Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF. It's about more than just Nvidia, but also about the "architecture of the AI industry that really depended on the vision" and expertise of Huang, Houri told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

events.title: Debate in New York City over city-run groceries is not just about food, but something bigger
events.summary: Five city-run groceries in a city of 8 million won't substantially lower food prices, but the experiment might cause shoppers to think differently about the role of government. Spencer Platt/Getty Images New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow. Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices. Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses . What explains this pushback? As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs. The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food. It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see. That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly. If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide. Some immigrant owners of New York grocery stores have warned that city-run alternatives will undercut them. Scott Gries/Getty Images How the plan will work New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all. While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices. In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals. Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable. At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.” A fresh form of intervention Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses. In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business. A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods. These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them. FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers. Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets. This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare. This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .” Bringing the state into the open Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways. First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food. If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate. Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable. To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. events.title: UK’s biggest insurer hit by rise in subsidence claims after record hot summer
events.summary: Increase reported by Aviva after Hastings Direct said claims were up 140% in August and Axa said it had been a ‘surge year’ The UK’s largest insurer has been hit by a rise in subsidence claims after an extremely hot summer left households across the country grappling with the fallout from the growing climate crisis. Aviva said on Friday it had experienced the jump amid an industry-wide surge in households filing subsidence claims with their insurers to cover repairs, which typically are needed to address cracks, sloping floors, and off-kilter doors and windows. It follows two record hot summers in the UK; August this year was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Drier summers cause the ground under houses to shrink, which undermines a property’s foundations. It then expands in wetter winters, which can further damage homes. Aviva experienced a “peak subsidence period” between July and September, with claims continuing into October, its chief executive, Amanda Blanc, told Bloomberg in an interview on Friday. Aviva would not provide any further detail on the scale of the increase in claims. Blanc said homeowners could reduce the risk of subsidence by keeping a close eye on drains, pipes and gutters, and fixing any leaks that could affect the ground under homes. “It’s about managing trees and plumbing,” she said. A number of fellow insurers have also experienced a rise in claims in recent months. Hastings Direct said it received record subsidence claims in August , up 140% compared with a year earlier. Axa, one of the UK’s biggest home insurers, has said it has been a “surge year” for subsidence. The value of claims have also hit a record high. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a high of £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers. Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, according to the British Geological Survey, which estimates that up to 11% of UK homes – more than 4.2m houses – could be at risk by 2070. Older properties with shallow foundations and those built on clay-rich soil are facing the biggest threat, with areas including London, Essex, Kent and areas around Oxford among the most vulnerable. We continue to deliver strong, profitable growth, particularly in the capital-light areas of general insurance and wealth.”

events.title: Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?
events.summary: What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. The departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking company which has become the backbone of the modern AI industry, has shaken the US’s Silicon Valley. Nvidia, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is a critical pillar of the US economy where AI and tech companies make up some 40 percent of stock market valuations. The furore over Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the company’s market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. While CFO Colette Kress has temporarily stepped into the top job at Nvidia, the search for cofounder Huang’s successor continues. What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. So, what’s next for Nvidia? On October 29, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang, had been tapped by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information from Nvidia’s Huang. The newspaper reported that the two were involved in an intimate relationship, later confirmed by the cofounder of the company in an internal memo. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote in an internal memo to Nvidia staff. The business links go beyond just the affair, however, fuelling further concerns. Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over roughly two years. Separately, The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5bn in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising even more questions about skirting US export controls. Then, on Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. The next day, Huang was forced out of the company and off its board. Hours later, Reuters reported that Huang had allegedly been involved in a third affair with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. In simple terms, if Nvidia sneezes, the AI industry and modern computing catch a cold. Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips which are used to train frontier AI models, giving it an extraordinary degree of influence over the global AI industry and the infrastructure powering it. Observers say the company holds the keys to next-generation computing. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres. That’s also why Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China. Nvidia’s Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors. That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing has “always opposed the abuse of export control measures”, as pressure gains momentum yet again in Washington. Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as “baseless”. In China, investors have been selling shares in Chinese AI-linked companies over worries that recent developments at Nvidia could deepen the technological divide between Beijing and Washington. On Friday, shares in Z.AI, one of China’s top AI model developers, tumbled more than 10 percent in Hong Kong while shares in rival MiniMax hit record lows. A Reuters review identified more than $3bn in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia’s restricted processors – despite the American chipmaker claiming that US export controls effectively shut it out of the AI data-centre market in the world’s second-biggest economy. The examination shows projects stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, and underscores how deeply Nvidia’s technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. What’s happened to Nvidia’s share price and will it recover? Nvidia shares rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday after losing around 11 percent of their value this week up to Thursday, when Huang exited the company he built. The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012. US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, next week in Shenzhen at the APEC leaders’ summit.

events.title: Global oil supply returns to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, says IEA
events.summary: Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’ The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said. Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”. The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported. It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes. The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April. However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “ effectively over ”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday. There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes . However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter. The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes. Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

events.title: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
events.summary: Watch: What we know about the Microsoft global outage overnight Published 13 November 2026, 07:12 GMT A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products. Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems". Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues. How many people have been affected? More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening. The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting. Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected. From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed. In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected. The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted. Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage. Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report. Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure. The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do. In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these. On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added it is focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" and warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue". In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected". Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming for some, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

events.title: Microsoft outage live: millions still affected as disruption stretches beyond 18 hours
events.summary: Readers in the US may be surprised to wake up to the news that Microsoft's outage is not fixed! While North America was asleep, there has been widepread disruption around the world – from schools, courts and public services in Australia , to companies and government services in Japan , and then schools, the police and the NHS in the UK . The cause of the mega-outage, which began around 18 hours ago, is still not known. Microsoft says it has “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” at this time. Reminder, it reported around 45 minutes ago that the situation was improving in Europe, Japan and North America . Many Microsoft 365 services are affected, for example: Problems with Exchange Online mean users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web Microsoft 365 Education features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted. Microsoft Copilot 365 – users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps The Microsoft To Do app may not load, and users may see operation failures. Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats. Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. events.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
events.summary: Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high. Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover. Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers. The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices. The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate. Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say. Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month ( see the chart above ), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft. A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens. "The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states. Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too. The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning . Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states. With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA predicts the global market will return to a surplus this quarter. Yes, but: Insurance and shipping costs are elevated, and that puts upward pressure on prices. "Both Iran and the Houthis have demonstrated that they can severely restrict oil flows from the region using a range of attacks and tactics. This is something that will have to be priced in," Torbjorn Soltvedt, a senior Verisk analyst, tells me via email. And there's no guarantee that higher tanker transit and increased shipments through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz won't be curtailed by fresh attacks. Zoom in: Goldman Sachs estimates that the tanker market's "adaptation to Mideast shipping risks" accounts for most of the $20-per-barrel year-over-year increase in average costs for shipping oil. These freight rates reflect vessel availability, insurance, fuel cost, logistics, travel distances and more. What we're watching: It's unclear how much more oil can keep leaving the region in the near term, as intermittent attacks keep happening. "The current recovery may be close to the limit of what the existing logistics system can sustain," HSBC's Kim Fustier said in a recent note. The bottom line: "We would not equate [oil] exports with normality," Fustier writes. She cited substantial volumes of well production that remain curtailed, lower refined product shipments, and "and the cost of sustaining exports." events.title: Oil market to return to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, IEA says
events.summary: The global oil market is to return to a surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war, despite supplies remaining tight, the International Energy Agency has said. Global oil supplies have outpaced demand for the first time since the conflict broke out in late February. Crude inventories rose by 1.7 million barrels per day in October as exports from the Gulf recovered faster than worldwide demand, the Paris-based IEA said in its monthly market report on Friday. Inventories climbed by 2.3 million bpd to 105.4 million bpd last month, raising output by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million bpd since August, the IEA said. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, hit 18.4 million bpd in October, which was 26 per cent below prewar levels as attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz continued. That narrowed the year-on-year output decline to 2.9 million bpd, compared with an average loss of eight million bpd loss from March to September, the agency added. The higher export rates also prompted the IEA to "significantly" raise its expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of 2026, with fourth-quarter estimates now 3.3 million bpd higher. The oil market is "straightening out" and "showing tentative signs of rebalancing", the IEA said. But the agency acknowledged that global oil demand continues to be weighed down by high prices and disruptions to exports of refined products and liquefied petroleum gas from the Gulf, which largely remain at about half of prewar levels. The agency forecasts that global oil demand in 2026 will fall by 2.7 million bpd to 102.3 million bpd, a slight decrease from its October projections . Demand is to recover by two million bpd in 2027, it added. While LPG, ethane and naphtha will account for about 80 per cent of the expected increase next year as supply chains normalise, transport fuels will see a modest gain, "as high prices accelerate electrification and fuel efficiencies across the global car fleet", the IEA said. The "severe tightness" in supply is still particularly pronounced for diesel, which has soared to record levels, especially in the US. Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country’s diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East, the IEA said. "At the same time, Atlantic Basin refineries, particularly in the United States, are running hard to capture high margins, while improved crude availability in Asia and fresh Chinese product export quotas could support higher refinery throughput rates in the region," it said. "Notably, the accelerated release of IEA emergency diesel stocks over the coming months will provide a critical bridge across the supply gap until the global refinery system and product output recover." The oil market is gradually recovering from the effects of the Iran war, which is now in its ninth month. While the US has signalled that it does not plan to carry out further military action against Tehran, a resolution to the conflict remains unclear. Oil prices have been volatile throughout the war, but have markedly declined over the past weeks. At 5.02pm UAE time on Friday, Brent was up 0.35 per cent at $96.16 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate shed 0.18 per cent to $88.58 a barrel. The IEA's supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a more substantial build in 2027. "As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery," the agency said.

events.title: CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade
events.summary: CFTC Chairman Michael Selig says major crypto exchanges and new entrants are showing interest in using the agency's federal oversight framework. The CFTC published an advance notice on Oct. 5 seeking comment on a framework for retail crypto commodity transactions after the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act on Sept. 15. Democrats' 2026 congressional gains are expected to bring greater scrutiny of crypto regulation and President Donald Trump's crypto ties in 2027. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig. The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement , Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world. Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading. "We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added. After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities. "We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said. "Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said. Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes. But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration. "I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said. Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory. "I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable. When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate." "I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said. Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets. Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps. "We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling." CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

events.title: Microsoft’s latest email outage turned into a full blown global cloud crisis
events.summary: Microsoft is slowly recovering from its day-long outage after much of the company’s systems were hit by a cascading software issue. The problems, which started Thursday, were initially flagged as affecting the company’s services in the U.S. and the Americas, but quickly spread around the world, as engineers struggled to recover downed servers. What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full blown meltdown, affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools, Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers. Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.” The company said it continues to investigate the cause. The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email. We’ve reached out to Microsoft for comment about the incident. As of Friday morning on the U.S. east coast, Microsoft’s Outlook email service had begun to recover and some emails have been trickling in. The recovery comes after engineers initially could not find the cause of the issue that was causing servers in Microsoft’s data centers to fail. Doug Madory, the director of internet analysis at Kentik, a company that monitors internet traffic worldwide, said in a post on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime. Microsoft said in its latest status update on Friday that there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident.” That may be some solace for the millions who went without their email and online services yesterday, but the company is likely to face questions about its inability to swiftly recover from an outage of its own making. A Microsoft spokesperson did not respond to our questions asking if the company has the technical means to detect malicious activity, such as logs, or if Microsoft has a way to check what happened. The last major incident affecting Microsoft services was in September , when a days-long outage hit Microsoft’s cloud services. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service. events.title: I binged 100 TikToks in an hour at a movie theater — and had some surprisingly deep feelings about it
events.summary: Content creator Max Zavidow screened over 300 of his TikToks on the big screen at Cherry Lane Theatre. Michelle Paradis I spent my Wednesday afternoon bingeing one creator's TikToks in a movie theater. Max Zavidow, a New York-based comedian and content creator, screened over 300 of his TikToks. Zavidow wanted people "to feel the agony" of re-watching all his videos — and see his career arc. One hour, 100 TikToks, one big screen. That's how I spent my lunch break on Wednesday. Max Zavidow , a New York-based content creator with 1.4 million TikTok followers, booked the historic Cherry Lane Theatre to screen more than 300 of his TikToks. Perched in the front row with a camera livestreaming his reactions, Zavidow watched (almost) every single video he's made in the past five years flash before his eyes. He cringed, laughed, and reflected on his career. Zavidow's live reactions to his own TikToks: cringing and laughing. Max Zavidow "It is hard to watch your old work," he told me. The screening was, in part, a parody of Shia LaBeouf's "#ALLMYMOVIES," in which the actor livestreamed himself for 72 hours watching his films in 2015. Zavidow, who started posting TikToks at the end of 2021, wanted the screening to "paint a complete picture" of what it means to have a career as a content creator and "evolve on the internet." "I wanted people to feel the agony of me having to look back," he said. The whole ordeal took four hours. I stayed for one. Meanwhile, TikTokers and creator-economy peers popped in and out of the dark theater. The event was free and invitation-only, done in partnership with the theater, which is owned by A24, and produced by Love Letter. "I had six days to pull it together," Zavidow said. Zavidow sat front row at the screening of his TikToks. Michelle Paradis My viewing experience may not have been as groundbreaking as sitting through Nathan Fielder's " You Can See Everything ." Still, I walked out of the theater with more thoughts about TikTok, entertainment, and the creator's career arc. Here are three lingering takeaways. 1. TikTok and Instagram on the TV may not be a bad idea after all I'll be honest, I've been skeptical about social media coming to TV. That's partly because I don't use a TV to watch TV. I usually watch HBO and Netflix on my iPhone . Watching Zavidow's TikToks on the screen, however, was great. Who would have thought watching TikToks while sitting at a 90-degree angle would be pleasant? Zavidow's "#ALLMYTIKTOKS" is a parody of Shia LaBeouf's "#ALLMYMOVIES" stunt from 2015. Michelle Paradis "Getting it on a big screen was a way to say, 'I take this really seriously, and you guys are saying that the big screen is serious. Great. Let's put our TikToks on the big screen,'" Zavidow told me. There was an added cinematic effect to watching videos one would usually watch alone with headphones, on a big screen in the company of dozens of other people. 2. Doing the same thing again and again — sometimes — pays off Zavidow's 316 TikToks were split up into chapters, starting with "See What Sticks." Then, there was the era of "Walk and Talk," "Still Talking, Less Walking," a brief moment of shanties and comedic rhymes, and eventually, "Really Short Films," where Zavidow zeroed in on more narrative fiction. Zavidow split up his TikToks into chapters. Michelle Paradis At certain points, we watched pretty much the same video slightly tweaked. A new angle, a different setup for the joke. "It was so hard to watch all my old videos and be like, 'Oh my God, dude, another one?'" he told me. Making it as a creator requires testing out formula after formula. "At a certain point I found something that worked," Zavidow said. "So I did that for a while." 3. I love screen time — it's the ads and distractions that give me dread When I walked out of the theater to a sunny corner in the West Village, I felt … at ease. Sitting through an hour of uninterrupted short clips designed to make me laugh felt almost as satisfying as a nasal rinse. There were no ads. No buttons to press. No comments to read. No need to move my thumbs. My mind was still — empty. Peak brain rot . Maybe that's OK. Read the original article on Business Insider
