events.title: Microsoft's outage is in its 2nd day, and it's causing chaos for businesses. Here's what we know.
events.summary: Microsoft 365 is suffering an outage affecting services including Outlook and Teams. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Microsoft's Outlook outage enters a second day as global recovery efforts continue. Microsoft says a fix is making its servers more stable, but Outlook is still unavailable. The outage is disrupting governments, airlines, and some AI tools. Microsoft's global Outlook outage has dragged into a second day, leaving users unable to access email and disrupting Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 tools. It has also affected AI tools . Anthropic and OpenAI said in status update pages that their connectors to Microsoft 365 tools had been disrupted. Anthropic said the issues were fixed by 6:58 a.m. ET on Friday. Here's what we know so far about the Microsoft outage that's causing chaos for businesses. What's the latest? Microsoft said in a 7:58 a.m. ET update that it was seeing "sustained improvements" in Europe. Asia Pacific was seeing "encouraging recovery signals," it added, and North America was also improving. It warned that some users could still face intermittent problems. About an hour earlier, Microsoft said that email delivery was improving, but warned some users could still run into problems while it works to restore the rest of its systems. Microsoft said in that earlier update it was focused on clearing the backlog of delayed emails. It is keeping messages in the system for up to 48 hours, giving them more time to be delivered rather than immediately returning an error. The company has not provided a timeline for a full recovery. What happened? Microsoft first flagged the outage on Thursday around midday ET, writing in an X post that users in the Americas were having trouble accessing Exchange Online mailboxes. It later said in a follow-up post that the issue could affect users "in any region." By Friday morning, Microsoft's public service status page was still showing "service degradation" for both Microsoft 365 business customers and consumer products. Microsoft said in a later X update on Thursday that some of its infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions. It said the strain was not caused by an increase in customer traffic, but because a number of servers had unexpectedly become unavailable. Microsoft also said in that 3:34 a.m. update that it had "no indication" the disruption was caused by malicious activity. In further X updates on Thursday, it said it had taken steps including restarting servers. Early Friday, Microsoft said that servers initially returned to service could become unresponsive again once traffic hit them. What's the impact? The outage has caused significant disruption for businesses, with many workers unable to use systems such as email or Teams. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US at the outage's peak on Thursday. That figure reflects user reports, not a confirmed count of affected people or businesses. Other Microsoft services are affected too. It said in its service advisory that the disruption could affect Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, Microsoft Defender, Intune, Power BI, and other Microsoft 365 products that rely on Exchange Online. Reuters reported on Thursday that the US House of Representatives said the outage had affected its users, while electric-truck maker Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings call because of the disruption. Air India said in a Thursday X post that it had rerouted email services, while IndiGo said in an X post on Friday that its email support channel was disrupted. Both airlines said their flight operations were unaffected. AP also reported that government agencies in Singapore, the Philippines, and Japan had reported knock-on effects. Is this unusual? Microsoft — and other Big Tech companies — have been here before. But this outage is unusually long. It has now lasted more than 19 hours as of 8:00 a.m. ET — longer than a major Microsoft 365 disruption in June 2022, which took 16 hours and 27 minutes to recover from, according to a Microsoft service alert , potentially making it the company's longest 365 outage ever. Microsoft also suffered a separate outage for Azure, its cloud service, on September 30 and October 1, affecting customers across several regions. Microsoft said it rolled back a change after some customers had trouble using its cloud networking services. Other cloud providers have faced similar problems. Google said a global Google Cloud and Workspace outage in June 2025 lasted three hours. Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing arm, also had a major disruption in Northern Virginia in October 2025. It said it fixed the initial problem in about two and a half hours, though some services took longer to return to normal. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Outlook outage continues as Microsoft flags 'encouraging recovery signals'
events.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company said it did not suspect malicious activity was the cause and it was attempting to restore operations. Amazon Web Services said it was "operating normally" and noted inaccurate reports of outages on its platforms. Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, causing disruption to millions of its customers as engineers scrambled to fix one of its biggest-ever server issues. Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit. In an update shortly before 8 a.m. ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email. However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific. Intermittent issues are expected as recovery efforts continue. Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users on Thursday afternoon and evening, throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected. Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported. A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more. Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users. The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone. "We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities." "Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said. Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

events.title: Kenyan building collapse near Nairobi kills six people
events.summary: Following on the heels of a similar accident three weeks ago, the incident is encouraging calls for improved safety oversight on construction sites. The collapse of an unfinished eight-storey building in Kenya has killed six people. The structure fell on Friday morning in Syokimau on the outskirts of Nairobi. Coming on the heels of a similar recent incident in the capital, the accident has revived calls for stronger safety oversight. list 1 of 3 Who is Kenya’s starvation cult leader? list 2 of 3 ‘Boxed through my skin’: British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali wins first title list 3 of 3 Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, awaits disease-free status Construction workers were reportedly at the site when the building’s uppermost concrete slab gave way, bringing down part of the structure, according to a preliminary report from Nairobi City County’s emergency team. The report did not establish why the slab failed. The Kenya Red Cross initially reported that three people had been rescued and one person was reported missing. TV reports later said that five people had been pulled alive from the rubble and taken to hospital. The emergency report said the number of workers present when the building fell had not been confirmed, leaving open the possibility that others were trapped. Firefighters and specialist rescue teams were continuing to search for survivors. Patrick Makau, a member of Kenya’s parliament representing Mavoko, the constituency that includes Syokimau, urged rescue agencies in a post on social media to act quickly. “Every second counts,” he wrote, offering condolences to the victims’ families. The accident follows a similar deadly building collapse in the city on October 23, which killed eight people. The twin disasters have prompted calls for tougher construction oversight. The Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, a state research body, has identified poor workmanship, inadequate supervision, substandard materials and faulty designs as wider causes of building collapses.

events.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers. Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think . Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China. The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve . —James O’Donnell More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want. events.title: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force
events.summary: Trump said he wants to “get Cuba done” before leaving office in 2029 and would “certainly consider” a short U.S. military operation. The comments come as Washington intensifies economic pressure on Cuba, including new sanctions targeting oil tankers and shipping companies. Cuba is grappling with severe fuel shortages, blackouts and economic strain, while analysts see further economic pressure as more likely than military action. U.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to " get Cuba done " before leaving office in 2029, adding that he would "certainly consider" military intervention against the communist-run Caribbean island. In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump said his administration was monitoring the situation in Havana "very closely" and described Cuba as a "failed" state. "I want to get Cuba done before I leave," Trump said. His comments marked the first time he has put a timeline on possible military intervention to topple Cuban authorities, according to Politico. Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio , whose parents are from Cuba, "would love to do it" and said he would "certainly consider" a short military operation. It comes as the U.S. continues to enforce a comprehensive economic embargo against Cuba, a campaign which has contributed to a deepening energy and economic crisis on the island. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts in recent months, as well as fuel and food shortages. The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., estimated on Thursday that the cost of the U.S. blockade to Cuba between March 2025 and February 2026 amounted to $8 billion. Earlier this month, the Treasury Department imposed further sanctions on Cuban oil tankers and shipping companies and threatened to target any international entity or person doing business within its marine or maritime industries as part of a push "to end the Cuban regime's malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere." In response, Cuba's Embassy in Washington, D.C., said these steps "deepen an energy siege that already leaves hospitals without reliable power and families facing blackouts. The blockade is not targeted at a government. It is collective punishment that hits ordinary people every day." Trump has previously talked up the prospect of a " friendly takeover " of Havana and said the White House could turn its sights on Cuba after the Iran war . The U.S. president has also said he could do anything he wanted with the country, adding that he thinks he will have the " honor " of "taking Cuba." In May, Cuban Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy said the country of roughly 10 million had run out of fuel oil and diesel, describing the country's predicament as "extremely tense." Analysts have typically been skeptical about the prospect of a U.S. military campaign against Cuba, suggesting that further economic pressure against the island's authorities appears more likely.

events.title: Huang's downfall may undo cozy ties between business and government: analysis
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit and the recent election results could make corporate leaders more cautious about close public ties to the White House. The two developments may also create pressure for increased regulation of companies. A poll of midterm voters showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision. The resignation of Jensen Huang , together with the results of the recent congressional election , could make this a watershed moment in the relationship of American business to government, one that sees the pendulum swing back toward greater regulation and greater separation of finance from politics. Corruption topped the list among issues that motivated voters in the overwhelming and nationwide midterm election victory for Democrats, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. It showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision, a percentage point higher than the cost of living. When voters were asked which party was best able to deal with the corruption issue, Democrats led Republicans 37% to 30% — though, significantly, 32% said neither party. It's impossible to know exactly what voters mean when they say corruption, but there are hints it involves the relationship of business to government. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey, taken two weeks before the election, asked respondents if elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should personally own or trade stocks in companies that have contracts with the federal government. An overwhelming 93% said it should not be allowed . A similarly bipartisan 89% objected to the president's family members receiving government contracts. The upshot: The very close relationship between business and the government, which has existed under both political parties but has come plainly and brazenly to the fore in President Trump's second administration, is now a major issue for voters. The Huang affair encompasses all of that. Nvidia, along with several other large corporations, made large donations to the president's ballroom . Meanwhile, there are allegations that the administration did not act when informed of potentially illegal sales of Nvidia chips to China. It may be that the president ignored warnings from inside his own administration that Huang was involved with a woman who was reportedly a potential Chinese spy , instead bringing Huang on a state visit to China and giving him say in U.S. export policies for chips. The Trump era has seen the virtual creation of the CEO Statesman: Huang and other tech execs draped around the president during foreign trips, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiating with Russia , Elon Musk deciding who the federal government fires. Could the Huang affair be the end of that phenomenon? Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., wasted no time in signaling the new Congress was ready to get tough on tech execs. "It's clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China's hands." The enormity of Huang's fall cannot be overstated. Imagine J.P. Morgan resigning — or Jack Welch or Steve Jobs or Tim Cook. Few have stood astride the pinnacle of political and corporate power during their era like Huang during the AI boom. This comes at a time of massive wealth increases for the elite that have helped undermine faith in capitalism. The CNBC Voter Poll showed 56% with a strong or somewhat favorable opinion of capitalism, with 32% reporting an unfavorable opinion and 12% saying they don't know. But those numbers are overwhelmingly driven by older Americans. Younger Americans, ages 18 to 34, have a deeply negative opinion. Those aged 35 to 49 are favorable toward capitalism by only a 46%-41% margin. For starters, it could result in a return to more traditional separation of business and politics, where business has less of a direct say in policy. But this could be the start of a more significant change. In the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the banking system was put under such strict regulations, many of which exist to this day, that one commentator remarked it was "in receivership in everything but name only." One can go back even further to more extreme measures taken when the public was deeply dissatisfied with business — to the fallout from the robber baron era when the trusts were busted up, or the wake of the Great Depression when the government put stricter regulations on banks and Wall Street and gave unions more power. Democrats will be limited, even with large gains in both houses, in their ability to overturn presidential decisions with veto-proof majorities. But executives themselves may decide that it's not a good look any longer to be seen being too cozy with the White House.

events.title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
events.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts . Dyania Health , a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would. The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision. Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital. Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on. Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers. Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021. Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand. “Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson , chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic. The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries. events.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
events.summary: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition. Big tech’s opening pitch about datacenters was typical: they told Americans that these facilities brought jobs and tax revenue . They spread this message through mailers , text messages , TV spots and targeted digital ads . But much of the spending behind these multimedia campaigns flowed through opaque non-profits and dark money groups with tech industry ties, hiding the source of these efforts. Groups like “ Elevate New Mexico ” have passed themselves off as local initiatives while obscuring their connections to corporate entities in the datacenter space. As environmental concerns mounted, the industry turned to misdirection and jargon to obscure datacenters’ impact. Developers continue to use terms such as “ closed-loop cooling ” and “ behind-the-meter power ” to deflect concerns about water and power consumption. But while these approaches can mitigate consumption, the effect is smaller than often implied: closed-loop systems may simply shift demand for water up the supply chain to power plants, while behind-the-meter generators still rely on the grid for backup and stability while competing with it for components. And those industry figures about job creation? They are often presented without any context. To give an example, an ad by Build American AI – an industry advocacy group connected to Lead the Future, an industry Pac funded by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz – boasts that datacenters have created 57,785 jobs in Texas. But industry figures can also be misleading: of the promised jobs, how many are permanent jobs remaining after construction? How many are cafeteria workers, landscapers, and custodial staff – who often work for subcontractors without benefits? And are those subcontractors included when industry reports the average salaries for the jobs they do create? A similar story applies to other tax benefits. When companies mention the tax revenue they bring to communities, they rarely include the exemptions and abatements they received. Those incentives are often unnecessary to attract projects and eat directly into budgets for schools and social services. Some jurisdictions even track the precise number of dollars they forgo through such abatements. But even when agreements allow communities to claw back money from underperforming projects, local leaders are often hesitant to do so because they don’t want to admit a project has failed. In other words, accountability is rare. The industry fights to keep critical details about projects under wraps, sometimes working with local authorities to do so. In The Dalles, Oregon, for example, Google paid the city’s legal fees after it withheld records about a datacenter’s water use. (The city agreed to release the information in a settlement with the Oregonian newspaper.) Most datacenters do not report their water consumption at all, hampering policymaking. As for the public, their visibility into the process is limited by non-disclosure agreements. Local and state officials, operating in a low-information environment and starved of resources by anti-tax policies, welcomed these facilities at first. The public has been more skeptical. With time, some government officials have joined them. Yet, local organizers and activists told us that they now see decisions about their economic future as pre-determined by big business and opaque governments. They criticized the lack of transparency, the late stage at which the public was consulted, and community benefits agreements they felt were inadequate compared to the burdens they were being asked to bear: higher electric costs, air pollution, noise, water depletion, and a change in the character of their communities. Industrial tycoons have historically manipulated leaders, laws, and regulations to their advantage. This time, though, resistance has been fierce. Perhaps that is why the industry has stooped to smearing its opponents as useful stooges of foreign propaganda. In May, Kevin O’Leary – the millionaire Shark Tank star who is developing one of the world’s largest datacenters – called two activists “proxies for the Chinese government”. He later admitted he had “ no evidence ”. Even so, similar theories have gained traction among tech executives and Washington policymakers. And it has percolated to the local level, where activists and organizers tell us they face this invective – and much more – online.

events.title: FTC to block $3.5B veterinary merger
events.summary: The Scoop The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again. The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival. The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said. Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment. Rohan’s view Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission — even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested. It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trump’s agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires. The FTC is also planning to block a $5 billion merger of two uniform and office equipment suppliers, Semafor reported . The FTC plans to set a last-rites meeting — a precursor to that formal suit — in the coming days, other people familiar with the matter said. Notable Merger investigations neared a record low in 2025 , according to the DAMITT database maintained by law firm Dechert.

events.title: A private equity giant just snapped up a creator company, and it points to the next phase of investment in the sector
events.summary: Eric Tencer, managing director at H.I.G. Growth, and Jake Rosen, founder of Jake Rosen Entertainment, are hunting for creator-economy deals. H.I.G. Growth H.I.G. Capital is betting on the creator economy, starting with the acquisition of Jake Rosen Entertainment. The PE giant envisions building a Whalar Group-style company serving brands and talent. PE is playing a small but growing role in the creator economy, a sign of the sector's maturation. The creator economy is catching private equity's eye. H.I.G. Capital, an investment giant with $76 billion in capital under management, has formed a platform called Waveborn to acquire creator-economy companies, starting with the management firm Jake Rosen Entertainment. The effort comes via H.I.G. Small-Cap & Growth, an arm of H.I.G. Capital. Terms for JRE weren't disclosed. The plan is to build on JRE by acquiring other companies that span the core parts of the creator-economy ecosystem: brand relationships , content production, and creator monetization . The companies didn't give details on the war chest, but cited Whalar Group as the type and scale of company they sought to build. Whalar spanned an agency, talent management, and influencer-tech companies and was valued at $400 million in 2025 before selling its agency to Accenture Song earlier this year. The creator economy has seen explosive growth. Ad spending in the category has grown four times as fast as media overall and is set to hit $44 billion this year in the US, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . H.I.G. Capital's entrance into the sector reflects financial giants' increasing recognition of the creator economy's potential. It also shows how financial buyers are taking a roll-up approach to fuel the industry's expansion, rather than waiting for it to reach scale. Eric Tencer, managing director of H.I.G. Growth, said factors like the IAB stats, along with his personal experience, forged his conviction in the space. "I've got a 10th grader and a 7th grader at home, and I've been fighting a losing battle around, 'Why don't you just watch normal TV or movies,' and they go straight to TikTok and Instagram," he said. H.I.G. Capital's view is that the ecosystem of businesses serving brands and creators is fragmented, while creators are building increasingly complex companies that require more expertise. Tencer said H.I.G. Capital chose a talent management agency for its first acquisition because it believed that putting creators at the core would help it determine its growth road map. Its plan is to acquire more companies to complement or bolt on to JRE, helping it offer more services to its roster of 400 mid-tier to macro lifestyle creators . "I never want one of our creators to leave us for a different agency because they say, 'I want to go to them because you're not able to offer X services,'" said Jake Rosen, JRE's founder. Rosen said he's bullish on the middle-income creators his agency serves. "A lot of brands on the high side do not want to risk their entire budget on one mega creator," he said. "On the other end, yes, a lot of people are seeing success with micro, smaller creators, but it's a lot on the brand and agency to have 100 creators on a campaign." Private equity is getting more active in the creator economy Private equity firms are playing a small but growing role in funding creator economy companies. That's happening mainly by backing or setting up firms like Fixated (funded by Eldridge Industries) and Wonderloom Media (backed by Content Partners) that become acquirers, said James Creech, founder of the advisory firm Quartermast , which wasn't involved in the JRE deal. That's similar to H.I.G.'s strategy. Creator economy companies haven't traditionally fit private equity's criteria for mature companies large enough to meet its investment requirements. Strategic buyers — such as ad holding companies or talent agencies — are often willing to pay more for creator economy companies than PE firms are. Rosen, who founded 25-employee JRE in 2019, said that when he started a sales process earlier this year, he decided that going the PE route would allow him to be actively involved in future M&A and JRE's growth. He felt that the corporate buyers he spoke with wanted him to adapt to their processes. "Having a seat at the table, and to be able to have that voice for the future, was something that was really important to me," he said. Creech predicted private equity's role in the creator economy would follow H.I.G. Capital's lead. "Other private equities have the same thesis," he said. "There are growth equity players who want to buy a core business, put in more capital to fuel expansion. It reflects the continued maturation of the space." 2026 continues to be the busiest period on record for the sector, with 118 deals involving creator-economy players so far, compared to 93 in all of 2025, according to Quartermast Advisors. events.title: France slams Israel’s ‘demagogic’ ban on opposition leader Melenchon
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Israeli ban on France Unbowed leader comes after Paris turned away a prominent advocate of illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank. Paris has condemned Israel’s “demagogic decision” to bar French opposition figure Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering the country. Late on Thursday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot slammed Israel’s earlier announcement that Melenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party (La France Insoumise), was not welcome. list 1 of 4 French far-right author Zemmour launches second bid for 2027 presidency list 2 of 4 Russia bans two French lawmakers, two journalists in tit-for-tat move list 3 of 4 Prominent Israeli settler denied entry into France list 4 of 4 France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’ Israel barred the party’s parliamentary group chair Mathilde Panot, alongside Melenchon, due to the “extreme anti-Israel stance” of the party and “outrageous statements” made by its leaders. “This demagogic decision, coming from a government that has repeatedly violated international law, plays into the hands of those who, like La France Insoumise, make a living out of exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” Barrot, who belongs to the centrist ruling coalition, wrote on social media. “France will continue tirelessly to work toward a two-state solution and peaceful coexistence between the Israeli and Palestinian peoples,” the minister added. Israel accused Melenchon and Panot of making “blood libel” statements against Israel. At the weekend, Melenchon had said that if he was victorious in the upcoming presidential election in April 2027, he would order French ships to escort flotillas taking aid to Gaza. The Israeli military has previously raided such fleets and detained activists. “Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it and will not allow individuals who act against Israel and incite against its citizens to enter the country,” a statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry said. Speaking to French radio, Melenchon said that he had been “banned from entering a territory I did not ask to enter”. The Israeli move came after France barred a prominent Israeli settler last week. Yossi Dagan, a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, who heads one of six Israeli regional councils in the occupied West Bank, was denied permission to enter France after landing at Charles de Gaulle International Airport. France’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that Dagan was barred “due to his active role in implementing Israel’s settlement policy,” which violates international law. France was one of several European countries this year to step up restrictions on Israeli settlers, spurring outrage from Israeli officials. Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet and have encouraged accelerated settlement in the West Bank and pogroms targeting Palestinians.

events.title: South Africa’s Ramaphosa takes AI pitch to Musk's turf
events.summary: The News South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment. The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as “openly racist” and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africa’s biggest economy. The working visit , which kicks off on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World summit , unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program. US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africa’s mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Africa’s racist past, are holding back “billions with a B” in American capital. Ramaphosa, whose itinerary includes meetings with Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, and Microsoft, is bringing eight cabinet ministers, including his finance, trade, energy, and communications chiefs — in a bid to capture a slice of America’s $650 billion AI capital expenditure this year. Speaking to the press ahead of the trip, Ramaphosa’s spokesman Vincent Magwenya said South Africa aims to court American capital while firmly “safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection, and responsible AI governance.” The BEE controversy Under South Africa’s BEE rules, companies in regulated sectors like telecoms and mining must hand at least 30% of their local ownership to Black people to secure operating licenses — a redress policy that prompted Bozell to say that “time for dialogue has ended” after South Africa failed to meet US demands for regulatory reforms, and executive condemnation of inflammatory political rhetoric. The stand-off has triggered US visa restrictions on unspecified South African officials deemed responsible for “government sponsored discrimination,” led Washington to pull PEPFAR funding to the country, which poured $8 billion into treating the world’s largest HIV/AIDS caseload over two decades, as well as the AGOA ejection. Tiisetso’s view Ramaphosa’s flight to California deliberately skips a potentially frosty reception in Washington. The itinerary, which starts off at Semafor’s inaugural Silicon Valley & The World summit, tells you everything you need to know about Pretroia’s game plan. It is a bold geopolitical arbitrage, an attempt by Pretoria to wall off diplomatic tensions to chase a slice of billions of dollars in AI spending. Pretoria has reasons to believe US boardrooms can look past Washington’s hostility. To start with, boardrooms seem to have a high tolerance for political noise when the economics make sense, if what has been happening in the background is anything to go by. The value of trade between these two countries rose in 2025, industrial giants such aluminum producer Alcoa and transportation behemoth Wabtec keep writing checks despite tariffs, visa curbs, and Bozell’s warning that billions in investment are frozen over South African domestic policies. Next week, we will find out if commerce can keep outrunning politics. Room for Disagreement Sakeliga, a pro-business lobby group, took South Africa’s telecoms regulator to court, arguing that forcing companies to hand over 30% of their local equity to obtain a license acts as a hard barrier to entry that shuts out global players like Starlink . Notable SpaceX has floated a $110 million local infrastructure commitment alongside hundreds of millions rand in free satellite broadband for rural schools as an alternative to handing over its local equity to Black South Africans.

events.title: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs
events.summary: Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO raises questions about the company's role in AI financing. Investors are watching whether a leadership change alters Nvidia’s role in backing AI companies. Smaller AI infrastructure companies may be more sensitive to any pullback in Nvidia’s support. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny. Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive. Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change. "Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday. The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers. It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday. CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress. It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li. "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said. "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person." "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us." Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted. The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions. "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies." — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

events.title: The dark side of reselling apps: ‘If you include your pants, I’ll pay more’
events.summary: Ministers consider banning under-16s from online marketplaces amid reported misuse of messaging functions and users’ photos In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged. “So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle. After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”. Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function. The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent. In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times , over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December. Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance. Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.” She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit. “These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.” About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.” Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services. Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.” Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.” However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18. A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.

events.title: Israel’s VCs see opportunity for challengers in Nvidia’s turmoil
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation has been received with worry in Israel, the company’s “second home,” as Huang described it in 2023. The company’s importance flows both ways, as the semiconductor giant has provided a major boost to Israel’s economic forecasts in recent years. Intel, Microsoft and many homegrown startups also conduct a sizable share of their R&D in Israel. But owing to Nvidia’s stronghold on AI given the centrality of its GPUs for training LLMs and using them, many in the country are wondering how much of a reshuffle will result from its leadership crisis. As with everything at Nvidia, Huang drove the company to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox for $6.9 billion in 2019 and use the company as the base for its largest R&D facility outside of the U.S. Nvidia also made plans to build a multibillion-dollar campus in northern Israel. “Jensen brought Nvidia to Israel with the acquisition of Mellanox, so there is a strong positive sentiment towards Nvidia and Jensen in Israel’s tech community,” Israeli repeat cybersecurity entrepreneur Pavel Gurvich told TechCrunch. Beyond the 6,000 locals Nvidia employs, the bigger question is whether the company will remain as committed to Israel with someone else at the helm. As a result, his line of succession is being observed just as closely by those who hope the company continues to do so as by those who don’t want it to happen. The latter have already gathered that they may be in for disappointment. In a 2023 interview that is now doing the rounds on X, interim CEO Colette Kress had declared that as Nvidia’s CFO, she typically started her day “with Israel meetings, and only then continue[d] to California.” Kress may not remain in charge in the long run, but the many names floated for the role include two Israelis , Apple’s Johny Srouji and Nvidia’s Michael Kagan — although they’re not at the top of the still quite tentative list . Regardless of who gets chosen, Huang’s successor will likely have less of a grip on Nvidia and the tech industry as a whole. But investors don’t think that would cause demand for Nvidia’s product to fade away. According to Yanai Oron, a general partner at Vertex Ventures Israel, “slower decisions at Nvidia could give competitors an opening, but if that uncertainty also slows AI spending, they could end up with a bigger share of a smaller opportunity.” Nvidia has been responsible for a vast share of the spending in the global AI industry. Under Huang’s leadership, the company used its cash reserves to massively invest across the spectrum, both in companies and in its own next-generation chips . Such an empire may not be doomed to fall with its architect’s ouster, but it does seem less likely to become a full-on monopoly. According to Adi Levanon, a founder and managing partner at Selah Ventures, “[Huang’s] departure doesn’t dismantle Nvidia’s technology or ecosystem, but it could give competitors more room to shape what comes next.” And now that companies globally are deploying increasingly demanding AI agents into their workflows, there’s been a lot of interest — and some venture capital — flowing into developers of AI-specific chips and inference software that could compete with Nvidia’s. “These challengers now have a window to prove a different approach delivers better economics; a leadership change alone won’t win them the business,” Levanon said. events.title: CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations 2026: How the 32 franchises stack up
events.summary: For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold. CNBC's NHL valuations are led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion. The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago. For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold, with CNBC's NHL valuations led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion. The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago . Don't be fooled by the lone NHL control sale to close over the past 12 months: the $1.8 billion sale of the Pittsburgh Penguins to the Hoffmann family. Although the transaction was approved by the league in June, the price was negotiated about 18 months ago. Look instead at the latest minority stake transactions. In March the NHL approved the sale of a 12.5% stake in the Carolina Hurricanes by Tom Dundon in a transaction that valued the team at $2.66 billion. Scott Malkin and other shareholders are close to selling a 15% stake in the New York Islanders at a $3 billion valuation. Sports bankers tell CNBC these deals are representative of what control stakes in the two teams would sell for given the hot market for sports teams. "Like the other major sports leagues there is a strong demand to own hockey teams because their media content values are high and there is a scarcity of teams," said Sal Galatioto, whose firm, Galatioto Sports Partners, advises clients on both the buy and sell sides of sports team transactions. "Capitalism and technology are creating more wealth and the NHL, like the NFL, NBA and MLB, is an industry with a very long product life cycle, a hedge against risk in AI." The NHL's current national media rights deals with Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery are worth a combined annual average of close to $650 million through the 2027-28 season, but given the league's strong television ratings last season, a big increase could be in the offing. "The 2025-26 NHL regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from last year and the highest average in more than a decade," Sports Media Watch wrote. "The 25% increase is on the high end of a general rise in sports viewership that includes gains of 35% for the NBA, 19% for men's college basketball and 10% for the NFL." Sports Media Watch also wrote that the 2026 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs averaged 1.8 million viewers in the U.S. across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports. That's up 68% from 2025, and it's the highest average on record for the playoffs on American television, going back to 1994, it said. The NHL is pondering adding teams in cities such as Houston and Atlanta, and another factor fueling NHL valuations is the belief that the expansion fees paid by the new teams would surpass $2 billion. The Seattle Kraken, the NHL's most recent expansion team, paid a $650 million fee to join the league for the 2021-22 season. According to CNBC's figures, revenue for the league's 32 teams averaged $257 million for the 2025-26 season, 6% more than the previous year, while EBITDA — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — averaged $48 million per team, a decline of 11% due to arena expenses. The league's profitability should rebound as money spent on hospitality, concessions and merchandise stores boosts revenue. In April 2025 the NHL and Rogers Communications agreed to a 12-year national Canadian media rights deal worth $7.79 billion, based on exchange rates as of Nov. 24, that will begin with the 2026-27 season. That's more than twice the amount the league is getting from its existing 12-year deal with Rogers. This will help push up the league's hockey-related revenue — which includes media rights, sponsorships, premium seating, tickets, concessions and parking — to around $7.25 billion for the 2026-27 season, 7% more than last season. CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations are current enterprise values — equity plus net debt — calculated using revenue multiples, and include the economics of the team's arena, including non-NHL revenue that accrues to the team's owner. The valuations are meant to represent what a control stake valuation would go for in an arm's-length transaction and do not include the value of the arena or the real estate it sits on. Revenue figures are net of revenue sharing and the 35% of home playoff non-premium gate revenue that goes toward the league's revenue-sharing pool. Revenue multiples are based on historical transaction prices, as well as what investors, league executives and bankers say about the current market. CNBC values exclude other businesses related to the teams with separate financial statements, such as the Edmonton Oilers' mixed-use real estate project .

events.title: Why a Western defense giant is helping Ukraine build its own version of a battle-tested British artillery gun
events.summary: Ukrainian soldiers are using the L119 Light Gun, and now BAE Systems is helping Ukraine to develop its own variant. Scott Peterson/Getty Images BAE Systems is helping Ukraine develop its own version of a British artillery gun. The agreement paves the way for Ukraine to manufacture a version of the L119 Light Gun domestically. BAE says the goal is to help Ukraine build and sustain its own weapons. A major Western defense firm is helping Ukraine build its own version of a battle-tested British artillery gun, part of a broader push to help the country produce and sustain its own weaponry. BAE Systems signed an agreement this past summer with a Ukrainian partner to develop and test a locally tailored version of the 105mm Light Gun, paving the way for domestic production of the towed howitzer. BAE Systems' Light Gun family includes the L118 used by British forces in the Falklands War and the L119, adopted by the US Army as the M119 and used in Iraq and Afghanistan. BAE Systems describes the Light Gun as "one of the world's most battle-tested artillery capabilities," while the US Army characterizes it as "one of the most versatile weapon systems in the US Army inventory." Giles Ambrose, the engineering, technology, and strategy director at BAE Systems, told Business Insider that Ukraine needs the ability to produce its own weapons rather than depend on foreign suppliers. "The need of the Ukrainians is sovereign capability as opposed to equipment supply ," he said. Ukraine has increasingly embraced producing its own weaponry rather than buying or receiving it from allies, as it seeks greater control over its defense, shorter production and repair times, and reduced vulnerability to allies' changing political priorities. A Ukrainian Light Gun variant would be made to Ukrainian standard. Scott Peterson/Getty Images Ukraine is already using the L119. The UK began supplying them in 2022 to help fight Russia's invasion. Ambrose said that "it's been proven that it really works for the operational needs of the end users in Ukraine," citing its reliability, lightweight design for easy movement, and smaller size. Although drones have transformed the battlefield, artillery systems remain essential to Ukraine's fight, with a recent major operation showing that artillery still matters. Guns like the L119 can deliver sustained fire against Russian positions, complementing drones used for surveillance, targeting, and precision strikes. The new agreement between BAE Systems and a local strategic partner is intended to build on that experience by giving Ukraine the ability to manufacture its own version of the weapon. The agreement grants a license to a Ukrainian partner, which BAE will not name publicly, and provides the engineering expertise, product specifications, and technical information needed to produce the artillery gun. Ambrose said the variant will "be performing to the same specification, albeit built to Ukrainian standard." The goal is to achieve "the same product specification, the same performance," he said. The difference is that "there will be manufacturing processes, specifications pertinent to Ukraine, unique to a Ukrainian industrial base, which will make it easier and maybe more preferable to use in building this gun." Ukraine's battlefield is dominated by drones, but artillery can still play a big role. Chris McGrath/Getty Images This variant "gives Ukraine the ability to optimize for their industrial base" and "will then maximize the battlefield availability," Ambrose said. "But our role in it will mean it will still perform the same as what is out there performing today." The new license agreement allows BAE's partner to produce a test article, which must be successfully manufactured and qualified before production can move forward. BAE will continue providing engineering expertise and support. The agreement also advances efforts to help Ukraine maintain and repair its weapons domestically, reducing the need to send equipment overseas. BAE Systems works with another British company, AMS Integrated Solutions Ltd, in Ukraine to maintain, repair, and overhaul the light guns already in service there. Keeping that work in Ukraine speeds up repairs and gets weapons back into action faster. Ambrose said it "means we're able to upskill in-country engineers and build industrial capability around those systems." "We, BAE Systems, provide the engineering expertise and with that, decades of through - life artillery support capability," Ambrose said. "AMS bring their in-country facilities, their maintenance expertise and Ukrainian engineering skills, to deliver repair and overhaul capability." BAE Systems also has a contract to repair Archer artillery systems donated by Sweden inside Ukraine, and that includes working with Ukrainian soldiers who receive technical training on maintaining the equipment. BAE Systems is a major player in artillery systems. It has a new 94,000-square-foot artillery development and production site in the English city of Sheffield that is now operational. events.title: Creator marketers reconsider their approaches as hauls and unboxings lose their cool
events.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI A version of this post appears in CMO Insider's Creator Brief. Sign up for Business Insider's twice-weekly marketing newsletter . Watching influencers unbox free things or detail their latest splurge is starting to lose its luster. For years, creators have posted videos showing off heaps of products on social media. Brands and retailers often sponsor these "haul" or "unboxing" videos or pay creators for the sales they generate, providing an inexpensive onramp for many to join the creator economy. "The volume of what someone had bought was the story," said Lucy Kruszynski, global head of brand at Buttermilk. "The bigger the bag in the thumbnail, the higher the views." Now, these video styles are losing their heat — and some marketers are moving on. "We're doing fewer hauls, fewer unboxings," Grace Murray Vazquez, an EVP at influencer marketing platform Fohr, told Business Insider. Industry insiders said brands and creators were focused more on content that integrated products into a story. As a share of sponsored posts, hauls declined from 2.4% for January through September 2025 to 1.2% for the same period in 2026, according to data from the influencer marketing platform Traackr, pulled exclusively for Business Insider. Sponsored unboxing videos fell from 1.3% to 0.7%. That decrease could be driven by a simple fact: audiences are tuning out. CreatorIQ data run exclusively for Business Insider found that likes, comments, and shares across all haul and unboxing posts had leveled off over the past year, after a period of growth. Sponsored haul posts, in particular, have seen a dramatic decline in average monthly engagements per post, falling from 2,633 in 2025 to 1,780 in January through October this year. In 2022, sponsored hauls averaged 5,900 monthly engagements per post. The volume of sponsored posts has been growing rapidly overall, and more haul and unboxing posts are being produced this year than in 2025, according to Traackr's data. That said, they represent a smaller percentage of paid posts than they did last year. The shift shows how creator commerce is maturing, with audiences becoming more selective as social feeds fill up, and brands recognizing the importance of audience trust. That raises the bar for sponsored content but could also make creators a more valuable marketing channel in the long run. The approaching holiday season will be a test of the format's staying power, as it's a time when its prevalence spikes. "That'll be a key indicator if it underperforms in its strongest time period," said Alex Rawitz, director of research and insights at CreatorIQ. Swapping surplus for storytelling Creators and their managers say their experiences line up with what we're seeing in the data. Amanda Acevedo, director of talent at G&B Digital Management, estimated that she used to receive 10 outreach requests a month for haul-style fashion and makeup videos. Today, she says she can't remember the last time she got such a request. Acevedo said that brands are now asking creators to focus on a single product, like a pair of boots or eyeliner, and to emphasize its value. "That whole 'styling 10 dresses in one Reel' is really outdated," she said. The change in brands' briefs mirrors a shift in what creators post when they're not being paid. "We're seeing a broader shift towards content that gives people a reason to care about a product beyond the fact that it's new," Buttermilk's Kruszynski said. "Think cost-per-wear breakdowns, wardrobe re-styling, genuinely useful recommendations, product demonstrations, and creators explaining why something has earned a permanent place in their routine." For some creators, the development is a welcome one. Julia Comil, a creator who often promotes luxury items, said brands used to ask her to do haul-style videos. She said that lately, they'd been asking for "more creative ones, with storytelling." In a recent Instagram Reel for a Longchamp bucket bag, she moves through the day, showing the bag's versatility. "When you do the haul, you don't have any storytelling," Comil said. "I think for clothing when you're in the high-end business, you need to create an emotion with the clothing." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Julia Corot Comil - Mode Rsvp (@juliacomil) Comil added that these videos cost her more to make than the old haul-style ones — she has to hire a videographer — but she says they get more views and, importantly, drive more sales. Why people are tuning out — and what still works Creators and marketers have a range of explanations for the waning interest in hauls . People may have grown tired of being constantly pitched as the format's use has mushroomed. There are also the " underconsumption core " and "deinfluencing" trends that have taken hold in response to online shopping culture. Inflation, meanwhile, has some people trading down and cutting back on splurges. A Harris Poll found 59% of holiday shoppers surveyed in October said they expected to make financial trade-offs this season. "It's a simple thing for people to skip away from," Fohr's Murray Vazquez said, especially "when they're not in a place to purchase 10 things." Lily Comba, CEO of Superbloom, said people are tired of being sold to on social media. Superbloom Other creator economy insiders feel the shift from hauls has more to do with consumers getting savvier. "They don't want to feel like they're constantly being sold to," said Lily Comba, CEO of Superbloom. Natasha Valerie, cofounder of The Viralist Group, said that people are "exposed to ads every day" and "being more selective." Brands are getting used to giving creators looser briefs, believing videos that feel more organic will resonate — and convert — better. Meanwhile, the rise of short-form video may have disincentivized longer, haul-style videos. This all doesn't mean unboxing or haul videos will go away completely. It's hard to deny TikTok Shop , whose US sales have eclipsed Target.com's. The platform's unboxing and product-led content can still be incredibly effective at driving sales, especially since it's so easy to buy there, Kruszynski of Buttermilk said. Valerie said product-focused videos can work if there's an element of surprise or the product itself is interesting or out of reach for most people. "They're getting a glimpse into a lifestyle they wouldn't have access to," she said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: For creators, higher incomes mean more pressure to use AI
events.summary: Gracie Schram of Epidemic Sound says high-earning creators face pressure to keep up with production and distribution expectations. Epidemic Sound High-earning creators and music artists face intense pressure to adopt AI tools, a new survey found. That pressure rose steadily with income level. Creators have to balance AI's efficiency benefits with the risk of backlash for using it. Content creators and music artists are feeling pressure to use AI , and the higher up the income ladder you go, the more acute it is. That's the key takeaway from a new survey, shared exclusively with Business Insider, which found six-figure creators and artists in the US were more than three times as likely (64%) to say they felt "large" or "very large" pressure to use AI, compared with the lowest earners (19%). That pressure rose steadily with income level. The findings come from Sapio Research, which surveyed 2,000 professional content creators and music artists in the US from March to April on behalf of Epidemic Sound, a music and sound platform based in Sweden. Those earning $50,000 or more also embraced AI at higher rates. Forty-four percent of those earning $50,000 to $100,000 said they used fully AI-generated music or content in their work, as did 45% of those earning over $100,000. Only 23% of those making under $5,000 said the same. Gracie Schram, global head of creator partnerships and strategy at Epidemic Sound, said higher-earning creators face bigger output and distribution expectations, adding that they tend to be early adopters in general and have access to more tools. "They're distributing multiple videos every day, on YouTube, Snapchat, Spotify," she said. "It comes with this distribution predicament. They're getting invited to do more stuff on platforms, which leads to more pressure to make more stuff. With these big creators, it's a huge amount of pressure to stay relevant." AI presents competing challenges for creators. The tech can be a time-saver and a creativity enhancer, but creators draw value from the trust their audiences place in them, and the US public remains uneasy about AI. Some creators have also feared reputational damage from platforms labeling their work as AI-generated if they use AI tools. The risk varies by creator. Those who use AI to pump out a lot of content or use it in ways their followers see as inauthentic are especially at risk of backlash, said Victoria Bachan, CEO of talent management agency Hyphen. "It comes down to, 'What is your social contract with the audience you serve?'" she said. "You aren't going to have AI make a recipe. We do have creators who have done AI deals, but it aligns with their content like tech, finance education." Henrik Olsson, a Stockholm-based music artist who creates for Epidemic Sound, said that as an artist who makes a "comfortable living," he depends on AI for scripting and editing to help produce his social media content. Schram said the creators she works with often use AI to speed up their workflow, including editing and testing A/B concepts. A creator could use AI to make storyboards that wouldn't be part of the final creative product, for example. In the survey, 77% of all US creators said human-made content was becoming a premium offering for audiences in the era of AI, and 78% said clear AI disclosure was essential to maintaining trust. "They still want human creativity to be at the center," Schram said. Olsson predicted the rise of AI would push artists to be more creative, rather than replace their art. "We have to be one step ahead," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider
