events.title: Apple, Alphabet and Uber survived major founder transitions. Nvidia will be a harder test
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation leaves Nvidia facing an unusually difficult transition after losing its founder CEO. Companies like Apple, Alphabet and Uber have prospered after losing high-profile leaders, but those transitions were generally less abrupt. Nvidia’s next permanent CEO will need to manage the fallout from Huang’s departure while maintaining its competitive position as rivals develop their own chips. Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build. But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation f rom Nvidia at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that's powering the artificial intelligence boom. In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China , made the company he co-founded the world's most valuable. Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was "indispensable" but "the graveyards are filled with indispensable men," referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle. While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang's charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate. "I'm not sure we've seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world's largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal," Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC. Whoever follows will "face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder," he added. Apple 's image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor. Tim Cook invested in Apple's chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple's supply chain. Cook had "considerable preparation" for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple's market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure. Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet in 2019, 21 years after founding Google. Page and Brin's departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the "natural time" to simplify the company's management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai. Travis Kalanick left Uber in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns. But his departure "unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing," Withers added. Former Expedia CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability . What's different about Huang's departure Withers said successor CEOs often struggle "under normal circumstances" to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership. "It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company's founder," he added. Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies. Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company. "We're talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That's a pretty remarkable situation," he added. As well as having to "step out of his shadow," the new CEO will have to deal with the "scandal" arising from Huang's conduct and "the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia," Withers said. Huang's successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy, while picking up the relationships he managed. Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May . Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world's second-largest economy. He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company's key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung. Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain. The supply chain was "where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology," Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially "when supply chains are already so tight." Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.

events.title: Mauricio Pochettino announced as new Manchester United manager
events.summary: Pochettino replaces Michael Carrick, who was sacked after United’s disastrous start to the season. Manchester United have appointed ⁠⁠Mauricio Pochettino as the new manager to replace the ⁠ sacked Michael Carrick , as the Premier League ⁠giants sit in the relegation zone after their worst start to a league ‌campaign in 40 years. Pochettino will lead the United States national team in their upcoming matches against Haiti before joining ⁠Man United, US ⁠Soccer said on Friday. list 1 of 3 ‘Utter nonsense’: Australia’s Cummins denies involvement in Sandpapergate list 2 of 3 Henry and Young shine as New Zealand thrash India by 244 runs list 3 of 3 WTA Finals: Pegula wins thriller as compatriot Gauff eliminated “The club has reached an agreement with the US ⁠Soccer Federation for Mauricio and ⁠his staff to ⁠be released after the conclusion of their responsibilities with the ‌US Men’s National Team,” United said in a ‌statement. Pochettino, a former Chelsea, Paris Saint-Germain, Tottenham Hotspur and Southampton manager, was the favourite for the managerial role at Old Trafford ever since rumours about Carrick’s departure hit the headlines. The 54-year-old arrives at Old ⁠Trafford with United having earned one win and eight points from 10 Premier League games. They are 18th in the standings, one point above bottom side Crystal Palace. United have won only three of their 15 matches across all competitions. Pochettino, who returns to club football, had been in charge of the USA national team since 2024, and under him, the cohosts reached the round of 16 at the 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America. “The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honours of my career,” Pochettino said in a statement. British media reported United would have to pay substantial compensation to release Pochettino from his US Soccer contract, which had been due to run ⁠until the 2030 World Cup. Pochettino becomes the eighth permanent man in charge at Man United since Sir Alex Ferguson’s departure in May 2013 after more than 26 years in the job. United said in their statement that their new manager is known for “his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players”. Pochettino took charge of Spurs from 2014 to 2019, leading the North London club to the Champions League final in the season before he was sacked. He guided Spurs to the League Cup final in his first full season and to a runners-up finish in the Premier League in 2017. Pochettino also spent a season at French giants PSG, leading them to the Ligue 1 title that year, and later guided Chelsea to a League Cup runner-up finish in 2023-2024. He inherits a Man United squad assembled at considerable expense ⁠but lacking confidence and identity, with supporters booing the players off the pitch after the Bournemouth defeat. United’s hierarchy, which has often attracted the fans’ criticism, will hope his experience can help stabilise one of football’s most scrutinised clubs. Pochettino’s first assignment at his new club will be a trip to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool in the league on November 22.

The five-year agreement covers Bedfordshire Police, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and Hertfordshire Constabulary, despite warnings from campaigners and politicians about dependence on the supplier. A contract award notice says the east of England police forces expect the Palantir platform to provide "an enterprise-wide data integration and analytics capability, enabling the secure ingestion, linking, and analysis of data from multiple systems and sources across the policing environment." The contract runs until October 2031, with the estimated value covering all three forces. News of the award coincided with revelations that former Metropolitan Police commissioner Dame Cressida Dick has worked as a paid adviser to Palantir since September 2025. A Palantir spokesperson told the Bureau of Investigative Journalism : "Dame Cressida is advising us on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles." Dick said her role was limited to advising on how such products could assist public services. She said she had never lobbied or advocated for Palantir, or introduced the company to her contacts. Dick led the Metropolitan Police, the UK's largest force, between 2017 and 2022. She left after Khan said he had lost confidence in her. She later said she was " intimidated " into leaving. Separately, Khan stepped in to block the Met from awarding a £50 million contract to Palantir. His office cited serious concerns about the procurement process. Palantir later sued the Met, but the case was settled in October. The new police contract award follows a report from MPs warning of vendor lock-in to US suppliers, including Palantir. It said : "Our view that Palantir's increasing presence across the public sector represents an unacceptable point of weakness is not ideologically motivated or driven by concerns about the quality of their products. events.title: Johnny Depp's Hollywood comeback in 'Ebenezer' comes with one catch, PR pros say
events.summary: Johnny Depp attends the London premiere of "Ebenezer." Mike Marsland/Getty Images Johnny Depp stars in "Ebenezer," his first major Hollywood feature since his defamation trial. The film's marketing campaign leans heavily on this being Depp's comeback role. PR experts say he's primed to succeed, but the box office will be the ultimate referendum. Johnny Depp became a household name playing misunderstood monsters , eccentrics, and Disney-friendly scallywags, but in the last few years, Hollywood has turned him into a different sort of outcast. "Ebenezer," distributed by Paramount Pictures, is Depp's first major Hollywood feature since he sued his ex-wife, Amber Heard, in 2019 for publishing an essay about domestic abuse , widely assumed to describe her relationship with Depp (which he denied), and the explosive defamation trial that followed. Jurors found both Depp and Heard liable for defamation, and they reached a settlement in 2022 — though not before testimonies and documents entered into evidence exposed disturbing details, from a photo of feces on the couple's shared bed (Depp blamed Heard, while Heard blamed their dog), to texts that Depp wrote about burning and drowning his ex-wife, and having sex with her "burnt corpse" (Depp said he's "not proud" of the messages, which he described as "dark humor"). Depp's professional reputation had suffered blows long before he took the stand. He lost a similar libel case in 2020 after the British newspaper The Sun  called him a "wife-beater," and was subsequently ousted from lucrative franchise roles in the next installment of the "Harry Potter" spin-off film series, "Fantastic Beasts," and " Pirates of the Caribbean 6 ." Before that, Depp was mired in complex legal battles with his former business partners over his admittedly lavish spending . Rumors swirled about Depp's tardiness and unprofessionalism on set amid a series of box-office flops . But the years have passed, and Hollywood may be cautiously welcoming Depp back into the fold. Many thousands of Depp supporters have stayed staunchly, outspokenly loyal to the star. Social media reactions to the defamation trial were overwhelmingly sympathetic to Depp amid reports of a targeted smear campaign to discredit Heard. By the time the actual jurors handed down their judgment, it looked like Depp had already been vindicated online. Johnny Depp stars as Ebenezer Scrooge in "Ebenezer." Paramount Pictures "Ebenezer" is positioned as Depp's big Hollywood comeback , complete with a splashy marketing campaign and top-line billing for its embattled star. "The Master of Misfits returns," one of the studio's taglines declares, with marketing materials drawing a connection between the film's title character and the man who "brought us Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands, and The Mad Hatter." Yet "Ebenezer" isn't just another misfit role for Depp to add to his résumé. Scrooge's near-two-century life in the pop-culture canon is proof that audiences love a redemption story. Is Depp about to get his? Paramount is certainly manifesting it. The first shot of Depp in character as Scrooge in the "Ebenezer" teaser trailer breaks the fourth wall, as Depp delivers his line to the camera with a knowing expression: "It's good to be back." Depp's path to redemption depends on his commercial value Paramount's marketing campaign for "Ebenezer" relied heavily on Johnny Depp's name recognition. Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for Paramount Casting Depp in "Ebenezer" was a gamble for Paramount, but a cheaper gamble than one might imagine. Where Depp once fetched $25 million up front for 2017's "Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales," the total budget for "Ebenezer" was $38 million. The New York Times reported that Depp accepted a reduced salary of roughly $5 million in exchange for a larger share of the proceeds if the movie performs at the box office. In other words, for an established movie star, he was a steal. Representatives for Depp and Paramount did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Paramount is certainly throwing its weight behind "Ebenezer," with the presumed expectation it will pay off in ticket sales. Depp has appeared in full Charles Dickens drag — top hat, overcoat, heavy prosthetics — for several promotional stunts, from New York's Bryant Park holiday market to San Diego's Comic-Con, where he drew an adoring crowd. According to The New York Times, one woman even called out to him, "Have my baby!" The movie's trailers and posters have relied heavily on name recognition for the actor and the character, betting on audiences to re-embrace both. As far as the promo is concerned, Depp and Scrooge are one and the same: a man with his feet to the fire, seeking salvation. "The studio is trying to test the public's willingness to embrace Johnny Depp again after all of the personal crises," said Tara Goodwin, founder of Goodwin Consulting and a crisis PR veteran. "This is allowing him, through the character Ebenezer, to be judged by his work rather than in a court of law or the court of public opinion." "One movie, one PR stunt, does not rebuild a reputation," she added. "But it does change the conversation from his personal narrative to his professional one." Will that be enough to get butts in seats? As PR professionals have told me over and over, the public is more forgiving than you think — especially if the celebrity in question has nostalgia to leverage. "Johnny Depp, his fans go back 40 years. They still remember him as the kid on '21 Jump Street.' In a lot of ways, he's a symbol of Generation X," said Ryan McCormick, cofounder and managing partner at Goldman McCormick PR. "Some of his iconic roles automatically pull people into a different era of time, like when they were younger and maybe when the world wasn't so crazy or intense." In that sense, Scrooge is the perfect character for Depp: a familiar face who learns to appreciate the generosity of others. He's the universal shorthand for second chances. 'Ebenezer' doesn't have to be great, as long as it makes money Johnny Depp interacts with a fan at San Diego Comic-Con 2026. Daniel Knighton/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures According to early reviews from critics — including this one — "Ebenezer" isn't a great movie; it currently holds a 49% critics score on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of publication. Helmed by horror director Ti West, it's meant to be a spookier-than-usual adaptation of Dickens' classic novella. I found it to be insipid and tedious, caught somewhere between a trite Christmas parable and a Halloween fright fest. Your opinion of Depp's performance will depend on your tolerance for hammy commitment, as a prosthetic-laden Depp gesticulates and mugs his way through a series of ghostly encounters — clearly attempting to recapture the smarmy charm of Jack Sparrow, reincarnated as a 19th-century grump. events.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
events.summary: One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades A s a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents. The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty. “All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.” Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height. As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements. The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website. The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years . If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate , as well as local, hazard? “We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies. “There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.” Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create. “We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.” Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added. The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city. Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.

events.title: Fox's Tubi is putting $250,000 into its latest effort to court creators
events.summary: Rich Bloom of Tubi and Everette Taylor of Kickstarter are joining forces to support emerging creators. Tubi, Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TIME Fox's Tubi and Kickstarter created a Fandom Fund to back indie horror, YA, and fan-driven films. Tubi is putting in $250,000 to back projects, and Kickstarter will help identify creators. Tubi will get an exclusive window for projects, but won't own the IP. Fox's Tubi is teaming up with Kickstarter in its latest move to bring creators to the streamer. Tubi is pledging $250,000 to what it's calling the Fandom Fund to support TV and film projects. Kickstarter will recommend creators. The new effort is an expansion of Tubi's and Kickstarter's 2025 FilmStream Collective Fund, which helped creators finish films and bring them to the free streamer. For the Fandom Fund, $150,000 will be spread across about eight to 15 creators working in areas that are popular on Tubi , such as stories centered on Black characters and experiences, horror, young adult, reality, and true-crime content. One project will get $100,000 in matching funds to produce a full film or series. The fund is part of Tubi's larger effort to boost its standing with creators as audiences' attention moves to social media. Tubi already has more than 700 creators distributing their nonexclusive content on the platform, but also wants access to new, exclusive fare. Other streamers including Netflix and Disney are also vying for YouTubers and other creators. Fandom Fund recipients will own their IP and get access to 110 million monthly active users. Tubi will premiere their projects and run them for an exclusive window of varying month-long periods, starting in 2027. "This is an opportunity for more emerging creators, versus bigger, more established creators, who, even with this big push across media to do more with creators, aren't necessarily getting those opportunities," said Rich Bloom, GM of Tubi's creator programs and its EVP of business development. Everette Taylor, Kickstarter's CEO, said cuts to programming spending across Hollywood have left a dearth of funding for independent creators. "What I'm hearing from creators is, I have my own audience, I have a great idea, I want to shoot this thing, but I don't know how I'm going to monetize it after," he said. events.title: Jensen Huang didn’t show confidence in his successor, report says
events.summary: Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang described Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who has now replaced him as interim CEO, as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation earlier in the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported , citing an anonymous source. Huang made the comment during a meeting with Nvidia’s finance team about the company’s plans to provide guarantees worth billions of dollars to data center operators that couldn’t afford to buy its chips upfront, according to the report. He reportedly also said Kress was a person who couldn’t help him steer strategy or decision-making. Kress has been with Nvidia for over 13 years now, after serving as SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance. The report said she has questioned Nvidia’s program-focused, credit-based deals involving Huang’s son-in-law Nico Caprez, and wanted to know how to decide which deals are beneficial, how to value guarantees, and determine returns. Earlier in the year, she had scaled back on Nvidia’s commitment for OpenAI’s ambitious Ohio data center project. The company was in talks to provide $250 billion in credit to OpenAI, but ended up committing $105 billion . Huang resigned Thursday after reports of two extramarital affairs , including one with the company’s VP for healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The company is also investigating a possible Chinese espionage plot . After his resignation, Reuters reported that he was having a third affair with another employee . Nvidia is currently searching for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, who had the top job for over 33 years. events.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
events.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet, with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing. 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves. In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings. Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire. AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence. Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters AI doubts trigger market turbulence The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly. Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple , Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day. In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy . On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged marital affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still. Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts. In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion. "We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "show me the money." Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction' Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction." "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie." In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates. Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share. Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. “Is this the best timing?” he asked. While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion. Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of over $600 billion in revenue by 2030. "If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued." Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects. “Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.” Signs to watch, not reasons to flee With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing. This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

events.title: Commonwealth Fusion’s CEO sees UAE primed for new energy tech
events.summary: The Scene When Massachusetts-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems looked for companies that could produce large metal components and complex machinery for its prototype, it landed on the oil and gas industry. CEO Bob Mumgaard said the hydrocarbons industry shares many of the same skills and tools that fusion developers need to achieve a breakthrough and eventually take a share of the energy mix. The UAE is well positioned to use its expertise in oil and gas to adopt fusion technology, Mumgaard said, especially after it has developed a track record of building nuclear power plants and its embrace of AI. “They understand what energy leadership and first mover advantage, advanced technologies can bring to their society, their place in the world,” he said. Abu Dhabi’s government-owned fusion fund, Plynth Energy, acquired a minority stake worth more than $100 million in Commonwealth this year, according to Axios. The US company raised $1 billion in July, bringing its total funding to $4 billion, which Mumgaard said would be enough to build the prototype and prepare for a larger, utility-scale plant in the early 2030s. Next decade Scientists have long predicted that the fusion breakthrough is a decade away. The prospect of unlimited, clean, and safe power is tantalizing, and it now appears that mastery of the reaction that essentially powers the stars is within reach. Commonwealth’s Massachusetts prototype uses powerful magnets and hydrogen isotopes (deuterium and tritium) to produce a reaction that’s hotter than the sun’s core. The machine is about 80% complete, Mumgaard said, and is due to start up in 2027. Its goal is to show that it can release more energy than it takes in. The company then plans to build a 400-megawatt plant in Virginia and has secured Google and Italian energy company Eni as buyers, Mumgaard said. Global adoption at scale is still decades away, but Mumgaard said the US-Iran conflict is also making the case for accelerating research and deployment. “Fusion is one of the most secure, resilient energy systems because it doesn’t need pipelines or ships, and it doesn’t have emissions,” he said. events.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang? The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China. Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China. Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities. But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country. Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits. But that relationship now looks rather more complicated. The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it? That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections. A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist. There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department. This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle. Now the political pressure is building. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 10 hours ago The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 20 hours ago Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach. And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure. Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips. Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.

events.title: Masdar completes $950m solar and battery storage project in US
events.summary: Masdar has completed its $950 million Lockhart Solar and Storage complex in California as the Abu Dhabi clean energy company continues to expand its renewable energy portfolio in the US. With 365 megawatts of solar generation and 173.7MW of battery storage, the project can produce electricity to meet the annual needs of about 350,000 homes and businesses, Masdar said on Friday. The project was developed by Terra-Gen, which is owned jointly by Masdar and Igneo Infrastructure Partners. It has offtake agreements with corporate buyers and long-term power purchase agreements with California load-serving entities to help meet their energy needs. “We are delivering reliable, affordable power, creating skilled jobs and supporting economic growth,” said Khaleefa Almheiri, president and chief executive of Masdar Americas. Engineering and construction of the complex is expected to generate more than 1,000 on-site jobs. The plant is also expected to generate more than $40 million in property tax revenue over its operating life, along with additional contributions and benefits to the local community. “As electricity demand accelerates, driven by AI, advanced manufacturing and wider economic growth, Masdar is proud to be a long-term partner in powering America’s future,” Mr Almheiri said. There has been a growing demand for power from the US and other countries amid the AI-driven data centre boom. “Solar is one of the most economical sources of new electricity and storage extends its value by making that energy available when it’s needed most,” said John O’Connor, chief executive at Terra-Gen. Masdar has invested about $3 billion in the US and plans to invest a further $20 billion over the next decade, with an ambition to grow its US portfolio to up to 25GW by 2030. Owned jointly by Abu Dhabi's Taqa, Adnoc and Mubadala, Masdar is targeting a portfolio capacity of 100GW by 2030 as it continues to develop new renewable projects globally.

events.title: Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks?
events.summary: Finland says Ukraine struck a Russian warship near its coast as Kyiv and Moscow held US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi. Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region. The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February. It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea . So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know: “The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement. The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected. It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg. On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response. The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain. Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia. Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv. “We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe. “You can still cruise with peace of mind,” he said. Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic. “Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera. Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks. “According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram. On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts. Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year. The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks. Territory remains the main sticking point. Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region. Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO. Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday. The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported. On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland. Why has Ukraine carried out attacks during talks? “Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.

events.title: Russian crude production rebounds after Trump diesel deal, IEA says as oil markets return to surplus
events.summary: Russia’s crude oil production rose by 210,000 barrels a day to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, according to the IEA. Global oil supply rose to 105.4 million barrels a day in October, lifting supply above demand for the first time since the Iran war began. Diesel supply remains constrained because attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and Middle East disruptions continue to limit product exports. Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, as a rebound in Gulf shipments pushes oil markets into a surplus for the first time since the Middle East conflict began, the International Energy Agency said Friday. Global supply and stocks have both swelled, though Middle East disruptions and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure tightened diesel supply, according to the agency's latest monthly oil market report. "Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country's diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East," the IEA noted. U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to global markets on Oct. 9. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a general license authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. Crude supply can rise even as diesel remains tight, with refinery capacity and refined product exports still constrained. Global oil supply reached 105.4 million barrels a day in October, up 2.3 million barrels a day from September, the IEA said, adding that supply rose by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million barrels a day since August, despite ongoing attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers. Inventories also rose for the first time since June, with observed global stocks increasing by 52 million barrels in October, or 1.7 million barrels a day. "The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," IEA analysts observed. Higher export flows have strengthened supply expectations for the fourth quarter, with Middle East and Russia losses partly offset by growth from the U.S., Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana, which together are set to boost output by 1.6 million barrels a day this year. The IEA has raised its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million barrels a day, and now forecasts a 6.6 million barrels per day increase in 2027.

events.title: Senate Banking Committee asks Jensen Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify over ‘significant national security concerns’ next month, or face subpoenas
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been asked to appear before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee next month to address national security concerns. Senator Tim Scott (R-SC), who leads the committee, confirmed overnight that Huang and Lutnick have been asked to appear on December 3. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” he said. “The American people deserve answers.” Senator Scott’s letter added a weighty conclusion: If either fails to appear before the committee voluntarily, it is “prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas, to conduct this legitimate and necessary oversight.” The Banking Committee hearing is the latest in a series of inquiries into the conduct of Jensen Huang , the former CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia . Huang resigned from the company he’s spent the past 30 years building after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Reports have since surfaced that Huang had an affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Reuters reported yesterday that the entrepreneur had a second affair with a member of staff, quoting unnamed sources. Nvidia’s CFO, Colette Kress, has been named interim CEO following his resignation. President Trump told reporters earlier this week that the FBI is investigating the affair between Huang and Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy. China has denied its involvement. Nvidia’s board has also said it is conducting its own independent investigation and has hired Joon H. Kim, former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York at Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to lead the review. Senator Scott laid bare the Senate Banking Committee’s authority to request both Huang and Lutnick, a member of the president’s cabinet, to appear before it. His letter to Huang says the committee has “jurisdiction over matters relating to ‘export controls,’ including their application to NVIDIA’s exports of advanced semiconductors.” The committee is “seeking answers to questions that raise grave national security concerns,” it added in a post on X. Chairman @SenatorTimScott has requested that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang appear on December 3 and Commerce Secretary Lutnick on December 10. The Committee oversees advanced semiconductor export controls and is seeking answers to questions that raise grave national security concerns. https://t.co/HpSxJH213J — U.S. Senate Banking Committee GOP (@BankingGOP) November 13, 2026 Committee questions Members of the committee have suggested Lutnick had allowed loopholes to persist that allowed high-end chips to continue to be sold to China. Senator Jim Banks (R-IN) told Fox News last night that he believed Lutnick had “defied President Trump’s directive not to sell these high-end chips to China or to allow them to be sold to Chinese customers, that ended up happening anyway.” “Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military,” added Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), currently the ranking member on the committee. Huang is also likely to face disbelief from Senator John Kennedy (R-LA). Senator Kennedy told CNN in an interview last night: “I’m not naive; I’m not Bambi’s baby brother. I know people have affairs; I wouldn’t recommend it, but if you do, you ought to make sure it’s not with a Chinese spy. I mean, check their LinkedIn page for God’s sake.” Senator Kennedy referred to the debacle as an “intergalactic freak show,” adding: Here’s a man, head of one of the most powerful companies in the world, more than anybody else in the private sector; he’s been making AI policy for America, and certainly with respect to our relationship with China. And then we learn about this.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
events.summary: DOJ said it obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance. U.S. government and private-sector efforts have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the more than $6 billion stolen from Binance on Oct. 29. DOJ also disrupted cloud infrastructure tied to FaceStealer, a separate social-engineering campaign it says stole more than $400 million over 18 months. U.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, the Department of Justice said Thursday, as it vowed action to tackle cyberscams originating from North Korea. Over $6 billion was stolen from industry giant Binance on Oct. 29, which the DOJ attributed to actors linked to the North Korean military. Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen. The FBI blames the attack, which shook confidence in crypto market security , on members of the North Korean military it refers to as "TraderTraitor." The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency." That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said. DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets. But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels. Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said. The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts — sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise. Individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries are prime targets. Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy, of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, called FaceStealer "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user." "It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," Grandy added. "North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement. "America will fight back against that corrupt regime's effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea's ill-gotten gains."

events.title: Duquesne’s Michael Buckley says young investors skip over learning these critical skills. They could prove to be invaluable in the AI boom
events.summary: As investors race to identify the next big winners in the AI boom, standing out requires more than just spotting the next breakthrough. Michael Buckley, managing director and head of equities at investment firm Duquesne Family Office, says young investors often overlook the fundamentals of corporate finance. In the age of AI, that could give them an edge. Buckley has built a diverse investing résumé. He’s worked across private equity, venture capital, and public equities—and his early days in debt and credit helped set him apart. Right after graduating from Harvard, Buckley learned the ropes of accounting and corporate finance at Sankaty Advisors, the now-renamed credit arm of private equity giant Bain Capital. With credit as the focus, Buckley poured himself into capital and corporate structures, as well as bonds and loans. His responsibilities unwittingly set him up to be recruited for one of America’s top private investment firms. “I learned the importance of things like capital structure and debt, which I think a lot of people—for example, that start out their career in things like equities—oftentimes will skip that stuff over,” Buckley tells Fortune. “It’s because it’s tedious and it can be complicated,” he added. Early-career analysts who have their heads buried in stock charts, earnings growth, and revenue projections could get a leg-up by returning to those basics. There’s a simple reason: The AI boom hinges on debt. Buckley explains that in this new ecosystem, debt is suddenly very important not only to distressed debt companies, but also to public markets and venture firms. As AI companies and their infrastructure partners take on more borrowing to finance data centers, chips, and computing capacity, investors need to assess how quickly a business might grow—and whether they can afford to pay back what they owe. It particularly stands out for those involved in data centers or funding next-generation labs, Buckley adds; tech hyperscalers issued more than $100 billion in corporate bonds last year, according to the Bank for International Settlements.  Buckley recognizes that doors opened thanks to his debt and credit expertise. During his two-year stint as an analyst at private equity firm CPMG, a headhunter came calling; Duquesne was looking to hire a credit and equities wiz to work under the family office’s founder and leader, legendary macro investor Stanley Druckenmiller, whose claim to fame was helping George Soros make $1 billion betting against the British pound in 1992. He joined as an analyst at 27. Today, at Duquesne, he’s steering some of the firm’s biggest wins. Over the past 11 years he’s leaned into investments in AI, as well as healthcare and biotech—which he believes will vastly innovate over the next decade. Recently, Buckley says the firm backed pharma company Formation Bio. As a self-proclaimed “non-dogmatic” investor, he’s continuing to keep his horizons open, a philosophy shared by Druckenmiller: Keeping a broad perspective on the market—and a set of skills to meet the moment—could mean the difference between spotting an opportunity or missing it entirely. “Now, we’re seeing that in the AI venture world, these concerns about credit and interest rates suddenly have this big impact on AI infrastructure, private companies, and the venture community,” Buckley says. “I think it’s something I’ve learned from Stan, to always be thinking about the top-down and the bottom-up.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Pakistan’s army has reported that it has killed 74 armed fighters in multiple raids in areas along the country’s borders with Afghanistan. Another 35 fighters were killed in the past two days during separate raids on Mir Ali, while eight were killed in Orakzai, and weapons were recovered, the force added in an update. Both districts are in the northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where the Pakistan Taliban, known as the TTP, and several other armed groups are based. Islamabad accuses India and Afghanistan of backing the armed groups, although Delhi and Kabul deny involvement. “The security forces’ continued successes in the war against terrorism reflect national resolve and professional capabilities,” President Asif Ali Zardari said in a statement. “Operations must continue against externally sponsored terrorist elements seeking to undermine Pakistan’s security.” The army identified the fighters as “Khawarij”, a term it uses to refer to fighters it says are backed by Afghanistan, including the TTP. Although separate, the TTP is allied with the Afghan Taliban, which took power in 2021. Pakistani authorities believe the group operates from areas on Afghanistan’s side of the border and is responsible for increased attacks on Pakistani territory in recent years. The issue has strained relations between Islamabad and Kabul and led to armed confrontations resulting in civilian deaths. At least 11 policemen were killed, and another 12 were wounded after alleged TTP fighters ambushed a convoy in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Thursday, authorities said.

events.title: Nvidia's leadership vacuum could create a unique opportunity for its customers
events.summary: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang. ANTHONY WALLACE / AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . It's technically 2026 AD, but the tech industry is now in 1 AJ (After Jensen). Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation Thursday closed a chaotic chapter for the chip giant. Huang turned gaming chips into the engine of the AI boom, building an empire in the process. In the end, Nvidia's biggest risk was its founder himself. But the saga isn't over. His unique org structure and lack of succession planning mean there's still a lot of mess to clean up. (Speaking of messes, Huang's resignation was followed by a report of yet another "intimate relationship" with an Nvidia employee .) BI's Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis have more on why flat organizations built around powerful founders are great … until they're not . Now it's the job of Colette Kress , Nvidia's longtime CFO and interim CEO, to calm nerves and steady the $4 trillion ship. She'll have the help of veteran tech investor Harvey Jones , an Nvidia board member since 1993, who was named the company's first chairman. Read the memos they sent to employees after the shakeup. In a bit of an eerie twist, Huang talked about succession plans just a few weeks ago . But his comments offered little in the way of concrete plans. "Just as I can be fired, the next CEO has to be hired," Huang said. Nvidia's biggest challenge could be maintaining stability as major changes still loom. Kress' interim tag means she's a temporary solution to Nvidia's leadership problem. According to prediction markets , longtime hardware executive Ian Buck could land the permanent gig. Buck's claim to fame is a big one: creating CUDA. The platform bridges the gap between GPUs and AI models, serving as a key technological moat for Nvidia . The company could also look outside its ranks. President Donald Trump, who had a close relationship with Huang, already suggested one name: Tim Apple Cook . Trump also said he spoke to Huang the day before the resignation and that Huang was " going through hell ." Meanwhile, no clear succession plan and a placeholder CEO could create an opportunity for customers looking to renegotiate deals on better terms. I raised this point to Alistair Barr, author of the AI Insider newsletter, on BI's live Q&A yesterday . He highlighted Huang's reputation as a "brutal" negotiator. "He had a stack of customers, and if they did anything wrong, you go down the list, and you have to wait longer," Barr said. But a new face on the other side of the table negotiating a deal changes the equation. Especially one who might not be in that position for long. Granted, tech companies' appetite for GPUs isn't going anywhere. Nvidia still holds an incredible amount of power and leverage in the AI trade. But thinking something will simply last forever is a recipe for disaster. Just ask Jensen Huang. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UN watchdog calls on Iran to reopen nuclear facilities to inspection
events.summary: Tehran has told the IAEA that it is not possible to resume inspections in the current security situation. The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme. Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation. The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported. The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”. The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency. Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility. Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons. But he blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Since the bombing of the nuclear facilities last year, the watchdog has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, the report noted. The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it. The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities. However, the report notes that Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections in the country cannot resume amid “persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression”. Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.

events.title: NHL’s next media deal will test the league’s strength
events.summary: The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB. One of the biggest developing stories in entertainment and sports is how the world's biggest media companies judge the value of non-NFL rights — and the NHL is giving us our first window into this new era in media values. My colleague Mike Ozanian is out with his new NHL valuations this morning. See the full list here . The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. Sources tell me the league wants an increase in overall rights fees between 50% and 100% over its current deal. The NHL inked a 7-year, $4.5 billion deal with ESPN and TNT Sports in 2021. Whether the league actually gets that type of increase is still unclear — and that will be one of the most watched data points in the world of sports business next year. National media rights for the NHL currently make up about 13% of its annual revenue, which is around $8 billion, according to CNBC estimates. I'm told both Disney/ESPN and Skydance want to renew a deal with the league. Both companies have engaged in preliminary conversations with the league in the past few weeks, and while there's still work to do in terms of price, there's mutual interest in getting something done. In its current deal, ESPN has access to 100 exclusive games for the 2026-27 season. Fifty-three of them air on ESPN or ABC, and the other 47 exclusive stream on ESPN. Under current terms, the league's playoffs are split between Disney and TNT Sports. I'm told Disney is particularly interested in acquiring the rights to more playoff games. The NHL had its most-watched playoffs on record last season, averaging 1.8 million viewers per game. The Stanley Cup averaged 5.2 million viewers — the largest audience since 2019. It was played between the Carolina Hurricanes and the Vegas Golden Knights — not exactly marquee NHL franchises. Last year's regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from a year ago — the highest average in more than a decade. The sport is also having a moment culturally. Earlier this year, HBO Max said its hockey-romance series "Heated Rivalry" averaged a whopping 10.6 million viewers per episode. International hockey competitions, such as the league's annual "4 Nations Face-Off" midseason tournament and the 2026 Winter Olympics, have drawn huge ratings. The last "4 Nations Face-Off" game — 2025's U.S. vs. Canada final — drew 9.3 million viewers. This year's Gold Medal men's hockey game between the U.S. and Canada averaged a stunning 26 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in the U.S., according to Nielsen data. That made it the most-watched sporting event in U.S. history with a start time before 9 a.m. ET. "We think we've got the best content," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said on CNBC last month . "Our ratings have continued to increase. We were up dramatically into the double digits last year. So we view ourselves coming into the marketplace in a very strong position. Having said that, the marketplace is extremely competitive and extremely fragmented. But, I believe that with fierce competition that's going on between traditional television and the newer media platforms that there'll be a great opportunity for us to both expand our reach and get paid what we think is an appropriate reflection of our value." Recent history suggests the NHL will get the rights increase it wants. The NBA nearly tripled its national media rights revenue, signing an 11-year, $77 billion contract with Disney, Amazon and NBCUniversal in a deal that started last season. The NHL also renewed its TV rights deal in Canada just last year with Rogers Communications, scoring an increase of more than 100% annually when adjusting for currency fluctuations. But recent history may not match up to present reality. While I've been told Skydance is interested in getting a deal done, sources also tell me Skydance's top two priorities are paying down debt and saving money to pay for what's going to be a huge NFL rights increase — potentially $1 billion per season or more. Skydance is dead set on renewing the NFL, I'm told. Those talks will likely occur in 2028, as the league has an opt-out clause at the end of the 2029-30 season. The NHL was a meaningful sports property to Warner Bros. Discovery. The company could use its loyal fanbase and sizable playoff ratings to help justify distribution fees to pay TV providers while marginally adding some subscribers to HBO Max.

events.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
events.summary: Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach... And look, the Boss has his office door open! C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D ! ... The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open. His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us. And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas. "AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop. He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town. ... "For the security system," the Boss teases. I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same. The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea. >clickety< >tap< "Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed." >tappity< "And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too." "It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to. "A virus?!" the Boss gasps. "I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing. ... So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him. Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow... >tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety< On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously. >tappity< >tap< The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight. On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling. >bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip< >ring< "Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback. "It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!" Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard. "What do I do?" the Boss gasps. "It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!" "I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks. DAMMIT! >tappity< >click< >tap< >tap< Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device... The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan. ...two hours later... "So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden. "Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor." "It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation." "It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used." "Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask. "No, more like lighter fluid." "Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know." "Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks. "Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie. ...Later, in Mission Control... "So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building." "Yes." "Simply to stop a dumb idea?" "Yes." "And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad." "Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.
