events.title: Why Jensen Huang's Nvidia scandal has everyone quoting Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger
events.summary: Warren Buffett (left) and Charlie Munger. credit should read JOHANNES EISELE/AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday following fresh reports of alleged affairs. X users responded by quoting Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger on risks and reputation. Munger famously warned about the dangers of "ladies, liquor, and leverage." Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger are having a viral moment following Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO. The AI chipmaker's founder stepped down Thursday following a scandal-filled week surrounding his personal life and relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The dayslong saga prompted many online commentators to share famous warnings from the former chairman and late vice-chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. "My partner Charlie says: there's only 3 ways that a smart person can go broke -- he says 'liquor, ladies and leverage'" - Warren Buffet https://t.co/r9DOOfcnEZ — Financelot (@FinanceLancelot) November 12, 2026 "My partner Charlie says that there's only three ways that a smart person can go broke: liquor, ladies, and leverage," Buffett said in a 2018 interview. Charlie Munger seeing his “Liquor, Ladies, Leverage” quote being used more times in a 72 hours timeframe than any other time in human history https://t.co/NA5yNOOKdL — Trung Phan (@TrungTPhan) November 11, 2026 "Now, the truth is the first two he just added because they start with 'l' — it's leverage," Buffett added. Charlie Munger once said liquor, leverage, and ladies are the downfall of men. Everyone thought AI would blow up over leverage, but no one was prepared for it to be women. — Anthony Pompliano 🌪 (@APompliano) November 11, 2026 Huang admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife following reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. He resigned as CEO after fresh claims that he had an affair with a subordinate. Charlie Munger once said smart people go broke in three ways. Liquor, ladies, and leverage. https://t.co/6Ip17Gs9XH — ProblemSniper (@ProblemSniper) November 12, 2026 Munger's caution about the risks of romantic entanglements has even been translated into other languages in recent days: «Solo hay tres formas en las que una persona inteligente puede arruinarse: el alcohol, las mujeres y el apalancamiento». Charlie Munger https://t.co/rYsqGdBRM0 — Roberto Chamorro (@robchamo) November 8, 2026 X users have also been relaying a classic piece of Buffett wisdom about how reputations are hard-won and easily lost. “It takes 20 years to build a reputation and 5 minutes to ruin it.” Buffett tried to tell them all and no one listened — Ben Carlson (@awealthofcs) November 12, 2026 Buffett has been issuing similar refrains for decades. He famously warned Salomon Brothers employees as their interim chairman in 1991: "Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding. Lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless." Buffett has similarly told the managers of Berkshire subsidiaries: "We can afford to lose money—even a lot of money. But we can't afford to lose reputation—even a shred of reputation." “It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it.” — Warren Buffett https://t.co/wZcic1lkQx — Brew Markets (@brewmarkets) November 12, 2026 The legendary investor has also famously advised people to never do anything they wouldn't want printed on the front page of their hometown newspaper for all their friends and family to see. Munger, Buffett's right-hand man for over 45 years, died at age 99 in November 2023. Buffett, now 96, stepped down as Berkshire's CEO at the end of last year, and as its chairman in September. Berkshire stock has rallied strongly in recent days as investors have soured on AI stocks like Nvidia amid concerns about overinvestment and fears of a regulatory crackdown. The Class B shares have jumped 13% in the past month to trade at $590, close to a record high. Nvidia stock is down 27% over the same period. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Inside the aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting
events.summary: It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot five people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and four others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said. The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place. By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch. Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil . People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA . "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another. But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour. Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness. The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said. Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed. Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline. The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Police say the gunman then returned to his apartment, where he fired at people below from an upper-level private balcony. Two men and two women were hospitalized. One suffered serious injuries. The standoff: Lambert barricaded himself in his apartment, where he broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, per police. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze. Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials. Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C. People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Behind the scenes: Lambert had been fighting his condo association over alleged leaks and mold, per court records. He filed a lawsuit against the group in March 2025. Months later, he told now- Washington Sun reporter Michael Brice-Saddler that he'd spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees. In those interviews, Lambert said he knew Stuart's daily gym routine. What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the four surviving victims or deliberately targeted them. The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation. Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies. Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed. President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force . In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country." Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors."

events.title: Nigeria election body to comply with presidential candidate ruling
events.summary: The News Nigeria’s electoral commission will obey any court ruling on whether the main challenger to President Bola Tinubu is eligible to contest January’s presidential election, its chairman said, potentially handing the judiciary a key role in Africa’s biggest poll. Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is set to appeal last week’s high court ruling that invalidated his candidacy . The chair of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Joash Amupitan, speaking at the Chatham House think tank in London, said the body would be constitutionally “obligated” to “obey every court order” if the appeal fails. INEC’s position adds to uncertainty around the vote in Africa’s top crude oil producer with less than 10 weeks until polls open.The commission is currently embroiled in more than 300 legal cases related to local elections, Amupitan said, adding that unresolved disputes could complicate its preparations for the forthcoming polls. Credibility test Bukola Idowa, executive director of civil society group Kimpact Development Initiative, warned any impression that the electoral process was opaque would undermine the validity of the vote. “We’re looking at an election that will put the credibility of all our constitutional institutions to the test,” he told the Chatham House event, adding that this was particularly true of the judiciary. Tinubu won the 2023 election with 36% of the vote with Atiku coming second with a 29% share. But voter turnout stood at just 27% — the lowest since the return to civilian rule in 1999. Atiku has vowed to restore a fuel subsidy the removal of which by Tinubu has been blamed for driving up the cost of living. The price of fuel has increased five-fold since the president announced the scrapping of the subsidy at his inauguration. The View From London Nigeria’s net direct investment inflows have improved significantly since Tinubu took office in 2023 and, in recent years, the nation has received credit rating upgrades. The president has campaigned on a strengthened economy that is projected to grow 4.2% this year. In a tacit acknowledgment of the criticism aimed at him over the higher cost of living, last month Tinubu said the country would shift its economic policy goal from administering “emergency treatmen t ” to delivering shared prosperity. Meanwhile, the oil industry is booming. Africa’s top crude oil exporter has benefited from higher prices sparked by the Iran war and in the past year the regulator has approved 145 new well operations . “The macroeconomic backdrop for these elections are probably the strongest that we’ve seen in a very long time,” said Yewande Sadiku, senior investment banker, international, at Standard Bank. But she stressed that investors care most about consistency around policies. “Elections matter, but the identity of the winner is not as important as the commitment to policy continuity,” she said. Notable Nigerians have limited confidence in the credibility of the upcoming elections, according to polling firm Afrobarometer which found fewer than four in 10 people it surveyed believe the poll will be free and fair .

events.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
events.summary: Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk. The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it. The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment. ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see. "Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said. In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping. Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't. Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order. The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news. This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison. That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't. Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed. The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025. And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018. Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch. "I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said. With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

events.title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
events.summary: Eccentric and overhyped, Tesla’s Cybertruck became a stand-in for Elon Musk during his ascent in the Republican party. It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year. Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era. Eccentric and overhyped, the Cybertruck became a kind of automotive stand-in for Musk himself amid his political ascent. Like so many of his projects, it was massively promoted, heavily delayed, and ultimately fell short: Musk once predicted he could sell 250,000 a year but ultimately sold 70,000 in three years , losing $1.9bn in the process, according to Quartz. The design seemed to prioritize science fiction over robust engineering: the unveiling was in November 2019, when the film Blade Runner was set , as Musk proudly pointed out – but it didn’t arrive on the roads until four years later. At that unveiling event, Musk infamously showed off the Cybertruck’s durability by having a designer throw a ball at its window, which cracked. While Musk called it apocalypse-proof , it often seemed like the opposite: Cybertrucks suffered at least five vehicle fires , four of them deadly – making them deadlier than the notorious Ford Pinto, according to an analysis . They were subject to 11 recalls amid technical issues, including a loose pedal that could get stuck and cause unintentional acceleration. They routinely got stuck in the snow . Like its creator, the Cybertruck was highly divisive. Many observers were repulsed by its bizarre, boxy appearance and its road-hogging size (a parallel parking nightmare). “It is the ugliest vehicle I think I have ever laid eyes on,” the automotive expert Mike Caudill told Fox Business . Others, however, were deeply devoted to their Cybertrucks. “I’ve got 6,000 miles on my Cybertruck; I’ve had zero issues,” Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin, told the Houston Chronicle . Indeed, the Cybertruck had its strong points, according to experts. “People at Tesla were rightly proud of the engineering they put into it,” said Ezra Dyer, a senior editor and columnist at Car and Driver . But “a lot of the engineering problems they solved were self-imposed” – driven by the need to incorporate Musk’s super-epic design choices. “Why is that important to you that it be bulletproof?” Jay Leno asked Musk during a test drive. “Because it’s badass and super cool,” the CEO replied. All this, of course, coincided with Musk’s political rise in the Trump administration. The truck, as the Guardian’s Andrew Lawrence put it, became essentially “a Maga hat on wheels”, indicating its driver’s political beliefs – or at least the politics onlookers would ascribe to them. The archetypal Cybertruck driver was a guy, “probably with some kind of goatee, likely compensating for something, so desperate for attention that he will take negative attention”, as an automotive analyst told the New York Times. Many drivers of various Tesla models rushed to distance themselves from the CEO with bumper stickers that say, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.” The Cybertruck, meanwhile, “became this totem and symbol of Elon Musk himself”, says Dan Neil, an auto columnist for the Wall Street Journal. While Cybertrucks took to the streets, Musk was taking a literal chainsaw to the US government as head of the department of government efficiency (Doge), which bore plenty of similarities to the truck, beginning with the empty promises. Musk said Doge could cut $2tn from the federal budget; its website now claims it has cut just $215bn. In the process, hundreds of thousands of workers left the government due to workforce reductions, early retirement and other reasons – before, in a move reminiscent of the Cybertruck’s recalls, many were rehired. And like the Cybertruck, it all came to an embarrassing end: Musk left government under a cloud as he feuded with Donald Trump over spending in his “big, beautiful bill”. Now, when it comes to the Cybertruck, “you’ve got this expensive luxury product with a very off-putting aesthetic and all this political baggage,” Dyer says (the 2026 model runs from about $72,000 to $102,000 ). So it’s little surprise that sales have struggled. “It’s following the trajectory of any cult vehicle,” Dyer says. The hardcore fans line up, but once they’ve all got theirs, demand fizzles. As it reaches the end of its short road, the Cybertruck – outwardly mighty, inwardly fragile, a poorly conceived product of an increasingly oligarchical system – feels alarmingly apt as a symbol of Trump 2.0 Phase I. Ten years from now, spotting an ageing Cybertruck on the street will serve as a reminder of the bad old days.

events.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
events.summary: The Georgia State Election Board meets in Marietta in March. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election. The board sets the swing state’s election rules , oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.  Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.  The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes. At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA , Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said. Janice Johnston and Janelle King at a March meeting of the State Election Board. Johnston resigned from the board in June. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.  The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.    EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.  “Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.” The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.  “The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.” John Fervier has chaired the Georgia State Election Board since 2024. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday , in part to discuss personnel matters . In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.  “There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan. “As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.” When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded. events.title: Jensen Huang shows the risk of becoming an indispensable leader
events.summary: When he ran Nvidia, Jensen Huang said a flat structure at the top kept information flowing and decision-making nimble. Mark Schiefelbein/Associated Press Jensen Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia exposes the risks of building a company around a powerful founder. The chipmaker's flat structure may have helped it move fast, while also leaving it without a clear successor. C-suite observers say boards need to build a leadership bench before a crisis hits — even if they do so quietly. For years, Jensen Huang embraced a flat leadership model as he molded Nvidia into one of the world's most powerful companies. His sudden exit Wednesday amid scandal puts that arrangement to the test like never before. After cofounding the chip giant at a Denny's restaurant in the early 1990s, Huang went on to lead Nvidia with as many as 60 direct reports . That deliberately flat structure at the top was something he credited with helping the company keep information "fluid" and employees empowered. Yet the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers , can leave a company with a thin succession bench, C-suite observers told Business Insider. "It's hard to imagine any of those direct reports are able to get the scale, scope, and experience to even be qualified to be the CEO," said David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership consulting firm RHR International. Nvidia hadn't publicly disclosed a succession plan. The company's appointment of an internal interim CEO to replace Huang while launching a search for a permanent replacement, including internal and external candidates, suggests it also didn't have an obvious candidate in mind behind the scenes, said Astorino. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. 'Key-person risk' Astorino said Huang's outsize status created "key-person risk," in which too much control rests with a single executive. He said the problem is particularly acute for Nvidia because of its central position in the AI ecosystem. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and head of the HR practice at the consulting firm ZRG, said founders can be conditioned to brush off doubts after years of being told their ideas would fail, making it especially hard to persuade them to plan for a future without them. "They're not great at hearing no," he said. "They develop the thickest skin possible" after years of hearing from skeptics while building their companies. "When you have a flat organization like this, it's great for speed. It's not great for developing leaders," Kaplan said. Nvidia's succession crunch reflects a broader corporate dilemma: Boards too often begin planning only after the window to prepare has narrowed. In a 2025 Nasdaq survey of about 700 board members, CEOs, executives, and governance professionals, 21% said their boards had no CEO succession plan, while another 16% said they had only an emergency plan. Identity tie-up Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs and a board investigation into concerns that he may have been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia named Colette Kress, its CFO, interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. The abrupt transition underscores a common vulnerability for founder-led companies, said Bradley Akubuiro, a partner at Bully Pulpit International and former Fortune 50 chief spokesperson. The reason, he said, is that founders' identities often become tied to an organization's success or failure. Boards in general can mitigate that risk by adding an independent director, lead director, or chair who can bring more governance to a founder-led company and keep succession planning on the agenda, Akubuiro said. They should ensure that someone can provide continuity if a CEO leaves unexpectedly. "It isn't always going to be misconduct," he said. "Any number of things could happen." A viable succession plan requires more than putting a name on an org chart, Akubuiro added. Potential successors need substantial operational experience, exposure to the board, and sufficient visibility with investors, customers, and other stakeholders to inspire confidence that they have what it takes to step in, he said. Avoiding a lame duck Even when companies do that planning work, however, they often keep it quiet, said Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at the executive search firm Kingsley Gate. That's because publicly naming a successor can turn the sitting CEO into a lame duck, prompt passed-over contenders to resign, and invite internal jockeying for influence around the heir apparent, he said. "The organization starts gravitating toward the successor because they know that's where the power center is going to be," Ramakrishnan said. Still, he said that boards should begin succession planning well before a crisis, cultivating two or three serious internal candidates, giving them substantial operating responsibility, and creating incentives for them to stay through the transition. Lior Prosor, cofounder and managing partner at the venture fund Deep33, said Nvidia has been a "super sticky organization" for years, in part because employees could take part in the company's extraordinary stock run-up. With the company's shares taking a hit , the leadership upheaval could give rivals a fresh opening to recruit some of its most valuable talent. "For the first time ever," employees may be asking, "How much will my equity be worth? How quickly does it come back?" Prosor said. Nvidia's troubles could serve as a learning opportunity for companies that have flattened management structures, said Alexander Kirss, a director analyst in Gartner's HR practice. "No employee is irreplaceable," he said. "That includes the CEO." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Target shoppers are visiting more often as the holidays gear up
events.summary: Target is riding into the holidays on a robust wave of customer traffic growth. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Target is nearly three fiscal quarters into a major turnaround effort. A focus on better merchandise and nicer stores is paying off in customer visits. The momentum may set Target up to deliver a strong performance during a pivotal holiday season. Target's bid to get shoppers back is showing results as it gears up for the holidays , recent data show. The bullseye retailer has seen strong growth in customer visits this year, with some of the highest year-over-year increases in retail, according to multiple foot traffic data firms. Those signals have analysts optimistic about the company's turnaround efforts as it heads into its busiest season. Placer.ai found that Target stores saw a 7.2% increase in chain-wide visits for the third quarter, including a 5.9% increase in same-store visits. In addition, roughly half of shoppers visited Target twice a month or more, and nearly one in eleven shoppers visited five times or more. Other data from Advan Research found a 4.7% year-over-year increase in foot traffic at Target in the third quarter, compared with 1.7% at Walmart. Target and Walmart report quarterly earnings next week. Unlike most of its competitors, Target is nearly three fiscal quarters deep into a major turnaround effort under new CEO Michael Fiddelke, and several of his bets appear to be paying off. "They picked off some of the easiest, low-hanging fruit to begin with," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger told Business Insider. Between a focus on tighter store operations and an initial refresh of categories like food and beauty, Target showed it was serious about winning shoppers back , Bellinger said. The company was also well dialed in to viral cultural moments, including the 30th anniversary of Pokemon, to get people lined up outside its stores. "The real parts of the store that Target needs to fix, they haven't touched yet, so that's mainly home and apparel where you get better margins," he added. "If those categories turn, then the Target turnaround is fully in force." Of course, Target's past success in home and apparel may be challenging to replicate as Walmart has become a more formidable player in recent years, Bank of America analyst Chris Nardone said in a note earlier this week. A recent bump in inflation, coupled with stalling wage growth, could point to a dicey road ahead for retailers of all stripes, but Jefferies analyst Corey Tarlowe told Business Insider that Target has been proactive about offering a strong value for shoppers' dollars. "If we are in an environment where, let's say, the consumer needs to turn a little bit more toward a value focus, Target plays well into that," he said, adding that the company has been regaining its trademark balance of affordability and style . Some investors have also raised concerns about an apparent slowdown of traffic growth in October, but Bellinger said he attributes that to an exceptionally strong September. The company is also starting to encounter stronger year-ago comparisons. That said, with this being Fiddelke's first holiday quarter as CEO, it's particularly important that Target sticks the landing this year. "They definitely have a lot of momentum going into the holiday. The stores are a lot cleaner. They're a lot sharper. Better staffed. So it seems like they're on pace for a good holiday," Bellinger said. Target's chief merchandising officer Cara Sylvester said at a media briefing last month that the company is taking a high-cadence approach to the holidays that she's betting will keep shoppers coming in more often. "It's one thing to set product in November and then forget about it and have it sell down. We want to have that consistent newness," she said. "Right up until the end." events.title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee after Chairman Tim Scott asked him to testify on Dec. 10, according to NBC. Lawmakers are scrutinizing the Commerce Department’s oversight of Nvidia chip exports to China and its enforcement of export controls. Scott also asked former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear on Dec. 3 as lawmakers examine national security concerns tied to recent reporting about Huang and Nvidia. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies. Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security. Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns." "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment. The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns." Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday. There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick. Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June. Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

events.title: Entrepreneurs have a secret weapon that anyone can invest in to get ahead. For me, it costs $400 a month.
events.summary: Rafael Nadal and his uncle, Toni Nadal, who coached him for most of his career. Julian Finney/Getty Images The secret weapon of the super successful? Coaches. No matter how talented, successful, or wealthy someone is, they're rarely doing it entirely alone. Business owners share how they've used coaches, mentors, and courses to get ahead. Bill Gates famously said , "Everyone needs a coach. … We all need people that give us feedback. That's how we improve." The best athletes have coaches in their corner. Influential business leaders and CEOs have advisors in theirs. No matter how talented, successful, or wealthy someone is, they're rarely doing it entirely alone. And coaching isn't reserved for people at the top. I hired a life coach at 31. I pay him $400 a month, and it's some of the best money I spend. I wrote about why here . Many business owners have told me something similar about the mentors, coaches, and classes they invest in: Bet on yourself, they say. It can pay off. Kyle Ray, who grew a window-cleaning side hustle into a six-figure business operating in multiple Texas cities, compares the right coach to a cheat code that can help you "collapse time." "When there's something I don't know or need to learn, I start to look for coaches or somebody who can help me speed up through time," he told me. Ray has worked with multiple coaches, joined mastermind programs, and taken classes on everything from using AI to training door-to-door salespeople. At this stage of his career, he said he's willing to pay for knowledge that can speed up his development: "It's like, I need to learn this skill. I need to find out who's doing it better than I am, who can teach me, and what it costs. And then I'm just going to pay for it so I can learn." If hiring a coach isn't in your budget, start with a mentor. Find someone who is already doing what you want to do — and doing it well — and ask whether they'd be willing to share some advice. That's how Ray got started when he was strapped for cash. He bartended and waited tables to pay the bills while gradually building Geek Window Cleaning. It took about seven years before he was earning enough from the side hustle to leave his service jobs. "I just found somebody who was doing better than me," he said. "I asked: What are you doing that I'm not doing? And what do you see that I'm doing that's preventing me from breaking through to the next thing?" Stavya Nilawar, a 19-year-old college student running a creator-marketing agency from his dorm room, took a similar approach. "I would reach out to agency owners who were in the position that I wanted to be in," he told me. "I literally asked them what they're doing now in their day-to-day business and how they got to the next level." Nilawar recommends that early-stage founders do the same: Look for someone running a similar business at a more advanced stage, then reach out. Those conversations can offer guidance now, and potentially lead to collaborations down the line. There are other accessible ways to invest in yourself, too: Attend a conference, join a mastermind group, enroll in a class, or pick up a leadership book. Before Ray had money to invest in coaches, he read to get ahead . He credits much of his business's success to principles he picked up from business and leadership books. His top recommendations include "Drive" by Daniel Pink, "Dare to Lead" by Brené Brown, and "Beyond the Hammer" by Brian Gottlieb. As for networking events, I've been in rooms with top Amazon sellers and real-estate mavens . Each time I've attended a conference for reporting purposes, I've come away with the same realization: I'm missing out by not getting out more. Read the original article on Business Insider

Expensive rocket launches, heat management, radiation, and server costs pose major hurdles, he said. "These are all technically solvable problems," he said. "It's just going to take a while." AI data centers in space aren't taking off anytime soon, according to Amazon cloud chief Matt Garman . On an episode of the Sources Podcast released Tuesday, Garman cast doubt on the near-term prospect of orbital data centers, saying they are "highly unlikely to be economically feasible or practical in the next decade or two." Space-based data centers "sounds good," Garman said, because they could tap free energy in orbit, but explained rocket launches into space are still "relatively infrequent and expensive." "We as a world don't do one launch a day today," said Garman, the CEO of Amazon Web Services , adding, "We're landing in a data center today one GPU every 14 seconds." The idea of orbital data centers has been championed by Elon Musk , the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, as a potential solution to AI's soaring energy demands. Earlier this year, SpaceX said it aims to build a "constellation of a million satellites that operate as orbital data centers" and that it had begun hiring engineers to make the vision a reality. In January, Musk said that within three years "at the latest" space could be the cheapest place to put data centers. Amazon and Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos is also among the tech billionaires who have embraced the idea of space-based data centers to scale AI. In a CNBC interview in May, Bezos called data centers in space "very realistic," though he said the timeline could take longer than some expect. "Some of the timelines we hear are very short," Bezos said. "People would talk about two or three years. That's probably a little ambitious." On the Sources Podcast, Garman said space-based facilities would face a major engineering challenge in managing heat. "Dissipating heat in space is actually quite hard," Garman told podcast host Alex Heath. "It's just a really hard environment. There's radiation everywhere, so you have to build things." Garman said it would be "way more" expensive to build servers in space, but the feat is not impossible. "These are all technically solvable problems," he said. "It's just going to take a while." Garman also expressed skepticism about underwater data centers. "Oceans, there's some of those same problems," he said. "I find oceans to be also probably impractical." Deserts, however, seemed to strike Garman as a more plausible frontier. "I think deserts of those three that you mentioned are by far the most likely," Garman told Heath. "You have relatively good environmental areas. You actually have heat sinks. You have solar areas that you could do it." Though Garman argued building data centers far from communities would mean towns miss out on the increased tax base and high-paying jobs data centers can bring. During the interview, Garman pushed back on concerns about data centers' water use , saying Amazon's largest facilities use less water than 40 US households. events.title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
events.summary: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence in hospitals and clinics is leading the nation's biggest physicians group to lobby for new legal protections if AI harms patients. Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software. There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight. The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong. Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended. The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states. Between the lines: The group's push comes as AI clinical tools are flooding the health system, unlocking new efficiencies but giving algorithms increasing power to make decisions like whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug. Legal and medical experts point to the possibility of triage errors, in which AI systems that process clinical histories, vital signs and imaging can misjudge the severity of a case without the attending doctor's knowledge. The AMA also raises the possibility of an AI system making a plausible recommendation for treatment, but with incomplete laboratory results or an outdated diagnoses. In such cases, a physician may be unable to verify the inputs. In cases where a patient is harmed, responsibility should fall on AI manufacturers and vendors — and possibly on health systems that require the AI systems' use — instead of through a medical malpractice claim against the physician, the AMA argues. Context: There already have been lawsuits around algorithm-driven medical decisions, including a wrongful death case in Alabama involving a screening tool for heart abnormalities. The software developer wasn't held liable because its licensing agreement left final medical decisions to doctors. The big picture: Courts around the country are concluding that companies that design, train and deploy AI systems bear responsibility for what the systems do, said University of California, Davis professor Martin Hilbert, who studies the role of digital information and algorithms in society. Accountability hinges on factors including who shares responsibility when multiple parties build an AI system, how to prove fault inside an opaque model, and what to do when damages surface only after the system is deployed. "Different parties are responsible for different cases, and you can't just hold the end user responsible," he told Axios. The AMA wants to address situations when use of an AI system is mandatory. What we're watching: The Food and Drug Administration is weighing whether a new framework is needed for regulating AI-enabled medical devices. But the agency oversees software that meets the definition of a medical device, not all of the AI in health care. Hospitals generally support putting the onus on developers and vendors for monitoring the systems' performance, saying the "black box" nature of many systems can make it hard to identify flaws. AdvaMed, the trade group representing device makers, is urging the FDA to continue using its current approaches for evaluating generative AI-enabled medical devices. It also wants the agency to avoid post-market monitoring that imposes added burdens regardless of a product's actual risk.

events.title: ‘I’ll be buying more’: Singapore investors pour into Nvidia shares on Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov 12 sent Nvidia shares down another 14% by the opening of US trading, and down 4.3% at closing. Singapore retail investors bought Nvidia shares after Jensen Huang resigned, seeing the dip as a chance to invest more. Trading on local platforms jumped sharply, with buy orders rising fast and many clients staying net buyers despite the sell-off. Investors now worry about Nvidia’s leadership and governance, while watching interim chief executive Colette Kress, earnings on Nov 17, and a congressional briefing on Nov 18. SINGAPORE – When news broke of former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang being ensnared in an alleged honey trap espionage , retail investor Asiya Bakht was quick to snap up shares in the world’s biggest chip company. “Nvidia shares had already been on a steep decline even before news of Huang’s resignation broke, so I was monitoring it closely… When the price dipped further following the announcement, I picked up a few more,” said the 52-year-old. Her current Nvidia holding is already worth five figures, and she plans to plough more into the stock, having picked up shares throughout the week. “I feel this temporary dip could be a major opportunity for investors like me,” said the founder of public relations company Beets PR. She is among a wave of Singapore-based retail investors who rushed into Nvidia amid the sell-off on the night of Nov 12 , betting that the company’s long-term growth prospects would outweigh the uncertainty surrounding its chief executive. Trading activity surged in several brokerage platforms when US markets opened overnight, with investors largely buying the dip or holding on to their existing positions. Nvidia shares had already been battered by a broader sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks , even before reports emerged over the weekend of Huang’s extramarital affairs. But as the AI rout retraced some losses, Nvidia was hit by an alleged espionage accusation. Huang was reportedly involved with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of espionage . The national security scandal was compounded by a governance issue when it was revealed that he also had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , Nvidia’s vice-president of its healthcare business. With the chipmaker’s board under pressure to terminate his appointment, Huang resigned on Nov 12 , sending Nvidia shares down another 14% by the opening of US trading, and down 4.3% at closing. The Nov 12 close represents an 11% decline in Nvidia’s share price over the week, wiping about US$490 billion (S$630 billion) off the chipmaker’s market value over the period. Despite the sharp sell-off, intrepid Singapore investors pounced on the buying opportunity on the night of Nov 12 . “Customers were placing buy orders within minutes of the price drop (when US market opened),” said Arpit Agal, head of brokerage at Syfe. Nvidia orders on the platform surged to about 13 times the daily average over the preceding six weeks on the platform, following news of Huang’s resignation on Nov 12 . Of the clients who traded US stocks on Nov 12 , 70% were dealing in Nvidia. Similarly, FSM Global recorded a surge in Nvidia trading on Nov 12 night. Trading volume rose to 11 times its October daily average, with Singapore clients remaining net buyers of the counter at a buy-to-sell ratio of 1.35. Over at brokerage firm IG, trading activity among Singapore peaked on Nov 12. Trading volume surged nearly six times over the past week compared with the preceding week, while the number of clients trading Nvidia roughly doubled. The increase in activity was broad-based, spanning existing Nvidia shareholders, first-time traders of the stock and new IG clients. “Investors are not necessarily losing faith in Nvidia’s business, but are reassessing the risks associated with iconic founder Jensen Huang’s departure,” said Jaycee Lai, head of clients at IG. He added that client trading activity suggested that confidence in Nvidia’s underlying business remains relatively resilient. Singapore-based investors were already increasing their positions in Nvidia from earlier in the week, when news of Huang’s scandal broke out. At FSM Global, Nvidia’s buy-to-sell ratio among Singapore clients touched 3.3 on Nov 9 , compared with 1.1 in October. Saxo also reported that Singapore clients remained slightly tilted towards buying, with the number of clients holding Nvidia positions increasing around 3% on Nov 12 . However, unlike the spree on that day , investors appeared more cautious earlier in the week as the controversy unfolded. While Moomoo Singapore recorded a near three-times increase in Nvidia sell orders and shares sold between Nov 6 and 9, put option contracts rose by more than five times. Despite the increase in selling activity, clients remained net buyers on both days.

events.title: His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose.
events.summary: Photo illustration: Mauricio Rodríguez Pons/ProPublica. Source images: Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian, courtesy of the Phillips family. What if you had to pick between your deeply held faith and the life of your child? That’s the gutting choice that faced Marshall Phillips, an Oregon dad who was born into the Followers of Christ, a sect whose creed bars medical treatment. When his 11-year-old son was stricken with a dire health crisis, Phillips became caught between his faith, his family and the state of Oregon, which had begun cracking down on faith-healing parents who don’t seek medical help for their minor children. A decade later, Phillips was pulled into another one of his church’s life-or-death dramas when he was asked to care for a newborn whose twin had died because her parents had refused to seek medical attention. Read More Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher To examine the power of faith-healing churches and the toll of their teachings, The Oregonian investigative reporter Noelle Crombie, senior staff photojournalist Beth Nakamura and videographer Samantha Swindler spent months with Phillips and his family, piecing together rare accounts from inside the deeply shuttered world of the Followers of Christ and of the state officials who fought to protect children who need medical treatment. The documentary, produced by The Oregonian’s managing producer of video, Teresa Mahoney, not only lays out in visceral detail the agonizing choices that families like the Phillips have to make, it also chronicles how they overcame the clash with their religious beliefs. Go inside the secretive Followers of Christ sect and watch the extraordinary journey . Read more in this riveting print narrative , and meet the man who dominated and shaped the sect . events.title: Henry and Young shine as New Zealand thrash India by 244 runs
events.summary: New Zealand trail India 2-1 and can no ​longer win the five-match series, but they can level it in Sunday’s final game. Matt Henry took six wickets and Will Young struck a century as New Zealand thrashed a ragged India by 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui on Friday. Henry removed Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer, all without scoring, in the first over of India’s chase to tear the top order apart. The visitors needed a massive 334 for victory. list 1 of 3 WTA Finals: Pegula wins thriller as compatriot Gauff eliminated list 2 of 3 Australia’s friendly against Jordan moved to Qatar over security concerns list 3 of 3 NBA: Cunningham scores 52 as Pistons win double OT thriller against Wizards New Zealand made 333 all out in the last over after being asked to bat, with Young punishing two simple drops by Indian fielders to bring up his fifth ODI hundred. India never stood a chance of chasing the total after Henry’s heavenly opening over. Rohit edged his first ball to slip, Kohli was bowled facing his fourth ball, and then Iyer was pegged on his back leg to fall lbw. India’s rebuild never happened, with Ishan Kishan top-scoring with just 27 as India were rolled for 89. Henry ended with 6-27 and Matthew Fisher took 3-31. New Zealand’s imposing total came off the back of Young’s 125 from 108 balls, including 14 fours and four sixes. Young and Tim Seifert combined for an 85-run opening partnership. While Young rode his early luck – dropped twice in two balls when on five in the second over, first by slip Rohit and then by wicketkeeper Kishan – Seifert played the aggressor with a brisk 39-ball 50. When Seifert fell for 58, Nick Kelly and Dean Foxcroft soon followed, playing reckless shots. Young found better support in Finn Allen, the pair putting on 90 runs in just 65 balls as they seized on wayward Indian bowling. Young’s first 50 came from 49 balls, and his second from just 39 balls as he hit regular boundaries through the middle overs. Allen made 41 from 30 deliveries, including five fours and two sixes. Axar Patel took 2-39 from 10 overs as India pulled the innings back late, while Auqib Nabi had 2-59 and Gurnoor Brar 2-69. New Zealand trail India 2-1 and can no longer win the five-match series, but they can avoid defeat if they ⁠win the final match at the same venue on Sunday. The third match was abandoned due to rain.

events.title: Why is Trump saying ‘no deal necessary’ with Iran as he sidelines JD Vance?
events.summary: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats? The US-Iran war is trapped in an ongoing ‘no war, no peace’ situation, analysts say, as the Trump administration appears divided over the conflict. Just hours before Iran claimed it hit the United States military’s early warning radar system in Bahrain early on Friday, US President Donald Trump said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, that, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.” Instead, Trump said, he has told Vance to focus on unearthing what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states – after Democrats stunningly took over Congress in the midterm elections. Vance is a known critic of the US-Israeli war on Iran. He has blamed Trump’s military strikes on Iran and the subsequent energy crisis and inflation in the US for the Republicans’ losses in Congress. Meanwhile, several commercial vessels trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz have hit naval mines, or were struck by the Iranian military, over the past week – but Trump continues to claim that Washington controls the critical waterway nonetheless. So, where is the war headed – and is Vance being sidelined by Trump? Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he had asked Vice President Vance “to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.” “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he added. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on the foregoing arc of war on Iran since the midterm losses. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added. Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war. Despite threatening that he might “destroy” Iran last week, this week Trump has said that further strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely”. What role has Vance played in talks with Iran? Vance favours a deal with Iran, which Trump believes is not possible currently. Vance led the US negotiations in April in Islamabad, where he helped secure the June memorandum of understanding with Iran. That quickly collapsed over glaring gaps in each side’s understanding of what had been agreed, however – particularly in reference to control of the Strait of Hormuz. The US vice president also led direct talks with Iran in Switzerland and is part of renewed diplomatic efforts, engaging Qatari and Pakistani mediators and seeking continued negotiations with Iranian officials. On November 4, following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections, Vance publicly questioned whether the war had been worth the political and economic costs. In a post on X, he wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” endorsing diplomatic resolution as sound advice. He added: “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” Political analysts say Vance’s rather blunt assessment is also an effort to distance himself from Trump’s war on Iran, when the president is facing his all-time low career approval ratings. On June 17, speaking at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France – when both parties had just signed the Islamabad MoU – Trump told reporters: “This way, if it works out, I’m going to take the credit. If it doesn’t work out, I’m blaming JD. You better be careful, JD.” The next day, Vance told reporters he believed the president was “joking”. Where does the US-Iran war go from here? On Friday morning, Tehran said it had attacked and destroyed an early-warning radar system belonging to the US military in Bahrain, in what it said was retaliation for an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran’s port city of Sirik. Meanwhile, on Thursday, Trump said Washington’s allies in the Middle East had asked him to hold off on renewed large-scale attacks against Iran. He added that the US could destroy Iran’s energy infrastructure, bridges and manufacturing facilities within three days, if it wanted to. “Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while,” he said at White House, adding that Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain preferred the current approach. Asked whether he would have launched further attacks without those requests, Trump replied: “Yes, I would.” Though Trump acknowledged that rising fuel prices caused by the war contributed to the Republicans’ defeat in the midterm elections, he defended his decision to attack Iran.

events.title: Democrats in power confront the social media trap
events.summary: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both cautious, calm, compromise-minded leaders fantasizing about a serious, sensible Democratic-run Congress. But social media is a temptress no party leader has tamed. The seduction of attention, likes and followers invariably proves too strong for the savviest, most self-promotional politicians to resist. Why it matters: That's the lesson of the Internet Era of American Politics — the algorithms always win. A few provocative members of Congress and online activists dominate the national conversation because they master the biggest social media platforms. That creates the impression that their views reflect a party, or a nation, when in reality they don't. And it shapes the party's image and agenda. Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), vice chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus , told us: "Governing isn't about getting the most followers on X — it's about delivering actual results ... It's easy to scream and yell, and say no — it's much harder to figure out a way forward." By the numbers: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed had 1.6 million Instagram followers as of Sept. 13. Today: 7.6 million and rising. One clip of him pulled an estimated 50 million-plus views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, sits at 466,000 Instagram followers . A man who hasn't been sworn in has roughly 15x the leader's audience. El-Sayed telegraphed this in July: "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous!" True. Jeffries has nearly 1 million followers on Instagram. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has 9.8 million on her personal account alone. Yes, President Trump remade the GOP. But social media sucked in countless others to try to copy him, pushing rhetoric or ideas few politicians would've touched in the past. You see this in the rise of celebrity politicians who do little legislating but lots of instigating. You see this in the explosion of not just Instagram, X and YouTube followers by politicians, but also in the many starting their own shows — unthinkable a decade ago. Several see themselves as content producers: California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas host podcasts while doing pretty important day jobs for big states. Trump started his own social media platform, Truth Social . You see this in the daily media feeding frenzy when someone, somewhere goes viral because they lit up social media with a meme or menacing post. The trap is springing before Democrats have even been sworn in: Several incoming senators have publicly said they won't support Schumer as leader, calling for new blood and more fight. James Talarico of Texas has sidestepped the question for months. Petitions to replace Schumer passed 100,000 signatures a day after launch. At Crooked Con, the post-election summit hosted in Washington last weekend by the parent company of "Pod Save America," the crowd booed and jeered his name all day. The pressure worked: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's thinking about a 2028 presidential run, announced Thursday night on MS NOW he'll challenge Schumer for majority leader. Doug Sosnik , a top official in Bill Clinton's White House and closely followed analyst of Democratic politics, told us: "You would never know it from the internet or press coverage, but the fact is there are only 130,000 members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)." "It has taken a while, but I think that Democrats have finally figured out that X/Twitter is not the real world," Sosnik added. "The best proof point of Democrats' 'getting this' was our success across the entire country." What we're watching: The biggest siren song of the algorithm this next year will be impeaching Trump. Schumer and Jeffries have tried to set a disciplined path focused on affordability, not impeachment. Trump is prone to taking provocative actions that would juice talk of impeachment. A crowded presidential primary field will make the topic even more tempting — a massive distraction for the new Democratic majorities. Reality check: Schumer only needs about 29 of his members to vote for him in a secret caucus vote. He'll likely win the room. But he's losing the feed, and the feed sets the narrative. Among the senators-elect who say they won't vote for Schumer are Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson of Maine. Running against your own leader is now a red state play, too. Accountability creep: In December, Jeffries waved off a Hegseth impeachment push. On Sunday, he said he was a " hard yes ." (House Republicans tanked the effort on Tuesday.) Bernie Sanders, the incoming HELP chair, says Democrats may go after RFK Jr. next, alongside aggressive investigations into Trump's staff and family. To be fair: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky forced the vote, and Jeffries tied it to an Iran war he says has driven up prices. But removal would take two-thirds of the Senate, which Democrats don't have. It was a Week 1 fight they couldn't finish. The bitter truth is there's little market for moderation or sanity or heads-down, excruciating policymaking. This wasn't always true: Pre-internet, politics wasn't minute-by-minute combat and most media played by similar rules and stuck to daily rhythms. So how can Schumer and Jeffries overcome this? You could argue no party is better positioned than Democrats to resist, or at least tame, the social media temptation. The scale of the win gives them cover: at least 54 Senate seats to 44 and 255 House seats to 168, with some races still uncalled . That's Democrats' largest House majority since 2008, with a lead of nearly 14 points in the total House vote. Democrats clearly won because voters are tired of Trump's ideas, rhetoric and tactics. They clearly won because they fielded very moderate candidates in very red states: flips in Kansas (which hadn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century ), Iowa, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina. They clearly won because those candidates uniformly talked about the economy, the cost of living and things that matter to real people in real states. Only the most delusional Democrats think they won because of the mass appeal of their party. They know they have a golden opportunity to reposition and rehabilitate the Democratic brand. Flashback: The last time Democrats held a majority this big, after 2008, they lost 63 House seats two years later. Big majorities have more members, more factions and more people chasing virality. Some top Democrats think the House and Senate should agree to focus on the one topic that unites them all, affordability, and allow room for debate but not distraction. Schumer and Jeffries could state this emphatically every day. They could also make plain that they plan to hold Trump and others accountable, but leave that to oversight committees and make it secondary to bringing down prices. The bottom line: Democrats won the election on prices. They'll lose the majority on posts. Axios' Alex Thompson

events.title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
events.summary: UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used. According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing. The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation. It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards. Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence. In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken. "We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action. "Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent." Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning." Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system. However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries. The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted. The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes. Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high. Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute , as well as the King's College London Policy Institute , showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively. Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience. The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition. Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns. "Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said. "A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence." As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK. Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made. Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped. The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements. A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming. Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals . "The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said. "This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited , as we've seen before. "Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused." Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®
