events.title: The unglamorous leadership strategy behind Hilton, the world’s best workplace
events.summary: In today’s CEO Daily: Hilton CEO Chris Nassetta plays the long game. The big leadership story: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit adds uncertainty to Anthropic’s IPO. The markets: Mixed globally as investors weigh the fallout of Huang’s departure. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. On one level, the best leadership strategies can sound obvious. “There’s nothing proprietary about it,” says Chris Nassetta, president and CEO of Hilton Worldwide . “It’s about grinding it out, investing in people, having the top-down purpose-driven north star, getting everyone unified, and doing the ground-up granular work. It’s about doing it and doing it and doing it and doing it. And then, when you-know-what hits the fan, it’s about continuing to live the values of the company.” In a world of shorter cycles, faster innovation and an increased urgency to transform and adapt, Nassetta preaches the power of playing the long game. He became CEO of Hilton in 2007 and told me that transforming a fragmented hotel company into a cohesive high-performing culture took years. It has paid off as Hilton was just named the No. 1 World’s Best Workplace by Fortune and Great Place To Work for the third time and second consecutive year. Leadership, or the lack thereof, is top of mind. Running a founder-led tech company like Nvidia is obviously different from managing a people-centric global hospitality company like Hilton. We’re paying a lot of attention this week to the perils of tech titans who make it all about themselves . Let’s also look at the playbook of a very different style of leader. We don’t just pick who gets on the Best Workplace list. It’s determined by data like employee engagement, where Hilton scored 93% in a company of more than 500,000 workers across 9,600 properties. And 93% of the leaders across those properties got their start in frontline jobs. They get training, perks, and opportunities to rotate in different roles. What matters most is who’s in charge. Nassetta thinks a lot about the art and science and execution of leadership. He talks about the need for humility, agility and communicating a “vision in unique and different ways so that people feel part of something bigger than themselves.” And of course he thinks about AI. “There’s so much money and time being spent trying to scare people as opposed to trying to educate people about where … the different possibilities are,” he told me. “AI, as well as other forms of technology we’ve used, have been tools that we can put in the hands of our frontline team members that help them do their job better, faster, easier.” Is he replaceable? You bet. He believes building a bench of talent is part of the job, arguing “you take way too much risk trying to bring somebody in from the outside.” And there’s no shortcut when it comes to listening, learning and building a great workplace. As with diet and exercise, it can take years to see the full results. “If you said to me, you have five years to ring the bell, high-five it, and you’ve totally rebuilt the culture, based on what I know now, I would have said, not possible,” he said. “It’s a marathon, not a sprint. events.title: Russia and Ukraine report overnight attacks amid US diplomatic push
events.summary: Overnight attacks reported on both sides as US efforts to broker a ceasefire struggle to make progress and Europe continues to ponder its role. Russia and Ukraine have reported numerous overnight attacks, despite a diplomatic push to end the conflict. Russian officials reported on Friday that a swarm of about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets. Ukraine reported that a hospital was struck and that strikes on the port of Odesa were ongoing. list 1 of 2 Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys list 2 of 2 The real winner in Poland’s constitutional battle is Putin The reports show that hostilities continue unabated despite the renewed effort of United States envoys to mediate a ceasefire. Russia’s Ministry of Defence reported it had intercepted 1,198 Ukrainian drones overnight, across more than 15 regions. Attacks in Volgograd in southern Russia killed four people as they hit an industrial area and left two others injured, regional Governor Andrei Bocharov said. Volgograd is home to a major oil refinery, which unverified video posted on social media purported to show was on fire. There was no immediate official ⁠confirmation that the refinery had been attacked. Ukraine has concentrated its fire this year on Russia’s oil infrastructure in a bid to cut off its earnings from energy exports, which are being used to power its ongoing invasion. Sergei Sobyanin, mayor of Moscow, said 467 Ukrainian drones had hit the capital overnight, according to the RIA Novosti news agency. Ukraine reported that Russian forces had been attacking the southern port city of Odesa since early on Friday morning. The city’s military administration reported that at least two people had been killed. The Russian Defence Ministry said it had targeted a cargo ship in the Black Sea that was transporting weapons and military equipment for Ukrainian forces, according to the TASS news agency. Ukrainian emergency officials reported six people injured in Russian attacks in the southeastern Zaporizhia district. A hospital in Kyiv caught fire overnight after being struck during a Russian drone attack, leaving one person injured. Reporting from the hospital, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the building was hit at about 3am local time (01:00GMT) and was severely damaged. “This is a hospital that treats civilians, it’s close to the centre of the city,” she said, noting that many people had been forced to evacuate their homes amid the strikes. The attacks came amid the renewed diplomatic push by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday, reporting an agreement on a major prisoner exchange but no progress towards ending the war. Territory and security guarantees remain crucial obstacles. Russia is reported to have repeated uncompromising demands, including its right to control the entirety of Ukraine’s Donbas region. Unconfirmed reports also said it had made demands regarding wider European security, including calling for Finland to leave NATO and for the Western military alliance to pledge not to base troops in the Baltic region. The US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday. Kushner said late on Thursday that Putin has agreed to include Europe in the negotiations. “We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” he said. “I think it is self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in Dublin. However, Europe continues to struggle to coordinate its approach, with disagreement over naming a lead negotiator persisting before an expected return to talks between Russia and Ukraine next week. The Dublin summit is focused on resolving the issue. In Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s MacAlpine said that the Ukrainians worry that Russia is using the move to include the Europeans in the talks to distract from its refusal to concede occupied territory. However, Moscow on Friday afternoon stated that it has not yet agreed to include European mediators in the talks. “Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

events.title: The biggest problem facing America's economy: not enough people
events.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI America isn't empty empty. Its population is still growing. Its cities remain raucous and crowded. Its suburbs are buzzing. But the country is starting to feel a little less full. For years, economists and demographers have warned about the coming " Great People Shortage ," a time when the US population would begin to decline thanks to lower birth rates and aging baby boomers. While the current situation is not yet as dire as those predictions, the ground is shifting in ways likely to reshape the American economy. The decrease in babies born years ago is now becoming more perceptible, as fewer people are reaching adulthood and joining the labor force. Plus, the Trump administration is giving America's ongoing demographic shifts a shove by making it harder for foreigners to enter the US, closing off one of the country's main buffers against a workforce that's getting smaller and older. Tourism is weakening, too, amid rising prices and hesitant international visitors. The effects may not show up in the national head count yet. But the slowdown will start to appear in the places and industries that depend on a churn of newcomers. The US population isn't expected to fall off a cliff soon: The Congressional Budget Office expects the number of people living in America to peak at 364 million in 2056 before it starts to decline. But in a country where the fertility rate crested in 2007 and isn't likely to go back up anytime soon, there are a lot of unanswered questions lurking underneath that topline number — namely, will there be enough working-age people in the places that need them to power the economy? Immigration has historically been a crucial part of the answer. The last few years have seen some wild swings in the country's net international migration. Under the Biden administration, it ballooned to 2.7 million in 2024, per the Census Bureau. It fell to 1.3 million in 2025 and is expected to decline to 321,000 in 2026. In terms of the workforce, that's a big deal. "Immigration is usually about half our job growth," says Pia Orrenius, a labor economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas. When fewer immigrants arrive, it becomes harder for employers to fill jobs, especially in regions that need workers. That means lower output, slower growth, and less demand, because immigrants aren't just workers, they're also consumers. Orrenius points to Texas, which is in the midst of a manufacturing boom and building out data centers. "If you have a stagnant economy anyway that doesn't really grow much or really generate a lot of new jobs anyway, you're not really going to feel it as much," she says. In Texas, however, "we grow fast, and we depend on immigrants and migrants from other states to fuel that growth." While incoming immigration numbers have waxed and waned over the decades, America is in novel territory regarding its broader attitude toward foreigners already in the country. Not only has the White House undertaken mass deportation efforts and cracked down severely on entrances at the border, but it has also revoked thousands of visas for students and workers and ended protections for hundreds of thousands of people living in the US from countries such as Venezuela and Haiti. Whether they're a white-collar tech engineer or a blue-collar roofer, non-natives across the economic spectrum are less welcome in the US. Immigrants don't simply take jobs that would otherwise go to US-born workers. The two groups often do different, complementary work. Immigrants also create demand — they buy groceries, rent apartments, and start businesses that fuel local economies. Fewer tourists from abroad impact economies, too. Many foreigners have decided to avoid Stateside visits under the Trump administration. The president's antagonistic stance toward Canada and ongoing tensions with our neighbors to the north has resulted in a steep decline in visitors from there. Tourism from Europe and Asia has fallen. People are just a little less footloose. Leigh Barnes, the North America president of Intrepid Travel, an international travel company, tells me they've seen a 67% decline in Canadians traveling to the US from 2025 to 2026, a 30% decline in inbound visitors from Australia and New Zealand, and a 24% decrease from Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. He attributes the drop-offs to a mix of politics and economics. Canadians have had a "visceral" response to Trump's stance toward their home country, while visitors from Australia and the United Kingdom, for example, are more put off by financial pressures at home and increased costs in the US. Once tourists arrive in the US, he says they often discover "everyone's bloody lovely," but the problem is that they're nervous about getting here. "It's that trepidation and concern coming into the border," he says. The cumulative effect is an uneven demographic era. There will be some places with fewer workers and some places that continue to grow. Attractions and cities that depend on international tourism will take a hit, whereas others that don't get many visitors won't see a difference. Some colleges will survive the drop in international students, navigate a world with lower attendance, or successfully entice enough young people to enroll. Others will struggle to weather the storm. The competition for an increasingly scarce number of young people is also complicated by the fact that Americans are moving less than they once did, says William Frey, a demographer and senior fellow at Brookings Metro. "People are just a little less footloose," he says. The result will be more parts of the country emptying out, especially rural areas that don't have the same kinds of job opportunities they used to have. They can't offer the jobs and amenities more populated areas do. One thing that is true across the country: the population is aging. "That's probably a bigger, broader concern," Frey says. Baby boomers are exiting the workforce, and there aren't enough young workers to backfill them, take their jobs, and replace their tax dollars. This is also changing the nature of jobs the country needs — someone has to care for these older people. For up-and-coming American workers, this setting isn't necessarily terrible news, says Steven Ruggles, a regents professor of history at the University of Minnesota. Workers entering the workforce in 2040 — about 15 years down the road — will have a "pretty darn good" labor market, he says. Companies will have to compete for the available workforce, which will mean greater leverage, stronger job prospects, and higher pay. "When the baby boomers entered the labor market, the labor unions disintegrated because they no longer had any bargaining power because workers were a dime a dozen," he says. On the flip side, it also means companies will try to squeeze more out of every worker they can hire. events.title: I’m a 'Mormon Wives' star, business owner, and recently divorced mom. My chaotic life runs on coffee, DoorDash, and dirty sodas.
events.summary: Jessi Draper, star of Hulu's "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives," runs hair businesses in Utah. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/Getty Images This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jessi Draper, a 34-year-old star on Hulu's "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives" and the owner of JZ Styles, who is based in Utah. It has been edited for length and clarity. No two days are the same for me because the scope of my work is huge. I run a hair salon, a hair school, and a hair-extension company . I'm also filming a reality show , "The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives." I have two kids, half the time now that I'm divorced. I don't have a routine. Every day is different and chaotic. One thing stays the same, though: I always start the day with coffee. I start my day at 7 a.m. with a coffee, then it's onto dirty sodas I'm usually up at 7 a.m. On the days I don't have my kids, I like to sit outside on my porch or in my living room by the fireplace and take a moment for myself. My life is so crazy, so it's nice to decompress, whether that means journaling or slowly drinking coffee. At my rental home, I have a full coffee bar in my butler's pantry, with a machine, syrups, and everything else I need. Sometimes, though, I still DoorDash Starbucks . Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. Coffee gets me going in the morning, but dirty sodas get me through the rest of the day. In Mormonland , dirty sodas — sodas mixed with creamer or syrup — are a big deal. At my salon, we have a whole dirty soda bar, so I can unfortunately end up having four a day. I'm often having Dr Pepper with vanilla cream and English toffee syrup. If I have my kids, I get myself ready before they wake up: hair, makeup, feeding my dog, and letting him out. Then I go to my 6-year-old son, lay out his uniform, wake him up, and let him get himself ready. Next, I wake up my 3-year-old daughter. My kids need to be at school by 8:30 a.m. It's always a shit show trying to get everyone ready and out the door. If we have time, I'll prepare Little Spoon meals . Depending on the day, breakfast is sometimes a cup of cereal in the car. The kids have to be at school by 8:30 a.m. During the ride, they get jealous of each other, so we make sure everything is fair. My son chooses a song, and then my daughter chooses one. We go back and forth between hot DJs' music and "We're Going on a Bear Hunt." If I'm not filming, I head to the salon or academy After drop-off, if I'm not filming, I could be teaching at the school one day and at the salon the next. I opened the JZ Styles salon in 2016, then launched a company that sells hair extensions and other hair-care products. Since 2022, we also have a hair-styling academy . I wrote the curriculum for our nine-month academy program, but our amazing director now runs most of it. I'll often start the workday by going to the office at my salon to discuss logistics and coming launches with the team. I also like to hang out in the salon's break room and see my employees. When I'm filming, I'm so removed from them, so I want to make sure everyone is feeling good. Before the show, I used to joke that I lived at my salon. It was my whole life. Nowadays, I pop in when I can. I don't take clients anymore because it would be too hard with my schedule, so I focus on everything that happens behind the scenes. Later in the morning, I might go to the hair school down the street to talk to the director, say hi to the students, and check in. There's always something to do on my phone, too, whether it's brand deals , the show, or the business. Filming runs my days When we're filming a season , my day is determined by the production schedule, and I usually don't know what I'm doing until the night before. I bounce from place to place to film scenes. The show is my friend group and my real life, but I also see it as a job, so I'm always on time. This season has been especially tough because I was going through a divorce while filming. There were times when we were shooting a scene, and I'd get news from my lawyer. I DoorDash lunch whenever I can Lunch is whenever I have time, and it's usually DoorDash. I eat like a child: chicken nuggets, mac and cheese, or my go-to, a turkey sandwich. Every hairdresser will tell you lunch breaks don't exist. I'm usually multitasking, and I can't remember the last time I sat and ate lunch in silence. I have a sweet tooth, so my guilty pleasure is always having Smarties in my purse. On a typical workday, I'm in my salon office responding to emails and texts, approving marketing materials, or shooting and editing content. I'm always asking ChatGPT random work questions , but we have a graphic designer, accountant, and other in-house professionals, so we don't need to use AI for that. I love a personal touch. From 5:30 p.m., I focus on my kids If I'm working or filming, my nanny picks the kids up at 3:30 p.m. and watches them until about 5:30 p.m. Then I'm home with them for homework, a game or activity, dinner, and bedtime. I cannot cook to save my life, aside from tater-tot casserole. We usually have Little Spoon meals or DoorDash pasta from Olive Garden. Luckily, I eat like my kids. Dinner is around 6:30 p.m., and then we start the wind-down routine around 7:30 p.m., so they're in bed by 8 p.m. If I don't have my kids, I try to decompress I listen to podcasts in the bath, like "The Toast" and "Call Her Daddy." I do my skincare routine, put on cozy pajamas, and watch a show with popcorn and a HydroJug of water. A month ago, I deleted social media from my personal phone. There was so much chatter and negativity around the show that it was easy to spiral. Now I can actually decompress instead of scrolling. It's a game changer. Before bed, I check Google Calendar At the end of the day, I look at Google Calendar to see what's coming up and figure out my priorities for the next day. I'm Type A and organized, but my life is Type B: I never know what's going to happen. Google Calendar is my best friend. I'm in bed by 11 p.m. By 11 p.m., I need to be in bed. I rarely stay up past midnight. I dread the next day if I have nothing going on because I like to know I'm busy. I normally look forward to tomorrow because I feel blessed to love everything I do. I get to work with my best friends and family, and to me, that feels like success. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I was addicted to my phone for years. Now I only check it on Mondays, and my life is completely different.
events.summary: Tom McHenry helped kick his phone addiction by communing with nature. Courtesy of Tom McHenry Tom McHenry started gaming at six, and it triggered his addiction to video games and social media. He would compulsively "doom scroll" on his smartphone, isolating himself from others. McHenry followed 12-step programs to break free of the habit, helped by fitness and cold plunges. This story is based on an interview with Tom McHenry, 36, a mental health worker from Southeast Michigan. It has been edited for length and clarity. I started playing Game Boy when I was 6. I loved it. It was awesome. Then, in my teenage years, I graduated to computers and played games like World of Warcraft. Smartphones became mainstream in my 20s, and I immediately jumped on them. I was an electrical engineer at the time, and I would sneak to the bathroom to play video games. Social media was my dopamine fix Things progressed to me having my work screen open and, in the corner, Facebook or YouTube. I kept up appearances, but my attention was always on games and social media . I got a dissociative effect, which helped me self-soothe and self-regulate. And it spiraled out of control from there, becoming my dopamine fix. McHenry tried to hide his addiction to his iPhone. Courtesy of Tom McHenry At least I recognized I had a problem. I was naturally isolating myself, and technology was my best friend. I would commit to being off Facebook for a month, before relapsing or moving to a different platform. I enjoyed the doomscrolling. It didn't matter if it was a friend or not; I liked seeing people write stuff. I would go to Reddit and read 500 comments under a post. It was an endless desire for more. My mom would say, "It's time for dinner." I wouldn't respond for an hour. I would tell myself, "Once I finish this up, I'll come." I'd stay up until 4 a.m. Appreciating nature helped It started to become miserable, and I was desperate to break the addiction. It was detrimental to my life, and I committed myself to stopping. Well, I tried to. I quit my job in 2019 and did the Camino de Santiago in Spain. Being off screens and in nature helped, but I'd fall into old habits. Once I was done with the hike, I'd get on my phone in the car. McHenry stays in the moment by going to the gym every day. Courtesy of Tom McHenry The next few years were a constant battle as I went in and out of sobriety. Luckily, I had the support of my family. At one point, I lived in my brother's basement because he was trying to help however he could. I found out about two 12-step programs in the spring of 2025: Internet and Technology Addicts Anonymous (ITAA) and Media Addicts Anonymous. I started putting down my phone It was the breakthrough I needed. I would attend recovery meetings with people in the same situation. I could talk to them about being addicted to YouTube , for example, and they understood exactly what I was saying. The connection broke the shame and isolation. I started putting down my phone, coming back to real life, and socializing again. My sober date is 6/7/25, so I'm celebrating 17 months of not checking my phone seven days a week. I will now only look at it for an hour or two on Mondays. I'll respond to text messages or calls I've gotten over the week. I still need my phone to get paid for my current job in mental health, and there's two-factor authentication for certain things like my taxes. McHenry practices cold plunging to focus his mind. Courtesy of Tom McHenry On Mondays, I'll write a list of things I need to do and work through it. It usually ends up being a busy day for me, but I've learned to only use my phone for essentials. Still, I haven't completely turned my back on technology. I check my email on my laptop daily and use it to play video games with my friends strictly once a week. I like to cold plunge The other factors in my recovery are nature, meditation, pickleball, and general fitness. I can spend hours at my Life Time gym every day, not necessarily working out but walking around and talking to other people. Best of all, I do a regular cold plunge . It's one of the ways I center myself spiritually. If I ever get a little head crazy, I'll jump into the water or dunk my face. It's a simple thing that really works. It's hard to explain how free I feel now. When I think about my everyday life, I'm grateful that I'm healthy and my mind is clear. I'm enthusiastic again. It used to be that I was at war or something comparable. Now I'm no longer at war. I'm at peace. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: GTA 6 has Logitech telling its 7,000+ employees to log off and game for a day
events.summary: Logitech is offering employees a day off to play "GTA 6." Or "The Legend of Zelda." Or "World of Warcraft." Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images, Rockstar Games A lot of big video games are coming out this month — and some companies are facing a PTO logjam. Logitech has a very different answer: give all 7,000 employees an extra day off to play the games. The video game hardware-making company argues that gaming is actually good for work readiness. Employers are facing down a potential rush of PTO requests amid a packed run of blockbuster video game releases — and Logitech has an unconventional answer. The tech company is giving its more than 7,000 employees an extra day off to play a game of their choice, a new perk it calls "Logi Game Day." Workers can use the day when they choose — but the initiative, announced on Tuesday, comes amid a surprisingly packed month of nostalgic AAA video game releases . Last week, Blizzard Entertainment, owned by Microsoft, launched "World of Warcraft: Forever," a day before Nintendo published "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time." That's all ahead of the release of "Grand Theft Auto 6," the most anticipated video game in years, debuting on November 19, roughly 13 years after the franchise's runaway hit, "GTA 5." Logitech isn't the only company that's turning major game releases into an extra holiday: UK-based Raptor PR recently told Business Insider that they've given their nine-person team an extra day off for gaming, and the US Army's 9th brigade engineer battalion in Georgia went viral for offering a four-day pass for reenlistees to boot up their consoles. View this post on Instagram A post shared by U.S Army WTF! Moments (@usawtfm) Logitech, which builds some gaming hardware , is among the largest corporate employers to offer time off tied to video game releases. The company says it benefits when its workers disappear into Vice City , Kalimdor, or Hyrule for a day: it cites company-commissioned surveys where gamers said playing builds real-world confidence. "We believe that the time employees spend playing will enhance the time they spend working," Robin Piispanen, the general manager of the tech company's gaming brand, told Business Insider. "We know excellence doesn't come from constant grinding. It comes from having space to recharge and have fun." Piispanen, himself a former competitive gamer, is set to host a community streaming event at the company's San Jose headquarters on the day of "GTA 6's" release. Game day will transport Logitech employees into a bunch of virtual worlds. "With 'World of Warcraft: Forever' just launching, my spouse convinced me to jump in with him," Heath Cleveland, the company's manager of marketing analytics and insights, said about his video gaming day off. "There's definitely a steep learning curve, but with some extra time on my hands, I'm ready to dive in and hone my skills." events.summary: A bipartisan 82% majority of Americans think that prediction markets should be regulated as gambling products instead of financial ones, a poll conducted by Qualtrics on behalf of the American Gaming Association found. Jim Jordan’s election as minority leader, given the Ohio Republican has few relationships across the aisle — but next year, they might not have to work with him much. Republicans’ procedural hijinks on a veterans benefits bill this week won’t help cross-party ties: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark registered her objections with Republicans but was rebuffed about reversing course, though that courtesy has typically been extended to the House minority, according to a person familiar with the situation. — Nicholas Wu

events.title: Microsoft struggles to restore services as outage hits companies and governments worldwide
events.summary: Microsoft is dealing with a major outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams HONG KONG -- From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue. Microsoft said in an update Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.” The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.” Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Roughly 130,000 users from dozens of countries Downdetector reported problems on outage tracker with accessing Outlook on Thursday although new reports have since fallen from that peak. A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control. Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue. Its most recent post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution. “We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote. In a more recent update Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.” U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage. In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024. Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption. "They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney. In July 2024, a massive global tech outage grounded flights, disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers, with Texas-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike blaming a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer machines. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts could not receive updates from their U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted. Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement. IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected. Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue. The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses. In Japan , Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that they were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said. OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

events.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
events.summary: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.   The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.  The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors. “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.” The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.) Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again. Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights. Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that. Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low . The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference . “This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.” This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. events.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
events.summary: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats. In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones. Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next. Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

events.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
events.summary: The Vineyard Wind farm off the coast of Massachusetts in May Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.  Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea. He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast. Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.  The company never came. Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Then-President Joe Biden gave a speech at Brayton Point in Somerset, Massachusetts, in 2022. Four years later, the promised factory has been canceled. Prysmian Caleb Kenna for ProPublica An architectural rendering of plans for an offshore wind cable factory on Brayton Point, compared with a 2026 photograph of the same area. A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.  In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out. Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Union members worked for three years assembling turbines on New Bedford’s waterfront. The wind developer that planned to use the port facility next has instead delayed its project indefinitely. Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.  ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts. James Estrin/The New York Times/Redux Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light A factory that made turbine components on Providence’s waterfront is now sitting empty. Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views. But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction , further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.  The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.  At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”  The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”  Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms. Read More About On-the-Ground Impacts From Our Partners The Connecticut Mirror: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for Connecticut. Trump scuttled the plan. The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying up Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertain. As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.  In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry. Wind turbine components are stored at the State Pier in New London, waiting to be loaded onto installation vessels en route to Danish wind developer Ørsted’s offshore wind farms. The last of three consecutive projects is expected to be completed next year, but no others are fully permitted. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore. “I think the future just looked limitless, ” said New London Mayor Michael Passero. Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt. New London Mayor Michael Passero in front of the New London State Pier. Danish wind developer Ørsted is currently using the pier as a staging area for its offshore wind projects, but no tenants are lined up once that work is completed. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.   “They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.  Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunit

A global outage for Microsoft web services disrupted email accounts and some other applications worldwide but appeared to have scant direct impact on markets. Microsoft said in an update Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. events.title: The AI boom will survive without Jensen Huang, but there's a $500 billion funding hole to fill
events.summary: The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook. Why it matters : With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia. But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder. The big picture : The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons: 1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain. At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer. The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI , as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever. AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days , compared with six to 12 months in the past. 2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales. Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access. Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI. Reality check : Alternative chips and leaps forward in software won't solve the near-term computing crunch that all the big players in AI are facing. Nvidia's chips remain the most sought-after because they are the most widely supported, making them critical for the industry's smaller players and important for the big companies who need maximum efficiency out of each data center they build. There are two reasons a strong Nvidia still remains essential: 1. Finance - The company's checkbook will be far more difficult to replicate than its computing power. Nvidia has made $530 billion of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees , including to buy memory and backstops for data centers and certain companies building them, according to data firm SemiAnalysis. Smaller cloud providers, often called neoclouds, as well as a vast array of startups all over the world, have lost perhaps their most enthusiastic champion . Nvidia will remain a formidable competitor, but it will almost certainly become less aggressive about startup funding, acquisitions and backstops, tempering its efforts to spread exposure among institutional investors in ways that some critics said resembled the mortgage bubble. 2. Open models - Nvidia has been the most enthusiastic funder and champion of the Western open-model ecosystem—giving developers cheaper alternatives to the expensive offerings from frontier AI companies. Its pending acquisition of Hugging Face , licensing agreement with model-developer Poolside, backing of Reflection and development of the Nemotron family of open models extend well beyond chip sales. Without Nvidia, it's not clear whether the U.S. will be able to develop open-weight alternatives to China, since many don't have a clear or easy path to financial returns given that such systems are often free to download. What we're watching : Whether the industry's growing freedom to choose its chips can compensate for an Nvidia that is suddenly much less willing to finance its ambitions. Bottom line: Huang's departure won't derail America's AI ambitions. But it leaves a hole in the ecosystem that will be harder to fill than any shortage of Nvidia chips.

events.title: ‘I’m in the trenches’: The payroll processor on her own front line
events.summary: The Signal Insight Jennifer Morgan, who became the first female leader of a DAX-listed company when Germany’s SAP named her co-CEO in 2019, now leads a US business processing $1 trillion of payroll data each year. UKG, formed in 2020 from the merger of Ultimate Software and Kronos, provides HR services and workforce management technology to organizations employing 65 million hourly and frontline workers in industries including retail, healthcare, and manufacturing. Since arriving in 2024 from Blackstone, one of UKG’s private equity owners, Morgan says she has not seen those jobs become much more vulnerable to AI disruption. But she has struck partnerships with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, seeing opportunities to “give the worker agency” with AI-powered tools that let them plan schedules around their childcare, or volunteer for overtime when they need to earn extra money. Morgan’s pitch to employers is that pairing these tools with data-driven insights into wages, absenteeism, and inefficiencies in schedules can cut billions of dollars from corporate America’s $1 trillion-a-year attrition bill. Replacing just one hourly worker costs the average employer about $5,000, she notes. Morgan’s strategy is to reposition UKG from a provider of administrative support tools to a “workforce intelligence hub” that uses shift data to inform operational decisions in real time. She has overhauled the company’s leadership, replacing about 80% of her direct reports and 40% of the tier below them, to bring in more people with experience of operating at the scale and speed this moment demands. But she has also tried to stay on her own front line, spending a quarter of her time with customers, which include Marriott, the Mayo Clinic, PepsiCo, and the Transportation Security Administration. And she says that sharing their positive and critical feedback with her staff has been equally important. Here’s how she sees AI bridging the gap between companies and the workers who are often furthest from their headquarters, yet closest to their customers. Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson: What will AI mean for frontline workers? Jennifer Morgan: Think about a world where that frontline worker on their app can say, “I need to make $500 extra between now and the end of the month. What are the shifts that are available for me to do this? Oh, and by the way, here’s my school schedule; schedule around this.” Or workers who need access to their pay before [their] paycheck arrives; one of our customers [who offered early “earned wage access” saw] the retention for people who took advantage of that was 14% higher. AI gives the worker agency because AI can be a better advocate for what they need. That’s what’s been missing. If you think about the person who’s trying to put the schedule together, they don’t have all that texture, and they definitely don’t have it in real time. So that’s where the expectation gap gets bigger and bigger, because what the worker needs and what the operation needs are different. Do you think you have better insight into what’s happening in companies’ workforces than they do? Yes. Whether we’re talking to Pepsi or T-Mobile, we can show them what we see happening. We can talk to them about their overtime, their wages, absenteeism, and the attrition that’s happening because people don’t get the hours that they want. If they get too many [hours], or they don’t get enough, they leave. That information is ready in real time, [but] companies look at that after the fact. What does private capital bring to this very expensive and uncertain AI transition? I remember when I read my first investment memo at Blackstone for a company we were looking at, my first reaction was, “I wish somebody had given this to me when I was the co-CEO of SAP.” Having somebody who can unemotionally look at your business and tell you all the opportunities, all the great things, and all the things that you can address to make it even better, as a leader, that’s what you’re looking for: Just take out the filter and give it to me. I love having a board with both investors and operators, because operators understand all the nuance and all of the intended and unintended consequences of what could happen if I do X or if I do Y. Investors tend to look at things very unemotionally, factually. And it helps bring a level of focus. Do you ever see tension between that left-brain and right-brain way of looking at the business? Absolutely. I remember, again, my first investment committee meeting at Blackstone. We were talking about [investing in] this one company and all of a sudden there was this strong intellectual debate. I’m thinking to myself, “Oh my goodness, they don’t like this company.” But it was really about just getting to the right answer. There were no corporate politics. It was just that intellectual honesty about what this was, what we could do, what you needed to believe in order to get to where everybody wanted to go. So that is really positive when you’re able to have those discussions, and make change at a pace that I don’t have to constantly worry about the [next quarterly earnings]. Because the amount of change that we’re making to the organization is a lot, and the longer you wait to react, the more you have to catch up, and the change is twice as much and twice as hard. UKG was put together from two different companies. To what extent has your job been about defining a single culture? [I was asked] as a new CEO, “Jen, are we going to be a product-led culture? Are we going to be a sales-led culture? How are we going to define it?” I said we’ve got to be customer-led. To be a winning culture, you’ve got to understand what’s going on outside the four walls. And so I spend a lot of my time sharing what I’m hearing. I’m used to being in bigger companies, and when you’re talking to tens of thousands of employees, you don’t tend to just go out there unscripted, off-the-cuff. But because things are changing so fast, people don’t want [a script], they want perfect imperfection. Like, “Give it to me straight. I don’t want to feel like you’re giving me the glossy. Tell me the challenges. Tell me what’s happening.” The more that I bring the outside in, the more that becomes a common language [across] product, engineering, marketing, and sales. And one of our challenges as you continue to grow, is you have to connect all those dots. Leaders today have to be on their own front line. As a CEO, I’m trying to find the most unfiltered, real-time feedback and people who are going to give it to me straight. CEOs get concise, need-to-know briefings. But the nuance really matters. How do you spend your time, between customers, employees, and your top team? I try to spend at least a quarter of my time with customers, because that contextualizes everything. So if I look at something that’s not going well in a company, you can usually find the answers by going out and hearing from your customers. My biggest fear is to have one

events.title: With every rainfall, Gaza risks losing access to power and healthcare
events.summary: Heavy rains flood shelters, damage solar power systems and threat essential healthcare services. Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – As the rain intensified, 65-year-old Abu Sajed rushed to place buckets and pots strategically around his modest room in central Gaza. The stone walls and tarpaulin roof offered little protection to his makeshift home, east of Salah al-Din Street, near the “Yellow Line” in Bureij refugee camp. “We could no longer stay in bed because of the heavy rain. We moved to chairs in the only part of the room the water had not reached and waited for the rain to stop,” said Abu Sajed, who has diabetes. He searched for his blood glucose monitor in the darkness. But it was soaked and no longer working. His family’s solar power system, used for lighting and charging phones, was also damaged. Water also flooded his daughter’s neighbouring tent, soaking her clothes and belongings and destroying the inverter connected to her solar system. “I did not know what to do. I could not protect myself or my family. Even going to the toilet had become difficult because of all the water,” he said. His ordeal continued after the rain stopped. The following morning, as he tried to leave the room, his foot slipped on the muddy floor and he fell. Because of poor health, he could not get up alone. His wife and daughter struggled to lift him. “I felt helpless and exhausted,” he said. Recent rainfall has added to Gaza’s suffering, and due to Israel’s siege, most people lack adequate housing. But the impact extends beyond flooded shelters and damaged belongings. It also threatens the energy sources residents depend on, particularly amid Gaza’s continuing electricity crisis. In a room inside a damaged building in northern Gaza, Mohammed al-Hour uses sunlight to charge people’s phones through his solar power system. But rainwater also seeps through the cracked walls and damaged ceiling of his room. “People come to me asking to charge their phones, even for a little while, so they can have lighting at night. But when the clouds persist and the sun disappears, it becomes difficult,” he said. “Whether you live in a tent or a house, rainwater will find its way in. The bombardment has destroyed almost everything.” Companies trying to maintain electricity services are struggling with the damage. Despite preparations in advance of the winter, Abu Zayed Electricity Company could not prevent water from entering several facilities, damaging equipment and causing generators to malfunction. It temporarily suspended services at affected branches over fears of electrical contact and short circuits. Aya Shaheen, the company’s general manager, said distribution panels and electricity metres were covered with plastic sheeting and tarpaulins, exposed wires were insulated, and municipalities were asked to pump out accumulated water. But the damage exceeded available resources. “However much we try to prepare and protect our equipment, we continue to face major obstacles because of the extensive destruction of infrastructure,” she said. “Municipalities are also dealing with enormous pressure. Flooded tents need urgent intervention, so they cannot respond to every request for assistance.” Water entered one of the company’s sites, even though its generators are housed in specially equipped prefabricated structures, Shaheen said. Restoring services and repairing equipment can take hours or days, depending on the damage. According to UNICEF, the recent rainfall affected more than 106,000 people. About 950,000 displaced people live in flood-prone areas, including 400,000 in particularly high-risk locations. A joint assessment by the World Bank, the United Nations and the European Union estimated that 80 percent of electricity generation and distribution assets had been destroyed or rendered inoperable during the war. This has severely limited access to reliable electricity, particularly as solar generation declines on cloudy days and equipment becomes vulnerable to water damage. Mohammed Abu Khaled, an engineer specialising in energy systems and equipment used in the health sector, warns that rainwater entering solar systems can damage batteries and inverters, causing short circuits and corrosion of electronic circuits. “The inverter is the weakest link and the component most likely to fail. It contains sensitive electronic circuit boards that are often not adequately protected against water,” he said. He estimated that malfunctions in household solar systems and those used in displacement camps increased by more than 40 to 50 percent following recent rainfall. Repairing a damaged inverter can cost between $200 and $500, while families may have to replace an entire battery if it is damaged. Solar panels’ electricity output can also drop by 60 to 80 percent on cloudy days, slowing battery charging and reducing the hours households can rely on stored electricity, he added.

events.title: Nvidia scandal: Howard Lutnick under pressure over alleged lack of action
events.summary: US commerce secretary faces sack as warnings emerge about alleged Chinese spy’s ties to Jensen Huang and delays in adding Megaspeed to trade blacklist Analysis: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached? One of Donald Trump’s top lieutenants reportedly could soon be fired, as criticism mounts over commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal . Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer, Colette Kress , after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Pressure is mounting on Lutnick after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration . Lutnick is scheduled to testify alongside the ousted Nvidia chief before Congress in the coming weeks. He is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration. White House officials are now discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported. John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”. Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls” and that: “Heads should roll.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang. “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News. Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge . The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported . On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia. Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, because: “Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.” The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded. Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters. House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China . Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them. “The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“ Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters .
