events.title: Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why?
events.summary: Outlook, Teams and Copilot remain disrupted in 74 countries as Microsoft reports ‘marginal success’ in fixing outage. Microsoft says it has had only “marginal success” in restoring its most widely used workplace services, more than 12 hours after a global outage knocked out Outlook and disrupted Teams and Copilot for users in 74 countries. In a statement on its service health page early on Friday, the company said it was monitoring activity across regions to assess server status and find ways to improve capacity. “This includes reviewing server performance and confirming that developed patches have been applied and working as intended after infrastructure reboots are completed,” it said. list 1 of 3 IBM’s biggest division ends most US foreign worker sponsorships list 2 of 3 Ireland fears undersea cables face growing threat from ‘malign actors’ list 3 of 3 Microsoft working ‘urgently’ to fix outages Here is what we know about the outage, what caused it and when services might return. Problems with Microsoft products began at about 16:00 GMT on Thursday, when users began reporting that they could not access Outlook, its email platform. Within about an hour, the outage tracker Downdetector had logged reports from 74 countries and territories. Microsoft first said it was investigating problems in the Americas, but later confirmed that users in any region could be affected. It said the affected infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which was likely contributing to the connectivity errors. The company later said a number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, and that the elevated load had not been caused by an increase in traffic. The disruption dragged on through the US working day and into the night. By Friday morning in Europe, it had still not been resolved, and servers Microsoft had restored were failing again. “I don’t think it’s unprecedented. I mean, the scale is impressive,” Rupert Goodwins, a technology analyst and journalist, told Al Jazeera. “It’s very embarrassing for Microsoft and really, really annoying for the rest of us.” Microsoft has not confirmed the number of users who have been affected. Data from Downdetector, through which users can report problems with online services, gives a partial picture, however. At about 07:00 GMT on Friday, it had received at least 43,000 reports of problems with Outlook from users in 72 countries. The true number is likely far higher, since the figure only counts people who visit the site to report an issue. “There’s about 430 million people who use Microsoft services,” said Walter Pasquarelli, an affiliate researcher at the Bennett School of Public Policy at the University of Cambridge and an AI specialist. “What we do know so far is that this is first and foremost a communication risk.” Government systems in Singapore and Japan have been disrupted, as have communications at the Supreme Court of the Philippines. In Australia, the country’s spy agency and federal police were among the organisations hit. Which Microsoft services have been affected? Outlook has been hit hardest. Users have reported being unable to open their mailboxes via the web, the app or through mobile devices, and many emails which do go through have arrived late. Other services have been partly disrupted. The disruption has spread beyond Microsoft’s own products, hitting integrations which other companies, including the AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic, rely on. “For the most part, we don’t really think about it too much, a little bit like our health, that we kind of take these tools for granted until they’re suddenly down or they’re not there,” Pasquarelli said. What caused the Microsoft outage? Was it a cyberattack? Microsoft has not published a root cause but said the outage was not the result of a cyberattack. On Friday, it was rolling back a network change, but did not say if that change was to blame for the problems. “We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said in a post on X late on Thursday. Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft had also told him it did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack. “They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told a news conference in Sydney. Goodwins said elevated load usually comes from one of two places. “Either there’s an external attack and some aggressor is trying to put lots and lots of artificial loads on the system to break it,” he said. “Microsoft says that hasn’t happened, and I believe them because there are ways to mitigate that.” The other common cause, he said, is a faulty update to internal systems.

events.title: Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users
events.summary: Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting. Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment. Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use. In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent. The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP. Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients. In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer . Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here . In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request . It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months. However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply. Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year. The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy. One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app. No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it. East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response . In its FoI response , Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements. Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app. In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP. Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website. Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million. Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract , but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology. Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

events.title: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?
events.summary: Installing a heat pump is a big decision Floorplans. Air duct diagrams. Heat pump specifications. Most people in the market for a new heating system probably don't want to think about this level of detail. But, perhaps surprisingly, some do want to think about those things. In extreme depth. Every day, roughly 150 new users sign up to an app called Cool Calc, which works out the heat requirements of properties in the US. Just over one third of those new users are not tradespeople but private homeowners, says founder and chief executive Bill Fiore. When choosing a heating system, people can find themselves bombarded with information – how powerful a heat pump do they need, for example? It isn't always easy to take a tradesperson at their word. "As an overall trend, we are seeing homeowners be more informed," explains Fiore. "They want to do a calculation on their own." Cool Calc is used by tradespeople and homeowners to work out heat loss A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. It's worked out room by room and is a key part of designing an efficient heating system. This estimate is especially important to get right when installing a heat pump, which is sized fairly precisely, according to the projected heat loss. Should that calculation be off, the heat pump will likely perform poorly. You could be left with an underpowered device that struggles to warm your property, for example. Given the costs involved, homeowners are often anxious to ensure installers avoid such mistakes. Certain new technologies are not, for the moment, helping, adds Fiore. "People are going to AI and they're getting a lot of misinformation because it's not backed by anything credible," he says. Cool Calc is planning to integrate with AI chatbots to try and improve the quality of the advice they spew out. It is probably a good idea to be cautious about your new heating system's design, says Kevin Kircher at Purdue University. He and colleagues recently conducted a study, yet to be published, examining the heat loss calculations provided by tradespeople to roughly 75 US homeowners. "We were surprised," says Kircher. "The heat loss calculations often led to overestimating the design heat loads by a factor of two or more." That would result in oversized systems that use much more power than necessary. Not only that, some people reported charges of more than $1,000 (£745) – and in one case as much as $2,500 – just for a heat loss survey, adds Kircher. Besides using excessive amounts of energy, an oversized heating system can also feel uncomfortable, says Dan Dempsey, a former senior engineering fellow for a major heating and cooling provider in the US. Dempsey, who took part in Kircher and his colleagues' study, lives in Indiana. He says it is his retirement hobby to monitor the performance of heating and cooling systems in the homes of friends and family members, by analysing data from their smart thermostats. "I spent five years manually downloading everything, every week," he says. He points out that oversized systems tend to cycle a lot, meaning they switch on and off again in quick succession. This leads to discernible swings in temperature: rooms that fail to remain at their target temperature of, say, 20C, but rather fluctuate, which feels uncomfortable, says Dempsey. For people seeking a better understanding of their home's heat loss, various free or partially free apps, including Cool Calc and AutoHVAC, are available. There are options for UK homeowners, too, such as web app Heatpunk. Heat loss apps help drive business to renewable energy firms says Andy Rankin Many things can influence the heat loss figure, including the amount of insulation in your home, whether the building has double or triple glazing, and also the size of your radiators. Heatpunk allows people to draw a floor plan of their home and input data about the property in order to estimate its performance. Thousands of people use it every month, mostly professional installers, says Andy Rankin, founder and managing director of Midsummer Energy. The web app also suggests specific heat pump models for each property, based on the results of the calculation. Naturally, these are models available through Midsummer Energy. "It's been a very effective marketing tool," says Rankin. Dwellow, another company that offers heat pump installations in the UK, is keen to follow suit. The firm recently launched its own heat loss estimator. While professional heat loss calculations remain essential, getting people to do their own "self surveys" first could ultimately reduce how much time professional heating engineers must spend analysing properties says Ian Mclaren, Dwellow's co-founder and director. "Going into a home and just being able to check the information rather than start from scratch could turn a survey into a half-hour trip – far more efficient and less costly," says Mclaren.

events.title: Microsoft outage to have 'cascading impact' on businesses
events.summary: The continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools will have a “cascading” effect on businesses, with the financial impact increasing the longer it stretches, experts say. Microsoft 365 tools Exchange Online and Outlook were affected, with Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot also likely to face an impact from the interruption that began on Thursday. The company is still working on fixing it. “The continuing outage of Microsoft’s collaboration tools, especially emails and scheduling, will not only impact communications, but also have a cascading impact on decision-making, revenue and service delivery,” said Saurabh Verma, vice president, ICT growth advisory at consultancy Frost & Sullivan. “The actual dollar impact or revenue loss would go up with every passing minute, as millions of organisations across critical and non-critical sectors are deeply embedded with MS 365 suite.” Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector, which monitors internet disruption. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector. Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25,… pic.twitter.com/7FQ4dDsfbm — Downdetector (@downdetector) November 12, 2026 The financial consequences from such an outage are significant, said Morey Haber, chief security adviser at BeyondTrust. “Lost productivity, interrupted transactions, missed revenue and recovery expenses can quickly accumulate into millions of dollars across affected organisations,” he said. “While Microsoft may offer contractual service credits under applicable Service Level Agreements (SLAs), these typically represent a fraction of actual business losses. Credits generally offset future service charges rather than compensate customers for lost revenue, operational disruption, or reputational damage.” The outage may also affect software as a service (SaaS) tools using MS’s 365 application programming interface (APIs), which refers to rules that allow software apps to communicate, Mr Verma said. “With MS having a significant market share in collab tools, there is no escaping and second solution to it. No product in today’s age and time is immune to such outage,” he added. The outage “exposes the severe operational fragility of single-vendor cloud concentration” across global businesses and financial markets, said Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. It has caused a considerable amount of disruption to financial workflows, although on the capital markets side, the core stock exchange matching engines are largely unaffected, he added. The Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange said on Friday that some of its electronic services may be temporarily unavailable, while email notifications may take longer than usual to reach users. The exchange said it is closely monitoring developments and working to restore all services and operations to normal as soon as possible. “Institutional execution desks lost their primary email channels during a turbulent week of trading and were therefore forced to revert to phone calls and WhatsApp to confirm settlements,” Mr Valecha said. Richemont, the Swiss luxury group that owns Cartier, was forced to delay its results. On the banking side, payment clearing was not affected at all, although payment networks and banking portals that required a secondary login were all having problems, he added. Technology disruptions have been common in recent years, as digital usage continues to soar. In October last year, Microsoft's Azure portal went down, affecting hundreds of thousands of people trying to access apps, games, websites and other services. That came in the same month that an outage of Amazon Web Services, which lasted for about 15 hours, disrupted several AWS-hosted services and platforms. In June this year, several web platforms, apps and internet services including X , Zoom, Reddit, Canva, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Teams , Fortnite and Discord also experienced significant disruption. Managing outages The lesson from the outage isn't that Microsoft is unreliable, but that every cloud platform will have a bad day, said Samir Elabed, cybersecurity engineer and founder of SECyber. For companies to reduce the impact, they must have an out-of-band communication channel agreed in advance, such as a phone tree, SMS or a secondary messaging app, so staff aren't left guessing, he said. “Keep your business continuity and incident-response plans somewhere you can actually reach during an outage. If your continuity plan lives in SharePoint, you don't really have one,” he said. It is also important to identify the most critical processes, such as payroll, customer service and sales, and decide on a manual or alternative workaround for each, he said. “Run tabletop exercises that treat a major cloud outage as a realistic scenario, not a remote one,” he added. For finance companies to mitigate risk, they must use out-of-band communication channels such as independent messaging platforms, dedicated voice lines and secondary SMS modes so trading desks and crisis teams can co-ordinate immediately when primary email services go dark, Mr Valecha said. “This is exactly what desks in Singapore have used,” he added. “Decoupled identity and access management can also be explored. If a single vendor handles both email and single sign-on, an outage locks staff out of third-party applications that are otherwise running normally.” Also, although the Microsoft outage is not a cybersecurity issue, hostile actors could be looking to take advantage of those affected, offering a resolution or assurances, said Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at Sophos Counter Threat Unit. “People should exercise caution when receiving emails, texts or calls purporting to be from Microsoft or other affected businesses, particularly banks or shops,” he said. “Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email.” Mr Elabed agreed, calling an outage “a gift to attackers”, with phishing emails typically sent within hours. “Businesses should send a short message to staff early on, through a channel that isn't affected, explaining that the issue sits with the provider, that IT will never ask them to re-enter passwords to fix it and how to report anything suspicious.” He called for phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and conditional access, and urged IT teams to review sign-in logs for unusual activity even after services are restored. “The attack often comes after the outage, not during it,” he added. events.title: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed
events.summary: At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law. (Source: Bloomberg)

The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Bank of Thailand today published the findings from their collaboration on foreign exchange (FX) settlement under Project Meridian FX APAC. footnote [1] The project showed that synchronisation – a service that coordinates movements of central bank money – could be one approach to supporting interoperability across wholesale settlement environments built on different technologies and operating models. This marks significant progress in making cross-border FX transactions safer and more efficient, and supporting interoperability as different forms of money evolve in different ways. In light of the Bank of England’s plans to launch a live synchronisation interface in 2028, footnote [2] the findings provide valuable insight into how the approach could be developed into a live service. Building on the earlier work, footnote [3] Project Meridian FX APAC tested payment-versus-payment FX settlement footnote [4] and multilateral net FX across the three central banks’ test environments, spanning both Real-Time Gross Settlement and Distributed Ledger Technology-based settlement systems. The project encompassed a wider range of currencies, technologies, infrastructures and time zones. Partior, the project’s delivery partner, developed, integrated and tested the Synchronisation Operator footnote [5] prototype for the trial. The trial demonstrated that synchronised settlement can be achieved across central bank systems with different technologies and capabilities, while identifying the requirements and trade-offs involved. They also demonstrated how multilateral net FX settlement can support banks in using their liquidity more efficiently by netting payments against each other. The project also examined the legal, regulatory and oversight considerations for applying synchronised FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. The analysis was informed by perspectives from the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, who participated as observer central banks. The project’s findings and insights are published across three complementary reports: Introduction and Executive Summary , Technical Report , and Policy Report . Together, they set out the experimental results, key technical findings and policy considerations. These results provide insights for further exploration of synchronisation as a means of enabling safer and more efficient FX settlement across diverse wholesale settlement systems. Future work could involve extending the existing approach to additional jurisdictions and industry participants, a wider range of currencies and transaction scenarios, and further consider the legal arrangements needed in practice. Tom Mutton, Executive Director of Payments, Innovation and Fintech at the Bank of England, said, ‘Innovation has the greatest impact when it addresses real world challenges. Project Meridian FX APAC provides practical evidence of how synchronised settlement could help reduce risk and improve efficiency in cross-border FX transactions. events.title: Nvidia’s turmoil is prompting a rotation across chip stocks. Here's what we know
events.summary: Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its rivals. AMD to Broadcom and even TSMC sees greater investor interest as they rotate out of Nvidia. Nvidia 's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated. From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC , chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead. "What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management. That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy . Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks. Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil. "Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC. Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit , irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme. The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said. Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively. Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis. Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals. That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production. The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers. "If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said. The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market. Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom. Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit. The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said. For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors. Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery. He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis. The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

events.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Elon Musk says hiring him would be ‘an honor’
events.summary: Before Nvidia publicly announced Jensen Huang’s departure, Elon Musk said he wanted to hire him. “That would be an honor,” Musk wrote on X Wednesday evening, responding to a post that read: “Elon please hire Jensen.” The exchange followed a Wall Street Journal report that Nvidia’s board was preparing to oust its cofounder, according to Reuters . By Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and a director, effective immediately. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, and longtime director Harvey Jones becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. The exit removes the cofounder who built Nvidia into the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom and No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500. Investors had already felt it: Nvidia lost $450 billion in market value in the days after Huang admitted to an affair, Fortune reported. That affair was with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner . U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe she was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence, which Beijing denies. Huang publicly apologized for his infidelity on Sunday. Nvidia’s board initially stood by him, saying on Sunday , “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team,” even as it announced an independent investigation. It said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised. But on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him. The board reportedly met later that day to decide his future. After the resignation was announced Thursday, Reuters reported that Huang had also had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia and Huang have not confirmed the report. Musk’s five-word response did not specify a job, a company, or whether the two had discussed working together. But it suggested that losing the job Huang held for 33 years had not entirely spoiled his employment prospects. Musk and Huang go back years Musk once “begged” for Huang’s chips. In September 2024 , Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison recounted a dinner with Musk and Huang at Nobu in Palo Alto, where he and Musk found themselves pleading for more of Nvidia’s coveted graphics processing units. “I would describe the dinner as Oracle—me and Elon begging Jensen for GPUs,” Ellison said. “Please take our money. Please take our money. By the way, I got dinner. No, no, take more of it. We need you to take more of our money please.” Musk has since made his admiration public on several occasions. “I am a huge admirer of Nvidia and Jensen btw. That market cap is well-deserved,” he wrote on X in March , adding that SpaceX AI and Tesla expected to keep buying Nvidia chips at scale. The relationship extends beyond business. In May, a user posted photographs of the pair taken a decade apart with the caption: “The most important thing in life is having true friends.” Musk reposted it with one word : “True.” In October, he struck a more personal note on X : “Old friends are the best friends. Jensen rocks.” The post accompanied a clip of Huang discussing the companies’ collaboration on computing infrastructure for space. The admiration goes both ways. Huang said Musk was “working on exactly the right things,” Fortune reported in January 2025 , and later that year called Musk “the ultimate GPU,” comparing his ability to juggle complex information to the chips Nvidia sells. Tech and finance leaders lined up behind Huang Musk is far from the only prominent business figure who thinks Huang still has something to offer. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney urged Nvidia’s board to retain him on X , comparing a potential dismissal to “ Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.” He credited Huang with driving successive eras of technology, from gaming graphics to AI supercomputers. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman took a more personal approach , arguing that even exceptional people make mistakes and urging support for Huang and his family. Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire criticized Huang’s conduct but described him as “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Musk endorsed Maguire’s post with a brief reply: “I agree.” Others who publicly backed Huang include Anduril founder Palmer Luckey , Binance founder Changpeng Zhao , and 37signals CTO David Heinemeier Hansson . The support offers a glimpse of the network Huang could draw on for whatever comes next. Congress comes before Huang’s next job For now, that next chapter remains unannounced. Musk’s public welcome has not come with a job description, and it is unclear whether Huang intends to join another company, start something new, or step away from running one. His departure also does not resolve Nvidia’s internal investigation or the FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang , which President Donald Trump has said is underway. Financially, Huang has plenty of room to weigh his options. He still holds about 3.6% of Nvidia, making him its fourth-largest shareholder, according to Reuters . His net worth fell roughly $10 billion this week to about $145 billion, Fortune reported , knocking him out of the world’s 10 richest people. A divorce could cut that net worth substantially. His wife, Lori Huang, could be entitled to half, depending on any marital agreements and which assets qualify as separate property, Forbes reported . Neither has publicly announced plans to divorce. Before any new role, Huang has a date on Capitol Hill. He has agreed to testify before lawmakers, with an appearance expected before Thanksgiving, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said, according to Bloomberg . Mast has said Huang has “very serious questions to answer.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Innovations A wave of announcements this week, including several from SEMICON Europa and electronica 2026 in Munich, highlighted advances in semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, automotive chips, and AI hardware. Manufacturing and test Infineon reported an industry-first milestone in 300mm silicon carbide manufacturing , fabricating functional power devices at its Villach, Austria fab using existing silicon processing equipment. The larger wafers can accommodate 2.3 times as many chips as 200mm wafers, potentially lowering manufacturing costs for automotive, industrial, and AI data center power devices. imec completed baseline process flows for its NanoIC silicon-interposer platform , including TSVs and multiple routing layers for chiplet and 3D integration. A silicon-interposer PDK is planned for early 2027. Chips and systems AMD introduced its 6th-gen EPYC server and embedded processors, including models for semiconductor ATE; an AI GPU with 288GB of HBM4; and tamper-resistant FPGAs for security-critical systems. Arm introduced the Cortex-M42 processor to bring ML and DSP capabilities to cost- and area-constrained intelligent endpoints in a compact, AHB-based design. Google added two new 8th-gen TPU systems : TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and higher rack compute density, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. TPU 8tx pairs Google accelerators with AMD EPYC CPU hosts. Fallout continues after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation : Congressional investigations: Senators are seeking the preservation of records related to chip exports and Megaspeed, calling for tighter AI-chip export controls . House committee leaders also requested a closed-door Nov. 18 briefing from Huang. Inaction questioned: President Trump authorized tougher action on suspected Nvidia chip diversion three times this year, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted over concerns that tighter restrictions could escalate trade tensions with China , Axios reported. Separately, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter contacted a senior Commerce Dept. official in late summer 2025 seeking information about the Megaspeed chip-smuggling investigation, indicating Nvidia’s legal leadership was aware of the investigation before the current scandal. The company subsequently characterized its Megaspeed dealings as “ normal .” Circular financing: Nvidia’s web of financial ties across the AI industry is facing fresh scrutiny after Huang’s resignation. The Financial Times says Nvidia made more than 120 investments this year and held or committed about $124B in equity investments by July, raising questions about whether its aggressive dealmaking and financing of companies that buy its chips will continue without him. Policy fallout: The episode has renewed debate over export-control enforcement and Chinese intelligence targeting of U.S. technology companies, with CFR highlighting enforcement gaps and CSET urging scrutiny without overreaction . Deals and funding Siemens plans to acquire Lauterbach , a provider of hardware-assisted debugging and real-time trace tools for embedded software and complex SoCs. The deal is expected to close in H1 2027. Mitsui Chemicals confirmed it will acquire JSR in a transaction valued at approximately ¥1.84T ($11.9B), combining two major Japanese materials suppliers, including JSR’s photoresist and advanced materials businesses. TSMC approved investments of up to $1B in OpenAI and Anthropic , allocating up to $500M for each, plus a separate $500M investment company focused on the semiconductor ecosystem. Fractile raised $720M to develop frontier AI chips that stack DRAM directly on top of logic to speed up output token generation. Memory Samsung Electronics broke ground on a previously announced HBM advanced-packaging facility in Asan, South Korea , accelerating the planned start of production by a year to June 2028. TSMC is reportedly considering 3D DRAM production at Nvidia ’s request, potentially through new capacity or an acquired fab. Still, TSMC said that it remains focused on its core logic foundry business. Vertical Compute and imec expanded their collaboration to integrate magnetic memory directly above 16nm logic . Winbond approved NT$73.1B (US$2.2B) in spending to expand its 300mm memory fab in Kaohsiung, Taiwan . Reports and analysis Lowy Institute estimates U.S. AI data centers have nearly 40 times China’s computing power , with U.S. AI chips providing about 31 times the compute. China, meanwhile, leads in critical-mineral production and downloads of open AI models. CSIS says Chinese rare-earth shipments to the U.S. remain about 75% below pre-restriction levels , despite agreements intended to restore supply. U.S. chipmakers have also faced scandium shortages and delays in obtaining Chinese export licenses. Counterpoint Research says soaring memory prices are driving up smartphone costs , with memory now accounting for 54% of a low-end phone’s bill of materials, up from 20% in Q3 2025. Prices are expected to keep rising through Q1 2027. Chiplet standards and interoperability The UCIe Consortium published UCIe 4.0 , which takes the specification beyond chiplet-level interfaces to the integration of multiple chiplets into an on-package system. New features include an on-package memory link between SoCs and memory logic chiplets, co-optimized link profiles with improved energy efficiency, and enhanced manageability, security, and reliability. ASRA and imec released requirements for interoperable automotive chiplets , covering connectivity, power management, and functional safety. Results Year-over-year revenue change: Applied Materials Q4 up 53% , Infineon Q4 up 19% , Onto Innovation Q3 up 88% , Silicon Labs Q3 up 22% , SMIC Q3 up 34% , and TSMC October revenue up ~60% . events.title: How Novig became the third biggest prediction market site despite launching only months ago
events.summary: Since bursting on the scene two years ago, prediction markets have become one of the buzziest new sectors in finance, pulling in billions of dollars in revenue, and driving daily news headlines. The young industry is dominated by two giants, Kalshi and Polymarket, but numerous other companies are trying to muscle into the field. That includes the sports-focused prediction market Novig, which only launched as a federally regulated prediction market in August, but has already claimed the number three spot by one widely used industry metric. Over the past 30 days, Novig handled $1.8 billion in trading volume on U.S.-regulated exchanges, according to the PM Pulse, a newsletter that tracks prediction market volume using data from research firm Aldrin. That figure is small next to Kalshi’s $33.3 billion and Polymarket U.S.’s $6.3 billion. But it’s about $300 million ahead of Crypto.com, the fourth-place contender, and its volume is up 80% from the previous 30 days. The volume figures don’t account for combos, or multi-game parlays, which Sam Schwartz, who runs the newsletter, says can inflate volume without producing proportionally more revenue for the exchange.  Novig’s ascent is notable given how little money it has raised compared to other prediction markets. Founded in 2021, the company enjoyed modest growth and raised $30 million as it pursued a sweepstakes-based business model that allowed it to operate in certain states. But a shift in the legal landscape led Novig this year to become a federally regulated prediction market, helping it raise a new $75 million Series B round in February at a $500 million valuation. The company is also reportedly raising a new round of capital at a $2 billion valuation, though Novig declined to comment on future fundraises.  While Novig has raised $105 million in total, that figure is dwarfed by Kalshi’s fundraising, which amounts to roughly $3.8 billion across 13 funding rounds, according to Tracxn data, including two $1 billion rounds since May. Polymarket, meanwhile, has raised roughly $3.3 billion across eight rounds, including $1 billion from New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange, and another $1 billion in a round led by Donald Trump Jr.-backed venture capital firm 1789 Capital. “There are very few companies I think outside of AI that have achieved our level of growth in the span of two months,” Novig cofounder and CEO Jacob Fortinsky told Fortune . Novig’s explosive growth, which has seen it swell from 20 to 100 employees this year, is due in no small part to Sydney Sweeney. The actress, who is a part owner of the company, starred in a viral ad campaign called “Just Sports” that made Novig a household name for millions. In the 30 days after the campaign launched in September, Novig says first-time deposits rose 362% and mobile app downloads jumped 261%, compared with the 30 days before, according to internal data the company provided. During the rollout, the app briefly hit No. 1 on the App Store’s top free sports apps chart. Novig’s early success comes at a time when conventional sports betting platforms like DraftKings and FanDuel are diving into the prediction markets industry too, while a host of smaller startups are also fighting to carve out a niche. It has been a difficult race, given how much weight the behemoths pull. Kalshi, which has held the top slot for months, accounts for roughly 64% of trading volume excluding combos over the past 30 days, and Polymarket’s U.S. and DeFi arms together hold about 23%. That leaves just 13% of the market split among the rest of the field, with Novig capturing 3.5% of that—edging out established competitors like Crypto.com and DraftKings’ DKeX platform to claim third place. Why sports only Like other prediction markets, Novig makes the case that it offers sports traders a better deal than conventional betting platforms. The company notes that it runs a peer-to-peer exchange where users trade against each other, not against the house, which gives traders tighter prices and lower costs than traditional sportsbooks and most prediction markets. “That’s the main reason Novig saw growth early as a company—it’s just such a natural draw to the professional and sophisticated users out there… they want to get the best odds possible,” Schwartz explained. Unlike many of its competitors, the company has zeroed in on the most popular event contract category out there: sports. Much like it marketed in its Just Sports campaign, Novig repeatedly emphasizes that it does not offer trades on politics or pop culture, and that its users must be 21 or older—a distinction from Kalshi and Polymarket, which allow 18-year-olds to bet on their platforms.  At first glance, focusing only on sports contracts might seem like a missed opportunity for Novig to capture huge, headline-grabbing volume spikes. When the midterm elections arrived, for instance, trading in politics and election contracts on Kalshi reached $729 million on Election Day alone. Over the full week, elections accounted for more than 70% of Kalshi’s volume growth excluding combos, according to data published by the PM Pulse. All of this, of course, resulted in a wave of free marketing since political news reports frequently cited odds on the platform. But once election week is over, political trading drops off sharply. Schwartz noted that on most other days this year, elections made up less than half of 1% of Kalshi’s daily volume. Sports, on the other hand, are on the calendar nearly every day, and they drive more than 80% of prediction market trading. That steady pace is what Novig is built around. Limits to growth While Novig’s low-fee model has succeeded in drawing sophisticated, high-volume traders, it doesn’t appear to be a major factor when it comes to the average retail bettor. “The majority of users out there are not price sensitive,” Schwartz said. Sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel, along with Kalshi, keep winning customers despite charging more. There is also an ongoing legal battle over the legality of sports-related prediction markets, which is widely expected to land at the Supreme Court next year, and has already led several states to move aggressively against the platforms. So far, state-level restrictions haven’t badly dented growth, but Schwartz said a drawn-out battle could slowly shrink access. Kalshi has already had to shrink its footprint from 50 states to 47 after bans in three states, including Nevada and Michigan, and Schwartz predicts a handful of others may do the same. The timing of a Supreme Court ruling matters, too. Schwartz called it about a coin flip whether the justices rule in June 2027 or June 2028, and said the court would likely need to take the case by mid-January for a 2027 decision. events.title: Microsoft outage hits MAS, banks’ e-mails; banks offer customers alternative contact channels
events.summary: The Association of Banks in Singapore said banks affected by the disruption had also put up notices on various channels to alert customers to the outage. SINGAPORE – Banks in Singapore whose e-mails and communications have been affected by the global Microsoft outage have reached out to customers with alternative ways to access help, including customer service hotlines and relationship managers. Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it was closely monitoring the situation. The financial regulator has also experienced disruption to its e-mail services, but said its operations remained unaffected. The Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) said banks affected by the disruption, particularly those providing retail banking services, have put up notices on various channels, including their websites, to alert customers to the outage. Checks by The Straits Times show that DBS, UOB, OCBC, HSBC and Maybank Singapore are among those affected. ABS director Ong-Ang Ai Boon said banks were making alternative contact arrangements available to customers while the disruption persisted. Customers are advised not to click on unknown or unsolicited links or respond to messages relating to the disruption as these could lead to phishing attempts, scams, credential theft and malware infections. The advisory comes amid concerns that cybercriminals could take advantage of the disruption to impersonate banks or send fraudulent messages to customers seeking information or help. DBS, Singapore’s largest lender, said responses to e-mails would be delayed because of the Microsoft outage. DBS customers can, however, continue to perform transactions via the bank’s ATMs, debit/credit cards, DBS/POSB digibank and PayLah!, all of which remain unaffected. They can use DBS/POSB digibank to receive push notifications. DBS wealth and corporate clients can also contact their relationship managers. The bank also warned customers to beware of scammers claiming to be from DBS or technology companies offering to resolve system issues. Maybank Singapore said in a Facebook post that all its digital and physical banking services remain safe and operational, though e-mails may be delayed. It directed customers to its digital channels, ATMs and self-service terminals. OCBC said responses to customer inquiries may be delayed. Those requiring urgent help should reach out to their relationship managers or the bank’s customer service hotlines. It too reminded customers to be vigilant against scammers taking advantage of the disruption. Microsoft suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including e-mail and cloud storage, to a standstill. In Singapore, Downdetector began recording reports at about 2am overnight, with numbers continuing to climb on the morning of Nov 13. MAS, in a banner displayed on its website, said it was monitoring its systems and the broader situation closely. Members of the public can continue to contact the central bank through its online feedback form. events.title: C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute
events.summary: The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature. Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup , who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself. The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language. In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies. The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay. Contracts dispute Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior. Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel . Developers have proposed adding Contracts to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults. But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal ( P2900 ) that made it into C++26. “The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested , and could be more effectively implemented as a library. Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig , a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself. “The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post . The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust . Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language . Sore losers Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers. “Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust." Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself. “The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.” Where to now? With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”) ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final. According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy , the group faces a number of choices. They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts. Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology. Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

events.title: Why Singapore keeps turning up in the fight over Nvidia chips and China
events.summary: Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February 2026 after authorities said she provided inaccurate information about her role in Megaspeed. The country repeatedly sought intelligence on Super Micro from U.S. authorities, but received "limited information or assistance," the ministry said. Singapore has faced international scrutiny over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight. The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country. A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year. The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday. Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday. Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China. The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development. Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue. Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up. Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year. Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering. Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added. "Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said. Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators. Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation. Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement. The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said. Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025. In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.

events.title: Oil on track to post second weekly decline as Trump eases fears of renewed war with Iran
events.summary: Oil prices were on course to post a second weekly decline as supply concerns eased, after US President Donald Trump signalled that he is not keen to restart the Iran war. But further attacks on ships in the region mean prices remain volatile. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was down 0.24 per cent at $95.59 a barrel at 8.53am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 0.54 per cent lower at $88.26 a barrel. Both Brent and WTI are set for decline of more than 2.5 per cent decline for the week, after plunging about 13 per cent last week. Mr Trump this week indicated that he is not planning to resume the war with Iran after his Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections. He also said on Thursday that the US was no longer looking to reach an agreement with Tehran. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we’ve got their strait,” Mr Trump said in a post on Truth Social. But attacks continue on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for two thirds of global crude supply and liquefied natural gas, putting upward pressure on oil prices amid supply risks. This week, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed there were explosions on two supertankers carrying more than four million barrels of oil in the strait. A tanker was also struck by a projectile while travelling east in the Arabian Gulf, with casualties reported, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said yesterday. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure by Yemen's Houthis also pushing prices higher. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said that a pumping station on the kingdom's East-West oil pipeline and the Yanbu oil installation on the Red Sea coast were hit on Thursday. Saudi Arabia has been exporting much of its crude through the pipeline since the beginning of the war, owing to disruption in the strait. Meanwhile, gold rose on ⁠Friday after prices ​reached a more than one-year low in the previous session. Spot gold climbed 1 per cent to $3,917.70 per ounce at 9.55am UAE time. Gold prices dropped below the $4,000 level as markets expect a December increase by the US Federal Reserve.

As The Register reported yesterday , the outage started on Thursday at around 18:00 UTC and saw Microsoft 365 users unable to access email, attend Teams meetings, use cloud PCs, consult Copilot, or enjoy full access to another 15 hosted services. The software giant says the outage impacts Microsoft 365 services “that interact with Exchange Online and email services.” Services that don’t need Exchange Online remain functional. The software giant initially blamed the outage on a mysterious “problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” Microsoft thought it found a fix but quickly admitted “Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief.” In the hours since, the situation has not improved markedly, and Microsoft is still struggling to restore service. It has also changed the language it uses when discussing the possibility that a cyberattack is the reason for the outage. As of 04:11 UTC, the company said it could find “no indication this is the result of malicious activity.” An update time-stamped 05:46 UTC stated “As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.” Microsoft’s status page includes only the company’s most recent update, but its RSS feed preserves each missive. That feed tells a tale of woe that we have distilled into lowlights and present in chronological order: We’re applying infrastructure capacity improvements where possible in an effort to help support traffic in regions coming online; We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected; We’re reviewing traffic flows and affected infrastructure to identify opportunities to optimize routing. This includes verifying the reasons for service failures so we can develop specific actions to improve stability; We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances; We're observing partial recovery across regions in which we've applied these adjustments; however, these actions aren't resulting in sustained recovery; Current actions we are taking include scaling up virtual machines to increase capacity and reduce load. However, we are encountering issues with the machines being stuck in a bad state, preventing our changes from syncing as expected. Microsoft’s latest status update doesn’t suggest this will be over any time soon. “We’re continuing to pursue multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx and advance the recoverability of the backend servers,” Microsoft wrote. “We’re taking a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure to improve the ability to confirm the developed changes were applied. We’re tracking the results of this approach to verify the servers are showing the anticipated recovery and performance intended.”

Which is why, each Friday, The Register runs a new instalment of On Call – the reader contributed column which ensures your work to keep tech alive doesn't remain unnoticed. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Tim" who told that while working for a phone company he once rewrote 2,650 lines of C as a six line shell script. He performed that feat after being asked to fix a data transfer program that, strangely, included a bespoke implementation of the venerable File Transfer Protocol (FTP). "Writing the script took eight hours, most of it tracking down the source code of FTP so I could see if it would do what I wanted," Tim wrote. This story took place before the World Wide Web became the way to find information online. To find the code he needed, Tim therefore used a Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) to search remote databases. "In those days, there was no Linux and AT&T had licensed the Unix source code to universities with the struct proviso that it never be made publicly available," Tim explained. "It took me quite some time using WAIS to track it down – the security could have been better – and read the code." Having found what he needed, Tim wrote his script, which ran overnight to collect data from the telco's switches, tidied up the raw info, and uploaded it to a mainframe. "It would automatically page me if it couldn't connect to a switch or mainframe after three attempts," he explained. The script worked fine, but the telco's networks didn't. Tim's pager was soon going off two or three times a night, every night. After two weeks of interrupted sleep, Tim's manager kindly told him to give the pager to a colleague. But that colleague habitually left the pager at work, forgot to turn it on, or conveniently placed it out of earshot. So Tim reluctantly took back the pager and endured another few weeks of nightly interruptions. How many consecutive sleepless nights have you endured while On Call? events.title: Politicians back focus on cost of living
events.summary: Targeted action on the cost of living is among the Government of Jersey's priorities for the next political term Politicians have backed the Government of Jersey's key priorities for the next political term which includes action on the cost of living. States members adopted the Common Strategic Policy , external which lays out the Council of Ministers' priorities for the political term until 2030. The priorities are centered around four pillars including targeted action on the cost of living, restoring Jersey's competitiveness, investing in homes and infrastructure and maintaining financial stability. Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was determined "to make Jersey a more affordable place to live" but Reform Jersey co-leader Lyndsay Feltham said the policy lacked "real action". The policy was backed with 31 votes in favour, 10 against and two abstentions. Ministers first published the proposed policy in September and this week politicians debated a number of amendments proposed by backbenchers. This included adding a priority about government transparency and promoting democracy , bringing the total number of priorities up from 11 to 12. Reform Jersey co-leader deputy Lyndsay Feltham does not support the government's Common Strategic Policy Listen to the latest news for Jersey Deputy Feltham's amendments to add actions to the policy about household affordability and employment rights were rejected and members also voted not to include reference to rental stress. The Reform Jersey co-leader said she was worried about the gaps this left behind. "What I really wanted to see from government was something more sustained and a sustained commitment to reduce everyday cost of living," said Feltham. "They've committed to a review of household affordability. A review doesn't put food on the table or a roof over somebody's head. "I am really concerned that ministers aren't going to actually take any action." Chief Minister Senator Lyndon Farnham believes the Common Strategic Policy reflects islanders' interests However, the chief minister said the policy recognised islanders' concerns such as affordability, housing, economic growth, investing in infrastructure and protecting the environment. In his closing speech, Farnham said their contributions "reflected a shared commitment to securing the best possible future for our island". He said the policy "will send an important message to islanders that we are putting their interests before our political disagreements". events.title: Cider makers fear future for orchards as costs grow
events.summary: Cider maker Matilda Temperley said the budget had been "disappointing" Rising costs could force the cider industry to reduce their reliance on British-grown apples, according to several well-established businesses. Higher alcohol duty, energy bills and packaging costs are making it harder to stay profitable, according to a producer in Somerset. The government said it was supporting the sector by increasing the value of Small Producer Relief, which provides lower alcohol duty rates for some smaller and medium-sized producers. Matilda Temperley, director of Burrow Hill farm near Martock, said it would be a "tragedy" to stop using its own apples due to climbing costs. Temperley, whose farm has been growing apples for 300 years, said recent increases had added to pressures already facing the industry, adding at 6% alcohol, their traditional cider is taxed at a higher rate than mass produced cider. Christmas market fears as roadworks cause long delays Published 7 hours ago Gritters out for the first time this autumn Published 21 hours ago No radical change after nationalisation, GWR says Published 18 hours ago "By next February, we will have seen a 61% increase in tax on our standard 50cl bottles," Temperley claimed. She welcomed the rise in Small Producers Relief but said other mounting costs outweighed it. "We've got huge, energy costs, then almost a 90% increase in tax costs since 2020." "The thing that will happen is that if you're a big cider maker, you're going to look to cut your costs and the only way to cut costs is to stop using British apples," she said. "That's a real tragedy because cider should be made from these beautiful orchards". Isaac Stell says ultimately it will be the consumer who pays Isaac Stell, a financial analyst at Wealth Club in Bristol, said that having pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT for working people, the recent budget focused on other areas to "help plug the fiscal hole." He said producers were also dealing with higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases in the minimum wage. "Inevitably, some of those additional costs will find their way through to the pubs, clubs and restaurants that producers supply, and ultimately to an already squeezed consumer. " Matthew Showering said like his apples - his business is growing The Showerings family, known for producing Babycham, has been making drinks in Shepton Mallet for more than 14 generations. "Our business has grown a lot in the last ten years - we've gone from having 80 employees to around 350 now," the firm's managing director Matthew Showering said. "We've had a good couple of years, we're making drinks that are popular and growing." While acknowledging rising costs, Showering said he would rather see less government intervention. "We don't want any help from the government, we'd rather they keep out of things as much as possible." Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider with his apple picker Johnny Matt Gillett from Tricky's Cider in Low Ham said the size of his operation means he will be eligible for the Small Producer Relief but adds he will not see a huge benefit as the Alcohol Duty is a "fairly substantial" part of his monthly outgoings. Gillett remains optimistic, and said he would not consider importing pulp or concentrate to cut costs. "We are a craft producer here in Somerset and are proud of the fact we take from local orchards, traditional orchards, and use the fruit that is available here in this county." A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The cider industry makes a vital contribution to our rural economy and communities, and cider continues to benefit from significantly lower duty rates than other alcoholic drinks. "But we know the industry is facing continued pressures, which is why the Budget provides additional support by cutting costs for pubs and bars that are vital customers for the industry and poured pints continue to benefit from draught relief."
