events.title: ‘They’ve cut all entry-level jobs’: unlikely seaside town on frontline of AI threat
events.summary: Bournemouth became a hub for thousands of finance jobs after the 1980s big bang, but new tech risks hurting Dorset’s economy A few minutes’ drive from Bournemouth’s sandy beachfront, on the site of a former farm, lies an unlikely nerve centre of international finance. Here, miles from the glass towers of London’s Canary Wharf, more than 5,300 staff including compliance officers, analysts and software engineers help process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day for the largest US bank, JP Morgan. The sprawling five-hectare (13-acre) campus, which hosted just 650 workers when it opened in 1986, has solidified Dorset’s status as one of Britain’s largest financial hubs outside London. Now, the financial services industry accounts for 10% of the county’s turnover – the total revenue generated by all businesses in the area – with 2,500 companies, including Nationwide Building Society, the insurer LV=, and the asset manager Canaccord Wealth, collectively employing 24,000 staff, according to the Dorset Chamber of Commerce. But along with other regional finance centres outside London, from Leeds to Birmingham, and Swindon to Cardiff, it faces an existential threat from AI. Bosses are considering how the technology can help automate costly human-led jobs, putting at risk a swathe of back-office roles, such as data processors, compliance checkers and entry-level analysts. The Barclays chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, last month announced 5,000 job cuts linked to advances in AI , while another London-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, said in May it was planning to slash 7,000 roles as it doubled down on artificial intelligence. AI now poses the biggest threat to the UK’s financial workforce since the 2008 financial crisis, says Caren Evans, a national officer for the Unite union, referring to an era when banks needed multibillion-pound taxpayer bailouts and subsequently embarked on swingeing cost cuts. Unite members, who include staff at NatWest, Lloyds and Barclays , are “very very worried about AI”, Evans says. “They’re worried about losing their job, they’re worried about having future skills, they’re worried about having sustainable careers.” All that is hitting staff morale. One Barclays employee said they felt “very undervalued and insignificant”, adding: “It’s kind of hard to be enthusiastic about your work when you know, at any moment, senior executives are thinking about how to get rid of you. You’re not seen as an asset, you’re seen as a problem to be removed.” The JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, has warned of the fallout from AI, saying widespread job losses could spark “civil unrest” unless governments and business supported displaced workers. He said retraining programmes, and even state-sponsored wage support, relocation schemes and early retirement could be needed to ease the blow. In Dorset, the banking tech push has already left its mark, with bosses closing Barclays House in Poole in 2022 after 46 years of operation. “It was the original site that all the cheques in the country used to go through, to be checked,” Gareth Sherwood, the president of the Dorset Chamber of Commerce, says. “And of course, that went with digitisation.” That office block still stands empty today. Sherwood’s organisation has been coaching local business to embrace AI and increase productivity. “There’s winners and losers in all change,” he says. But “we would still encourage people to use human beings”, both to support local jobs, but also mitigate cybersecurity risks and unplanned outages. “You can’t switch a human off in the same way that you can switch an AI off,” he adds. But if cost-cutting bank bosses start to axe back office roles at pace, there would be ripple effects throughout regional economies such as Dorset. Demand for professional support from law firms and consultancies could start to dry up, and the wider ecosystem of services, such as gyms, hairdressers, restaurants and estate agents, could start to suffer. “The collateral would be to some of the more service aspects of [the economy],” Sherwood says. “And it’s hard enough to keep young people in this area.” The Conservative councillor Lawrence Williams has served Littledown and Iford, the ward hosting JP Morgan’s campus, since 2011. He originally moved to the area in the early 1980s, shortly before the bank – then known as Chase Manhattan – took up its lodgings on former farmland. The 76-year-old regularly meets JP Morgan bosses, but says he has heard nothing of AI-related job cuts. The bank itself says the Bournemouth campus is a “centre for financial innovation”, adding: “AI will enable us to do more, and we train our people to make the most of it.” But if companies start to follow in Barclays’ and Standard Chartered’s footsteps, that “could hit quite hard”, particularly for an economy otherwise reliant on seasonal tourism, Williams says.

events.title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
events.summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube. Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name. Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény. The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks. Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital. The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.” The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983. While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year. At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand. The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually. Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.” Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.” Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today. “The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.” The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest. The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world. Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations. “If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said. 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation has sent ripples throughout the global technology industry, with competitors itching to take advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the chip giant Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, with rival chipmakers itching to take advantage of the uncertainty and others wondering if the downfall of one of AI's biggest cheerleaders will dampen the mood around the civilization-altering technology. Huang, who stepped down Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, was the very public face of a company that dominates the market for computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, Huang predicted Nvidia will be grappling with a $1 trillion backlog in orders for its chips by the end of the year, doubling his estimate from a year earlier. A linchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Some of Nvidia's biggest rivals, such as Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, saw their shares advance Thursday following Huang's departure as investors predicted that its customers will look to diversify their suppliers. In the end, analysts say, this might not be a bad thing. “This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand,” said Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at the global consultancy West Monroe. “Nvidia did not create that demand, and a shift in this part of the market could ultimately diversify the supply chain, create more choice for customers and strengthen the broader AI industry in the years ahead.” Nvidia carved out an early lead in tailoring its chipsets known as graphics processing units, or GPUs, from use in powering video games to helping to train powerful AI systems. Demand soared as tech companies scrambled for more chips to build and run AI systems. In annual filings, Nvidia has identified competitors including Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, Intel, Broadcom and cloud services companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft. While these other players are established and respected within the industry for their chips, they have been trying to catch up to Nvidia. Nvidia has had an advantage from the start and as soon as a competitor releases something just as good, Nvidia has put out the next better chip, said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer of International Services Inc. “Nobody’s just sitting still,” he said. While some competitors saw bumps to their share prices Thursday, “their gains are going to be smaller than Nvidia’s losses,” said Chester Spatt, a finance professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But Spatt said he also anticipates chip purchasers could also become “much more reluctant to concentrate their purchases with a single source.” The incident is also sure to prompt elected officials to seek stronger export controls on American-made chips, but that could be a boon for Chinese chipmaker Huawei , another Nvidia competitor. Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, said she suspects Chinese AI firms could accelerate efforts to secure overseas computing capacity ahead of tighter controls. “Chinese chipmakers have already rallied on Nvidia’s troubles, but China’s AI developers depend heavily on Nvidia’s ecosystem,” she said. “This could be both an opportunity and a headache for China.” While Huang is not the only face of AI — OpenAI's Sam Altman , Google's Demis Hassabis and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton are among the others — he's been an influential one. A celebrity-level industry evangelist with President Donald Trump's ear and support, he has advocated for a light touch on AI regulation and has been bullish about AI’s potential to transform society, creating faster economic growth and more scientific breakthroughs. Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE “Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” said Asa Hiken, a senior analyst for research firm eMarketer. “And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.” Lee, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the resignation fallout will ripple across the AI ecosystem. “Obviously Nvidia’s technological leadership won’t disappear, but Huang had played an outsized role as its chief strategist, dealmaker and — very importantly — political advocate, with close access to both Washington and Beijing,” she said. “This happens at a critical juncture when markets are already questioning the sustainability of massive AI spending.

events.title: Coal protest to go ahead on harbour after court rejects police objections
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supreme Court rejects police objections to approve Rising Tide anti-coal protest on Newcastle Harbour The group Rising Tide has staged protests in the Port of Newcastle for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) The NSW Supreme Court has rejected a challenge from the state's police commissioner to a climate protest planned in Newcastle. The protest, organised by Rising Tide, is set to see hundreds of activists paddle out in the Port of Newcastle. The court heard the flotilla will stretch across the harbour, blocking the shipping channel for up to 40 minutes. A climate protest on Newcastle Harbour will go ahead as planned after the Supreme Court rejected an application by NSW Police to stop it. Rising Tide's Paddle for the Plant flotilla is set to see hundreds of people in kayaks take to the water tomorrow. Handing down his judgement this afternoon, Justice Edward Muston said he had to balance the interests of the public with the concerns of police. "The public interests in the facilitations of political expression through assembly outweighs the legitimate concerns which have been expressed by the commissioner," he said. Protest organisers in NSW must submit a notice of intention to hold a public assembly to the police commissioner, known as a Form 1. The NSW Police Commissioner opposed this application and asked the Supreme Court to prohibit the event due to safety concerns for those attending and other users of the harbour. Without a Form 1, protesters run the risk of being charged by police for offences including obstructing people, vehicles or vessels. Police have argued their resources have been stretched on the water and land during previous anti-coal events. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) The court heard up to 785 people on kayaks and other watercraft would enter Newcastle Harbour tomorrow morning to unfurl a 20-metre-long series of connected floating letters that will read "Coal Exports Equals Climate Chaos". They also plan to form a continuous line spanning the harbour for about 30 to 40 minutes, blocking the shipping channel, before returning to shore. On Wednesday, barrister David Hume SC, who acted for NSW Police, told the court transport officials and police predicted dire consequences. "Everyone has looked at this [event] saying it poses an unacceptable risk," Mr Hume said. The Assistant Police Commissioner echoed those calls, citing an incident last year where protesters were washed hundreds of metres down the harbour. Police watch on as protesters previously demonstrated against fossil fuels at Newcastle's port. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) "I have not seen any Rising Tide event run safely yet," Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said. The number of watercraft will be capped at 785 — more than double previous anti-coal protests in the port. Rising Tide's barrister Michael Green told the court the event would have a kayak safety team, swimming in the channel would be banned, and life jackets mandatory. He said people attending would also be briefed on hand signals they could use to raise the alarm if they get into trouble. Rising Tide's Anne Hodgson told the court it would be a family-friendly event and ruled out the prospect of civil disobedience. Ms Hodgson told the court it was hoped global media would cover the event. The world's biggest coal port in Newcastle has been a focus for groups fighting climate change. ( ABC Newcastle: Carly Cook ) "Yes, as the COP31 meetings are on, we would like that," she said. COP31 is the United Nations Climate Conference — the largest international summit to negotiate and advance global cooperation on climate change. On the eve of the court action, Newcastle City councillors banned Rising Tide from protesting on community land "now and into the future", sparking fears among activists about their right to peacefully protest. Newcastle's Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote on Tuesday to pass a motion opposing the use of community land for the purpose of Rising Tide's events and protests. Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris used his casting vote this week to ban Rising Tide from protesting on community land. ( ABC News: Keely Johnson ) "The constant request for them [Rising Tide activists] to remain within the boundaries has been broken, and it's been a constant breaking of promises," he said. ( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) A Tasmanian cray fisher says the wild-caught fishing sector has been "impacted so deeply" by salmon companies' use of antibiotics. Following salmon company Tassal's use of an antibiotic, two commercial fishing areas are being closed from Sunday until February 14 to protect export markets. Premier Jeremy Rockliff says it is important "we get the balance right". A commercial fisher says the impact of salmon companies' antibiotic use in Tasmania is "completely unfair" on smaller, wild fishers. Kodey Rolston, who works as a deckhand on a cray fishing boat, said while he was a supporter of the salmon industry, "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done". The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) is closing two commercial fishing areas from Sunday until February 14. Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use. The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "therapeutic management area" (TMA). Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA. Under the state government's Aquaculture Therapeutant — Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, released last month, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed. The closures are to protect export markets as some countries have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild-caught fish. Man who burned shoebox of tax records fined for resulting bushfire Tasmanian premier apologises for 'outcome' of Christmas post AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community deal The two new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel. The company said the closure accounted for 1.6 per cent of the state's historical rock lobster catch. A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) But Mr Rolston said the closure area was "vital to the crayfishing industry". "Down south is our safe haven for abalones, for crayfish. "It's a multi, multi-generational fishing ground and it's being locked off all together because the salmon farms want to just dump as much antibiotics in the water as they can to try and save their own arse and not cooperate with other businesses," he said. "I actually don't have anything against the salmon farms. "In all honesty, I'm very much for them — they provide a lot of jobs all around the state. Tassal says the rock lobster fishery closure accounts for 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual rock lobster catch. ( ABC News: Bec Pridham ) Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said the government was expecting the wild-caught fishing industry to "do all the heavy lifting". "Wild fishers have been sidelined and the interests of big salmon companies have been put first by the government," Ms Woodruff said. "They've refused to put in place any regulations to constrain the operations of salmon farming in the Channel." 'Important that all industries work together': Premier Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was important "we get the balance right". "The industry is in a transition and a very quick transition in terms of antibiotic use because of the investment that's going into breeding, for example, will mean that in future years there'll be less reliance on antibiotics if at all, and that's the space we need to get to. "We're in a transition time now and I know it's difficult … I feel for industry outside of the salmon industry very much. "It's important that all industries work together, we get the balance right." In a statement yesterday, Tassal said the closure was a "precaution to protect export market access". "Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe. "We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible.

events.title: Outlook outage expected to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Microsoft Outlook outage cost to businesses 'billions' The Microsoft outage has been ongoing for more than 12 hours. ( Reuters: David Ryder ) Experts say the Microsoft outage is likely to cost businesses billions. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner, Ashwin Pal, says small business will be hit the hardest. The financial impact is expected to last weeks. The Microsoft outage is calculated to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars, with experts warning small businesses will be the hardest hit by the technology failure. A widespread outage, which started about 3:15 am AEDT, has hit platforms including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing emails and encountering errors across the Microsoft suite of products. Workers across multiple types of businesses have reported being unable to access email or SharePoint, with some resorting to using fax machines to keep operating. Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues affecting the tech giant's apps, read our blog. RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner Ashwin Pal said the cost to professional service businesses, such as lawyers or accountants, would be hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour. "It's not just the initial downtime, it's more actually about then the catch up effort because that costs money," he said. "Because now when things do normalise, you're going to have to spend money to actually catch up because of all the backlog." Ashwin Pal says Monday's backlog of work will be costly. ( Supplied ) He said the impact of the outage was amplified by the 3.9 million businesses globally that used the Microsoft suite, with many not having backup systems, resulting in huge costs to the economy. "This is what happened with CrowdStrike. So when the outage happened, because of where we are in the world in terms of time zones, we felt the impact first. "As the US and Europe come online, and they can't operate, it's going to get worse. So you're going to have a multiplier effect." Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today. He said the repercussions would be most keenly felt by small businesses, due to operating on thin margins. "You take a CBA as an example, they'll be able to absorb an impact like this a lot easier than the five-person accounting shop down the road," he said. "They were already actually working on very thin margins. All of a sudden they're actually out for three, four, five days or whatever it takes for them to recover. That could be the final straw." Owner of small Queensland business Regal Shower Screens, Tracey Tucker, said the lost day of business would cost at least $30,000, but there were numerous flow-on effects. "I'm paying my girls sitting in here in the office to do nothing," she said. "The phone rings, they can't order anything. "Then it puts undue pressure because if it's back online on Monday, everything we missed Friday, we're going to try to catch up on." Experts say the outage will hurt small business the most. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) She said the outage meant the business would struggle to meet its promoted deadlines because the glass manufacturers would also be inundated on Monday. "It's going to put pressure on everybody down the track because our girls are going to get yelled at, like, 'You just said my shower's going to be two weeks now, it's two and a half weeks', all because we can't send the order through today." Service delivery manager with telecommunication company Hubify, Chloe Mombeshora, said she had received numerous calls from less tech-savvy clients who were unsure what was happening. "They're thinking that their internet is down, they don't know what to do," she said. She added some clients had raised concerns the inability to communicate could impact their businesses' reputations. Some Outlook users were receiving notifications for emails they could not open. ( ABC News: Liana Walker ) IT support specialist James Coates said he had been inundated with requests for help but was unable to reply through his helpdesk because it used Outlook. "We actually have to call each client individually, every single personal phone number, every single Teams number, hope it gets through and update them that way because the email service is just not working on their end either," he said. He said he also could not do other work over concerns it would not be saved. Do you know more, or are you affected?

events.title: Outback cattle flown to Kazakhstan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hereford cattle from the middle of Australia flown to Kazakhstan Ben Hayes (second from right) alongside livestock agent Tim McKean, inspecting cattle with Kazakhstan buyers. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) A buyer from Kazakhstan has taken nearly 300 head of cattle from the Northern Territory after flying out to inspect them. Cattle producer Ben Hayes says Kazakhstan's government has an initiative to boost its national herd. Federal data shows Kazakhstan imported more than 1,000 head each of cattle and sheep in October. Nearly 300 head of cattle from a station near Alice Springs have been flown to Kazakhstan, in what local producers hope is the start of a new market. The distance from Alice Springs in the middle of Australia to Kazakhstan is roughly 10,000 kilometres. Ben Hayes from Undoolya Station said he got a call from his livestock agent one day with an interesting offer. "He asked if we had some heifers for this Kazakhstan job and we did," he said. "The buyer from Kazakhstan actually flew out here [with an interpreter], took a quick look and ended up taking them. "They got trucked down to Melbourne, where they stayed in quarantine for about a month and were then loaded into crates and onto the plane." Cattle from Undoolya Station ready for export to Kazakhstan. ( Supplied: Undoolya Station ) Mr Hayes said the animals were flown from Melbourne to Singapore and then onto Kazakhstan. "There was a weight limit on them of about 180 to 250 kilograms and they had to be preg-tested empty." He said the money paid for the animals was "on-par" with what he would normally receive in the Australian market. But he said the chance to be involved in the sale to Kazakhstan was "very special". "To know that our heifers are now becoming breeding stock for Kazakhstan is a feather in our cap, in Australia's cap," he said. ABC Landline has been told some cattle from Mt Riddock Station in the NT were also purchased for the consignment. According to data from the Federal Department of Agriculture, there were two flights of breeder cattle out of Victoria last month totalling 1,252 head. Another flight to Kazakhstan took 1,617 breeder sheep. It is understood Australia last exported cattle to Kazakhstan in 2019. It is a long way from Alice Springs to Kazakhstan. ( ABC Landline ) This is not the first time Undoolya Station has flown cattle to a distant market. In 1981, Undoolya steers were flown direct out of Alice Springs to Korea. "I was only a little fella at the time, but my father and grandfather flew steers out of Alice Springs on a Flying Tiger aircraft, straight to Korea" Mr Hayes said. "I don't know why they wanted steers, but that's what happened, Alice Springs is an international airport, it was a good opportunity." Undoolya Station is the Northern Territory's oldest pastoral lease. Established in 1872, the property has been owned by the Hayes family since 1906. events.title: World is now in ‘age of electricity’, energy agency chief says
events.summary: Exclusive: Fossil fuels no longer dominant energy source, IEA leader says, as summit considers electrification pledge The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said. Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war. Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures. “We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey . “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.” Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century. Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels , mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said. The more our lives can be powered by clean energy the better, say experts, not least because, as a result of the inefficiency of fossil fuels , most of the rest of our energy is wasted as heat, so when these activities are electrified, only about half of the energy needs to be replaced. Most countries back the electrification goal, according to Birol. He has worked closely with the Turkish and Australian governments, which are jointly presiding over this year’s summit . “It will be an unmistakable signal to the markets and investors that governments see that the future of energy is in electricity,” he said. “This will make the age of electricity even earlier and cheaper. It might be one of the most consequential decisions coming from Cops in the last several years.” But even if the resolution was not adopted – some governments, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, are said to be opposed, and owing to the convention by which consensus is needed to pass decisions, a small number of countries can hold the rest to ransom – the “staggering” progress would continue, Birol said. “The reason is there are three major drivers for electrification: one is AI and datacentres; second is the electrification transportation sector; and third, the most important one in terms of volume, is air conditioning. Air conditioners are growing explosively,” he said. In the US, about 90% of households have access to air conditioning, but in India it is fewer than 20%, and in Nigeria about 5%. “With the increasing effects of climate change, and if they have more money, [people] buy air conditioners,” said Birol. “These things are happening, and electrification is not bad. It is good for energy security, because it is your own electricity [generated within a country rather than imported, as fossil fuels often are], good for the competitiveness of countries, and good for climate change.” The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential He added: “Global energy demand is growing strongly, but global electricity demand is growing three times faster than total energy demand. And it is impossible to stop it. The one and only issue is making electricity affordable for people.” Birol placed the blame for the UK’s high electricity prices firmly on gas. “There is always a debate about this in the UK, but in fact the single most important reason why UK electricity prices may be on the high side is reliance on imported gas. Gas prices went up, so did the electricity prices, full stop. And the solution is not importing more gas, but building more [renewable] electricity at home,” he said. The transformation is happening fast. “Five years ago, only 5% of all the cars sold was electric.

events.title: ‘I spend less, that’s all that matters’: life in the world’s most electrified countries
events.summary: Owning an electric car, driving an electric motorbike taxi, riding scooters – we speak to people in Oslo, Kigali and Shanghai about their everyday routines T he race to electrification has emerged as a key theme of this year’s UN climate summit: increasing the use of electricity – particularly from clean sources – has the potential to improve daily life for people around the world. The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. The global figure currently stands at 23%, but some countries are already striding ahead. As 100,000 delegates, negotiators and world leaders thrash out the details in Antalya, Turkey , the Guardian spoke to three people in Norway, Rwanda and China to find out what life looks like in more highly electrified countries. Norway is a world leader in the race to 100% electrification. In September, a record 98.81% of new cars sold were electric, and hydropower produces 90% of all electricity . But with rapidly rising energy demands, including from new datacentres, authorities warn that the country could soon face a power deficit and higher energy prices. Unni Berge, 47, lives in Oslo with her husband and two teenage sons and works as the head of communications at the Norwegian EV Association. She describes how electricity features in a typical day: “I use electricity in my three-bedroom flat and I have district heating [where heat is transported around a local network from a centralised source rather than individual boilers to heat homes and buildings]. For electricity we are connected to the Norwegian central grid, which is mainly hydropower. “I live in a rather energy-efficient flat, so our electricity bills are comparatively low. In October, we spent 730 Norwegian kroner [£57] on electricity for our apartment, and in September it was 500 kroner. “I go to work by bus. Almost all the buses in Oslo are fully electric. I also have an electric car, but driving in the middle of Oslo for work is not an option because we have a lot of restrictions on cars in the city centre. In my street, the bus comes every fifth minute, so I don’t have to plan. I go outside and a bus comes. “I mostly use my electric car on weekends. A lot of the trips are driving to sports activities with my two children, who are 18 and 15. I also train a handball team, so I use it to go to a lot of handball matches and tournaments. “We charge our car with a charging box in our garage where, like most apartment garages in Oslo, we have built a collective charging system. If everyone put their charging on at the same time it would go slow, but in practice that doesn’t happen. “I have a large battery on my EV so I charge it once every two to three weeks. Of course we pay for the electricity and a system fee, but it’s much cheaper than petrol and diesel. “In my office, we have district heating, which is quite common in Oslo in larger buildings, then we use electricity for light and computers. Lunch is made in my office in the internal canteen with electricity. At work I use Microsoft Copilot, which is a really helpful tool, but of course there are big questions there – energy demands will get too high if everyone is using AI more. “I come home and use electricity to make dinner, watch television and go to the cinema. Growing up in a small village on the western coast of Norway , we also used wood for heating as well as electricity. But it is fair to say that electricity is common part of Norwegian life and has been for a long time. “What has changed is that our transport sector is also now run on a rising amount of electricity: passenger cars, buses and also ferries. That happened quite fast. Heavy goods vehicles are also increasingly electric, so of course that changes the system and society. “Perhaps because of the war in Ukraine and more extreme weather conditions, people are becoming aware that they are quite dependent on electricity, so in recent years there has been debate on how to prepare for a crisis. In previous power cuts, some people have used their electric cars as a battery to power electric equipment. “There is also a big debate about electricity prices. In Norway we have nearly 100% renewable electricity, but even so we are connected to the European grid. So the gas prices still influence our electricity prices. And when we have dry winters, electricity prices rise because if we have less snow, the hydropower gets less water. Rising numbers of datacentres is also something consumers are starting to wonder about – what this development is going to look like and how much energy it is using.” An e-motorbike taxi driver in Kigali, Rwanda Six years ago, the Rwandan government embarked on an enthusiastic promotion of e-mobility by removing a number of taxes on e-bikes and vehicles and offering incentives for businesses operating charging stations.

events.title: Haze-linked First Resources, Bumitama post higher profits for Q3
events.summary: First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter. First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in Q3 underlying net profit to US$122.7 million, helped by higher palm oil sales and stronger output after buying Austindo Nusantara Jaya. Bumitama’s Q3 net profit rose 1.9% to 614.1 billion rupiah, as better plantation and mill productivity lifted production, though dry weather hurt shipments. Both firms said biodiesel demand and higher energy prices may support palm oil, but they also stressed zero-burning policies and cooperation with authorities over the haze. SINGAPORE – Two palm oil companies linked to the transboundary haze in October reported higher profits for the third quarter ended Sept 30, in separate business updates published on the morning of Nov 13. Palm oil producer First Resources posted a 40.1% rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million (S$157.9 million) for the third quarter of 2026, from US$87.5 million in the year-ago period. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palms, it said. Sales were up 24.9% at US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation rose 26.6% to US$207.4 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from US$163.8 million a year ago. For the nine months ended Sept 30, sales grew 36.5% year on year to US$1.6 billion, driven by higher sales volumes. A net inventory drawdown of 28,000 tonnes over the nine-month period, compared with a build-up of 80,000 tonnes in the corresponding period in 2025, also supported higher sales volumes. The group’s stronger production output in the first nine months of 2026 was also attributable in part to the full nine-month contribution from Austindo Nusantara Jaya, an Indonesian agribusiness company acquired in May 2025. However, profits were partially offset by foreign currency translation losses resulting from the depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah against the US dollar. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. In addition, elevated crude oil prices arising from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East are expected to support biodiesel economics and crude palm oil demand. Performance supported by productivity improvements Meanwhile, Bumitama reported a 1.9% increase in its net profit to 614.1 billion rupiah (S$43.4 million) for the quarter ended Sept 30, compared with 602.9 billion rupiah in the previous corresponding period. For the nine-month period, net profit rose 30.6% to 2.4 trillion rupiah, up from 1.9 trillion rupiah in the year-ago period. Revenue increased 9.7% to 4.2 trillion rupiah in the third quarter, up from 3.9 trillion rupiah a year ago. For the nine-month period, revenue was up 20% at 16.3 trillion rupiah. Bumitama said its performance was supported by productivity improvements in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. In July, internal production of fresh fruit bunches reached 383,203 tonnes, accounting for almost 40% of the quarter’s production. Quarterly production of crude palm oil increased 14% year on year to 368,323 tonnes. However, exceptionally dry weather conditions in its Kalimantan estates during the third quarter put additional pressure on logistics infrastructure and disrupted shipments, said Bumitama. Consequently, third-quarter revenue declined compared with the second quarter. The prolonged dry season also heightened the risk of land and forest fires across parts of Kalimantan. Fires affected certain areas within or adjoining the group’s concessions, including community-managed, conservation and unplanted land, the group noted. Bumitama said that elevated energy prices and Indonesia’s biodiesel programme coupled with a relatively constrained palm oil supply growth could provide a “supportive backdrop” for palm oil fundamentals heading into 2027. However, market conditions remain subject to uncertainty. These include changes in global energy prices, supply-and-demand dynamics, and the potential effects of prolonged dry weather on future production, it added. Both First Resources and Bumitama reiterated their commitment to upholding a zero-burning policy, and cooperating with the Indonesian and Singapore authorities in relation to the haze.

events.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
events.summary: Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though. The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.  The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though. Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet. Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he cofounded in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing. In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.  The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.  Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks. Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ST Engineering Q3 revenue rises 9% to $3.4 billion, declares interim dividend of 5 cents per share
events.summary: Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion. SINGAPORE – ST Engineering’s revenue for the third quarter ended September rose 9% year on year to $3.4 billion, from $3.1 billion in the previous corresponding period, the group said on Nov 13. The technology and engineering company declared a third-quarter interim dividend of five cents per share, up from four cents a year earlier. Its first-quarter and second-quarter dividends were four cents and five cents per share, respectively, bringing the total for the first three quarters to 14 cents per share. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue increased 10% to $10 billion, from $9.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. Excluding LeeBoy, its US-based construction equipment business divested on Sept 4, 2025, revenue grew 13% on a rebased basis. Defence and public security was the group’s largest revenue contributor for the nine-month period, generating some $4.3 billion, up 7% year on year. Excluding LeeBoy, revenue from the segment grew 13%. Third-quarter revenue rose 8% to $1.4 billion, or 12% on a rebased basis. The increase was led by marine and digital systems and cybersecurity businesses. The segment secured $5.5 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, including $1.8 billion in the third quarter . These included a five-year contract to supply 40mm ammunition to the British Ministry of Defence, projects involving defence command-and-control systems in Singapore, and maintenance and support services for the US Navy fleet. Meanwhile, commercial aerospace revenue rose 12% to about $4.1 billion in the first nine months, supported by higher contributions from engine maintenance, repair and overhaul work and nacelles, a container for aircraft parts. Revenue for the third quarter increased 7% to $1.4 billion. The segment secured $4.2 billion in new contracts in the first nine months, of which $1.4 billion was won in the third quarter . The latest wins included its first Airbus A220 airframe heavy maintenance contract with an Asia-Pacific operator and airframe maintenance agreements with Asia-Pacific airline customers. Revenue from urban solutions and satellite communications increased 15% year on year to about $1.7 billion in the first nine months. Third-quarte r revenue also rose 15% to $600 million, with higher contributions from both businesses. The segment secured $3.5 billion in new contracts in the nine-month period, including $2.4 billion in the third quarter . Wins included turnkey rail services for the Taoyuan MRT Brown Line and Green Line Extension in Taiwan, integrated smart security management solutions contracts in Singapore and tolling infrastructure modernisation work for the Tampa-Hillsborough Expressway Authority in the US. Across the group, contract wins totalled $13.2 billion in the first nine months, including $5.6 billion in the third quarter. The nine-month figure excluded $1.7 billion in New Jersey Turnpike Authority order book recognition. The group’s order book stood at a record $37.7 billion as at September, up from $33.2 billion as at end-2025. About $3.1 billion is expected to be delivered in the remainder of 2026. ST Engineering also reported a record-low operating expenses-to-revenue ratio of 9% for the first nine months, compared with 10.2% for the whole of 2025. The 2025 figure excluded a one-off impairment loss of iDirect group. Separately, ST Engineering said it is exploring long-term opportunities in the nuclear energy sector, drawing on its capabilities in complex, safe and mission-critical environments and partnering organisations with complementary expertise. Its current collaborations include those with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, Sembcorp Utilities and Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Areas of activity include factory-fabricated structural modules, such as protective steel structures, and advanced materials for fusion reactors, including tungsten coatings for reactor’s inner walls. The group also sees opportunities to apply its capabilities in digital twin technology and artificial intelligence, advanced materials and manufacturing, and large-scale systems integration.

events.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
events.summary: Joon Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, have been retained by Nvidia to investigate allegations that then-CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang resigned Thursday after reports he had an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected spy for China, and a second affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Kim has a long track record as a federal prosecutor and lawyer in private practice. His investigations have included ones into former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and the FDIC. Joon Kim , the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia to investigate former CEO Jensen Huang , and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases. Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John "The Teflon Don" Gotti's son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo , the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp . and other high-profile people and companies. The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer , which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to "conduct a thorough and independent investigation" of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China . Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him. That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe. Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim. Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job. "I think he's the ideal person for this role," said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related. "I think they're going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead," Edward Kim said. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University. After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit. The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included "racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism," the office has previously said. Kim's trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti's nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries. "He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate," said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends. "He's incredibly smart," Conniff said. "I think he's known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned." Kim in 2006 returned to Cleary Gottlieb as a partner in the firm's litigation and enforcement group but then went back to the SDNY in 2013. During his second stint there, he served as deputy U.S. attorney, and then served as acting U.S. attorney from 2017 to 2018. events.title: A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
events.summary: CEO behind the meteoric rise of Nvidia stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements. March 2023 Megaspeed, a datacenter firm, is spun out from a Chinese video game company Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg. November 2023 Megaspeed is sold to a Singaporean shell company and becomes an Nvidia cloud partner Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry. Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. June 2024 Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are seen together in Taipei, Taiwan Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal. 2024 to 2025 Megaspeed receives several hundred shipments of Nvidia AI chips The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Ali Baba. September 2024 The US Department of Commerce begins investigating Megaspeed The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips. January 2025 Jensen Huang meets Donald Trump for the first time Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office. April 2025 Jensen Huang attends a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after. May 2025 Jensen Huang is again seen with Alice Huang The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reportes that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier. October 2025 Trump is reportedly briefed on the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this. December 2025 Trump approves the sale of more advanced Nvidia chips to China Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government. May 2026 Marco Rubio reportedly drafts a memo about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy.

events.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December. Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines. Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X. "The American people deserve answers," he added. Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony. Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 1 hour ago How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 21 hours ago Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China. A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee. Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang. On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive. Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing. Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday. According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company. Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close. Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently? Published 22 hours ago The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 20 hours ago Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company. It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said. Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public. Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared. Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information. The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures. Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming. But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data. Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

events.title: Outlook email outage: Microsoft says service recovery completed in parts of Asia-Pacific
events.summary: Microsoft said on Friday its email services were being restored in parts of the Asia Pacific region, as it extended its email timeout to 48 hours to resolve an outage that affected systems globally on Thursday. The disruption affected Outlook, Teams and the Copilot AI service for millions of people, companies and governments around the world on Thursday, and the issue continued into Friday. "We've made additional progress towards service recovery, with recovery actions completed across portions of the affected infrastructure in the Asia Pacific region," the company said in its most recent update on Friday. "Traffic is being gradually restored and we're seeing improvements in key customer scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing. However, some users may continue to experience intermittent issues." Reducing email queues and backlogs "remains a priority, and the extended 48-hour email timeout window remains in place to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up", it added. The focus is now on extending the recovery actions across affected infrastructure in other regions. "At this time, we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident," the company added. "We will continue to treat this with urgency until full mitigation, and we will share a full post-incident report with root cause and defence-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete." The company delayed its email timeout window to 48 hours to help protect and keep delayed messages, such as emails sent from other providers, from being bounced back. After hours of troubleshooting, the company said its investigation indicated that failed checks "may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health". "We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service", it said. “We're implementing these actions more broadly across affected regions as we seek to attain persistent recovery. ” The company said it was working to recover its front-end servers. To improve server stability and traffic, Microsoft previously said it was “adjusting traffic protocols, redistributing traffic and applying strategic traffic blocking measures”. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 were recorded in 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector, an online service that monitors internet disruption. Microsoft said its Exchange Online incident began at 4.17pm in the US (8.17pm UAE time) on Thursday. In two hours, reports on five Microsoft services reached 19,650 a minute, compared with fewer than 15 a minute on an average Thursday, Downdetector said. Outlook reports peaked at more than 2,000 times their normal level. “Reports about Microsoft 365, Copilot, Teams and OneDrive each rose more than a hundred-fold, and Azure about 100-fold. Xbox, GitHub and LinkedIn, also Microsoft's, rose far less,” DownDetector said. Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector. Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25,… pic.twitter.com/7FQ4dDsfbm — Downdetector (@downdetector) November 12, 2026 The outage "highlights the need for resilience in all our critical systems", said Jack Hidary, chief executive at tech company SandboxAQ. "The energy grid, the telco network and the applications layers are all now essential to business continuity. Often these outages occur not from cyber attacks, but from code updates within the system that has unforeseen consequences. "Code simulation [CodeSim] is emerging as a new field that can detect potential impact of code updates before they are committed to production. CodeSim will prevent many of these outages in the future," he added. Microsoft's status website first acknowledged the problem on Thursday. “Users may be unable to connect to their mailboxes in Exchange Online through multiple connection methods,” a message on the Microsoft page said. Over the course of the day, the company added to its tally of products that users might not be able to access. Services for technologists, including cyber security software, file-sharing services and administrator tools, were also disrupted. We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 For Outlook specifically, Microsoft classified the issue as being a “service degradation”. A social media post from Microsoft explained efforts to rectify the problem. “We've begun redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load,” it said. Later on Thursday, data from Downdetector indicated that services started to recover for some users. For many, however, problems continued for several hours. Microsoft later confirmed through its service health status update page that the technical issue broadly affected the company's Microsoft 365 productivity suite. The technology company also said it was able to gain more insights into the cause of the problem experienced by so many users around the world. “We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable,” the update said. Governments and various companies around the world were also affected by the problem. As a result, many sought to calm the frustrations felt by patrons and customers through social media posts. “Due to a wide-scale outage impacting Microsoft 365 across North America, the State of Michigan is currently experiencing technical issues with email and other Microsoft applications,” Michigan's Department of Technology, Management and Budget said in a post. “Responses to emails may be delayed during this time.” Later on Thursday evening, Microsoft said it was still looking at “all available pathways to restore service”, but that those efforts “have not provided the anticipated relief”. The company indicated that it was pursuing a different strategy of “re-isolating a portion of infrastructure” and also restarting certain components that it speculated were causing the problem. More than seven hours after the problem was first reported, Microsoft warned that certain servers that were returned to service might become unresponsive once traffic started moving through them.
