events.title: Nvidia fallout fuels questions about Lutnick’s staying power
events.summary: The News Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has kept his job through scrutiny over his ties to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; his cryptocurrency firm, Tether; and his former financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald. The Nvidia fallout may be the toughest test yet of his staying power. A growing GOP contingent is pointing the finger at Lutnick for not cracking down hard enough on Megaspeed, the AI chip firm with ties to an alleged Chinese spy with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair, and for what they see as the Commerce Department’s broader failure to restrict AI chip exports to China. In the wake of reporting that other administration officials had urged the Commerce secretary to move faster, Republicans on and off Capitol Hill are accusing Lutnick of defying President Donald Trump by not imposing curbs on the firm — and even positing his job could be at risk. “We’re hearing … Trump has directed three times that [Megaspeed be blacklisted],” Rep. John Moolenaar, the top Republican on the House Select Committee on China, told Semafor. “If that’s true … then clearly, it seems that those questions need to be answered.” But so far the balance of GOP officials are coming to Lutnick’s defense, suggesting the commerce secretary won’t be going anywhere soon. The president himself is so far standing by Lutnick despite the bipartisan backlash, reinforcing his willingness to go easier on China as he pursues a trade detente with Beijing. “What I would say to everybody: Just settle down,” Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. “We don’t need to shoot Howard today.” “There’s lots and lots and lots of stuff here that’s going to come out. Should it come out? Absolutely,” Justice continued. “Should we get on some witch hunt running through the wilderness? … I don’t do that.” Congress will get more answers soon: Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that Lutnick will testify before the chamber’s Commerce Committee. And House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., said that Huang, who resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following revelations of another affair with a colleague, will appear before his panel . Even Lutnick’s critics think he’ll eventually pull himself out of trouble, even as longstanding interagency tension threatens to boil over. “When you saw [Treasury] Secretary [Scott] Bessent blowing up at Lutnick in the Situation Room, you can rest assured the working level at Treasury was all over Commerce about chip sales for over a year,” Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and Bessent ally, told Semafor. “Now the issue becomes: Does Lutnick start inventing excuses to save himself?” A Commerce Department spokesperson said that “Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship,” adding that both “are committed to advancing President Trump’s agenda.” The Nvidia news landed just in time for Democrats, who are finalizing their oversight plans for the next Congress. Already, lawmakers have laid the groundwork to investigate Lutnick’s involvement with Cantor Fitzgerald , Tether , and Epstein . The detractors No GOP lawmaker has called explicitly for Lutnick’s firing. But they haven’t hesitated to blame him for many of the recent revelations about Nvidia — including the fact that Huang accompanied Trump to China earlier this year despite the since-revealed existence of a State Department memo outlining his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy. “How on Earth do you put somebody on Air Force One [when you have] been informed there was a suspected improper relationship beforehand? How is that protecting the president?” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president; to me, that’s a disqualifying moment for Lutnick.” Compared to Epstein, “this, to me, is next-level,” he added. Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., rebuked Commerce for not shedding more light on the circumstances, particularly when it comes to the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed. “If I were the secretary, I’d call a press conference and explain what happened,” Kennedy said. “This is as serious as an aneurysm.” Even some of the Trump administration’s staunchest allies have weighed in, accusing Lutnick of defying the president by failing to rein in Megaspeed. “Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen,” China hawk Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News. He urged Lutnick to testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The defenders Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor that “you’ve got to get the facts” before drawing any conclusions, adding that Lutnick has “always responded to my questions, so that’s all I can ask.” Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., also cast doubt on whether Lutnick really was at fault. “In a lot of cases, where they simply blame someone, I want to know what the rules are that he’s trying to comply with,” Rounds told Semafor. “Is there something that we’ve done, in terms of policy, that might have either delayed his ability or something else? I don’t know, and I’d rather get the facts before I make a decision as to guilt.” The AI industry sees little problem with Lutnick’s conduct either way. “Commerce’s job is to expand the economy, domestic and foreign, pretty much at all costs,” National Artificial Intelligence Association CEO Caleb Max said. “So if you zoom out, I don’t think it looks nefarious; I think it looks natural.” The View From the white house Far more crucially, the White House’s public posture on the debacle indicates that Trump is not particularly concerned about the fallout, let alone Lutnick’s role in it. “Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” a White House official said. “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” The White House pointed Semafor to the president’s comments earlier this week, when he told reporters that he didn’t think he’d bring up the subject during his upcoming meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Notable The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule to block China’s remote access to AI chips, The Information reported . White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out of his role, Reuters reported .

events.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
events.summary: The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r) Published 13 November 2026, 00:13 GMT Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person? Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw. From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place. But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing". So how much AI enhancement is too much? Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye. But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place. "The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different." For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison. AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI. But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time. "It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for." All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down. Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible. It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly. According to a recent survey , external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was. Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months. He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential. But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time. "I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person." He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated. Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove. In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter. In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down. Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing. "If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says. In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property". "It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold." Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology. But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

events.title: Advocates warn FIFO standards are slipping on mine sites
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts FIFO worker advocates warn 'bare minimum standards' not being enforced FIFO workers face long shifts away from family, with accommodation playing a crucial role in their wellbeing. ( ABC News: Cody Fenner ) Researchers say minimum accommodation standards are dropping on mine sites around the country. As a result, FIFO workers are more likely to experience psychosocial hazards like isolation and harassment. A code of practice for worker's accommodation is set to be endorsed by the WA government next year. With six years' experience as a WA fly-in fly-out (FIFO) worker, Vicky Pellowe still remembers the creeping sense of loneliness at the end of a 12-hour shift. "If you have had any kind of challenge or if there's anything going on at home, you are very much isolated with your own thoughts in your room," she said. "It needs to be comfortable, clean and connected." Mining camps are often built up with demountable "dongas". ( ABC: Jessica Shackleton ) As the Australian resources sector has exploded with year-on-year production records, advocates warn basic accommodation standards on remote mine sites are slipping. Ms Pellowe says the options range anywhere from extravagant camps to motel-style overflow to "donga" demountables. Ms Pellowe, executive director of the FIFO Family Project, represents one of 50 organisations that submitted to the WA government about a draft code of practice for workers' accommodation. Vicky Pellowe heads the FIFO Family Project, an advocacy group she founded after working in the mining industry. ( Supplied ) The code outlined best practice for amenities, including deadbolts on doors, better lighting in outdoor areas, king-single beds and reliable Internet connections. Triggered in part by revelations of widespread sexual harassment on site , it closed for feedback in June. The Department of Local Government, Industry Relations, and Safety says the code will receive final endorsement next year. Once the code of practice is in place, mining companies will not be legally bound to follow it, but it could be admissible in court if a hazard has not been properly managed. Ms Pellowe said there remained critical gaps when it came to connecting workers with their loved ones back home. She called for a mandated 24/7 contact point for families to raise welfare concerns. "They can be a real part of the safety net if they're included in these conversations about psychosocial wellbeing of workers," she said. Over-reliance on 'wellbeing washing' Architectural sociologist Jack Tooley, who also entered a submission, said mining companies had failed to connect the challenges to their bottom line. In a study published last month by journal Safety Science , Dr Tooley identified a reluctance to grant access to outside researchers, a lack of trust in survey data and an over-reliance on "wellbeing washing" like swimming pools. Mid-tier operator Mineral Resources built luxury-style Mungala Resort for its Pilbara workers in 2021. ( Supplied: MinRes ) Dr Tooley attributed 60 per cent of the psychosocial issues faced by mine workers to the built environment around them. Modelling by Dr Tooley's consultancy found simple improvements that lifted a worker's experience to a "neutral standard" — things like a better bed or noise-cancelling acoustics — could generate about $1.6 billion in annual revenue. Some advocates say the disparity is growing larger between rudimentary camps and resort-style accommodation. ( Supplied: Courtney Mason ) In 2025, Mineral Resources grabbed headlines by opening its $140 million Mungala Resort at Ken's Bore mine in the Pilbara, which boasts a pool and accommodation built for couples. The mid-tier miner has spruiked the 45-square-metre accommodation as three times the size of traditional FIFO rooms. Erin Turner delivers mental health training at Queensland mine sites and says growing workforces mean FIFO workers often feel shunted from room to room. "What that means is that people can't have their photos, they can't have certain homelike things that they would usually have," she said. Ms Turner said "creature comforts" were important to navigate the isolation and recover from long hours. Researchers from Edith Cowan University found employees in WA's Pilbara region were scared to speak up about the issues. They approached 20 for in-depth interviews across FIFO and residential rosters. Senior lecturer Heidi Vivian argued a wave of industrial action at BHP's iron ore and port operations earlier in the year was a reaction, having spoken with union-affiliated workers.

events.title: Cisco lifts annual revenue forecast on strong AI networking demand
events.summary: Cisco expects fiscal 2027 revenue in the range of US$74.8 billion (S$96.2 billion) to US$75.8 billion, compared with its previous forecast of US$72.2 billion to US73.4 billion. Cisco beat first-quarter estimates and raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to US$74.8 billion-US$75.8 billion, as demand for AI networking gear stays strong. Chief executive Chuck Robbins said: “We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle,” and Cisco lifted AI infrastructure revenue guidance from hyperscalers to US$9 billion. The firm is also building software for AI agents and cybersecurity, but investors still watch gross margin pressure from higher memory and component costs. Cisco beat Wall Street estimates for first quarter results and raised its annual revenue forecast on Nov 12, as the network gear maker bets on sustained strong demand from companies building out their AI infrastructure. The company has doubled down on its artificial intelligence efforts through strategic investments as Big Tech’s massive spending moves beyond artificial intelligence processors to the switches and routers required to connect large data centre systems. “We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking super-cycle,” chief executive Chuck Robbins said in a statement. The company raised its fiscal 2027 forecast for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to US$9 billion from US$7.5 billion. The segment generated revenue of US$4 billion a year earlier. Investors have been worried about a possible slowdown in data centre build-out following Democrats’ sweeping win in the US midterms , as well as rising borrowing costs and their impact on the debt-fuelled construction. Cisco reported first-quarter revenue of US$18.5 billion, compared with analysts’ average estimate of US$18.14 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. The company reported an adjusted profit of US$1.40 per share for the quarter ended Oct 24, above estimates of US$1.33. Cisco is also building software tools that businesses can use to build their own ​armies of bots, known as AI agents, to protect their IT ‌infrastructure against cybersecurity threats. They have risen about 32% so far in 2026 through the Nov 12 close. Cisco’s gross margin has been a worry for investors, as a shortage of memory chips has pushed up component costs for hardware makers while suppliers prioritise chips for AI data centre customers. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” said Bob O’Donnell, president and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. Cisco’s raised annual forecast and results above estimates are what the market wants to see from a company tied to AI infrastructure, he added. The company reported first quarter adjusted gross margin of 65.6%, in line with estimates, but down from 68.1% a year earlier. REUTERS

events.title: Anthropic’s IPO is about six times oversubscribed, say sources
events.summary: The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as US$64.4 billion (S$83 billion) in the IPO and US$26 billion in a private placement. Anthropic’s IPO is about six times oversubscribed, as strong demand builds for what could be the biggest listing ever. The firm aims to raise up to US$64.4 billion in the IPO and US$26 billion privately, with Nvidia set to buy about US$10 billion of shares. Anthropic is using investor events and a US$1.4 trillion valuation target, while its revenue run rate rose to US$81 billion by Oct 31. Anthropic’s initial public offering has drawn about six times the orders for the shares available, according to sources familiar with the matter, as interest increases for potentially the biggest first time share sale ever. The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as US$64.4 billion (S$83 billion) in the IPO and US$26 billion in a private placement, its filings show. Taken together, the offering would be bigger than SpaceX’s IPO, making it the biggest listing of all time. Bankers have told prospective investors that existing backers will be prioritised by Anthropic, and some would-be buyers will receive smaller allocations than they expect, some of the sources said. Details of the IPO including the demand for shares could change, said the sources, who asked not to be identified as the information is not public. A representative for Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The surge of interest in Anthropic shares contrasts with investors pulling back support for Nvidia Corp. after chief executive Jensen Huang was ousted from his post after reports of several affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. The chipmaker has agreed to buy about US$10 billion worth of shares in Anthropic as part of a US$26 billion private placement concurrent with its IPO, the artificial intelligence model firm’s filings show. Anthropic counts Nvidia as a strategic partner, and has committed tens of billions of dollars to deals securing access to its most advanced chips. Anthropic is looking to bolster demand for the IPO with a campaign of events for prospective investors, including a live-streamed event with its CEO Dario Amodei and JPMorgan Chase & Co CEO Jamie Dimon on Nov 13 , a source familiar with the matter has said. The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.4 trillion, below where some investors expected the company to settle, Bloomberg News reported. Some companies set terms conservatively when they begin formally marketing their IPO, in the expectation that strong demand will push up the final figure and set them up for robust trading in their debuts. Anthropic’s filing on Nov 10 supported the case for AI spending as sales continued to increase. The company reported a revenue run rate of US$81 billion as at Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, the filing showed. Anthropic had a US$65 billion run rate figure at the end of July, Bloomberg News reported. Anthropic defines the metric as annualising consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and subscription-based fees for a single month. Some investors are offering a portion of their Anthropic IPO allocation to other prospective backers, letting them collect additional fees and reduce their risk before trading begins, while others with pre-IPO stakes are marketing them to buyers via special purpose vehicles. Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley are leading Anthropic’s IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filing shows. The stock is expected to trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. BLOOMBERG

events.title: DOJ takes aim at $1.2B in Binance loot as FBI disrupts North Korean scam
events.summary: The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month's $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea's ongoing cryptocurrency theft. The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months. It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks. 900+ faces stolen The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers. Here’s how the attack works. First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible. “You're going to think it's real because it's going to be based on either conversations or interests you've expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles. “They're going to then send you a link to catch up, and it's usually a calendar invite, and it's going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday. The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite. Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told. “When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you're not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you're going to see their face, you're going to see them looking around, you're going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you're going to receive some instructions.” ‘You’re on mute’ as a social engineering vector The text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix. Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam. The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet , which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff. “The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.” Binance heist update The FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group. Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “ sophisticated, multi-stage campaign ” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.” Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department's court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®

events.title: Binance finishes covering US$6.3 billion of stolen customer tokens
events.summary: The crypto exchange said it had restored all crypto-assets lost as at Nov 12. Binance said it has covered all US$6.3 billion of stolen customer tokens after the Oct 29 hack, which the US and analysts blamed on North Korea. The exchange used profits and emergency funds to restore most tokens fast, but some obscure assets took longer to buy back and replace. The hack showed major crypto security risks, with thieves using thousands of wallets, 65,000 transactions and laundering networks to hide the stolen funds. Binance said it has covered all US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) in crypto assets pilfered from customers, marking a capstone to the largest cybertheft in history. The Oct 29 incident , which the US government and analysts have blamed on North Korea, involved not just common cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, but more obscure tokens that took Binance more time to find and purchase. As at Nov 12, the crypto exchange had restored all of them, according to a social media post. “To our users and community: thank you for your patience and understanding,” Binance said in its post on social media platform X. Binance spent a mixture of its profits and other emergency funds to quickly restore most of the stolen tokens in a matter of days, but said a remaining 10% would require more effort. It pledged throughout the process to completely cover lost funds. Hackers used a maze of tools to launder the cryptocurrencies stolen from Binance, including transferring the tokens through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins. The thieves used meme-coins to launder a slice of the proceeds, allowing them to pass through about US$430,000 of the stolen crypto. The automated nature of the transactions was also notable. Within a week of the hack, the laundering effort used more than 20,000 wallets and executed at least 65,000 transactions, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic. That equates to roughly one new wallet being used every 30 seconds and one transaction completed every 10 seconds. Blockchain security firm Chainalysis also recently highlighted the role of Chinese money-laundering networks in cashing out the funds. The enormous cyberheist of the world’s largest crypto exchange came at a time when the digital asset industry is pushing ever more into mainstream finance. It also highlighted the prevalence of cybersecurity challenges – especially since a key vulnerability appears to have been an engineer who was phished through a phoney job offer. Crypto exchanges Bitget and Bybit, as well as companies that helped keep tokens safe with physical hardware, such as Coinkite and Ledger, have all also experienced major incidents recently. events.title: Family Dollar to pay $63m to settle overcharging allegations
events.summary: Dollar-store chain’s settlement with FTC and state officials comes after Guardian exposé of its pricing practices Discount store giant Family Dollar will pay $63m to settle claims by state and federal authorities that it frequently overcharged its customers for milk, diapers, batteries, toilet paper and other household goods. The enforcement action announced Thursday by the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states followed a Guardian investigation that revealed Family Dollar and its larger rival, Dollar General, frequently charge more at checkout than the prices listed on their shelves. Family Dollar failed at least 2,100 price inspections in 20 states from 2022 to late 2025, the Guardian found. In a lawsuit publicly released for the first time as part of Thursday’s settlement, the FTC and the states allege that “Family Dollar knows that it harms consumers by persistently charging prices at the register that are higher than those it advertises”. Despite widespread consumer complaints and increasing government scrutiny, the suit says, the dollar-store chain has failed to put in place adequate safeguards to prevent continued overcharging. “Even now,” the suit asserts, “Family Dollar continues to overcharge customers.” The suit says that it was not until the fall of 2025 – after the company learned of the coming publication of the Guardian’s investigation – that “employees at Family Dollar’s corporate offices devoted more attention and resources to addressing state pricing inspections”. Family Dollar, which says it offers “affordable products and trusted values to families across America”, has roughly 7,000 stores. The company did not deny or admit to the state and federal authorities’ allegations. It previously told the Guardian that “we take customer trust seriously and are committed to ensuring pricing accuracy across our stores … We continue to be focused on providing a consistent and transparent shopping experience.” The Guardian has sent questions to Family Dollar about the settlement and lawsuit. The FTC made undercover visits to Family Dollar and Dollar General stores after the December 2025 publication of the Guardian’s story about the two chains. In January, the agency said, an FTC investigator was overcharged on 15 of the 50 items she purchased at a Family Dollar in Euclid, Ohio. The agency also sifted through large numbers of customer complaints to the company itself as well as to the FTC, state regulators and consumer groups. The lawsuits says that customers from at least seven states reported in January 2025 that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” offer for diapers advertised on shelf tags, its weekly flyer and its mobile app. A consumer in Michigan, for example, said they took a photo of the discount price displayed on the shelf for diapers but that the manager “told me that the price was wrong and he would not sell to me at that price”. A customer in South Dakota, meanwhile, complained they had been charged $25.50 for three packs of Dr Pepper that were listed as “3 for $12”. When they complained, the consumer said, an employee “freaked out on me” and screamed “in front of 20 people” – saying the higher price was correct and the customer was no longer welcome at the store. Under the settlement, Family Dollar will be required to set up a $40m consumer redress fund, provide $20m in discounts to customers and pay more than $3m to state authorities. It also must create a program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices, trains employees to identify pricing problems and promptly corrects overcharges. The settlement comes at a time of growing attention on overcharges at dollar store and convenience store chains. The Family Dollar lawsuit says the consequences of overcharges “fall most heavily on shoppers living on razor-thin margins – families who carefully budget every dollar and rely on accurate, transparent pricing simply to meet their day-to-day needs”. In October, the FTC and 20 states sued Dollar General, the largest dollar-store chain, accusing it of a “staggering” level of “pricing misconduct”. In response, Dollar General said it would “defend this litigation vigorously”. It added that, in the retail market, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer.”

events.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
events.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers. Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business. Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess. Ian Buck Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia. He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development. Chris Malachowsky Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page . "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads. Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership. Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position. René Haas Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports . He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes . Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products. Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition. Tim Cook President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia. Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse. Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation. Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO. Johny Srouji Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg has identified Srouji , Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor. Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices. Nikesh Arora Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks , has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name. Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity. He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography . Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development. Lisa Su AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry. Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, and she was just named " CEO of the Year " by Yahoo! Finance. Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried says Su might relish competing with a weakened Nvidia rather than taking over for Huang. Thomas Kurian Thomas Kurian speaks onstage during Oracle's OpenWorld conference in San Francisco in 2017. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud could also be considered . Kurian oversees cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience with major customers and technology essential to Nvidia's business. Yes, but: His resume does not feature chip design experience. Pat Gelsinger Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger holds up a processor while speaking onstage at the Computex technology conference in Taipei in 2024. Photo: Annabelle Chih/Bloomberg via Getty Images The former Intel CEO boasts decades of semiconductor engineering and leadership experience at one of Nvidia's longtime competitors. events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters ‘Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief’ Microsoft's massive M365 outage stretches past 20 hours as its fixes keep failing 7 hours ago Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era 23 hours ago Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update 1 day ago Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss 1 day ago Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit 1 day ago Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed. The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too. On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.” The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.” The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.” According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.” “We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote. But those efforts may not be working. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted. Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.” But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration. This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ® UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they " initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic." So not usefully healthy at all, then. "We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised. outage microsoft saas microsoft 365 Make us preferred on Google Oh my Word!

events.title: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
events.summary: Alan Milburn will publish his review next week Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to under a radical overhaul of the welfare system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review. As reported in the Times, , external Alan Milburn's year-long report, to be published on Tuesday, is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 16 to 24 year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet". He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants. His report is expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. Disabled people in Scotland can claim the devolved Adult Disability Payment. Instead, under Milburn's plan, under-25s would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit. Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions. Some claimants would receive less under the plans - although the exact amounts will not be clear until early next year, when the government publishes legislation to implement the changes. People can claim Pip to help them with the additional cost of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions. It is available to those both in and out of work. In his interim report, , external Milburn said survey data found that 19% of young people claiming disability or health benefits were in work. Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers. Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate. Milburn told the Times: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system. "But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances. "I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around." Speaking later on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said young people would be given support "when they need it as teenagers rather than leaving them on benefits in their 20s". He added: "The principle that we will be working on is that we will guarantee support for young people and that is the whole basis on which we will proceed." Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare changes last year under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Dame Meg Hillier, who helped spearhead a backbench rebellion against Starmer's reforms, suggested she and her colleagues were broadly supportive this time around. "What happened last year was a cut was being proposed and none of us could explain to people what would happen to them," the Labour MP told the BBC. "Milburn has done some very good work on this so I'm giving him a fair wind," she added. But Bell Ribeiro-Addy, one of the Labour backbenchers who revolted last year, said she was "not sure" she could vote to cut the benefit entitlement of existing claimants. Tom Ashforth, a 19-year-old student at Sheffield Hallam University, receives both components of Pip at the higher rate. He said the financial support helps him manage additional expenses linked to his visual impairment, including prescriptions, mobility aids and accessible learning resources. "If I were to lose it, I would struggle to afford essential things," he said. Student Tom said he relies on the money he gets from Pip to support him through his time at university He said he believes decisions over disability benefits should be made on a case-by-case basis, rather than according to age. "You cannot assume that everyone under the age of 25 is in the same position," he said. In his Times interview, Milburn acknowledged that changing the rules for existing claimants would be "difficult politically" but stressed it was necessary. James Taylor, from disability equality charity Scope, said Pip was a "lifeline" and restricting access to it "won't make young disabled people's extra costs disappear".

events.title: Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang’s ‘scheme’ with Trump
events.summary: Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang . He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees. Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs , with Nvidia employees.) The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers. Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal. “The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license. By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time. But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang. The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia. Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail , and after that, the exec “totally changed.” This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. On Thursday, after his resignation, he agreed. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: SEC enforcement actions drop to multi-decade lows
events.summary: Enforcement actions and penalties levied by the US Securities and Exchange Commission have fallen to multi-decade lows, reflecting a dramatic pullback by Wall Street’s top watchdog. The agency, which has seen budget and staff reductions under the Trump administration, doled out $1.1 billion in penalties last year, the lowest in two decades. The decline drew a rebuke from Democrats who vowed increased scrutiny of its enforcement program in the next Congress, though an SEC official cautioned that “ activity and effectiveness are not the same .” While some suggested the figures were consistent with the agency’s stated aim of promoting more IPOs , “the obvious risk is, with less enforcement, you have a greater risk of fraud ,” a law professor told the Financial Times. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Donald Trump Jr exits as paid adviser for prediction market Kalshi
events.summary: Kalshi announces ‘mutual decision’ as Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump family’s investments Donald Trump Jr is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday. Kalshi described it as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr’s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi’s biggest competitor Polymarket. But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family’s investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets. “We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer,” said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.” The president’s eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years. At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry’s efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts. Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration. 1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket’s latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr’s advisory role with Kalshi.

events.title: Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang
events.summary: News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley —including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation , after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned . As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave. Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure. Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company. That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report. Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate. Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman. On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.” Huang’s resignation left them in shock. The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure. The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says. Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week. Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision. Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer. events.title: Nvidia turmoil could shake up China's AI landscape
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia could spell a sea change in China’s AI fortunes, as heightened scrutiny from Washington threatens to choke off the supply of American compute to mainland tech titans and AI startups. Huang’s extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have helped funnel at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips to China, The Information reported, empowering lawmakers to push for tighter US chip export controls . The prospect of more Nvidia chips staying in the US provides one explanation for hyperscalers’ share rises Thursday . On the flipside, restrictions on American compute could benefit Chinese chipmakers with Beijing pushing more resources toward developing semiconductor self-sufficiency. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Muse can now place calls to US businesses — if you pay
events.summary: After initially testing the feature in September, Meta’s consumer AI agent Muse is now able to place calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. However, only paid subscribers have access to the feature, the company says. Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users , the company said last month, has been working to make consumer AI a mainstream product for everyday users. Placing calls is one of the ways it aims to get there, as it could handle another task on people’s to-do lists. Notes Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs division, the feature could be used to take care of calls people don’t want to make, like those to their cable company, the DMV, or to a restaurant that doesn’t offer online reservations. 🚨MUSE FEATURE ALERT!!!🚨 lots of you have been asking for this one… muse can make phone calls for you! ☎️📞📲 let muse take care of all those calls you don’t want to make. insurance? cable? DMV? dinner res? not your problem anymore. out now to paid subs in the US 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/dsyMNmI2Ub — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) November 12, 2026 Previously, only a select number of Muse early adopters were able to try this feature after asking the AI for access. Now, anyone who pays for Muse can make this type of request. Currently, Muse subscription plans start at $20 per month for 500 million Muse tokens per week. Heavier AI users can opt to pay $100 per month for 3 billion tokens. Muse is not the only AI agent able to place calls to businesses; the startup Instinct has been offering a similar option , as has Google’s Gemini . However, while the AI tools are now certainly capable of handling the task, the reception on the other end of the line can be mixed. Many businesses and receptionists hang up on calls from AI agents as soon as they identify that it’s not a human on the phone. But with AI now better able to mimic a real human voice, being able to tell the difference between a customer and an AI working on the customer’s behalf will get tougher. Despite the challenges, this feature is one that could appeal to consumers who have grown frustrated with the state of customer service over the years. For too long, customers have been forced to navigate complex phone trees, and then sit on hold waiting for a human representative to pick up. If they’re lucky, that person can actually help them, and not transfer them to another department. Now, those consumers could potentially use their AI, with its infinite patience, for this tedious task instead. While calls remain a paid-only feature for the time being, the recently added option to make a Muse email address will soon roll out to free users, Wang said this week. events.title: Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view
events.summary: It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy. As announced Thursday, Google has decided not to make wearables itself, instead turning Samsung and eyeglass makers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Like most of the rest of this generation of smart glasses, none of the nine styles available feature heads-up displays, just cameras and audio feedback from Gemini. Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video. Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times. Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10. Google promises privacy The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them. Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “ pervert glasses .” Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns. As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features. “We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us. The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. Google told us it does save audio recordings and transcripts of conversations with Gemini that users create while wearing the glasses but again insists that those aren’t used to train its AI models. We asked about serving ads too, but Google’s responses didn't address the topic. Lucky for those in range of a pair of Google glasses when wearers ask Gemini to interpret images captured by the device's camera, the tech specs redact the faces of strangers before they’re transmitted. Google told us that face redaction doesn’t apply to photos or videos saved to a wearer’s camera roll. Google’s terms of use require users not to record others without permission, or in "sensitive places." If users ignore that requirement, the company reserves the right to brick their devices. Another restriction means Google won't allow apps that use the glasses for real-time streaming or facial recognition into its Play app store. Given that it remains possible to use the glasses to store recordings of people around a wearer, it’s safe to assume non real-time facial recognition is still a possibility. Creeps will doubtless use such loopholes to behave abominably. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang Is Out. Will Nvidia’s Rivals Cash In?
events.summary: Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang officially resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. He also faces reports of at least two more alleged affairs with Nvidia employees. In this bonus episode, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down how Nvidia’s board turned on its founder, what interim CEO Colette Kress means for the company, and how this moment could be a golden opportunity for Nvidia’s competitors. Articles mentioned in this episode: Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim CEO Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett , Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer , and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger . Write to us at [email protected] . You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too. Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors. Leah Feiger : And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science. Brian Barrett : We're bringing you an extra episode this week because Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang , has officially resigned. His resignation caps a swift, stunning fall for the man who spent more than three decades building a company into the engine of the AI boom . We're going to talk about how a board known for deferring to its celebrity CEO finally changed its tune and who's going to be running Nvidia, at least for now. Let's get started. Just for the room, we released a podcast this morning before this happened and then it happened. So now we're talking again. Leah Feiger : I mean, who doesn't want multiple offerings from the Uncanny Valley crew, Brian? Brian Barrett : It's true. Constant updates. And I guess first, if you want some setup about what happened, you can listen to our previous episode, but I guess I'll first say really quickly, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was selling a lot of chips to—and then a report came out that he had another affair allegedly with someone who reported directly to him at Nvidia, and that feels like the final straw. So we're caught up. Are we surprised still? Zoë Schiffer : I mean, the first thing to say is the company does have rules on the books saying that you're not supposed to have a relationship with a direct report. And so when we talked and it was the Chinese spy, although that is the obviously more scandalous thing that has happened, it also really felt to me like Jensen was going to weather that storm. But then when the second affair came out, that felt like it gave the board a really good excuse if they needed one to say, "OK, we have to stop." Leah Feiger : But he still fought pretty hard to retain his role, right? Zoë Schiffer : I don't think the board wanted him to resign. I don't think Jensen wanted to resign. And now Nvidia has a new CEO in the name of CFO Colette Kress . Tell me about her. Brian Barrett : Interim. So yeah, she'll be there for the time being, but she's been at Nvidia for a long time. She's been there since 2013, which means that she's worked closely with Jensen since before the company was the darling of the AI world back when it was a graphics processor for gaming laptops company. She was at Cisco and Microsoft before that. She's a real industry veteran. I think my understanding is she's really a classic CFO. I don't know if she's a long-term visionary leader of this company, but she knows Nvidia inside and out.

events.title: ‘Win-win’ deal with EU could be done, Andy Burnham says
events.summary: Prime minister says reset could be a deal ‘like the Brexit people thought they were voting for in 2016’ Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”. The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe . At the bilateral summit the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, but the question of tuition fees for European students remains a stumbling block. Burnham said: “I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. “The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.” He said the reset would be about whether we can “take a step back to closer working relationships with Europe”. Burnham added: “We ended up with a far harder Brexit , I think, than people thought they were getting when they went to the polls.” The EU has said the prized food and drink deal and emissions-trading agreement may not enter into force without a deal on tuition fees in which European students would pay domestic rates. Burnham said it was a package deal, but would not be drawn on whether he accepted the link. “I’m going to be fighting hard for these benefits for Britain in the next seven days … they will make a real difference. If I can do anything to address the cost of living crisis, I should be doing it.” He has previously said the food and drink deal, which will ease Brexit red tape, will add 0.4% to British GDP. The prime minister also said David Cameron had been wrong to argue that Britain’s problems had “nothing to do with Brexit”, adding there would be “long nights ahead” to negotiate a reset with the EU before the summit. Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum, told Bloomberg News that Burnham should not seek to bring Britain back into the EU, arguing that the UK’s problems had nothing to do with its exit from the EU. Asked about those remarks, Burnham said: “I think he is wrong to say that the low growth that we’ve had over the last decade has, quote, ‘nothing to do with Brexit’. I would say the evidence says otherwise. “It feels like his intervention is more about unity in the Conservative party than it is about fighting for the British interests.” Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU. He said a deeper relationship would be the outcome of future talks “and it will be in the outcome of that negotiation that then we will take a decision as a cabinet, on what, if anything, comes next”. Earlier on Thursday, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said she wanted to see Britain rejoin the EU, but warned that negotiations would not be easy after the “trauma” of the Brexit years. She said: “I would very much like to see Britain back in Europe, but, of course, we also have in the European Union , a lot of, I would say, trauma from Britain leaving, so the negotiations will not be that easy.” Burnham is expected to make the EU reset the centrepiece of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet on Monday night – though it will range widely across foreign policy challenges. No 10 sources said the speech would be focused on the upcoming Brussels summit – and look ahead to the next stage in 2027 – rather than outline what a more permanent close relationship might look like. Officials at the UK-EU summit will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, expected to focus on a joint migration pact. It could also target collaboration on law enforcement and borders, visas for touring artists, and mutual recognition of qualifications. Ministry of Justice officials are also trying to water down an EU ultimatum on halting the deportation of foreign national offenders. “This is the classic wheeze that the EU always pulls at the last minute of negotiations,” one Whitehall source said. The next week is expected to be fraught with last-minute negotiations. Key will be access to Made in Europe, which has the potential to lock British firms out of continental supply chains and public contracts if no deal is done. Negotiations could be challenging despite the lure of the UK making a potential concession on tuition fees in exchange for inclusion in the Made in Europe legislation . The EU has long said there cannot be a deal on Made in Europe at the summit, because it has yet to finalise its own position. The joint communique for 2027 is expected to call for strengthening efforts between the UK and the most exposed member states to the small boats crisis in the Channel. This will centre on both the EU’s Channel action plan, already in place since June this year, and a possible framework for a wider bespoke EU-UK migration plan.
