events.title: Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients needing specialist care
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts A Regional Express plane at Albany airport in southern WA. ( ABC News: Mark Bennett ) Medical services in regional WA are directly affected by high airfares. Local practices say flight costs are hurting their ability to attract doctors and provide care. The Productivity Commission is due to release its final report on regional airfares next year. Residents and medical professionals say Western Australia's increasing reliance on fly-in,fly-out doctors for specialist care leaves country patients heavily exposed to skyrocketing regional airfares. An interim report from the Productivity Commission released this week found regional Australians are paying high fares to travel within their own state. The commission found short regional flights were on average 173 per cent more expensive per kilometre than major routes. The same flights, often only provided by one operator, are used by medical specialists to visit regional areas across WA. Latrice Porter manages a specialist medical centre in Albany. ( ABC News" Will Corbett ) Great Southern Specialist Centre practice manager Latrice Porter said airfare costs were a growing issue for regional practices. She said locking in visiting staff for her centre in Albany, 400km south of Perth, was becoming increasingly more difficult. "Rising airfare costs, limited flight availability, ongoing airline delays and cancellations are significantly increasing the cost of providing specialist outpatient care (in regional WA)," she said. "The disruptions require clinics to be reorganised, accommodation arrangements amended and patients' schedules adjusted. While remote healthcare such as telehealth is an option, Ms Porter said it is not fit for an "aging population". Latrice Porter says the tyranny of distance makes it hard to find staff willing to travel to regional areas. ( ABC News: Will Corbett ) "When we do provide telehealth services, we have a nurse sit in with the patient. It does take one of our staff members out of action," she said. She believes that if costs keep rising, specialists servicing regional communities will have to start passing the cost of their travel onto patients. While flights for regional residents are capped under a scheme subsidised by the state government, WA's Patient Assisted Travel Scheme (PATS) provides one of the lowest fuel and accommodation rebates in the country. The burden is felt particularly heavily in the Pilbara, where Karratha woman Kim Simpson has been a long-time advocate for cheaper flights. She said the expensive fares placed an unfair burden on regional patients seeking treatment. Kim Simpson has advocated for cheaper flights. ( ABC News: Alistair Bates ) "I've got to go have skin cancers cut off my nose, Mohs surgery; they don't do that in Karratha so I've got to go down to Perth," she said. "If it's something that you could have done in Karratha, but you don't want to wait, then PATS isn't going to cover that, so you've got to cover that fare yourself." The impact of high airfares on families is also something Ms Simpson sees in the north-west. "Lots of babies get born in Karratha, and then you want the grandies to come up, and that's going to cost them well over $2,000," she said. FIFO traffic ensures Karratha Airport is WA's busiest outside Perth. events.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
events.summary: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress Nvidia confirmed in an SEC filing on Thursday that the board accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

events.title: A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs
events.summary: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable , a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude. Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults. Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate. How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers). A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request. "Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style." The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose ," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research. While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition. Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage. Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model. Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper , "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses. Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project , as did numerous social media users. Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse. Chris Donnelly, Searchable CEO and co-founder, endorsed Anthropic's change of terms, suggesting that it could help make human interaction more civil. "For me, Anthropic's policy change is a positive move," Donnelly said in a statement. "It should help people get more out of chatbots, and it helps curb the kind of derogatory behavior that previous research suggests can spill over into how people talk to each other." ®

events.title: Top Democrat opens door to committee term limits
events.summary: A top Democrat is cracking open the door to implementing committee leadership term limits next Congress as lawmakers start to circulate proposals. “I have to look at exactly what it is, but I think that some change might be helpful,” outgoing Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee Chair Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., told Semafor. “Talent isn’t always just about one person in one position. It’s about using the diversity of the caucus. So I hope we can do things so that people can play a lot of roles to help get things done.” Democrats are expected to take up potential changes to their rules in December, when an under-the-radar panel led by Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., will convene and make recommendations to the full caucus ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress next year. Senior committee leaders and members of the Tri-Caucus have historically resisted attempts to implement term limits. With House Democrats on a path to winning roughly 260 seats next Congress, DelBene also took a victory lap, touting the “great candidates” that helped Democrats overperform in 2024 and in 2026. “That absolutely was why we had such a big win,” she said. “I think we actually continued to expand all the way to the end. We added to our districts in play. We added, in fact, we sent out information asking for resources so that we could expand,” she continued. And she argued that a lack of national attention on some districts where Democrats notched surprise wins had actually helped candidates by not attracting big GOP money. “There are a couple folks that weren’t on the map at all who also won, and I think they ran good campaigns, got their messaging out,” DelBene said. “They weren’t inundated with outside money on the Republican side pounding on them, so they were able to get their message through.”

events.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
events.summary: In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks. Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations. “Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.” The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip. One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027. The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells. Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law. DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center. According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery. Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything. TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment. On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg. In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays. Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash. Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.” Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter. Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey.

events.title: ‘A high probability’: Congress pushes tighter export controls following Nvidia scandal
events.summary: The News Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year. In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidia’s now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. That’s raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that there’s a “high probability” that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China. Three measures were included in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation, known as the NDAA, however both Thune and Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., acknowledged there is no deal yet to include them in the final version of the bill currently under negotiation between both chambers. “I give it a better than even chance,” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told Semafor of the possibility of strengthening export controls, which are handled by the Commerce Department. “I understand people have affairs but if you’re going to do it, try not to have an affair with a Chinese spy.” What’s on the table There are three main bills that could be included in the NDAA and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass all three of them “to cut off China’s access to advanced American technology before it’s too late.” The Chip Security Act aims to prevent illicit smuggling of advanced AI chips to foreign adversaries, partly by verifying their location once they’ve been shipped out. The MATCH Act closes loopholes around chipmaking equipment and export rules in allied countries. And the AI Overwatch Act would make it so chip sales are treated more like foreign arms sales and give Congress oversight of how Commerce approves or disapproves a license to sell chips to a “country of concern,” including China. Johnson told reporters Thursday that there’s “a developing consensus in Congress” around more chip restrictions, calling it “an important position to take, especially in light of recent developments.” And Democrats like Jeffries have signaled their support for putting the AI-related provisions into the NDAA, as have some Republicans. “I think the NDAA does provide us an opportunity to put guardrails around AI” or export restrictions, said Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said he’d otherwise defer to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the incoming House Armed Services chair. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., argued the Nvidia debacle “reinforces” the need for Congress to include more export controls in the defense bill, adding that there’s “strong demand” to do so even as there’s no final agreement on what it will entail. “Which plan takes priority in the final product, I don’t know yet. I think there’s several different strategies to be vetted yet,” Rounds said. Why this year is different During last year’s NDAA fight, the GAIN AI Act from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Jim Banks, R-Ind., an earlier version of the AI Overwatch Act, made it into the Senate version of the NDAA but got dropped from the House version after pressure from Nvidia, the broader semiconductor industry, and the White House (including then-AI adviser David Sacks). Congress did include some investment controls, but senators in both parties wanted to do more. This year, the bills are much further through the process, buoyed unexpectedly by the Nvidia scandal and gaining momentum among GOP leaders, one Senate Democratic aide told Semafor. Anthropic has publicly supported all three bills, and OpenAI has been warming up to them as well after initially being reticent to support the proposals. Nvidia hasn’t stood alone in its opposition to the bills — the broader tech industry has also lobbied against them, with the Information Technology Industry Council arguing they would “undermine the American tech stack.” But Congress will feel more emboldened to act than ever giving the security risks exposed by the controversy. Still, the defense bill, one of the few pieces of legislation that passes on an annual basis, could be imperiled by Democratic efforts to add provisions to sunset the war in Iran. Many in the party are pushing to use the must-pass legislation or a December government funding deadline as leverage over President Donald Trump, which could poison Republican support for the bills. “We have leverage. Take when the appropriations bills run out. I want the war in Iran stopped. I think we should put provisions into that bill, into the NDAA for that matter to stop it,” said Smith, the incoming House Armed Services Committee chair. Democrats face tough decisions about how hard to push for those provisions now and risking a government shutdown or the failure of the defense bill, especially when they could put the legislation together on their own terms next year when they take control of the House and Senate. Room for Disagreement Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said Congress has already done “a lot before more than people probably realize” on restricting chip exports to China and that they need to think before they do more. There’s also worry about going too far and inducing more Chinese manufacturing of chips by denying China technology. “This is a balance. Until someone comes up with a better construct, we need to put very strong export controls on the most powerful computer chips. That seems like a no-brainer to me,” said Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind. “Then the question is, how robust in terms of processing power can those chips be that we sent to them? … I don’t think it’s formulaic.” Burgess, Nicholas, and Ashley’s view Scandals move Congress and boy is this a scandal. And it comes at the perfect time for supporters of stricter chip curbs on China. We’d be surprised if more export restrictions aren’t law in some fashion by the end of the year after the shocking downfall of Huang and national security concerns raised by his indiscretions.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Meanwhile, a group of nonprofits sue AI giants and cite AI-driven cyberattacks Alibaba's Qwen3.8 re-educated with a more Western worldview 12 hours ago OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models 2 days ago Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory 2 days ago Stanford's century-long AI study admits it's already out of date 3 days ago Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques 3 days ago OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. events.title: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test
events.summary: Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere. Now, Mississippi faces a new question: Was Scott Colom's victory a once-in-a-generation breakthrough, or the beginning of an era of Black political power? Driving the news: Colom's defeat of incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith broke a barrier that had stood since Reconstruction. Mississippi was the first state to send Black senators to Congress, before violence and disenfranchisement stripped Black residents of their political power. In Colom's race, Democrats gained ground in 75 of the state's 82 counties, Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, told Axios. "It wasn't just a fluke of super high turnout in one particular region," he said. "Scott Colom's victory can signal that maybe Mississippi is ready to govern differently." The big picture: During the Great Migration , roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South to escape discrimination and seek better opportunities. Many Black Mississippians built political power in Northern cities such as Chicago, said Keneshia Grant, a Great Migration expert at Howard University. For many, the question became, "should we go and try for a better life in these other places ... or should we stay and fight where we are?" Grant said. "It was about economic opportunity, but I also think it was about terrorism too," Cassandra Overton Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, told Axios, pointing to the lynchings that drove families away. Welchlin left Mississippi for graduate school and considered staying away. "I did not want to come back to Mississippi because it is hard here," she told Axios. Mentors encouraged her to return. She did, eventually becoming a voting rights organizer. Zoom in: "What Colom did is he really jazzed up his base. He didn't run from them," King said. "His campaign style and that strategy can certainly serve as a model" for future campaigns. Welchlin pointed to years of "nickeling and diming, doing organizing work to make sure that people had what they need to turn out the vote." Between the lines: Colom rode a Democratic wave and discontent with the Trump administration's economic policies, but those conditions may be difficult to recreate, said Andra Gillespie, who studies Black voter behavior at Emory University. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi's population, while most white voters favor Republicans. Unlike Georgia, Mississippi lacks the same diverse potential Democratic coalition. "[T]he conditions that we see this year are probably not going to be the new normal," Gillespie says. "It'd be way too early to diagnose that there's a realignment happening." Welchlin also cautioned that one historic victory doesn't mean Mississippi's racial barriers have disappeared. "We understand here in Mississippi that racism ain't over, ... Racism is still very much embedded in everything from our policies to our elections." What we're watching: Mississippi holds elections for governor, other statewide offices and state legislators in November 2027, testing whether Colom's coalition can hold. "For the first time in forever, Mississippi Democrats will go into an election with momentum," King said. The bottom line: Welchlin hopes Colom's victory changes how Black Mississippians view their futures: "I believe ... this election has given people hope that maybe I can stay here and be that change." events.title: Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women
events.summary: The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress , the new interim CEO of Nvidia —but her predecessor, Jensen Huang , failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic. Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry. We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod. As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts. He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive. Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure. As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy. Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls. events.title: AI industry execs brace for future without leading hype man, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
events.summary: Tech industry insiders awoke Thursday morning with an unfamiliar, and somewhat alarming notion to contemplate: life without Jensen Huang. Huang’s abrupt resignation as CEO leaves one of the world’s most valuable companies without the leader who has steered it for the past 33 years; the person who almost singlehandedly transformed Nvidia from a small maker of video game graphics chips into the driving force of the AI boom.  “NVIDIA’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” Stephanie Balaouras, Forrester’s VP, group research director, told Fortune .  The importance of Nvidia, and of Huang, to the AI industry extends well beyond the company’s own P&L statement. In addition to being the leading maker of the GPU chips powering AI services like ChatGPT and Claude, Nvidia has become the AI industry’s “central bank” financing scores of other companies. And then there’s Huang’s unique standing as AI’s senior statesman and cheerleader on everything from AI regulation to industrial policy. Whether the AI industry turns out to have lost its most famous champion with the ignominious exit of Huang and his famous black leather coat, or a more crucial, Jenga-like piece may be the most important economic question to be answered in the coming weeks and months. “Obviously Nvidia is more than Jensen Huang, but he kind of championed a whole range of investments,” a VC investor focused on early-stage companies told Fortune . “There is a question around whether the pace of investment in AI and the size of the amounts of capital going into companies can be continued. Because by any stretch of the imagination, it’s been quite extreme,” the investor said. In the immediate aftermath of the news, the stock market appears to be keeping its composure. While shares of Nvidia were down 6.3% in midday trading on Thursday, and certain AI-linked stocks took a hit, the broader market reaction was relatively muted, with the Nasdaq down only 95 points.  But with spending on AI and data centers so important to the broader U.S. economy, the extent of the potential fallout from the Nvidia shakeup is difficult to overstate. Looming largest on the horizon is Anthropic’s widely anticipated initial public offering , scheduled to occur next week. The Anthropic IPO (along with OpenAI’s IPO expected in 2027) represent make-or-break moments for the AI industry—closely watched events that will serve as proxies for the health, and momentum, of the AI business. If nothing else, one startup founder told Fortune , the Nvidia drama raises the stakes for Anthropic’s upcoming IPO: “If the Anthropic IPO doesn’t go well and if the OpenAI IPO [down the line] doesn’t go well, there’s a question of: Is there a path to profitability for any players in the AI space?” Anthropic is seeking to raise upwards of $60 billion in the offering slated for November 18, giving the five-year old AI company a valuation that could exceed $1.4 trillion when it makes its expected Wall Street debut next week. Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, argued that investors will recognize the strength in Anthropic’s business, regardless of the Nvidia shakeup.  “From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong and as good a position as it was before this news came out,” Alomar said. “I’m not sure it’ll have a massive impact on them. Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need,” he said.  Last stop for the money train? Anthropic’s business prospects are closely intertwined with those of the cloud providers, which provide the data centers and compute capacity to train and run AI models like Claude. (According to Anthropic’s S-1 filing, it has roughly $900 billion in compute spending commitments over the next several decades.) While the tech giants like Alphabet , Amazon , and Microsoft have the wherewithal to ride out whatever turbulence is caused by the changes at Nvidia, the situation may be trickier for the smaller “neo-cloud” companies —many financed by Nvidia—that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the computing power. Huang has championed these neo-cloud companies because it was good for business and the company’s influence, Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock. “He’d rather have 300 small customers who are dependent on him than three massive ones who you can’t negotiate with,” he said. With Nvidia CFO Colette Kress now serving as interim CEO, the company’s attitude towards neo-clouds could shift. According to a report in The Information on Thursday, Kress has occasionally pushed back against Huang’s deals in the AI ecosystem, including a deal to backstop $250 billion in credit for an OpenAI datacenter project. The “Nvidia money train” that has kept parts of the market that propped up could come to an end, said one venture capital partner invested in numerous AI startups. “ The idea that they could count on Nvidia for future financing is unlikely.” Shares of CoreWeave one of the leading neocloud providers were down 7.5% on Thursday, while Nebius Group, another neo-cloud company which gave a lighter-than-expected sales forecast during its quarterly earnings on Thursday, were down 18%.  Investors are likely to look harder at the numbers Huang used to justify the complex web of investments. Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, expects investors and policymakers alike may start re-examining “Jensen math.” Incoming: regulation U.S. policy towards data centers could also come in for harsher treatment, particularly after last week’s midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly registered their opposition to having the facilities built in their communities.  Huang gave much of the industry credibility, even amid the backlash to datacenters. He was well-liked and not seen as a polarizing political figure, said Goldberg, of Seaport Research. But with Huang gone, the data center industry becomes “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” he said Goldberg.  Similarly, lawmakers advocating stricter regulation of AI technology, both the large language models as well as the chips that power the models, now have a much stronger hand. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI. But his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has destroyed his credibility on the regulatory issues.  “This guarantees new export controls,” Ed Mills, policy analyst at investment firm Raymond James, said of the spy scandal that contributed to Huang’s downfall. “It was extremely likely before the scandal and this is the accelerant to push it over the finish line.” Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are currently attached to the defens

events.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
events.summary: Jensen Huang: in the spotlight and out of a job. Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.” Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies . She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair . And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026. The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked. Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose. Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .” As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors. The beauty stratagem of Ancient China “Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems ,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership. The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience. Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history. In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge. According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu ,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs. The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu. A 19th-century etching depicting Zheng Dan and Xi Shi. Wikimedia Commons Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery. Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly. A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms ,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature. It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo. The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor. The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap .” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War . Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu . The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s. Bernard Boursicot and Shi Pei Pu in the dock during an espionage trial in Paris in May 1986. Laurent Maous/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang , a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office. Why Jensen Huang is strategically important Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power. Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development . Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers. From Beijing’s perspective , advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition. This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang. However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation. events.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
events.summary: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

events.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
events.summary: Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ® Updated to add on November 31: Lego said on Friday that BrickLink is back online after acknowledging the "confusion and uncertainty" the downtime caused among Lego fans. A statement made via the BrickLink website confirmed that "some" usernames and IP addresses were accessed, as were "a very small number" of email addresses. "We have already emailed members whose BrickLink usernames or emails were accessed with further information," it said . "Based on our investigation, passwords and payment information were not accessed. You do not need to take any action at this time. We have addressed the issue identified through our investigation and will continue to monitor the platform closely." The site is back online, although its Studio Forum remains down, and the company said it will provide more information on this front "over the coming days." BrickLink will also waive sellers' fees for November and December as a token of appreciation for putting up with the downtime and disruption.

events.title: Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis
events.summary: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead. And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas. A marred reputation One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea. It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer. Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom. After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful . One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country. The consequences of controversy When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself. Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat. Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries. Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. Regardless, with Nvidia’s reputation marred and its future shrouded in uncertainty, once loyal customers may be more willing to explore alternative providers. There are certainly plenty to choose from. Amid a surge in custom AI chips from the likes of Broadcom, Marvel, and others, Nvidia’s main advantage wasn’t so much technological as it was simply considered a safe bet. AMD is the most obvious winner here. As we reported earlier this year , the House of Zen’s GPU tech has already surpassed Nvidia’s, at least on paper. What’s more, the company has a long and unblemished relationship serving the US government. AMD’s chips now power two of the Department of Energy’s three largest and most sensitive supercomputers. Meanwhile, hyperscalers with sufficient cashflow – think Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta – may seek to insulate themselves from Huang’s fallout by investing more heavily in homegrown silicon and offering it to customers. Then there's the threat from the man himself. Huang's ambitions and influence are such that he's unlikely to fade into obscurity. He may disappear from the spotlight while things blow over, but it’s a pretty sure bet that he’ll pop up at a new company eventually, and will still have enough sway to poach some of Nvidia’s top engineers. ®

events.title: SA gives green light for gas to help power future data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts SA government gives green light for gas to help power future data centres The proposed data centre at Bundey in SA's Mid North would require up to 800 megawatts of electricity to operate. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) South Australia's energy minister says he is "absolutely fine" for gas-generated power to be used to help supply energy to proposed AI data centres across the state. The SA Greens leader says it is a "total backflip" by the state government. Plans are underway for at least four major data centres in SA. The South Australian government has been accused of doing a "backflip" by allowing gas-generated power to be used to supply energy for proposed AI data centres. Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis has told the ABC that he was "absolutely fine" with gas being used to help run the new large-scale centres that are proposed in various regional locations around the state. "We support the idea of gas use to firm data centres the same way we support the idea of gas firming our renewable energy right now," Mr Koutsantonis said. The government's own Data Centre Strategy, released just under five months ago, focused on the promotion of the state's renewable energy sector. That strategy document stated: "South Australia can produce the clean energy needed, at scale and on time, to power the artificial intelligence revolution". But Mr Koutsantonis said that data centres needed large amounts of energy continuously, and that gas could be used to "firm" up or guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres "if the sun stops shining or wind stops blowing". Tom Koutsantonis says gas would guarantee ongoing electricity to data centres. ( ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke ) As part of the strategy, new data centres would be required to supply their own power. Developer Quantum DC, who yesterday announced it was pausing its plans for a 1,200-megawatt data centre at Tungkillo , had previously estimated about 20 per cent of the energy it needed would be supplied by a gas power station to be built on a section of its 220-hectare Adelaide Hills block. The company had proposed that the rest of the centre's electricity requirement would be supplied by renewables. Apart from Tungkillo, plans are underway for at least three other major data centres in SA. Australian company Iren proposed a $10 billion 800MW facility at Bundey, near Robertstown in the state's Mid North, while AI giant Firmus previously announced plans for data centres near Tailem Bend and Port Augusta. Kirsty Bevan says using gas is a step backwards. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) Conservation Foundation of SA chief executive Kirsty Bevan said the use of gas to supply energy to SA's data centres would be a "step backwards" for the government and the climate. "South Australia has led the nation on renewable energy and is aiming for 100 per cent net renewable electricity by 2027, but that progress could be undermined by proposals to lock in more gas," she said. Ms Bevan said using gas would also be ignoring "community expectations". "With energy storage and other backup technologies available to support grid reliability, expanding gas supply for data centres and AI infrastructure is a step backwards," she said. When asked generally about the potential environmental impacts of using gas for data centres, Mr Koutsantonis said: "Well if you don't let them use gas, they'll use diesel or they'll use coal." Robert Simms is urging the SA government to reconsider its position. ( ABC News: Tony Hill ) SA Greens leader Rob Simms said green-lighting gas projects was a major step away from the government's previous policy. "This is outrageous," Mr Simms said. "We don't need more dirty gas here." "It's a total backflip from where the government was just a few months ago when they gave an assurance to the people of South Australia that these data centres would be self-sufficient, they'd be reliant on renewables." Mr Simms urged the government to reconsider its position, and proposed a moratorium on the construction of data centres in SA. In a statement, an SA government spokesperson said the Greens' suggestion of a policy backflip was "nonsensical". "Allowing large new energy demand without requiring it to be matched by new firmed renewable energy, as suggested by the Greens, would be a recipe for a more expensive and less reliable system," the spokesperson said. Political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development , and united in the upper house to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres.

events.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
events.summary: Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself . Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios. Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including: What will the investigations uncover? Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences. Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee. Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public. Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it. Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter. Who takes the permanent role as CEO? CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally and we are big fans of her strategically," tech bull Dan Ives wrote Thursday in a research note. Prediction markets point to Nvidia hyperscaling tech exec Ian Buck as the the leading candidate, but the political ramifications of Nvidia's position in the global economy may demand someone with more experience with geopolitics. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook, whom Ives also floated, but Kalshi traders rate that as a 1 in 25 shot. Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble? Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars — and Huang is at the center of that vast flywheel, Axios' Zachary Basu writes . Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says. "This Nvidia story is going to take a little air out of the balloon for the Anthropic IPO," he says. The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips: "The company was never the source of AI demand. It has been supplying the capacity to meet that demand," which remains "enormous," he wrote today. Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry? Competitors like AMD, Alphabet and Intel could benefit if chips customers are soured on working with Nvidia. "When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: did the clients sign with the banker — or with the bank? Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market," writes Mark Malek, CIO at Siebert Financial. What's the floor for Nvidia's stock? Nvidia shares were down another 5.7% just before 3pm Thursday and are now down 27% over the last month, having lost about $1 trillion in value. "With this kind of leadership uncertainty, it's very difficult to predict where shares go over the next several trading sessions," writes Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. "Sometimes huge news catalysts like this take all technicals out of the equation." The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang? Elon Musk has already hinted he could hire the former Nvidia chief as he moves toward a possible merger of SpaceX and Tesla . But it'll be hard for anyone to hire Huang unless and until the FBI probe in particular is resolved. The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

events.title: Master carver to engrave crystals from last year's New Year's Eve ball sold as mementos
events.summary: People who find themselves at the site of the iconic New Year's Eve ball drop can purchase one of the 5,280 Waterford crystals from the Constellation Ball that dropped in New York City last year in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026 Dropped in Times Square on New Year’s Eve, the Constellation Ball was created with 5,280 Waterford crystals that incorporated three different designs to represent life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness in honor of the nation's 250th birthday in 2026. On Thursday, people can buy one of those crystals and get their names engraved on it as a memento. They will be replaced with new crystals to ring in 2027 with a theme yet to be announced. It takes about three days to make each crystal by hand for the roughly 12-foot (3.7-meter) geodesic sphere that weighs 12,350 pounds (5,602 kilograms). The process involves the design, molding, kilning and the finishing of each crystal. Waterford, a longtime luxury crystal brand from Ireland, has designed the New Year’s Eve ball’s crystals for over 25 years. Some new crystals are swapped in every year. Richard White, a master cutter for Waterford, flew to New York City to engrave the crystals that vary in size from 1.5 to 4 inches in diameter. White will use a small electronic pen with a diamond tip to engrave names on the small crystal pieces Thursday. “To be actually here and to be up close, personal with it, is a real excitement for me,” White said of seeing the completed ball. Delfin Ortiz, general manager and senior vice president of One Times Square, the 26-story building from which the annual ball drops, said the crystals are part of “tomorrow's history.” Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE A New Year’s Eve ball was first dropped in Times Square in 1907. Built by a young immigrant metalworker named Jacob Starr, the 700-pound (318-kilogram), 5-foot (1.52-meter) diameter ball was made of iron and wood and featured 100 25-watt light bulbs. Nine versions of the ball have been featured in the century-plus since that first celebration. The only years no ball drop occurred were 1942 and 1943, when the city instituted a nightly “dimout” during World War II to protect itself from attacks. Crowds instead celebrated the new year with a moment of silence followed by chimes rung from the base of One Times Square. One Times Square began offering crystals for purchase last year, though Thursday marks the first time they will be engraved.
