events.title: Only four government ministers have saved money this year. Here's who
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Only four ministers have achieved net savings this year, budget papers show Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher have flagged further savings in the mid-year budget update. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Four federal ministers have achieved net savings in their portfolios this financial year, according to ABC analysis of the May budget. The most significant savings were in the infrastructure portfolio. The government is searching for savings ahead of the mid-year budget update, but has not committed to a net save. Only four out of more than 20 government ministers have managed to save more than they have spent this year, pointing to challenges across the board as the cabinet works to rein in spending. Stung by the accusation from the opposition and some commentators that the federal budget is worsening inflation and fuelling interest rate hikes, ministers have indicated they are searching for fresh savings ahead of December's budget update. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has indicated the government is looking "across the board" for savings, but has declined to commit to a "net" saving — that is, big enough to offset any new spending. A net save of $8.2 billion was achieved in the May budget, measured over the full five years of budget forecasts. But the government failed to achieve a net save for this financial year, when inflation pressure is most acute. Looking at this year alone, the government spent $8.7 billion more than it saved. It also raised an extra $2.2 billion in revenue, meaning the budget was $6.5 billion worse off overall. Only Infrastructure Minister Catherine King, Education Minister Jason Clare, Agriculture Minister Julie Collins and Treasurer Jim Chalmers achieved net savings for the 2026-27 financial year, according to an ABC analysis of budget papers. Of these, only Ms King's portfolio had substantial net savings with $1.3 billion overall, mostly from the decision not to proceed with programs including Inland Rail. The largest net spend for 2026-27 was Health Minister Mark Butler, whose total includes measures the government describes as "unavoidable", including the listing of new PBS medicines and a major hospitals deal. This was despite some savings from the NDIS and the private health insurance rebate for older Australians, which is yet to win support in parliament. Defence Minister Richard Marles and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, whose responsibilities include Services Australia, both spent in excess of $1 billion. Catherine King achieved the largest net save this year, with nearly $1 billion. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The government has offered few specifics about areas it will target for mid-year budget savings, but Senator Gallagher confirmed last week the public service would be subject to "belt tightening". The Albanese government has overseen a significant expansion in public service headcount, from 173,558 before it came to office to 217,256 as of May, spread across multiple portfolios. The largest individual increases were the National Disability Insurance Agency (more than 5,000 new staff) and Services Australia (more than 4,000). Labor fought former Liberal leader Peter Dutton's bid to reverse that increase during the 2025 election campaign, but has made quiet moves of its own to contain public service spending since then. Peter Dutton campaigned unsuccessfully to return public service numbers to their pre-pandemic levels. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) In 2024, it opted not to give departments any extra money to cover the wage rises in a new pay agreement worth 11.2 per cent over three years. That effectively required departments to find 11.2 per cent of savings elsewhere. Several subsequently offered redundancy rounds last financial year, with at least 1,500 redundancies confirmed but an exhaustive tally not yet available. But an ABC analysis of budget papers show departmental staffing costs still increased by $792 million last year, only partly offset by a $687 million reduction in "supplier" costs, such as consultants. Annual reports indicate further cost overruns are likely. Government won't promise net savings Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation. Earlier this year, ministers asked all departments and agencies to identify 5 per cent of their resourcing that was "low priority". Senator Gallagher emphasised at the time that this was meant as a savings shortlist, not as a 5 per cent overall cut.

events.title: David Jones closures present 'unique opportunity' for big shopping centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Economic pain of outer suburbs accelerated demise of David Jones, experts say Economic pain felt in outer suburban areas could have fast-tracked the problems that overtook David Jones. ( ABC News: Taryn Southcombe ) David Jones is closing 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the majority to close in metropolitan outer suburbs. Property analyst Howard Penny says outer suburbs were disproportionately feeling mortgage stress. According to retail expert Gary Mortimer, a changing business model is forcing major suburban centres to adapt to survive. Acute economic pain being felt in the outer suburbs may have accelerated the demise of David Jones, according to property and retail experts. The 188-year-old shopping giant announced on Wednesday that it would close 19 stores across Australia and New Zealand, with the vast majority being in metropolitan outer suburban areas. Among those are stores in areas like Hornsby, Parramatta and Campbelltown in Sydney, Maribyrnong and Glen Waverley in Melbourne, and Robina on the Gold Coast. Howard Penny says retail challenges reflect negative consumer impacts in emerging areas. ( ABC News ) Howard Penny is the head of Real Estate and Infrastructure Research for Australia and New Zealand at Citigroup. He said that was a symptom of the financial strain in those areas after five interest rate hikes this year. S&P Global Ratings data this week revealed that households in some outer suburbs in Sydney, Melbourne and south-east Queensland are more than twice as likely to be experiencing mortgage stress than the national average. "It's new home buyers, it's young families, et cetera, and naturally the areas where these types of consumers are, are in the newer areas further out in the cities," Mr Penny said. The announcement has also raised questions about how large suburban shopping centres will fare losing a large anchor tenant. Nine of the stores that are closing are in Westfield shopping centres, owned by Scentre Group. Scentre had offered David Jones discounted rents to continue trading, after the department store stopped paying rent in September. Howard Penny said there was likely to be a short-term impact on Scentre Group, but that was unlikely to threaten the viability of its shopping centres in the outer suburbs. "Although we are, in the short term, a little concerned as to the short-term impacts on income and rent due to the disruption, in the medium term, we remain optimistic, and we believe that in 18 months, these shopping centres may actually look even stronger on the back of this," he said. After Wednesday's news, Scentre Group chief executive Eliott Rusanow was similarly confident. "Our business is practically full, with occupancy at 99.8 per cent and strong demand for space," Mr Rusanow said in a statement. "We have a unique opportunity at 17 Westfield destinations to introduce and grow local and international brands and experiences that our customers want." Gary Mortimer says the fall of David Jones comes as major suburban centres shift. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Gary Mortimer is a professor at the Queensland University of Technology who specialises in retail and marketing. He said the closures represent the changing business model of major suburban centres. "A big centre once might have included an anchor tenant, be that a department store, and possibly a discount department store and a supermarket," Professor Mortimer said. "Today, those centres have changed. Those centres are now underpinned by precincts: health precincts, services precincts, libraries, gyms, childcare, car wash facilities and a whole wide range of experiences and offers." He said the changes in the composition and socio-economic pressures in outer suburban areas require shopping centres to adapt to survive. "As the demography of those suburbs changes and the centre now is better representative of a Kmart, Target, Big W discount department store than a traditional department store, I think they'll have no problems filling that space," Dr Mortimer said.

events.title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
events.summary: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.” While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement. The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level. In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode. In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question. Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains. The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode. Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models. The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens. On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out. In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform. events.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
events.summary: Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results. Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research. Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically. Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult. Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords. Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular. Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets. “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.” Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals. Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers. The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents. This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic. events.title: Salmon deaths at 'eye-watering' levels in Macquarie Harbour
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mortality data for salmon farms in Macquarie Harbour revealed after RTI documents release Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour. ( Huon ) It's been revealed that almost 2,000 tonnes of salmon died in Macquarie Harbour over a 15-month period. Salmon Tasmania says it equates to about 8 per cent of fish farmed there during that time. The EPA is yet to issue new licences for companies to continue operating in the harbour. Almost 2,000 tonnes of farmed salmon died over a 15-month period in Macquarie Harbour on Tasmania's west coast, new data shows. The Environment Protection Authority's (EPA) mortality data was obtained by conservation group Environment Tasmania, which submitted the Right to Information (RTI) request in December last year. But it took until this week for the information to be made public after salmon companies sought reviews of the EPA's decision to release the data, as they are entitled to do under RTI laws. The EPA regulates 10 salmon leases in the harbour. ( Supplied: Tassal ) The data shows a total of 1,907 tonnes of farmed salmon died in the harbour between October 2024 and December 2025. "Salmon has no place in Macquarie Harbour," Environment Tasmania campaigner Jess Coughlan said. Man who burned shoebox of tax records fined for resulting bushfire Tasmanian premier apologises for 'outcome' of Christmas post AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community deal Salmon farm antibiotic use impact 'completely unfair' cray fisher says Industry group Salmon Tasmania said up to 9,500 tonnes of salmon can be farmed in the harbour each year under a feed cap. The mortality data was obtained by Environment Tasmania. ( Supplied: Tassal ) Environment Tasmania said this would infer about 15 per cent of the total maximum haul had died. But Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said the maximum tonnage could not be used to determine a "mortality rate". "Mortality is measured by counting the number of fish that died, not their weight," Dr Whittington said. The new figures come after a separate RTI in late 2024 showed a total of 1,149 tonnes of salmon had died over a seven-month period between September 2023 and March 2024. Monthly data on salmon deaths doesn't show locations Since 2025, the EPA has released monthly data showing the total tonnage of mortality among salmon farms across the state, but it is not broken down by location. Macquarie Harbour, which is the only habitat for the endangered Maugean skate , makes up only a small portion of the salmon industry's annual production across Tasmania. Dr Whittington said mortality was "unfortunately part of all livestock farming". He said there was no standard "mortality rate" for farmed salmon. Salmon Tasmania CEO John Whittington said mortality was measured by numbers of fish not weight. ( ABC News: Madeleine Rojahn ) "As with other forms of farming, survival rates or losses vary by year, location and season," Dr Whittington said. "Salmon growers employ a range of strategies to maintain fish health and maximise survivability, including selective breeding, vaccination, specialised diets and growing fish larger on land so they spend less time at sea." The new RTI data did not include details about what caused the deaths of the salmon. Salmon Tasmania said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused other mass mortalities. ( ABC News: Sophie Zoellner ) But Dr Whittington said Macquarie Harbour was free of the bacterial disease that had caused mass mortality in salmon pens in other parts of the state. As such, he said the industry had not applied to use the antibiotic florfenicol in Macquarie Harbour. Ms Coughlan said there had been "near complete opacity surrounding operations where disease and mortality are concerned" in the harbour. The EPA regulates salmon farming at 10 leases within Macquarie Harbour. However, the environmental licences issued to the three salmon companies that operate there expired almost a year ago. A map showing the location of salmon farm licences in Macquarie Harbour. ( ABC News: Magie Khameneh ) Prior to the expiration, the companies applied for new licences, meaning they can continue to operate pending the outcome of their applications. The EPA told the ABC it was continuing to assess the environmental conditions in Macquarie Harbour to inform future regulatory decisions about salmon farming in the region. events.title: Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’
events.summary: With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms. In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc . But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products. The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028. "I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said. Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance. "My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot." All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio. Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you." They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir , while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants. Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power , and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority ." At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement ," he wrote in his shareholder letter. It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process. Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company. He told CNBC: " If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir . Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection." In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough . "And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet. Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight. Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®

events.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs B ritain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry. The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech. The conventional wisdom is that if startups are struggling to grow, the problem must be that they lack capital. That is why Rachel Reeves, as chancellor, wanted pension funds to invest in UK assets. But the paper says that this risks making things worse. Putting cash into startups risks inflating eventual sale prices without securing British ownership or control. The London School of Economics’ Nils Peters and David Kampmann expose a circular logic. The UK lacks tech giants that can acquire successful startups, but selling those startups overseas helps perpetuate that problem. The authors say US and European incumbents won big from the exit of the 38 biggest UK VC-backed tech firms between 2010 and 2023, including businesses at the forefront of AI, fintech and biotechnology. Selling British technology companies abroad can enrich investors while thwarting ambitions to build domestic champions. The social costs also matter. A system geared towards maximising capital gains favours businesses that promise lucrative exits. The paper argues that this has encouraged surveillance technologies, from wearables to AI chatbots, and exploitative gig platforms , concentrating wealth among a few rather than delivering social benefits. Gordon Brown is right: Britain should retain ownership of its innovations. But there is a difference between financial returns and industrial development – and improving the former doesn’t necessarily deliver the latter. Although industrial policy has returned rhetorically in the west, this has not translated into meaningful policy. The Common Wealth paper suggests that is a mistake and argues for democratic control over innovation, with investment directed towards social purposes. The paper’s preferred capitalism is one that is historically associated with the global south: curbing extractive intermediaries, limiting foreign capital and building domestic capacity. India’s publicly funded space programme and Ethiopia’s state-owned airline show how sustained public investment can support homegrown capabilities rather than hastily readying businesses for sale. Most daringly, Brazil linked universal healthcare for 215 million people to industrial policy, using public purchasing, laboratories and technology transfer. The payoff came during the pandemic: by August 2021, almost three-quarters of Covid vaccine doses administered had been produced at home. Brazil shows that a state can finance, research and produce a universal healthcare system that creates employment and productive capacity. It is surely a powerful idea that providing for people could be a way of sustaining output. Making the fulfilment of social needs a motor of economic development would give Labour a purpose beyond managing scarcity. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: Australia defends climate record after Greta Thunberg's 'snail' swipe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chris Bowen seeks pragmatic consensus heading into final COP31 talks Chris Bowen rejects suggestions Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter has damaged its standing in the negotiations. ( Reuters: Murad Sezer ) Chris Bowen has rejected criticism of Australia's climate leadership over its continued coal and gas exports. The climate change and energy minister says countries must be realistic about the transition to cleaner energy. Negotiations at COP31 will intensify next week as Australia seeks agreement on electrification and climate finance. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen has defended Australia's credibility as a global climate negotiator and signalled a pragmatic approach to securing a deal at COP31 amid pressure for a stronger international commitment to move away from fossil fuels. Mr Bowen has questioned why the Coalition sought to diminish Australia's role on the world stage and singled out Opposition Leader Angus Taylor for attacking expenses introduced during his own time as minister. "Does he want one lump of hypocrisy or two with his coffee?" Mr Bowen told the ABC in an interview on the sidelines of COP31 in Türkiye. Australia holds the presidency of negotiations at the summit, putting Mr Bowen at the centre of efforts to secure agreement between more than 190 countries on the next steps to tackle climate change. "My job is to steer consensus to the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow," he said. Anthony Albanese (right) and Chris Bowen have defended Australia's decision to expand coal and gas production. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) That task has become more complicated as momentum builds behind a renewed push for a plan to transition away from fossil fuels. Fossil fuel road map lacks consensus Despite efforts by Brazil and others to advance work on a global road map for moving away from coal, oil and gas, the COP31 agenda remains predominantly focused on electrification, adaptation and climate finance. Mr Bowen described the fossil fuels transition as a "challenging issue" and noted the failure to get consensus on fossil fuels at last year's COP showed the enthusiasm of some governments was no guarantee of a collective agreement. He said there was "good spirit" around the negotiations at this year's summit before adding there was a "long way to go", with talks to ramp up next week. Mr Bowen also drew a connection between the road-map push and Australia's efforts to accelerate global electrification, arguing that reducing the use of fossil fuels would depend heavily on replacing them with electricity. Australia rejects fossil fuel hypocrisy claims Australia's role at COP31 has brought with it scrutiny of the nation's continued expansion of coal and gas production, with environment campaigners arguing the country's domestic policies undermine its climate credibility. Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has criticised the pace of Australia's climate policy. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Speaking overnight at the summit, activist Greta Thunberg said even a "snail" would agree Australia was moving too slowly on climate action. But Mr Bowen emphatically rejected suggestions that Australia's role as a major fossil fuel exporter had damaged its standing in the negotiations. He said other governments understood the practical challenges of reducing dependence on fossil fuels, including their continued reliance on Australian exports. Mr Bowen said the argument Australia's exports undermined its leadership on climate was not one that "survives contact with reality in a COP negotiation". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also defended the government's approach, arguing resource companies contributed substantial tax revenue used to fund public services. Coal and gas policies under scrutiny at COP31 Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has put the Pacific at the centre of his COP31 pitch, but Australia's continued expansion of coal and gas is drawing criticism from climate advocates. Asked why he did not directly reference fossil fuels in his speech at the opening of the COP31 leaders summit, Mr Albanese said "you could pick out any number of things" that were not in the short address. Electrification presents its own challenges Australia is championing a commitment to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. But the proposal has attracted criticism because it does not explicitly require the additional electricity to come from renewable sources. Mr Bowen said linking electrification exclusively to clean energy would be difficult to achieve.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
events.summary: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. events.title: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check services
events.summary: The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services. By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services. In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks. The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org ® . Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website . events.title: How Nvidia's Veterans Day video inadvertently sealed Jensen Huang's fate amid scandal
events.summary: A seemingly wholesome social media post from Nvidia on Veterans Day inadvertently showed why keeping embattled Jensen Huang as chief executive was almost impossible. On Wednesday, as the US observed Veterans Day, Nvidia employees gathered and watched Marines methodically unfold and raise the US flag at the company's California headquarters. "This Veterans Day, we honour all who have served, including veterans across our Nvidia community ," read the caption accompanying the video on several of the company's social media platforms. "Thank you for your service." During any other time in Nvidia's history , and if just about any other company had posted something similar, the reaction would have mostly been positive. But its now former chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to infidelity with an accused Chinese spy, and reports that he also had an affair with a former Nvidia executive, opened the company's Veterans Day event to criticism. View this post on Instagram "Ironically, the Marines motto is 'Semper Fidelis', which means 'Always Faithful'. You can't script this," wrote one of about 160 people who commented on the post. "You should maybe take a break from posting," wrote another. About the same time as Nvidia's Veterans Day video was posted on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that people close to the company were claiming Mr Huang had another affair, with a former Nvidia executive. "What about Kimberly Powell?" read another comment on Nvidia's Veterans Day video post. Top executives have survived such media coverage in the past, but the problem for Nvidia and Mr Huang proved to be the national security concerns related to AI . For several years, Mr Huang has criticised export bans preventing US technology from being acquired and used by China , which the US has regarded with increased hostility over the past decade. Republicans and Democrats often criticised Mr Huang for his public statements that the strict export laws hurt the US more than helping, and that the policies should be changed. He was familiar with the Oval Office, where he seemed to successfully convince President Donald Trump late last year to relax some of the export policies affecting China . Republicans and Democrats were irked, but even more so after the revelation on Sunday about Mr Huang's romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a technology executive who US officials say was a spy for China. Subsequent media reports implied that he was doing everything he could to try to undermine US export laws, and that various companies in China were able to circumvent them. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations think tank in Washington, told Bloomberg on Monday that Mr Huang and Nvidia should be held accountable. "You have the CEO of one of the biggest companies in America, that is potentially compromised by the Chinese and they have some information on him – it really needs to be looked into," Mr McGuire said. So Rubio himself is worried about Jensen’s romantic relationship with the Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, meaning the intel was validated at the highest levels of government. But still, Commerce has done nothing to limit AI chip shipments to Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. Why? https://t.co/AkaxnPMKcB — Chris McGuire (@ChrisRMcGuire) November 8, 2026 In a post on X, Mr McGuire said some members of the Trump administration had tried to convey that Mr Huang had been compromised, while others seemed to disregard it. One year ago, during Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, the company wrapped itself in the US flag. Mr Huang walked on stage in front of thousands after a video played highlighting US achievements in technology. “It’s difficult not to be sentimental about America after watching that video,” he said. Last Sunday, however, Mr Huang's admitted affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese spy confirmed his critics' worst fears. On Veterans Day, Nvidia's video with the Marines showed that the repercussions of Mr Huang and his company's alleged actions were not going away any time soon. "Where is the Chinese flag?" another comment read adjacent to the video. "What about Chinese veterans?" wrote another. Others, however, were quick to say the main focus of all the anger directed towards Nvidia was that the company did not seem to mind its most powerful chips being used by China. "I'm not a Chinese spy, can I have a 5090?" another person commented, referring to the graphics processing unit that Nvidia describes as the "most powerful" consumer GPU "ever made". Nvidia's attempt to show that it was committed to US national security and the soldiers that protect it, had backfired. On Thursday, less than 24 hours after the Veterans Day video was posted, Nvidia's board of directors announced that Mr Huang had resigned. Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, will act as interim chief executive.

events.title: Google DeepMind Staff Tap the UK Government to Escalate Their Unionization Fight
events.summary: Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab. On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application with the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions. The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm that the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership. The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression that their demands weren’t being taken seriously. “They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.” “We respect the right of employees to make an informed decision about whether or not to join a union,” Google DeepMind spokesperson Tom Hewett tells WIRED in a statement. “We have consistently listened to both those seeking to unionize and those opposed, and have acted in good faith from the outset. We remain committed to constructively participating in this process, and have maintained open and transparent communication with our employees and the unions throughout.” The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Alphabet, Google’s parent company, removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development. “When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.” The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts. “We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee. The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations. “We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.” In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote. The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK. “It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.” Update 11/12/26 3:50pm ET: This story has been updated to add a statement from Google DeepMind. events.title: Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads
events.summary: eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined. Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television. Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back. First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month , eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort. eMudhra has since left the CA racket , saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue. What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of. eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing. By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task. “Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.” The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers. As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work. “It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo. It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads. “The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.” As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself. “I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained. We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

events.title: Worried doctors urge action on frequent shortages of critical drugs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lifesaving medicines repeatedly in short supply and doctors are worried New ABC analysis has revealed the important medicines that have repeatedly been in shortage, highlighting supply chain weaknesses that could get worse. If you've never heard of Bicillin L-A, count yourself lucky. It's a long-lasting penicillin and a lifesaver for many Australians with syphilis or rheumatic heart disease. Trouble is, there's a global shortage and Australia's emergency supplies ran out in September. And, as it turns out, this isn't the first time this important medicine has been in short supply. Medicine shortages are reported on the Therapeutic Goods Administration's (TGA) website. For this story, we tracked shortages going back to 2015, including some that were expected to continue into next year. Bicillin L-A 1.2 million units went into shortage in April 2025, and isn't expected to be back to normal until March next year. It's been labelled a critical shortage, which means there could be a risk of life-threatening or serious impacts. It also means there's not enough supply or no other suitable replacement on the Australian market. But we found multiple shortages of this drug, and most of them were critical . The current shortage is the longest recorded for this drug, and the company says it's due to manufacturing issues. And this is far from the only drug in critical shortage. Another is Creon, which is used to help people digest food, including patients with cystic fibrosis. Two different doses of this drug have been in shortage for more than a year, due to an unexpected increase in demand. One dose, Creon 25,000, has been in shortage multiple times in recent years. We found a low impact shortage in 2015, followed by four medium impact shortages. Like Bicillin, the current shortage is the longest and most severe. These are only two of the 40 medications recently in critical shortage. Our analysis revealed more than half of them have had at least one recorded shortage before. And 13 medications, or about a third, have been in critical shortage multiple times. We've put them together here, ordered by the number of previous shortages and the length of the current one. It's important to note that some of the medicines relate to a specific dose or formulation, and there are ways the health sector manages shortages, which we'll come back to. (If you're concerned your medication is in shortage, you can check the TGA website ). Most of the shortages continued beyond October 2026, when the data was last collected. Bicillin and Creon are among the medicines that have the most shortages recorded, with six each. The other drugs at the top of our list include a nuclear medicine used to assess how blood moves through the heart (Radpharm PYP), and an injection that reduces high blood pressure in late pregnancy (among other uses). The list also includes the only vaccine available for Q fever — a bacterial disease that can result in serious illness. Australia is due to run out of the vaccine this week. While many of us are lucky enough to never have heard of these drugs, some on the list are ones you'd commonly get from your pharmacy. They include the EllaOne morning after contraceptive pill, which is known as the gold standard , and Lyclear scabies cream. Some medicines haven't had as many shortages, but that's because they've spent several years in one continuous shortage. Again, the reasons given by the suppliers are either increased demand or manufacturing issues. And it's not just the repeated critical shortages causing headaches for medical staff and patients. More than 420 shortages were recorded between late September and early October, with critical ones making up the smallest share. Royal Australasian College of Physicians spokesperson and internal and addiction medicine professor John Saunders said repeated medicine shortages — including medium-impact ones — caused "great frustration" among doctors. While there were often alternatives available, he said sometimes they weren't as good, or were simply not available at all. "It's not something that I can say, 'Oh there, there, don't worry about it, it'll be alright' — far from it," he said. "Switching medications when this isn't part of a plan … is a very difficult thing for [patients] to experience." University of Adelaide pharmacy lecturer and pharmacist Jack Janetzki said the medicines on our "critical" list spanned a wide range of essential uses, such as treating life-threatening and severe fungal and viral infections.

events.title: Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month
events.summary: On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned from the company that had become, in many ways, synonymous with its chief executive. Less than an hour later, when the markets opened, Nvidia’s stock had lost roughly $546 billion in market value. Though it has rebounded somewhat, the last weeks of scandal—including a reported second affair with an Nvidia employee—have tanked the chipmaker’s valuation by more than $1 trillion. Huang’s very public downfall began in late October, when The New York Times reported that the CEO had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed and an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. (The two are not known to be related.) At that time, Nvidia’s market cap was around $5.2 trillion. On November 8, Nvidia announced it was investigating its CEO, after Jensen publicly acknowledged the affair. By the following morning, roughly $1 trillion had been erased since the scandal started. If you hang out with a certain type of person who thinks of themselves as a daytrader, they might have talked about “buying the dip” over drinks last weekend. If you believe Nvidia can thrive without Huang, there’s still time! The dip has dipped even further. But the early consensus seems to be that this could be more of a prolonged plunge. “Huang is irreplaceable,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, told WIRED last week. “He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution.” There are very real questions about what the end of Huang means for the global economy. Not only are Nvidia’s chips used to train most major AI models, but the company has also invested billions in a number of other tech companies. As of an August regulatory filing , Nvidia owned nearly $30 billion worth of Intel stock and roughly $21 billion of SpaceX stock. For now, Nvidia’s loss is other chipmakers’ gain. AMD shares are up 28 percent over the past five days, and Broadcom is up nearly 16 percent. Nothing to see here. More Numbers That Illuminate Huang’s Value: Nvidia’s market share of chips used in training frontier AI models: roughly 90 percent ; AI companies in which Nvidia has invested at least $100 million: eight, as of its August filing; Huang’s pay last year : $36 million; Portion of Nvidia owned by Huang: 3.5 percent, as of March—which means the scandal has devalued Huang’s own share of the company by more than $50 billion; PR firms hired with expertise in sex scandals: at least one ; Huang relatives employed by Nvidia: one son, one daughter, and one son-in-law ; Leather jackets owned: several, including a $960,000 Tom Ford number ( but not that vintage Saint Laurent jacket everyone was talking about on X ). Update 11/12/26 2:50pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that a third Jensen Huang affair has been reported. events.title: Dewa posts record nine-month profit on increased demand for its services
events.summary: The Dubai Electricity and Water Authority has posted record profit in the first nine months of 2026, underpinned by increased demand for its utility services in the emirate. Net profit attributable to owners of the company in the nine months to the end of September jumped 11 per cent year-on-year to more than Dh7.1 billion ($1.93 billion), Dewa said in a regulatory filing on Thursday to the Dubai Financial Market , where its shares are traded. Revenue for the period also hit a record, growing 3.3 per cent to about Dh25.7 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, a key metric of profitability, climbed 2.5 per cent to Dh13.43 billion. Dewa attributed revenue growth to increased demand across its electricity, water, district cooling and other businesses. "We continue to advance our journey towards net zero by 2050, while strengthening our contribution to Dubai’s sustainable economic growth and global competitiveness,” said Saeed Al Tayer, chief executive of Dewa, referring to the UAE's economic and societal push to zero emissions. For the third quarter of 2026, net profit grew 8.3 per cent annually to Dh3.9 billion, as revenue rose 5.4 per cent to nearly Dh10.9 billion and Ebitda inched down more than 1 per cent to Dh6.11 billion. The three months through to the end of September highlighted the continued expansion in Dubai's economy, which was reflected in rising electricity demand, increased clean energy generation and improvements in operational efficiency, Dewa said. "As the emirate continues to develop, Dewa remains committed to providing the essential power and water services and innovative smart and digital solutions needed to support households, businesses and economic activity," the utility said. Dewa continues to boost its portfolio with an increased focus on clean energy generation. The utility has announced plans for the seventh phase of the Mohammed bin Rashid Solar Park, which Dewa operates, that includes incorporating large-scale battery storage. Dewa also operates a network of electric vehicle charging stations, as more motorists opt for EVs. Dewa's moves demonstrate its "ability to keep pace with Dubai’s growing energy needs while steadily increasing the contribution of clean energy", Mr Al Tayer said. Dewa has also previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced. In June, the utility established Dewa International to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. The company aims to work with governments, developers and financial institutions to identify investment opportunities and participate in projects outside the UAE. Earlier this month, Dewa International signed an agreement with China's Shanghai Electric to explore energy and water investments in global markets, as the emirate seeks to expand its footprint in the international utilities sector. Shares of Dewa ended 1.11 per cent higher at Dh2.74 on the DFM on Thursday.

events.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025. “This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X. This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026 The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance. As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space. After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models. The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned. Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.” Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated. For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country. Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026 In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs. events.title: Measures restricting clean tech exports slowing down energy transition
events.summary: Major economies representing 58% of the world’s GDP have adopted at least one measure to restrict the import of clean energy technologies, many targeting Chinese goods, according to data published by the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor . In contrast, a large number of small economies outside China, accounting for about 8% of world GDP, are liberalising imports of EVs, batteries, along with wind and solar equipment, creating a de facto free trade area for clean tech. Analysis by the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford found that restrictions are making the transition slower and more expensive, but they may also be needed to balance effective climate policy with industrial development and economic security . “Openness and protection can be combined, rather than traded off wholesale,” it said. Large economies could pursue more selective trade restrictions instead of trying to build entirely self-sufficient industries, while smaller countries could specialise in particular stages of manufacturing. “Our findings show that many countries have begun to implement this strategy,” said Claas Mertens, the brief’s co-author. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Africa to press for more adaptation finance at COP31
events.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Dems cautiously optimistic for clean energy following midterms sweep
events.summary: Democrats’ sweep of Congress doesn’t mean a seamless victory for clean energy over the next two years, California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned COP31. “I don’t want to romanticize what this will mean. I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down,” Newsom said, adding that state and local leaders need to “hold on” and continue working on their own clean energy initiatives for the next two years. He was joined at the summit on Thursday by Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, and about a dozen mayors. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-RI., and a group of House members led by Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., will attend the summit tomorrow. Together they’re the only US elected officials to attend COP31, which has no federal representation. Walz was more optimistic: “They need to just get out of the way, and it will be much more difficult for them to put up barriers now,” he said. Meanwhile, other world leaders expressed a wide range of views on the main podium. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised “a new era of British leadership,” while Venezuela’s acting president Delcy Rodríguez insisted her country has a “sovereign right” to produce more oil, and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said the US should pay compensation for environmental damage caused by the war in his country. — Tim McDonnell

events.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks
events.summary: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.
