events.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
events.summary: BBC's Samira Hussain reports from Wall Street on what the fall of the tech superstar means. Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation. The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom. He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement. On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China. Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology. The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses. Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping. His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream. Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia. They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia. The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive? Published 23 hours ago Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products. So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit". But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said. Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation.

events.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system throttled again, Space X denies it
events.summary: The Ukrainian government has asked the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain new restrictions it says are disrupting the satellite system its military uses to intercept Russian drones. Why it matters: This is the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine reported that Starshield, made by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was impeded. The Ukrainian military uses Starshield — the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system — to control and operate its reconnaissance and to intercept drones. The other side: SpaceX respond Axios: "This is false. There has been no change." Driving the news: Ukrainian President Zelensky said Thursday he was briefed by the minister of defense and the commander of the Ukrainian military that "units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations" along the entire front line and in the parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia. "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he wrote on X. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side." Zoom in: A Ukrainian official said the restrictions have been happening for three days. "On the first day there were 10% limitations, on the second day 50%, and today 100% of the missions fail because of restrictions," the official said. Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said the Starshield system shuts down when drones fly at more than 100 miles per hour. "We don't have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment," he said. State of play: Zelensky said the new restrictions began shortly before President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky later on Thursday in Dublin. What they're saying: The bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus said in a statement that it was "extremely alarmed" by the reports of a Starshield slowdown and "demanding a full accounting" from the Trump administration and SpaceX. Catch up quick: Ukraine relies on two SpaceX satellite services. Starlink, the commercial service, supports battlefield communications and logistics. Starshield is designed for government and military customers. Ukraine accesses it through a U.S. government agreement and uses it to operate reconnaissance drones and intercept Russian attack drones. The Defense Department and SpaceX did not immediately return requests for comment.

events.title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
events.summary: SoftBank might not be the first to invest in a hot trend, but when it does, it goes big. Witness its $30 billion bet on OpenAI in early 2025 or its announcement in February that its SB Energy subsidiary would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. If you can’t be first, be biggest, I guess. That philosophy apparently spilled over into procurement, where orders were also supersized. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly put down deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed. The decision to over-order undoubtedly helped secure turbines and speed up SoftBank’s projects. “SB Energy did not have a choice except to overbook turbines in the future if they wanted some turbines right away,” Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva , told TechCrunch via email. The energy world was caught off guard by the swiftness and magnitude of AI’s rising power demands. Queues for turbine orders now extend into the early 2030s . As natural gas was shaping up to be a go-to power source for the AI boom, CEO Masayoshi Son bet that by deploying his investment firm’s significant war chest, he could corner a portion of the market. If the AI world wanted power for its data centers, it would have to come to him. Now that bet appears to have fizzled. SoftBank announced a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, with over half of that stemming from losses related to power-generating equipment. The investor had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and now it considered much of those worthless. The move was also a costly bit of price discovery, Gardett said. Rather than overpay and potentially still be short of turbines, SoftBank overpaid and over-ordered. “This charge is just that price discovery finally happening,” Gardett said. The magnitude of that misplaced bet — over $3 billion — reflects some of the electricity mania that has overtaken the AI world. Faced with years-long waits to connect to the grid, many hyperscalers and developers have turned to natural gas as a sort of energy security blanket, something that is proven and familiar. As AI data centers spend more time in operation, their operators are getting a better feel for what’s required to keep them operating. Natural gas might seem like a safe bet, but there are still risks, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes, Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics , told the Equity podcast Wednesday. In light of that, Nelson said the grid might still be their best bet. Most data centers would be best served by a grid connection, albeit a smaller one than they might normally request. To make up for the shortfall, large batteries are a cost-effective choice, Nelson said. They’d help shave peak loads or ride out requests from the utility to curtail electricity use. Data center operators might be coming to that same conclusion, leading the natural gas market to develop more slowly than SoftBank expected. SoftBank’s natural gas-related losses are unlikely to have a domino effect, leading to mass cancellations of gas power plants. AI’s power demand appears to be too large for that. For now, natural gas is riding high, though SoftBank may have found its ceiling. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots
events.summary: A new iOS app called Phota Labs gives users access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image. Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos. The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop. The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image. “Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.” The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot. Users can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives. While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like. “For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang said. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.” Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms. The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives. “We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia said. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.” Xia said beta users were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later. “We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang said. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.” In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year. Phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also plans to launch an Android app in the future. events.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it. Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday . Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month. Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated. The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%. Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June. The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace. The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May. The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI , which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025. More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X . Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation. Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates. Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning . What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing. President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border. Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran , raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

events.title: IMF holds new talks with Lebanon on bank restructuring strategy
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund said its staff held a new round of talks with Lebanon this week focusing on the banking sector's restructuring strategy, as Beirut looks to secure a new agreement with the multilateral lender. Lebanon's banking resolution law is seen as a critical component in securing an economic reform programme with the IMF. A staff-level agreement was initially struck in 2022 after the country's economy collapsed in 2019, although the government had been slow to implement the IMF's recommended changes. “This is part of our close discussions with the Lebanese authorities to underpin a comprehensive reform programme to restore financial stability in the country and to support an economic recovery in the country,” IMF communications director Julie Kozack said. Yassine Jaber, Lebanon's Finance Minister, said talks were being held with a view to reaching a new agreement with the fund. He said a law distributing losses between the state, the country's central bank, commercial banks and depositors remains a sticking point in negotiations. Ms Kozack did not say whether the IMF hopes to reach a preliminary agreement this week. “The mission is focused on the banking sector restructuring strategy and the mission will communicate at the end of the mission with whatever relevant updates they have,” she said. The Lebanese parliament passed a banking resolution law in August, a development welcomed by the IMF and characterised as a major step forwards in revamping the banking sector. Last month, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun appealed to the Constitutional Council over an amendment involving the central bank's independence and power. The IMF said it would assess any changes to the legislation to ensure they are consistent with international standards. The IMF has said Lebanon must implement a 2027 budget, a medium-term fiscal framework and other reforms to secure any agreement. Lebanon defaulted on its debt for the first time in the country's history in March 2020, resulting in hyperinflation, high unemployment and a soaring poverty rate. The banking crisis left depositors unable to access their savings and the Lebanese pound fell more than 90 per cent. Lebanese authorities estimated total financial losses from the 2019 economic collapse to be around $70 billion, although that figure is now thought to be higher. A World Bank report in August estimated Lebanon's economy would contract by 6.4 per cent this year due to reversing the economy recovery of the previous year, when growth accelerated at a rate of 4.2 per cent. Mr Jaber has said Lebanon must urgently bring an end to its economic crisis and restore a functioning banking sector.

events.summary: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News . Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month. The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees . Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed. events.title: Microsoft has an image problem with November's Windows security update
events.summary: Printing with Windows has always been something of a choose-your-own-adventure, and November's security update has added another unwelcome plot twist: documents containing certain images might not print. The issue affects images rendered with a height or width of zero at the selected printing resolution. These might not be visible to users, but can form part of a document's watermarking or layout. After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected." According to the notification (WI1549472), most versions of Windows are affected, from the latest Windows 11 26H2 through Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2016. Windows Server from 2025 to 2016 is also affected. Users need not have added these objects themselves. Microsoft says document-generation tools can insert them even when no graphic is visible. Printer problems aren't the only issue requiring attention. After installation of the November 2026 security update, Microsoft warned that "certain Windows activation and licensing operations performed using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail." This one is a little more niche, but it could be a headache for affected administrators. It primarily affects organizations that use command-line tools or automated processes to manage Windows activation and licensing. "Affected devices might encounter error 0x80041008 , Invalid parameter ( SWbemObjectEx ), when running commands to activate Windows, configure Key Management Service (KMS), or manage product keys," Microsoft said. "The failure has been observed while executing the command ' slmgr.vbs /skms-domain ' and ' slmgr.vbs /ipk '." The notice (WI1549486) currently lists Windows 11 23H2, Windows 10 22H2 and 21H2, and Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019 as affected. The printing problem remains under investigation, but Microsoft says a fix for the activation issue is due in the coming days. Administrators needing an interim workaround must contact Microsoft Support for Business. ®

events.title: Five ways Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia could damage the AI industry
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s confession that he had an affair (and reports of another one with a direct report ) that led the board to oust him on Thursday isn’t just your run-of-the-mill salacious billionaire CEO sex scandal. In this case, one of his lovers is suspected by the U.S. government of being a spy for China . She’s also an executive of a Singapore-based neocloud that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. These affairs show undeniably poor judgment by Huang and, I’d argue, unchecked hubris on many levels. Such choices are not only a betrayal of his wife of 40 years, they’re also a liability for his company. Sleeping with any Nvidia partner is bad enough, but he also chose one in a tinderbox of a geopolitical situation. Even if Alice Huang’s company wasn’t suspected of helping Chinese firms evade chip restrictions (and he was somehow unaware of this), it was still exploiting a legal loophole by renting powerful AI infrastructure to Chinese companies. It’s those potential national consequences that may land him in a hellscape of ongoing public humiliation. Republican committee chairs are already summoning him to testify in closed-door sessions about the security ramifications. Will Democrats, who are set to take over key committees when the new Congress convenes in January, also haul him in to testify on the Hill? No one knows yet, but Huang has flaunted his close relationship with President Trump. Remember when Trump called him while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in September? Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom, a deeply unpopular project with American voters. Several Democratic lawmakers have already vowed to investigate the money behind it. In other words, he is a billionaire close to Trump. He was — until Thursday — the face of AI and data centers (also a deeply unpopular political topic with voters), and he has publicly admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Even though he’s no longer CEO, that seems too juicy a target for Democrats to ignore. Beyond whatever may be coming, Huang’s influence has been lost right when he was using it to push the tech industry in a number of directions. These areas have now lost their biggest champion. Open-weight AI models as competitors to closed-source labs Huang has been the biggest, loudest advocate for open-weight AI models in the tech industry and among government policymakers. Nvidia not only offers its own open-weight models, it also offers a lot of other open source tech for agents, AI security, and more. It has even agreed to acquire the biggest site that hosts them, Hugging Face, for $12.9 billion. (That deal is supposed to close in the first half of next year, pending regulatory approval.) In July, when Anthropic and OpenAI were reportedly urging the Trump administration to ban Chinese open-weight models, Huang organized a letter of support for open-weight models generally (if not Chinese models specifically), signed by hundreds of tech companies. Open-weight models give enterprises choice in the market and reduce costs. Without Huang, the next biggest advocate for them is perhaps Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, but he’s not out there organizing the industry to speak up. Pushing the AI industry to clean up its security Both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed incident after incident this year as their AI agents hacked into others’ networks or performed other misdeeds. Huang loudly proclaimed the AI industry still didn’t need regulation and would deal with safety itself. As the industry mulled over what they should do ( auditors? a FINRA-like board? ), Huang rallied the tech industry again. Nvidia got over 100 companies to sign on to his Open Agent Safety Platform, a largely open source effort to solve the epidemic of misbehaving AI agents. Naturally, this effort hasn’t instantly solved the problem , and now the top spokesperson for self-regulation via technology solutions is out of his position of influence. Arguing AI is a tool, not a life form Huang has also been among the loudest voices insisting that AI is an engineered system that creates products, and so can be controlled like any other engineered system. This viewpoint counters the AI doomers and even the big AI labs themselves, which sometimes position their models as on the verge of consciousness (Anthropic) or as alien minds (OpenAI) . While Huang deals with the fallout of his actions, the loudest voice of this counter-narrative is, for the foreseeable future, silenced. A new Nvidia-powered AI PC industry Huang also just convinced a long list of PC makers to buy into his long-time dream of providing CPUs (the main processor chips) for them. In this age, when most Americans have not experienced AI beyond a chatbot, he orchestrated a new line of high-end AI PCs geared for running agents locally. These new PCs are due out this holiday season, and they may sell well for their intended targets: creators, developers, and others already savvy with agents.

events.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang’s successor
events.summary: In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position. In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote. Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company , but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China. Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday , suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs. Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess. “Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does . events.title: Trump sticks by Commerce Secretary Lutnick despite Nvidia inaction
events.summary: The White House is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite a view within the administration that Lutnick delayed action to address concerns over chip smuggling to China. Why it matters: Congress smells blood in the water following bombshell reports that U.S. national security may have been jeopardized by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers want to know what the Trump administration did or did not do in response to that intelligence — and Lutnick, the official in charge of the department at the center of export control policy, is squarely in their field of view. President Trump, however, is not distancing himself from the secretary. "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments," a White House official tells Axios. "President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history." Catch up quick: Lutnick was sent intelligence about Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and repeatedly did not take export control action — despite pressure from the broader administration and the president himself, Axios first reported. Lutnick's role is prompting scrutiny on the Hill from members on both sides of the aisle. "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. "The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told Politico. "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country," Kennedy added. "I mean, there will be a congressional investigation. But I don't think he ought to wait on Congress." The Commerce Department has not confirmed for the record whether or not Lutnick has seen the memo. Yes, but: " It's impossible that Howard Lutnick didn't know about this memo," one senior administration official told Axios. "Of course Commerce got the memo. It had to get the memo. That's the point of the memo. It's about chips. Commerce deals with chips," a second official said. Meanwhile, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of a second affair with a direct report. He previously admitted to an affair and apologized, but members on both sides of the aisle are also not letting him off the hook. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren said. Republican House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (Fla.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (Ark.) told reporters on Thursday that Huang's resignation doesn't change their plans to probe him and the company, Bloomberg Government reported. "Jensen Huang himself has been a pretty bold, some might even say arrogant promoter, sort of dismissing our concerns about China having access to these most advanced chips. And I do not take that lightly ... I would be happy to support a subpoena," Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said on CNBC. The bottom line: Resignations and apologies aside, Washington is ready to hold someone accountable as the FBI, Congress and Nvidia's board all investigate in tandem.

events.title: Whoop just launched a social network
events.summary: Whoop , the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data. The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us. Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example. I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention. Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents. Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members. He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.) But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed. As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls. Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties. He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health , a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.” He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end. As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty. In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year. As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band . But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

events.title: US equities close lower as Nvidia drop outweighs energy gains
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Nov 10, in New York City. US stocks closed lower as Nvidia fell after Jensen Huang’s exit, while energy shares rose on higher crude prices and Trump’s Iran comments. AI and chip stocks stayed volatile. Investors worried about tighter regulation, Nvidia leadership, and financing scrutiny, while some rivals and the energy sector gained. Markets now await the Producer Price Index. Traders expect a December Fed rate hike, with officials split on how aggressive policy should be. NEW YORK - US stocks closed lower on Nov 12, as a drop in Nvidia shares after CEO Jensen Huang’s exit outweighed gains in energy shares. The chip company’s shares fell but were well off the day’s lowest level after earlier dropping nearly 12%. Retail investors bought Nvidia shares worth about US$111 million (S$142 million) in the first half hour of trading, the biggest opening bid on record for the stock, according to data from Vanda Analytics. The S&P 500 energy index rose for a fourth straight session as the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors. Crude prices climbed after President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran. Global AI-linked stocks fell and AI cloud firm Nebius tumbled after reporting its quarterly earnings and outlook. But Nvidia competitors such as Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, Alphabet and Amazon moved higher and were among the biggest boosts to the S&P 500. Equities have been volatile in recent days. Sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have sparked investor concern about more AI regulation. Worries about Nvidia’s leadership have also pressured one of the foundations of the current bull market. Nvidia tabbed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. “Right now, the market is selling AI stocks and tech stocks and buying safe stuff, just like it did in the first halo trade in January and February of this year, but it will flip back,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management in St Louis. “That’s the tug of war the market is doing right now. It’s concerns about deceleration versus just pointing out that the absolute valuation and growth rates are still pretty compelling.” According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 25.99 points, or 0.34%, to end at 7,593.39 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 102.44 points, or 0.40%, to 25,363.75. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 190.29 points, or 0.36%, to 52,296.20. Even with Huang’s departure, some investors expect questions to persist about the future of AI companies with strong ties to Nvidia. The company has backed several firms, including its own customers, through financing arrangements that face greater scrutiny after Huang’s departure. “Nvidia is the circular-funder-in-chief; they’re the biggest by far at this point, and I assume that activity will moderate,” said Ellerbroek. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index declined after surging 17.2% over the prior four sessions. Along with Nebius, peer CoreWeave dropped. Shares of data centre-related firms IREN and Applied Digital also slumped. Investors are awaiting the release of the Producer Price Index on Nov 13, which will follow a hotter-than-expected consumer price reading earlier this week. Markets are completely pricing in a December rate hike of at least 25 basis points by the Federal Reserve, with a 15% chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to CME FedWatch. Comments from multiple Fed officials earlier this week suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen. Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack said on Nov 12 she does not believe the central bank needs to shift to more aggressive rate hikes to combat inflation, while San Francisco Federal Reserve president Mary Daly said she thinks the central bank will likely need to raise interest rates further to deal with elevated inflation, but did not suggest any urgency. events.title: Jensen Huang, an architect of the AI boom, resigns as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy. His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble. It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself. Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company. Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell more than 10% after news of Huang's resignation. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. 🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history. Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index funds because of its size, meaning this move has massive implications for every American with a retirement account. The intrigue: Huang's resignation doesn't look like it'll ease congressional pressure over his behavior either. "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. The bottom line: The fallout is just starting. This is breaking news.

events.title: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia — who is Colette Kress, his interim replacement?
events.summary: The Nvidia Board of Directors announced on Thursday morning that the company’s co-founder and CEO of 33 years, Jensen Huang, has resigned as president, CEO, and member of the board, effective immediately. This is a shocking twist for one of the most valuable companies in the world, which designs the chips that make the AI boom possible. Few people would have predicted this turn of events even just a week ago, as Huang has been so central to Nvidia throughout the company’s existence that he never even established a succession plan . But Huang has now been ousted after reports that he had affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and one of his direct reports at Nvidia. While the company conducts a more thorough search for Huang’s successor, Nvidia CFO and Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO. But beyond her name and job title, what do we know about the person who will now lead a company worth about $3.8 trillion? According to Nvidia’s website , Kress has worked at the company since September 2013. Before that, she spent three years as an SVP and CFO of Cisco’s Business Technology Operations Finance organization. She also worked at Microsoft for 13 years, where she spent four years as CFO of the Server and Tools division. She holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. The California-based 59-year-old has a very limited social media presence — on Linkedin , she has commented some well wishes on former colleagues’ posts about their retirement. But as CFO, she’s been a regular presence on Nvidia’s earnings calls, making her a familiar figure for analysts covering the company. According to Forbes’ list of America’s Richest Self-Made Women, Kress’ net worth is estimated to be about $1.2 billion. Her Forbes profile adds that she initially joined Nvidia in part because her two sons endorsed the company for its role in the video game industry, which it was best known for at the time. “Nvidias strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement . “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” Nvidia is slated to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, when we will likely hear more from Kress about her plans for the company’s immediate future. events.title: United Airlines wants you to check in, not your chatbot
events.summary: United Airlines has become the latest company to slap restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, warning that the bots could make unintended purchases, expose customer data, or bypass checks requiring human acknowledgment. The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies. United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind. And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems. AI agents are pitched as a way to outsource life's minutiae, and it's difficult to navigate the web without tripping over a breathless influencer explaining why you need one, or dozens, or hundreds of virtual personal assistants. The thing is that operating these assistants requires care and thought. Earlier this year, British mathematician Professor Hannah Fry conducted a cautionary experiment in which she gave an AI agent a bank card, and a bit too much agency, to see what it would do. Passwords were coughed up, and some ill-considered purchases were made. Still, as Fry said of the agent, dubbed Cassandra, "don't let her incompetence fool you, because these things are getting better fast." Last month, reports emerged of major US banks blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside accounts and taking actions on behalf of the customer. This month, several UK banks were reported to have followed suit. United stated: "Corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents and we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety." The Register asked United Airlines how it planned to implement the blocking. There are a few options, including physical biometric confirmation for actions or checking for signs of automated browser driving. Amazon has also moved against unauthorized AI agents, blocking Meta's Muse (the "AI that gets it done," according to Meta's marketing) in September . The airline has yet to respond. ®

events.title: Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
events.summary: Arm's boss Rene Haas (L), Nvidia's Colette Kress (C) and Chris Malachowsky (R) have been named as possible successors Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang. The influential co-founder of the AI chip-making giant resigned on Thursday over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is in charge, for now, as the tech giant faces one of its biggest challenges - finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies. We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors. Colette Kress is chief financial officer at Nvidia Colette Kress has been an industry veteran for more than 30 years, having previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft. Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice-president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse. She has "fronted every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro. But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair. Chris Malachowsky is one of Nvidia's three co-founders Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority. Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology. Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job. Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications. "He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo. Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development. Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced. Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap. Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts. Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair. Apple's Tim Cook (R) with Jensen Huang (L) and his wife Lori Huang at the White House Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant. Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung. Rene Haas is the boss of Arm Holdings Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana. "The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said. Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive. "The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies." Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company. An early indication came as markets opened in New York shortly after Huang's resignation was announced. Nvidia shares opened down more than 13%, wiping more than half a trillion dollars off the firm's share market value. Jensen Huang's departure leaves a void in the influential AI giant Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here". Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines.

events.title: Nvidia CEO’s ouster leaves AI world reeling
events.summary: The News Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia’s CEO Thursday, a stunning fall for one of the world’s most powerful figures. His downfall sparked fears of what his departure means for one of America’s chip champions and the unwind of the AI money machine he assembled. Nvidia’s CFO, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO while the board conducts a search for Huang’s replacement. Huang will also leave the board, which he chaired, and will be replaced by Harvey Jones, a board member since Nvidia’s founding in 1993 who ran chip design company Synopsys in the 1980s and 1990s. Semafor had earlier reported that Kress was in the lead to run the company on a temporary basis. The company said it will look at both internal and external permanent successors to Huang, whose departure leaves the giant chipmaker without a tested leader. Huang had nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the world’s AI boom, and the company has never had another leader. It has no succession plan and few apparent internal successors. One external candidate under consideration is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, Semafor reported Wednesday. Other names that have been floated are AMD’s Lisa Su, Huang’s first cousin once removed, as well as an offbeat suggestion by US President Trump on Thursday to tap former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the job. Huang’s ouster came four days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and followed a New York Times report that he had another affair with a subordinate. He is now wrapped up in a series of investigations by the board, congressional leaders, and by the Department of Justice , Semafor reported on Thursday. The ongoing saga has also shaved hundreds of billions of dollars off of what was once the world’s most valuable company — one crucial to the US remaining at the forefront of AI development around the world. Shares fell as much as 7% Thursday, adding to Nvidia’s losses since the first reports of Huang’s relationship with the suspected Beijing spy, who ran a Singaporean company that was a major buyer of Nvidia’s advanced chips. Shares of neoclouds Nebius and CoreWeave, which rely on Nvidia to help AI startups rent space in their data centers, fell as much as 19% and 9%, respectively. Shares in Alphabet, whose TPU chips compete with Nvidia’s GPUs, rose slightly. Key-man risk Huang’s ouster raises questions around Nvidia’s ability to remain the de facto central bank of the AI boom — and the fate of billions of dollars of chip financing from a slew of Wall Street firms that are tangled up with the company. Nvidia has provided tens of billions of dollars in financing to its customers, invested more than $50 billion in AI startups, and guaranteed huge data-center leases for firms including OpenAI. Much of that spending rested on Huang’s singular credibility and power in the tech world, as well as his close ties to US President Donald Trump. His successor will likely have far less leeway from the chipmaker’s board, which is facing its own mountain of litigation, government investigations, and public scrutiny. Still, Huang will remain one of Nvidia’s largest shareholders, with a 3.6% stake in the company worth about $160 billion at today’s price. While he doesn’t have the same sort of control afforded to other tech founders through super-voting stock, such as Alphabet’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, he’ll maintain a meaningful seat at the table. It’s unclear what his exit package looks like and whether the board will claw back any additional share-based compensation from previous years. Washington fallout Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee who’s been pushing for stricter export control laws, said Thursday that Huang agreed to come in for a closed-door briefing before lawmakers break again for Thanksgiving on Nov. 20. Other Congress members have sent letters asking Huang to come and testify in Washington. Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under increasing pressure from members of Congress over how his office allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to what reports allege to be a front for banned Chinese buyers. The Trump administration is made more vulnerable by Huang’s close relationship with Trump and its deference to the Nvidia CEO on chip policy matters. “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wrote in a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Thursday, asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia. Reports suggest government officials “were aware of concerns about Nvidia, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips,” the senators said. So far, Trump is standing by Lutnick. The president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position,” a White House official told Semafor. Winners and losers Huang’s exit could scramble the AI chip market, elevate rivals that have been relegated to operating in Nvidia’s shadow, and ensure more chips stay in the US rather than in China, which could explain hyperscalers’ share rises Thursday. While long chip design cycles mean it could take years for a competitor to eat into Nvidia’s lead, a few companies stand out as beneficiaries. AMD, whose stock is surging, competes most directly with Nvidia on data-center products. Broadcom and other custom silicon makers could gain as tech giants look to design more of their own chips, rather than relying on Nvidia’s. Google may also get more momentum on its TPUs, which it began selling directly to outside customers this year. And Qualcomm offers a competing line of chips for robots. China’s chipmakers are also poised to benefit: Any tightening of US chip export controls could push more resources toward building out China’s domestic chip sector, a long-term priority of Beijing’s. And China hawks in Washington are newly empowered to push for more restrictions on American chipmakers’ overseas dealings.

events.title: Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation
events.summary: Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals. In the short term, they’re probably right. There’s strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed China’s technological progress. The problem is that the US can’t win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation. And that’s where Huang’s ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valley’s great innovators. In the short term, his ouster won’t be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. Innovators burn a lot of money thinking about the long term. And Nvidia will never be as innovative as it was under Huang. Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat. That’s especially true now, in an era when AI allows pretty much any company to design a chip just like Nvidia’s, as OpenAI did in a matter of months. A less innovative Nvidia is not just a problem for Nvidia. It’s a problem for the entire technology ecosystem. Big, powerful incumbents tend to be barriers to innovation. Cook’s Apple built the iPhone and then sat on that invention by defending its turf — a great business strategy but one that let the entire mobile ecosystem stagnate. The key risk to the US tech industry isn’t that Chinese spies will steal its cutting-edge technology. It’s that Silicon Valley is at risk of seeing the magic formula that brought that technology into being in the first place weakened.

events.title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
events.summary: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned. Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)." And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server . This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves. According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide , the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®

events.title: Global AI stocks sink as Nvidia CEO’s exit deepens sector sell-off
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit plunges the US$4 trillion (S$5.14 trillion) company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after a scandal, and CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent leader. Global AI stocks fell as Nvidia shares slid 10.3% pre-market, with the firm losing about US$300 billion since its Nov 8 investigation and facing funding and regulatory worries. Rivals like AMD and Broadcom rose on hopes of market share gains, while other chip and neocloud stocks dropped and tech markets in Asia and Europe also weakened. Global AI-linked stocks tumbled on Nov 12 as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a deepening scandal around his affairs, upending the chipmaker’s leadership and posing fresh risks to a sector already reeling with funding and regulatory concerns. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said. As the centrepiece of the AI ecosystem, the chipmaker finances infrastructure built around its chips – a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding and now risks weighing on the sector as its crisis deepens. Nvidia’s shares fell 8.2% to a more than 16-month low in early trading and its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion (S$5.14 trillion) for the first time since July 2025. “Nvidia has been called the ‘Bank of AI’. If they have to take a step back because of what’s going on, will that cut off funding to smaller companies that need it? That’s an open question,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading. Nvidia-backed neocloud firms CoreWeave dropped 9.1 % after surging more than 27% in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks. Other neocloud stocks including IREN and Applied Digital were also trading lower. Nebius dropped 16.2 % after the company said its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its previous forecast. Nvidia has lost about US$550 billion in market value since the board announced an investigation on Nov 8 into Huang’s relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang , who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. “The interlocking deals that Nvidia has with so much of the industry raises the question of whether that created more stability or more fragility. We’re going to find out over the next few weeks as this whole situation unravels,” said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers. Nvidia short sellers have made US$9.6 billion in on-paper profits so far this week, according to data analytics firm ORTEX. AI sell-off continues after brief respite Chipmakers, widely viewed as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, led the sell-off, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3%. Marvell Technology, which Huang called as the “next trillion-dollar company” in June, slumped 3.8%. AI hyperscaler Oracle, which is expanding its cloud AI chip deals with Nvidia, shed 2.6%. Memory chipmaker Micron Technology fell 2.5 % and data storage firms Sandisk and Western Digital eased 6 % and 3.7 %. Photonic product makers Lumentum and Coherent and AI server maker Dell eased between 3% and 5.1%. Construction and power-generation equipment maker Caterpillar and power producer Vistra slipped about 0.5% each. Other hyperscalers including Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft were also up between 0.8% and 2.7%. AI stocks struggled and the Nasdaq entered a technical correction earlier in November after the Democrats swept the US midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out. Tech-heavy stock markets across the globe witnessed jitters. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7% lower. Tech stocks in Europe were also down about 1%. Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. REUTERS

events.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
events.summary: Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal. A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer. The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts. A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal. Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period. The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims. However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham. About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops. The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer. Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business". Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street". "They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said. "It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge." Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year". He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now". "It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added. Views on Poundland performance differ Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners. Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget. He added that the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year when there were losses of £68m. However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading". It has argued that the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers. There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland shops, which could mean continuing employment for workers at those sites. The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain. Are you affected by issues discussed in this story?
