events.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
events.summary: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company . “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “ totally irresponsible ” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton. Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc. Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive. It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.” In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.” “We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace ,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare. During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter. “Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war. “I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.” Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable. “We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said. Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations. However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.) “What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: Murders plunge 17% in America's biggest cities
events.summary: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 15.2%. Robberies fell 9.1%. Rapes declined 3.5%. Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses. Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

events.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
events.summary: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME. GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies. If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway. Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on , but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 , it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4 . The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen. As The Register mentioned in 2017 , in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course . The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty. Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear. The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here. It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock , shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell . ®

events.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
events.summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

events.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.  In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.” It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.” But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office. They are not just numbers.  Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.  Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica. Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In their own neighborhood Photographed at their home in a Boston suburb “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.” Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status. Both she and her brother are citizens. “Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.” DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.  As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.  DHS denies that they were ever detained. “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.” Andrea Velez On her way to work Photographed in Los Angeles In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.  “Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.” Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.  After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside. Quentin Williams At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant Photographed in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses when more agents arrived outside his building. Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe. “They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.  Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours. Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.  Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.” Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children Attending a horse race In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children . Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens. Photographed at a park in Meridian, Idaho Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.  Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”  She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.” On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. events.title: Some Democrats push to keep House’s China committee
events.summary: As House Democrats debate the future of the select committee on China, some in their party are arguing for keeping it around. “If you want to be able to look at the comprehensive issues facing the US-China relationship, there is not a single committee that covers all of it. It’s spread all over. So this puts it in one single committee,” said Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., who hails from a more centrist wing of the party and sits on the select panel now. Some progressive groups led by Just Foreign Policy are mobilizing to defend it, too, after Semafor reported some lawmakers were lobbying to kill it . A letter from the groups shared with Semafor praises the “different approach” from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., its current top Democrat. “We believe Democratic leadership now has an important opportunity to build on this progress and demonstrate a more responsible and constructive approach to US-China relations,” it states. There’s a bipartisan push to save the committee as members consult House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on its future. He told reporters Wednesday the discussions with committee leaders and the caucus on the future of the China select panel and a proposed AI select committee were “ongoing.” Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat, who favors folding the select panel under his committee, has been pushing to make it a “special” committee under House Foreign Affairs, a person familiar with the talks said. That would mean it would resemble a Foreign Affairs subcommittee that off-committee members could still join. Republicans made a similar move last Congress, putting a committee on the “Weaponization of the Federal Government” under the Judiciary Committee rather than standing up a separate panel. “We will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy,” a spokesperson for Meeks said.

events.title: Some Democrats want to pump the brakes on Hegseth impeachment
events.summary: Some top Democrats want to pump the brakes on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth next year after this week’s attempt came up short. “We have a very difficult set of decisions to make and I don’t think we should hastily make them,” said Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Democrat. He worries the party could get stuck in internecine conflict after a sizable number of Democratic absences on the impeachment procedural vote caused hand-wringing this week, which could take attention away from cost-of-living issues that powered their midterm gains. “Strategically and tactically, what’s going to best advance our agenda? And I worry that what you saw yesterday is a preview of one of our biggest challenges,” Smith added. With plenty in the caucus pushing for a Hegseth impeachment, though, another lawmaker could force a vote next Congress — whether Democratic leaders want it or not. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark told Democrats in a closed-door meeting Wednesday morning that the party had disappointed the American people by not having all of the members there for the impeachment vote, and that it was their job to show up for the people who sent them there, according to people familiar with her comments. Still, Democrats, including Clark, note that they likely couldn’t have won the vote, given the lack of GOP defections beyond Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced the resolution. Nearly a dozen Democrats missed the vote Tuesday referring the impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, with Democratic lawmakers blaming traffic and scheduling conflicts , among other issues. Looking ahead to the next Congress, top Democrats plan to conduct investigations into Hegseth on their own terms, rather than letting their hand be forced early. “I think we should do oversight and investigations under our own timetable, not Tom Massie’s,” said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the top Intelligence Committee Democrat. “And I’d really like to see affordability stay at the center of the agenda.” Still, others wanted to keep impeachment in mind. “Everything’s on the table there. I don’t think there’s a single Democrat or a lot of Republicans that think that Hegseth is qualified for the job and has done the job well,” said Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat.

events.title: Nvidia fallout could hamper US-China trade talks
events.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy may complicate US-China trade talks at next week’s APEC summit, where President Donald Trump is slated to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. That’s because the ordeal has heightened bipartisan scrutiny of the administration’s handling of export controls on AI chips, just months before Democrats assume control of Congress. “Up until this point in time, Trump and the Republican Party had full control over what to do with export controls,” Bloomberg analyst Michael Deng, a former Commerce Department official, told Semafor. “The issue going into APEC is the Chinese side is going to know that Trump may not necessarily be able to hold any commitments he makes.” China, which agreed this week to extend the current truce until January, is already seeking to exploit the GOP’s midterm losses. Deng predicted subsequent extensions “will get progressively harder to negotiate,” noting that lawmakers are already debating including multiple export-control proposals in defense legislation. “We already didn’t expect much from many of the previous meetings,” Deng said. “You could probably expect even less coming into this, because now the US side can’t even make true commitments to preserve the status quo.” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in September that negotiators had taken export controls “off the table” as a “national security issue.” Some doubted that Democrats would focus their new power on US-China trade over juicier priorities, like investigating the Trump family. “It’s probably too early to tell” given “there’s going to be a lot of things on the Democrats’ priority list,” Caleb Max, CEO of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said. “Do people go vote against Republicans because they didn’t like the [Nvidia] H200 [chips] getting sold to Shenzhen? Probably not.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Democrats mire themselves in Schumer debate after landslide win
events.summary: The News Some Democrats say they won’t vote for Chuck Schumer to be Democrat leader. Others are declining to endorse him publicly as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., weighs a challenge and dials up colleagues. But a confident Schumer is acting like he’s staying put. And many of his colleagues are itching to skip the Democratic infighting altogether and reach the moment when Schumer is reelected Democratic leader on Dec. 1. “Schumer has been an unpopular figure among people who don’t understand the role of the Senate party leader. And I think it probably helped them on the trail,” Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., told Semafor. “It’s not the first time that a Senate leader has helped elected members who have opposed his leadership.” He said he was confident when all is said and done, Schumer will emerge as the victor. Schumer is, too. The New York senator has asserted repeatedly he’ll be the majority leader again next year. And in a sign of that confidence, he’s already plotting out a unified Democratic agenda with House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries. He spent his Wednesday doing things that only a returning leader would: meeting with incoming newly-elected senators like Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., to discuss their priorities and what committees they’d like to serve on. Schumer is not acting like a guy who is short of the votes. Hamilton has called for new party leadership and told Semafor that Schumer didn’t ask him to reconsider that demand during their sitdown on Wednesday: “No, he didn’t at all, actually.” “We talked about being overwhelmed when you’re first getting into this and talked about stories, things that matter, committees,” Hamilton said. Path to victory Schumer recruited a number of strong Democratic candidates, including former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, and former Rep. Mary Peltola of Alaska (who is ahead of Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, in a race that has yet to be called). Still, there’s no question that the core of the Democratic Caucus is changing and Schumer has to adapt to it. Whitehouse is from the class of 2006, the year of Schumer’s first big Senate triumph, when he flipped the chamber as party campaign chair. He then achieved a stunning 60-seat majority two years later. Those Democrats were the bulwark of Schumer’s political power as he became leader in 2017, and his support remains strong within the caucus even as his reputation has eroded outside the Capitol. And despite Schumer’s relentless fundraising on candidates’ behalf and candidate recruitment, the class of 2026 has its own ideas. The Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates spent $67 million in Michigan, $65 million in Maine, and $14 million in Kansas, only to see those senators say they do not support him. “We have a lot of new voices coming into the Senate and folks who have been on the ground hearing directly from their constituents about how frustrated they are. So we just have to make sure that leadership recognizes the urgency of this moment,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn. “We’ll see who decides to step in,” she added, calling Van Hollen “fantastic.” Schumer also has moves to make to reshape his caucus. He may elevate progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., to a more prominent leadership position as Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., prepares to be sworn in as governor of her state. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a vocal critic of President Donald Trump who was elected to the Senate in 2024, is also making calls about a position in leadership. So far, no one besides Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., is raising their hand to be chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — a position appointed by the party leader. Gillibrand just enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 cycle. And most importantly, Schumer will have to decide whether he will run for another six-year term as senator in 2028. Votes in hand Even as a number of Democrats like Sens. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., and Mark Warner, D-Va., decline to publicly back Schumer, Democrats believe Schumer’s private commitments range far beyond his public ones. The long windup to the Dec. 1 leadership election, which is conducted by secret ballot, offers little upside for members with national ambitions to endorse Schumer early. But even so, a number of Democrats are still publicly backing him. Brown, who was first ushered into the Senate in 2006, says he’ll support Schumer after Schumer-aligned groups spent an eye-watering $150 million in Ohio. Sen. Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said on CNN that expects the caucus to unite around Schumer. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., said she’ll back Schumer, as did Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn. “When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” added Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz. And Schumer is already plotting out next year’s schedule. Senate and House Democrats are planning fast legislative action on potentially bipartisan bills by picking up the four or more Republican Senate votes they need to pass legislation. If Republicans block those bills, Jeffries and Schumer would move more quickly to party-line budget reconciliation legislation that can reach Trump’s desk. If Schumer were somehow dislodged as leader, the new Democratic majority would be way behind the eight-ball. Room for Disagreement As Gallego and Gillibrand lauded Schumer this week, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced he can’t support him, while Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said she’s a no until she gets a “concrete plan” from a Democratic leadership candidate. Sanders called for a “vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party” to show voters the party is changing. And Van Hollen criticized Schumer and Gillibrand’s electoral approach, accusing them of siding “with the crypto industry and AIPAC” in their candidate endorsements. Burgess’s view After their biggest victory since post-Watergate, Democrats are spending weeks picking apart Schumer and, to a lesser extent, Jeffries. That’s not exactly the thank-you one might expect after winning the largest Senate majority since 2010. Not to mention that Schumer is still being second-guessed for not spending more in Florida and Louisiana, on Senate races that ended up closer than expected. Talk about a thankless job. The infighting could extend for weeks if Van Hollen runs against him. Schumer would be the heavy favorite, but it would be an unwanted distraction for Democrats ahead of 2027. But for now, Schumer is the only one who wants the job. As Senate GOP Leader John Thune found out this week, your critics lose steam pretty quick if they can’t put up an opposition candidate.

In after-hours trading, Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6% after reports said Nvidia’s board was meeting late Wednesday to discuss the situation surrounding its CEO, Jensen Huang, whose affair with a Chinese woman has raised national security concerns in the U.S. Nvidia 's shares climbed 2.9% on Wednesday. Its shares have fallen after the company said it was investigating Huang, who has admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman who reportedly fed intelligence and advanced chips to China. The future for the S & P 500 slipped 0.4%, while that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly unchanged. Apart from Nvidia's situation, investors are worried about a potential slowdown in the overall AI industry given longstanding questions about whether it will prove profitable enough to make massive investments in the technology worthwhile. events.title: London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk
events.summary: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk. Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials. As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password. Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials. “With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.” An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings. Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password. “I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.” After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud. Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication. “The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.” ®

events.title: Data sovereignty takes more than keeping data close to home
events.summary: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. Data could be stored locally while remaining subject to another jurisdiction's laws, dependent on overseas service providers or exposed to disruption beyond your control. For enterprise IT teams, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore. Geopolitical tensions, evolving regulations and the growing use of AI are forcing organizations to reconsider what data sovereignty means in practice. Yet translating those concerns into a workable strategy is another matter. And simply throwing more money at the problem won't necessarily solve it. In The Register's on-demand webinar, Data Sovereignty By Design, moderator Tim Phillips speaks with Patrick Smith, Field CTO for EMEA at Everpure, formerly Pure Storage, about moving beyond compliance checklists and taking a more strategic approach to data control. Drawing on findings from Everpure's research, Smith explores a curious disconnect: organizations are increasing their investment in sovereignty initiatives, yet many still lack a coordinated strategy. Some of the risks attracting the most attention aren't necessarily those receiving the greatest investment. The discussion examines why sovereignty shouldn't be treated as an IT-only responsibility. Decisions about which data needs protection, which services must remain operational and what level of risk is acceptable require input from business leaders, security, procurement and legal teams. There's also the question of priorities. Not every workload needs the same sovereign controls, and attempting to protect everything equally can make an already complicated challenge considerably harder. Smith explains the concept of the "minimum viable company," identifying the critical services, applications and data an organization needs to keep operating through disruption. He also considers why visibility into data access, supplier dependencies and potential exit strategies should influence technology decisions from the outset. For IT leaders trying to turn sovereignty from an abstract boardroom concern into something actionable, the conversation offers useful questions to take back to their organizations. Because knowing where your data sits is one thing. Knowing whether you can maintain control when circumstances change is quite another. events.title: Your AI agent is only as good as your endpoint data
events.summary: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. Answering "where does this run, and can the internet reach it?" often means pivoting across an asset inventory, a vulnerability scanner and an external attack surface tool, each with its own view. Every hop adds delay. Every console is another chance to disagree with the last. The third is pace. Several security firms reported exploitation attempts before PHP released its fixes, and Cloudflare reported early attacks hours ahead of the patch. Frontier AI models helped find PHP2Shell, and in April Anthropic said its Claude Mythos Preview model had found thousands of previously unknown flaws across every major operating system and browser. With models like these in the picture, the old rhythm of disclose, patch and verify assumes a gap that keeps shrinking. Put an AI agent on top of stale, fragmented data and these problems don't go away. They scale. Why does real-time endpoint data make autonomy trustworthy? Endpoints are where work happens and where many attacks end up, so they are the ground truth for any decision about the estate. Four qualities make that data a sound foundation for autonomous action: Accuracy: Live data from the endpoints themselves, not a snapshot that was true last week. Speed: A short path from question to action, with no hopping between tools to reconcile answers. Control: Approvals and an audit trail, plus the ability to roll back, so any automated action can be reviewed and reversed. Shared truth: IT operations, security and the system of record working from one view, rather than arguing over whose data is right. Matt Psencik, a threat research engineer at Tanium, put the visibility problem bluntly when PHP2Shell broke: "The installations that worry me most are the ones a security team doesn't know it owns." How does AI fit in? AI sits on both sides of this. It helped researchers find the PHP2Shell flaws, and attackers can use it to build exploits too. For defenders, AI works best as the operator and the interface: it takes a plain-language question, works out what to ask of the data, and proposes or carries out the next step. But it is only as good as the data it is grounded in. A fluent answer built on outdated information is still wrong, just more confidently so. Keeping people in the loop where stakes are high is what makes automation safe to expand. What are the practical first steps? Teams don't need to hand over the keys all at once. Start here: Find every copy: Don't stop at the installed-applications list. PHP2Shell showed that software bundled inside other products can slip past it. Compare your CMDB against what is really on your network and record exact versions. Draw the lines: Rank systems by what the internet can reach, then decide which response actions run automatically, which need approval and which are never delegated. Write it down before an agent needs it. Pilot one low-risk workflow: Pick something contained, build approval into it, and read the audit trail before widening the scope. Teams can also shorten the pilot with a partner. World Wide Technology (WWT), a Tanium partner, works with many large organizations on technology rollouts and hosts a Tanium lab in its Advanced Technology Center, where customers can test an approach hands-on before moving it into production. That second problem, the hopping, is the one Tanium Atlas was built to close. Instead of moving between consoles, an operator asks a plain-language question, gets an answer from live endpoint data, and acts on it inside limits the team sets, with every action recorded. events.title: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
events.summary: A cargo ship is set to leave Ireland for Russia with alumina, a white powder that experts say is likely used to make weapons AUGHINISH, Ireland -- The Karin, a 400-foot-long (120-meter-long) cargo ship, sat moored this week on Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary. Soon it set sail for Russia laden with a white powder that can be forged into weapons vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine. Alumina, the key ingredient in aluminum, goes into everything from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones. A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland is Europe’s biggest alumina refinery and regularly sends shiploads of the substance directly to St. Petersburg and other Russian ports. Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine , alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy. That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where some ends up in weapons, experts say. “The material is clearly ending up in military supplies,” said Irish lawmaker Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party. “It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.” Ireland is facing calls to stop the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders. Irish government minister Niall Collins told The Associated Press that “there’s absolutely no evidence” the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to make public the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments. Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.” Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives. The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska , a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the U.S. and Australian governments. While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic analyzed by AP. The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia. These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories — one in Australia, the other in Ukraine — stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40%, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU. Roughly 17% of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU. An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times published earlier this year found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors. “Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU. Standing next to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin in June , Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.” Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.” Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it isn’t, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.

events.title: Adnoc L&S expects $4 billion full-year profit as tanker rates surge
events.summary: Adnoc Logistics and Services raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this year after third-quarter earnings more than quadrupled, as disruption from the Iran war drove up tanker charter rates. Net profit attributable to the equity holders of the company jumped 310 per cent to $842.7 million in the three months to the end of September, from $205.4 million a year earlier, the Abu Dhabi-listed company said on Thursday. Revenue rose 160 per cent to $3.29 billion, while operating profit nearly quadrupled to $898.7 million. The shipping arm of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company now expects annual net profit of about $4 billion, growth in the low-360 per cent range, up from its previous forecast of growth in the high-110 per cent range. “Resilience has defined our performance this year,” said chief executive Capt Abdulkareem Al Masabi. Daily rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) on the Gulf-to-Asia route reached about $1.4 million in early October, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That compares with about $30,000 to $45,000 before the war began in February, as fewer shipowners are willing to send vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping was the main driver of growth. Revenue rose 244 per cent to $5.09 billion in the first nine months, from $1.48 billion a year earlier. Tankers brought in $4.15 billion, up 249 per cent, on higher charter rates and a larger VLCC fleet. Gas carrier revenue surged nearly five-fold to $619 million, helped by new liquefied natural gas contracts and three second-hand very large gas carriers deployed with Adnoc. Dry bulk and container revenue rose 93 per cent to $318 million. Much of the growth came from moving the parent company's own oil and gas. Sales to other Adnoc group companies reached $2.26 billion in the third quarter, about 69 per cent of revenue, up from $620 million a year earlier, according to the company's bourse filing. Nine-month attributable profit rose 219 per cent to $1.96 billion, while revenue climbed 88 per cent to $6.96 billion. The board approved a third-quarter interim dividend of $85.3 million for shareholders on record as of November 23. The company has maintained its policy of raising annual dividends per share by at least 5 per cent to 2030. 'Challenging' as it enters 2027 Adnoc L&S chief financial officer Hugh Baker, in a conference call after the results were released, said the company had a "very high degree of confidence" in its newest guidance uptick. However, he acknowledged the difficulty of projecting its performance entering 2027, given the uncertainty surrounding the situation in the Middle East. "I have to say that I don't think we can really sustain any of the previous projections into next year. We are starting 2027 and with a very challenging guidance outlook, the ability to guide for 2027 is challenging because, obviously, there is uncertainty about the events," he said. Adnoc L&S is "sort of normalising our response to the current extreme market circumstances", Mr Baker said, adding that the carry-over effects of higher shipping rates won't result in a "dramatic decrease in earnings in the first quarter". Fleet expansion Adnoc L&S is using the windfall to expand. It has committed $7 billion in capital expenditure to 2030 and took delivery of 14 vessels in the third quarter, including six VLCCs, with another 10 due before the end of the year. After the quarter ended, some of its owned and chartered vessels were struck by projectiles while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, the company said. It added that the vessels were insured and the financial impact was still being assessed. On Tuesday, Adnoc L&S said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters in the Gulf, without identifying the ship or the extent of the damage.

events.title: Blackstone opens DIFC office to boost wealth management business in the Gulf
events.summary: Blackstone , the world’s largest alternative investment manager, has expanded its footprint in the UAE with the launch of a wealth management office in Dubai International Financial Centre. The new outpost in Dubai’s onshore financial centre will serve as the regional hub for the nearly $1.4-trillion investor , which looks to court the wealthy, as well as institutions and family offices, to boost growth of its wealth management business in the Gulf and beyond, it said on Thursday. “The UAE has built an extraordinary position as a global finance and investment hub and is becoming an increasingly important centre for wealth management,” said Jon Gray, Blackstone's president and chief operating officer. The company has been present in the UAE since 2010 and Mr Gray said the new Dubai office builds on that long-standing commitment, allowing the company to “deepen our partnerships and broaden access to alternatives” for investors. The DIFC office adds to the Blackstone’s presence in the Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM and expands its reach across the oil-rich Gulf region as well as the broader Middle East. Blackstone’s private wealth business aims to build on its partnerships with leading banking institutions in the region and has already established more than 40 distributor relationships across the region. Blackstone is the latest among global investors and money managers to set up a base in the UAE or expand presence in the Arab world’s second-largest economy as they look to capitalise on rapidly growing wealth management market in the region. Both DIFC and ADGM have attracted a steady stream of global financial institutions, and trillion-dollar dollar asset managers over past few quarters despite the geopolitical headwinds. Blackstone has already committed more capital to the Gulf region in the past 12 months than at any point in its history and it plans to invest more despite the continuing US-Iran conflict, its chief executive Steve Schwarzman told The National last month. Despite the months-long war , the investment appeal of the Gulf remains intact and the company aims to substantially grow the percentage of its assets under management in the Gulf by the turn of this decade, he said at the time. Blackstone has already upgraded its Abu Dhabi office licence to boost deal origination in the region. It also plans to open an office in Kuwait and expects to further expand its presence across the region over the coming year, the company said on Thursday.

events.title: Rethinking Memory For AI Inference
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Moving compute closer to memory can reduce data movement, power consumption, and latency. Different AI workloads require different approaches to memory architecture, interconnects, and processing. Software support, standardization, and thermal management remain major barriers to wider adoption. The shift from AI training in data centers to AI inferencing at the edge will require a fundamental rethinking of where and how data is processed and stored, how it is prioritized, and what needs to be traded off in terms of power and performance to stay within a limited power budget. At the center of these efforts is a recognition that the explosion of data — especially in physical AI where data is being live-streamed from sensors — requires much of that data to be processed as close to memory as possible. This has been a topic of discussion since the inception of the Internet of Things, but it really began gaining traction with AI due to the flood of data and concerns about the amount of power required to move and process it. In battery-electric vehicles and drones, for example, the less energy spent on processing data, the greater the range per charge and the more energy that can be allocated to critical and not-so-critical functions. The challenge is understanding what data needs to be kept, what can be discarded, and what needs to be acted upon. Those are very different priorities. Making those choices requires advanced processing, and the quickest path to results using the least amount of energy is to minimize the distance data needs to travel between processing and memory. “The realities of these LLMs getting into physical devices are causing everyone to rethink how they architect their memory,” said Frank Ferro, group director for product management at Cadence . “Even with conventional memory — without even talking about processing in memory — how do I partition these models to maximize the performance both of the overall processor and memory subsystem?” Solving those issues will require several new approaches, such as processing near memory (PNM) and processing in memory (PIM), as well as improvements across multiple technologies and approaches. Compilers and operating systems will need to catch up, and standards will need to be established. “AI in the data center and all these large language models have been the focus of everyone’s attention for the last couple of years, and now these models have been trained and pushed out into the field, into the edge of the network and physical AI,” Ferro said. “The reality is you have limited compute power and limited memory.” AI inferencing at the edge presents different challenges than training AI models in AI data centers. “Training almost always involves highly variable memory access patterns, and mostly involves the use of interpreted code — for example, Python to PyTorch — which necessitates the complexities of coherence across layers of memory,” said Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric . “Once inference begins, the use model changes dramatically. Whether you are looking at big LLMs running in a data center, or models running locally, such as smaller LLMs or VLAs (vision-language-action) in cars, the model is known before you run it. That means the data access patterns are known ahead of time. This is where ahead-of-time compilation can start to take great advantage of the various at-memory, processing-in-memory, or in-memory-compute (IMC) options. The system knows exactly where, when, and how the compute is going to occur. There is no need for one element of a compute solution to guess if something manipulated the data while it was in another memory subsystem, because the entire system orchestration was planned out hours, days, or weeks before, when the AI inference model was compiled.” Certain stages of the AI inference pipeline benefit from near-memory solutions more than others. “Pushing the compute into the DRAM or near the DRAM has interesting implications,” said Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder of Expedera . “You’re moving your communication pattern — my activation goes to memory, rather than my memory goes to activation — and that changes how much communication you need to do. These sort of solutions are okay for low-batch decode. For example, if you have batch one and you are trying to do decode and you are not reading all the weights, as soon as we move to large-batch decode, which is cost-optimized, or prefill, which is large-batch execution, the activation communication becomes the challenging part. These are the two ways to think about it. In the end, you have to break your execution into parts that are either storage-sensitive, in terms of how much data you need to store, or bandwidth-sensitive, or batching-sensitive.” Either way, bringing compute closer to data can reduce the time and the energy spent moving it, and processing in the same memory package (custom HBM), or on the same memory die (LPDDR6-PIM), provides two fundamental advantages. “One of them is performance,” said Kos Gitchev, product marketing director at Cadence. “If we’re looking at a CPU or a core sitting inside the SoC, and every time you need to do an operation you’ve got to go out to memory, there’s a transaction that says, ‘Okay, get me some data from the memory that’s going to hit a cache somewhere in the SoC.’ That will eventually go to memory. It will come back to the cache and eventually come back to the processor. This operation really takes some time.” So while chip architects can get compute running quickly on an SoC, the SoC has to wait for data to arrive. “Processing in memory to a large degree addresses this,” said Gitchev. “Now you can say, ‘I have this chunk of memory data in the memory, go do something with it, and I’m just going to go read the results. I’m going to skip this whole step of reading it, compute again, and putting it back. I’m just going to do a read, and that’s all I need.'” .heartland-swipe-cue{display:none}.heartland-desktop{width:100%;max-width:100%;overflow-x:auto;-webkit-overflow-scrolling:touch;clear:both}.heartland-desktop th,.heartland-desktop td{white-space:normal!important;word-break:normal!important;overflow-wrap:normal!important;-webkit-hyphens:none!important;hyphens:none!important}@media (max-width:800px) and (orientation:portrait){.heartland-swipe-cue{display:block;background:#EEF2FF;border:1px solid #17365D;font-weight:bold;font-size:14px;text-align:center;padding:6px 8px;margin:0 0 6px 0}.heartland-desktop table{width:900px!important;min-width:900px!important}} Swipe left to view all columns → Term Domain What it means Where the math happens Data form Examples CIM (compute-in-memory) / IMC (in-memory computing) Hardware The memory array its

events.title: Beyond Bandwidth: AI Inference Is Reshaping The Memory Wall
events.summary: AI infrastructure has spent the past several years in a race for compute. More accelerators, larger heterogeneous clusters, and higher peak performance have enabled increasingly capable models. As AI moves into large-scale deployment, infrastructure must support more users, larger models, longer context windows, and more complex applications. Performance still matters, but so do latency, power, utilization, predictability, and cost per inference. The challenge extends beyond bandwidth. AI systems must balance memory capacity, bandwidth, latency, power, data movement, utilization, and cost. Improving one dimension can create pressure elsewhere. The key-value (KV) cache illustrates this trade-off. KV cache reduces repeated computation during generative AI inference, but requires the system to retain and repeatedly access growing amounts of data. As context lengths and concurrent requests increase, the trade-off becomes more significant. The result is not simply another memory bottleneck. It is a coordination problem across compute, memory, interconnect, and software. Adding capacity or bandwidth helps only if the system can place, move, and retrieve data without allowing latency, congestion, power, or complexity to erase the benefit. The memory wall is getting wider The memory wall predates AI. Processor performance historically has improved faster than the ability of memory systems to supply processors with data. AI magnifies that problem. Increasing arithmetic throughput delivers limited benefit if accelerators spend more time waiting for data. But bandwidth is only part of the constraint. AI systems also need sufficient capacity for models, intermediate data, application context, and inference state. Latency affects responsiveness. Power constrains how much data can be moved economically. Packaging and physical connectivity limit how much high-performance memory can be placed near compute. These requirements frequently conflict. High-bandwidth memory close to an accelerator can deliver tremendous bandwidth, but its capacity, power, and cost are constrained. Larger-capacity memory may be more economical but may not provide the same bandwidth or latency. Moving data among tiers can expand effective capacity, but consumes bandwidth, power, and time. The memory wall is therefore becoming a multidimensional system constraint. Fig. 1: AI scaling turns the memory wall into a system-level trade-off among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, cost, and utilization. A system may have substantial aggregate memory, but not all of that capacity is equally useful. Data in a lower tier may technically be available, yet still be too distant, congested, or costly to move within the application’s service-level objective (SLO). The practical limit is not installed capacity alone. It is usable capacity within the workload’s latency, bandwidth, and power envelope . Inference changes the economics Training large models requires enormous compute resources and memory bandwidth, but it is fundamentally a process of building or updating a model. Inference is dynamic and ongoing. Every prompt, generated token, agent action, and application interaction consumes infrastructure resources. Inference also is not one workload. A conversational assistant may emphasize latency. An enterprise AI assistant may process substantial proprietary context while supporting many users. AI agents may retain information across multiple steps. Consumer services may prioritize throughput and cost per token. Batch inference may emphasize utilization. Each creates a different balance among bandwidth, capacity, latency, power, and cost. The architecture must follow the workload. KV cache exposes the trade-off During transformer inference, attention mechanisms generate key and value representations for tokens in a sequence. Retaining those representations allows subsequent decoding steps to reuse prior states rather than recomputing them for earlier tokens. That improves inference efficiency, but reduces repeated computation while increasing pressure on memory capacity and data movement. Longer context windows increase the KV-cache footprint of each sequence. Higher concurrency multiplies that requirement across simultaneous requests. An optimization intended to reduce compute demand therefore creates more data that must be retained and accessed. Fig. 2: Reducing repeated computation improves efficiency, but longer contexts and greater concurrency increase the data that must be retained, moved, and managed. KV state also has a lifecycle. It is created during prefill, repeatedly accessed during decode, and may be retained for reuse. Depending on the serving architecture, it may be moved, replicated, compressed, or evicted. Each phase places different demands on bandwidth, capacity, latency, and control. KV cache is therefore a data-lifecycle problem, not only a memory allocation. Moving KV state to a lower-cost tier is beneficial only when the higher-tier capacity it frees, or the recomputation it avoids, outweighs transfer latency, bandwidth consumption, energy, and the risk of missing an SLO. In other words, every movement of data must earn its cost . The workload determines the architecture A latency-sensitive assistant may benefit from keeping frequently accessed data close to the accelerator. A long-context enterprise application may emphasize capacity. AI agents may require longer-lived state and more frequent reuse. Large-scale consumer inference may prioritize throughput, utilization, and cost per token. Frequently accessed data may justify residing near compute. Other data may tolerate additional latency for greater capacity or lower cost, or move among tiers as access patterns change. The objective is not to eliminate the memory hierarchy. It is to coordinate that hierarchy efficiently. There is no single memory metric Bandwidth remains critical, but optimizing exclusively for bandwidth ignores other constraints. Capacity determines how much model and inference state can remain accessible. Latency affects response time. Power determines whether increasing data movement is sustainable. Utilization indicates whether expensive compute resources are working or waiting for data. High aggregate throughput can hide unacceptable time to first token, inter-token latency, or tail latency during congestion. A more meaningful measure may be tokens per watt or dollar while meeting latency targets. Headline bandwidth alone does not solve the memory wall. The relevant question is: Which combination of compute, memory, interconnect, and software delivers predictable performance within the available power and cost envelope? Adding memory is not enough High-bandwidth memory can supply data quickly near accelerators. Larger-capacity tiers can complement it where capacity matters more than maximum bandwidth. events.title: The Semiconductor Singularity: When AI Starts Accelerating The Silicon That Accelerates AI
events.summary: AI is entering the inner loop of semiconductor engineering by reducing the effort required to develop software, operate software tools and carry out engineering analysis. Ray Kurzweil described the broader pattern as the Law of Accelerating Returns: accumulated technical capability helps create the next computing paradigm. In my recent white paper, The semiconductor singularity: Accelerating IC innovation with AI , I applied that idea to semiconductor engineering. Better computing improves the tools used to design and manufacture semiconductors, and those tools help create the next generation of computing. Figure 1 places that loop in the longer history of computing. The technologies change, but each generation contributes tools, knowledge and capacity that help create its successor. Fig. 1: Successive computing paradigms have built the technical capacity used to create the next generation. Lowering the effort required for the next experiment Progress in semiconductor engineering never follows a smooth exponential curve. It advances when a bottleneck is overcome sufficiently for engineers to try something that previously cost too much money, time, computation or organizational effort. I saw this firsthand with machine learning in computational lithography. Early demonstrations were exciting, but production adoption required developers who understood both ML and semiconductor applications, representative data, model management, IP controls and customer confidence. Production adoption followed only after the model, data, deployment environment and customer requirements matured together. Generative AI relieves many of the user-complexity bottlenecks characteristic of EDA flows. When I created my original SPIE machine-learning course for lithography, the prototype work took roughly 200 to 300 hours, including some help generating training data. In a later experiment, I used generative AI to recreate and expand a surprising amount of that prototype functionality in roughly 30 hours. These were notebook-level prototypes, not production computational-lithography tools, but the change in exploratory effort was striking. The practical effect is more engineering exploration within the same schedule. Experienced silicon engineers can examine more alternatives and produce more usable results while spending less time on software and workflow mechanics. Extending the reach of engineering expertise Agentic AI extends this effect from delivering predictions or analyses to carrying out sequences of engineering work. The LLM interprets intent, assembles the workflow, retrieves relevant context and coordinates specialized tools. Engineering authority remains in the EDA tools, models, qualified data and deterministic analysis. Semiconductor workflows have traditionally depended on experienced engineers who know which analysis to run, which data matters, when a result is credible and when something requires closer examination. That expertise takes years to develop and cannot expand as quickly as computational capacity or engineering demand. Agentic systems can increase the reach of that expertise. In computational lithography, an agent might collect recent SEM data, configure model calibration, invoke the appropriate analysis, inspect convergence and runtime, and return exceptions to the engineer for judgment. More computation, data and tool activity can operate under the direction of each expert. Siemens Fuse EDA AI implements this architecture by connecting AI models to EDA tools, engineering knowledge, specialized languages and data formats. Manufacturing connects models to physical evidence Computational lithography shows how this works. A fab collects wafer and metrology data, calibrates models, uses those models to drive correction, measures the resulting silicon and feeds what it learns into the next calibration and process change. The model improves through repeated comparison with physical evidence. Different parts of that loop require different computational methods. Physics-based simulation predicts physical behavior. Qualified models, rule decks and deterministic verification establish engineering and signoff authority. Specialized machine learning supports prediction, classification and optimization. Generative AI improves access to knowledge and tools. Agents coordinate workflows. Accelerated computing expands the analyses that fit within practical schedules. The result of these workflows is usually the conversion of physical understanding and manufacturing observations into evidence-backed engineering interventions. Simulation directs exploration, metrology records what happened, models reconcile prediction with observation, and engineering action changes the design or process. As EDA tools, manufacturing systems and digital twins become accessible to agents, this loop can operate across more of the workflow. Agents can explore design-technology tradeoffs, run simulation and computational-metrology flows, evaluate alternatives and organize evidence for the next engineering decision. Trust is engineering infrastructure As engineering cycles accelerate, the value of trust increases. AI can generate hypotheses, assemble workflows and explore alternatives quickly. Semiconductor development advances through evidence that engineers can responsibly act on: verified designs, qualified models, measured silicon and data whose origin and applicability are understood. Agentic EDA needs engineering context, secure data access, traceable actions, deterministic authority and human control over consequential decisions. These properties belong inside the workflow and provide a foundation of trust. A Calibre nmOPC model earns trust through calibration against physical metrology data and continued comparison with what appears on the wafer. The model, calibration data, process conditions and physical evidence together establish where the model can be relied upon. As conditions change, the model is recalibrated and the evidence base grows. AI-enhanced metrology tools such as Canopus can strengthen that foundation by increasing the quantity and quality of SEM data available for calibration. Calibre, together with foundry-qualified rule decks and verification flows, establishes that a design complies with the physical requirements of manufacturing. Agents can orchestrate more work and explore more possibilities, while trusted engineering tools determine which results are allowed to move forward. With access to more tools within a well-designed trusted software foundation, engineering analysis may encounter bottlenecks in the larger organization or ecosystem. The time required to establish data access, protect IP or authorize a production change can become the limiting factor on acceleration. Reducing the time required to establish access, protection and authority becomes the next engineering problem.
