events.title: EGA’s nine-month profit and revenue fall as Iran war disrupts aluminium sales
events.summary: Emirates Global Aluminium has reported a 9 per cent decline in its nine-month adjusted net profit, driven by impairments for lost production after an Iranian attack on its Al Taweelah plant as well as disruption of exports. Adjusted net profit for the nine months to the end of September stood at $744 million, compared to $817 million in the same period in 2025, EGA, one of the UAE ’s largest non-oil industrial conglomerates, said in a statement on Thursday. Net profit during the period stood at $547 million, after recognising a net impact of $197 million linked to the war-related incident in March, which led to an an emergency shutdown of all of EGA’s Al Taweelah plants at Khalifa Industrial Zone Abu Dhabi (Kizad). The company’s revenue fell 16 per cent annually to $5.28 billion during the nine-month period. “In the first nine months of 2026, EGA has been tested like never before,” said Abdulnasser bin Kalban, chief executive of EGA. “During this challenging period of recovery, we have continued our focus on delivering long-term growth. While challenges remain ahead of us, across EGA we share determination and full confidence that EGA will come back stronger than ever.” The shutdown after the March incident resulted in a $53 million impact on adjusted Ebitda. However, operations at Jebel Ali and EGA’s international recycling plants remained uninterrupted throughout the period. Despite the setback, EGA said it lifted its adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation margin to 30 per cent in the January to September period, from 28 per cent a year earlier, helped by higher aluminium prices and disciplined cost management. Sales volumes The shutdown at Al Taweelah also weighed on aluminium sales volumes. Total sales fell 36 per cent to 1.33 million tonnes during the nine months, reflecting lower metal availability from Al Taweelah and constraints on outbound logistics from the UAE during the period, EGA said. The company then established alternative export routes through corridors to ports outside the Strait of Hormuz , supporting continued customer shipments. In September, EGA signed an agreement with Gulftainer to expand aluminium exports through the UAE's eastern coast ports. The arrangement will enable EGA to ship up to 250,000 tonnes in the first year, rising to 300,000 tonnes in the second year. The company has also diversified inbound supply routes and secured a renewed bauxite agreement with Guinea's Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinee for up to 4.9 million tonnes annually until 2044. EGA said on Thursday it is continuing to restore its Al Taweelah smelter , with 766 of the 1,262 reduction cells that need restarting now operational. This represents 61 per cent of the total, with the company aiming for a full restart in the first quarter of 2027. Production is increasing as more cells come back online. The disruption also affected the company’s alumina refinery , which produced 899,000 tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, down from 1.75 million tonnes a year earlier. After its restart in July, the refinery had reached about 70 per cent capacity in September. EGA estimates that fully restoring Al Taweelah production will require capital expenditure of about $400 million. This will be financed from the company's balance sheet and operating cash flow, EGA's chief financial officer Pal Kildemo told The National in August. The company's balance sheet remains robust, with $1.93 billion in cash and term deposits and a further $1 billion available through an undrawn revolving credit facility. Meanwhile, EGA is continuing its global expansion, having completed the acquisition of an 80 per cent stake in Italian aluminium recycler Eco Green in September. The deal takes its global recycling capacity to more than 400,000 tonnes annually, with another 200,000 tonnes under development. Although the aluminium market remains undersupplied, EGA expects it to move towards a more balanced position in 2027, Mr Kildemo said on Thursday.

events.title: Designing Edge AI SoCs At Near-Threshold: Why Foundation IP Can Help You Break Down The Power Wall
events.summary: Lowering operating voltage is a key to SoC power optimization. In advanced FinFET processes at ~0.4–0.5V, it can also start to become a design risk. As edge AI pushes inference closer to endpoints, edge-AI SoCs must deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits. Traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient. SoC designs are shifting towards much more extensive use of near-threshold operation to achieve step-function improvements in performance per watt. But this shift fundamentally changes how chips behave: delays increase non-linearly, variability grows significantly, and underpinning predictable operation becomes a critical enabler to minimizing power. Design success in this operating regime depends heavily on the underlying quality, modeling accuracy, and integration of Foundation IP with EDA flows and silicon validation. Embedded memories, logic libraries, and I/Os must be selected carefully and any targeted optimization carried out and fully validated at an early stage—not treated as a possible downstream option. What changes at near-threshold Every SoC designer understands that lowering supply voltage reduces energy—but at near threshold voltages, it changes transistor behavior and challenges traditional design assumptions. Fig. 1: Energy efficiency improves at lower voltage, but delay and variability increase sharply near threshold. As shown in Figure 1, reducing voltage lowers energy per operation, but comes with significant trade-offs: delay grows rapidly, variability increases, and noise margins shrink. In this regime: Timing paths become highly sensitive to small voltage variations IR drop and local voltage droop become first-order effects Guard-banding becomes less effective Nominal-voltage models no longer predict behavior accurately Voltage scaling is no longer an isolated optimization—it introduces tightly coupled challenges across the entire design stack. Foundation IP: The differentiating layer Meeting power targets at ultra-low voltage is not sufficient; designs must achieve this predictably and without introducing additional silicon risk. This can be where Foundation IP moves from an incidental enabler to a significant part of the design success. The quality of logic libraries, memory compilers, and I/Os can directly determine the robustness of design closure and silicon outcomes. A unified, silicon-proven Foundation IP platform—tightly coupled with EDA flows, built with the most accurate modelling and characterization methodologies and meticulously validated on silicon —provides the accuracy and consistency needed to enable PPA winning designs at ultra-low voltages, with reliable behavior from early design through signoff. Embedded memories: Where the voltage floor lives Memory is a dominant contributor to area and power—and often determines the system’s minimum operating voltage (Vmin) if not architecturally decoupled. This is addressed through flexible architectures: Single-rail memories with silicon-validated assist features support operation down to ~600 mV Vmin, enabling direct V² energy reduction without architectural disruption Dual-rail memories decouple logic and memory voltages, allowing deeper scaling of compute blocks. As shown in Figure 2, this approach has been validated at ISSCC 2025 with a 38 Mb/mm² dual-rail SRAM at 380/540 mV in 3nm FinFET Ultra-low-power register files support localized data storage in compute-intensive regions Fig. 2: Dual-rail memory architecture decouples logic and memory VDD, validated at ISSCC 2025 with a 38 Mb/mm² SRAM at 380/540 mV in 3nm FinFET. Different AI subsystems require different memory strategies: MAC tiles benefit from small, distributed SRAM blocks; activation units from ULP RFs with wide data-paths; and shared system buffers from high-bandwidth AXI interfaces. Logic libraries: Accuracy where it matters most Logic libraries must be engineered specifically with low-voltage operation in mind: Advanced characterization, such as moment-based LVF timing and noise models across wide bands of PVT coverage Delay and slew models that capture near-threshold non-linear sensitivities Enhanced verification checks—including MIS effects, pulse-width integrity, skew interactions, and mixed-device behavior—to address reduced noise margins Targeted silicon validation, including extended timing and functional sweeps, to ensure model accuracy This modeling accuracy is essential to avoid unexpected surprises during low voltage signoff or timing failures on silicon. I/O: Don’t let the periphery block the core In many designs, I/O domains define system-level Vmin. If I/O cannot operate reliably at reduced voltages, it blocks near-threshold logic benefits regardless of how well the core is optimized. The portfolio spans control interfaces (GPIO, I3C/I2C, SWI3S), high-speed data links (LVDS, RGMII), clock and reference inputs, storage interfaces (SD/eMMC), test I/O, and 2.5D/3D integration I/O for chiplet-based systems—each validated for consistent operation across varying supply levels. Co-optimization: Standard IP alone sometimes isn’t quite enough Achieving predictable, optimized operation at ~0.4–0.5V requires tight alignment across Foundation IP, EDA tools, modeling, and silicon validation. Fig. 3: A closed-loop methodology aligns Foundation IP, tools, and silicon feedback to ensure optimized low-voltage design. As shown in Figure 3, optimal low-voltage design depends on an iterative, closed-loop enablement process: Early exploration of PPA trade-offs, along with specific voltage targeting Selection of right IP architectures, technology options and configurations, maybe with specific cell tuning Flow and signoff refinement targeted for low-voltage conditions Feedback from silicon validation to continually improve accuracy and raise confidence Synopsys Application Engineers bridge the gap between IP/EDA R&D experts and SoC designers during the customer design engagement, ensuring that the features are fully exploited and technologies are optimally deployed. The co-optimization of tools and IP keeps device physics, modeling assumptions, and silicon outcomes tightly coupled—transforming near-threshold design into a low risk, production-ready solution. Proof point: ~20% power reduction, zero schedule impact A power-sensitive AI networking SoC targeting high volumes in an advanced technology node, using near-threshold design, needed expert enablement. Supporting extremely low operating voltages for a design executed under a very compressed schedule. The Foundation IP solution included specially tuned low-voltage logic cells, custom level shifters and a custom dual-rail memory compiler, with specifically targeted PVT corner set all specifically selected to achieve the optimum design trade-offs for the best power efficiency through near-threshold signoff. The results: ~20% reduction in power consumption Full achievement of performance and area targets No schedule impact R

events.title: IP Integration Challenges Evolve
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Integration challenges go beyond making sure a block is properly connected. Semantic issues cause the most problems, and many are due to incomplete or bad specifications. Complexity, including increasing software content, makes keeping track of everything included in a design more challenging. Many designs are pushing power and thermal boundaries, and this requires a new layer of information that must be specified and tracked. IP integration is not the most glamorous task in semiconductor design, but it often is one of the most troublesome. At the intersection of block-level verification and system-level interactions, bugs are often very difficult to find. The creation of the Virtual Socket Interface Alliance (VSIA) in 1996 was, for many, the first time the notion of designing a system by integrating third-party IP blocks became a reality. Its charter was to unify and standardize the way IP was constructed, verified, delivered, and supported. The alliance dissolved in 2008, considering its work to either be complete, or transferring parts of it to other organizations that were more focused on specific pieces of the problem. Eighteen years later, the problem continues to evolve. The idea was that each company should focus on developing the part of the design that was novel and unique, adding their expertise, and allowing the rest to be developed by domain experts. “Ten years ago, a design may have had tens of IP blocks,” says Pedro Pires, SOS product manager at Keysight EDA . “Today, a company may have thousands of IPs, dozens of different versions of the same IP, and you want to make sense of all of this. In addition, they are much more configurable than they were in the past. With the increasing quantity and different types of data now required for each block, it is becoming very difficult to manage in an ad hoc way. “ This puts a lot of stress on verification. “The nastiest failures are almost never inside a single block,” says Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . “They show up between blocks — message-dependent deadlock, credits that slowly leak away, a reorder buffer that gets corrupted, an ordering rule broken across a bridge. Each block passes its own verification, yet the system hangs because two teams read the same protocol rule slightly differently.” Over time, the number of cross-IP issues has increased. “From an SoC point of view, it could be a lot of different issues, including address mapping, interrupts, coherency, QoS, security,” says Madhumita Sanyal, senior director for technical product management for HPC IP portfolio at Synopsys . “Then there are physical implementation scenarios like DVFS, dynamic voltage scaling for lower power. Plus, there is software and operating system interaction. If you consider a die-to-die IP, there’s interoperability. There is known-good-die package, signal integrity, power integrity, power delivery network, thermal coupling, telemetry, and so forth.” While design size has steadily increased, that alone is not an indicator of complexity. “I may be designing a giant CPU with 32 cores, but that is just 32 copies of the same thing,” says Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. “It may have a giant cache on it. That is just one cell repeated 100 million times. The complexity is not always proportional to the size of the chip. They are complicated, but the complexity has not linearly grown with the size of the chips. The human brain can’t deal with it.” What matters is how many assumptions a block makes about the world around it, and that number climbs much faster than size. “A UART needs a clock, a reset, and a register interface, and that’s about it,” says Axiomise’s Darbari. “A coherent cache, a CHI home node or a NoC carries hundreds of assumptions. There are ordering rules, credit contracts, limits on outstanding transactions, reset and power sequencing, address-map expectations and security attributes. On top of that come configuration parameters whose effects the datasheet often doesn’t fully explain.” Increasing pressures Many areas add to the integration pressures, such as badly written or incomplete specifications for the IP blocks. At the system level, there is increasing software complexity, power and thermal issues – especially when associated with chiplets, increasing analog content, and added complexity with licensing, geopolitical restrictions, and export controls. Each of these will be touched on briefly. Bad or incomplete specifications: Specifications are notoriously difficult to make unambiguous or complete. “The information is oftentimes not complete enough to give you an accurate picture of how it’s going to behave under all circumstances,” says Keysight’s Pires. “Knowing the conditions in which the system is going to operate will probably help you, depending on the quality of the documentation of your IPs. It might be that the IPs have information that is relevant for that particular set of circumstances, and in that sense, knowing the circumstances where the system is going to operate will help you, but it might not.” The problem is often discovered when a bug escapes. “The architect, the designer, the software team, the DV lead and the formal team all look at the same failure and see something different,” says Darbari. “Nobody can agree on what the system was supposed to do, because nobody ever wrote that down in a form everyone shared. Those differences of opinion were there from day one. They just surface two years later, often in post-silicon debug, when they are most expensive to fix.” Software complexity: While some software is fully encapsulated and hidden from any external interfaces, much is not. “Even something as simple as a PHY has a significant software content,” says Synopsys’ Sanyal. “There is the boot firmware that will establish all the clocks, resets, and memory. Then the PHY has calibration firmware, which will do the initial calibration and adaptation, and it’s updated continuously. That driver needs to tie in to the operating system interrupt and the DMA framework, and the BIOS and hypervisor or coherency or IOMMU dependencies for PCI controller and stuff like that. These all extend the dependency to interrupt between topologies and operating system services and power management framework.” These issues are problematic enough that the UCIe standard attempted to address it. “UCIe 3.0 standardizes how firmware gets downloaded early in initialization,” says Darbari. “The trouble is that the hardware is often only correct under some software assumption. For example, registers might have to be programmed in a particular order, or a field must never be written while a transaction is in flight. Those rules are rarely

events.title: The Memory Challenge Of Physical AI
events.summary: Most AI hardware conversations start with compute, which is understandable since accelerators are visible, easy to compare, and often tied to headline performance metrics. Physical AI broadens that conversation by placing greater emphasis on how compute, memory, and data movement work together under real-world operating constraints. For intelligent systems that must see, interpret, decide, and act in the physical world in real time, it’s critical that the right data reaches the right engine at the right time. As a result, data movement has become an increasingly important consideration when architecting physical AI systems. A physical AI device may simultaneously handle sensor streams, model weights, activations, temporary buffers, control loops, and safety functions. If memory access becomes unpredictable, compute engines can stall. Power consumption rises when data is moved too often, and poorly planned buffering can cause latency accumulation that is hard to recover from later. As physical AI workloads become more complex, architects must now consider how predictably the complete system performs when multiple real-world workloads are active simultaneously. Avoid unnecessary data movement Physical AI systems rely on a memory hierarchy that coordinates on-chip memory with larger-capacity external memory. LPDDR or GDDR may hold model weights, sensor data, activations, and other working data, while on-chip SRAM and cache keep the portions currently needed by the NPU, CPU, DSP, ISP, or other processing engines close to compute. As workloads move through the processing pipeline, required data is transferred from external memory into on-chip memory, where it can be accessed and reused with lower latency and energy. The more effectively the architecture reuses that local data, the fewer times it must retrieve the same information from external memory. However, because SRAM and cache consume silicon area, their capacity is limited. Data that does not fit on-chip, or is used less frequently, remains in LPDDR or GDDR until it is needed. This coordination is important because every unnecessary transfer across the memory hierarchy consumes energy, adds latency, and uses external-memory bandwidth. Physical AI systems are also constrained by device size, package complexity, power delivery, and thermal headroom. The goal is therefore not to eliminate external memory access, but to keep the right data close to compute for as long as it is useful and avoid moving it more often than necessary. A well-planned dataflow coordinates compute engines, on-chip SRAM and cache, external LPDDR or GDDR, buffering, and interconnect around the workload. This helps keep compute resources productive while using external-memory capacity and bandwidth efficiently. Real-world applications clarify the tradeoffs Humanoid robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, smart cameras, inspection robots, industrial robots, and autonomous mobile robots may all run local intelligence, yet each stresses memory and interfaces differently. Their architectures must determine which data should remain close to compute for immediate access and which should reside in higher-capacity external memory. Humanoids may combine cameras, depth sensing, audio, inertial data, balance control, object recognition, path planning, and actuator feedback within a limited power and thermal envelope. If perception data arrives late, control decisions may be delayed. In addition, sustained performance drops and power rises if model weights and intermediate data are reloaded too often. In this kind of system, memory efficiency affects how smoothly the robot can perceive, decide, and move, all of which are key to successful real-time operation. A drone or autonomous mobile robot has a different set of constraints. It may need visual navigation, obstacle avoidance, stabilization, object tracking, wireless communication, and video processing, all while staying within a limited power and thermal budget. Unnecessary external memory accesses reduce operating time, add heat, or introduce latency into the control loop. For these physical AI systems, bandwidth per watt is as important as raw bandwidth. Autonomous vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) present an even greater challenge. With cameras, radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensors, vehicle telemetry, map data, and control functions, competition for memory access is fierce. Some data streams need continuous throughput, while others need fusion across sensor domains. Retaining relevant data long enough to support planning and decision-making is also an important consideration. In this environment, memory behavior affects both throughput and response predictability. Memory choices must follow the workload When building a memory architecture, architects should begin with the behavior of the physical AI workload itself. The objective is not simply to select the fastest external memory technology or provision the greatest possible bandwidth. It is to right-size the complete memory hierarchy, including local storage, external memory capacity, bandwidth, power, buffering, and integration, around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints. LPDDR and GDDR address different architectural priorities. LPDDR is often a strong fit when bandwidth per watt and memory capacity are needed to sustain local inference performance. When continuous image or sensor-stream bandwidth is the primary requirement, GDDR may be a viable option because its high bandwidth can meet those performance needs with fewer DRAM devices. Available solutions give architects considerable flexibility in making this tradeoff. For example, Cadence offers LPDDR6/LPDDR5X PHY and Controller IP supporting data rates up to 14.4Gbps, as well as GDDR7 PHY IP supporting data rates up to 36Gbps for high-bandwidth applications. These options allow the external memory interface to be aligned with the workload rather than treated as a one-size-fits-all design choice. A humanoid robot may prioritize power-efficient access to model weights, perception data, and control information. A smart camera or autonomous-vehicle perception processor may place greater pressure on sustained vision-stream bandwidth. In each case, the architecture should keep frequently reused and latency-sensitive data close to compute while selecting an external memory interface sized for the remaining capacity and bandwidth requirements. This helps avoid both memory bottlenecks and unnecessary over-provisioning. events.title: Introduction To FP8 Formats: Part 1
events.summary: The industry is moving from high-precision formats (FP32, FP16, BF16) to lower-precision data types for Machine Learning (ML) inference and training. In cloud and data center environments, lower-precision data types deliver higher throughput by packing more compute per cycle from the same platform. On edge and mobile devices, smaller formats reduce model size, memory footprint and bandwidth, which directly affects power consumption and latency. Arm, Intel, and NVIDIA published an OCP 8-bit Floating Point Specification (OFP8). It is an interchange format that allows software systems to share the models easily. FP8 is not a future concept, it is being deployed today. It is already supported by NVIDIA’s Hopper H100 GPU, with software deployment appearing in major ML frameworks. Arm added the FP8 support to the Arm v9 ISA and is exploring the best way to integrate the FP8 across all the ML platforms. This blog post explains the FP8 data formats, the new Floating-point Mode Register (FPMR), and the instruction set that makes FP8 practical on Arm CPUs. FP8 data format Unlike IEEE FP64, FP32, and FP16, FP8 is not a single format, it is a family. The whitepaper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning proposes an FP8 format consisting of two encodings: E4M3 and E5M2. Why a family of formats? With only 8 bits available, FP8 makes a trade-off between precision and dynamic range. A single encoding cannot fit all tensors equally well. Activations and weights usually have a smaller and more stable value distribution after training or calibration. They can therefore benefit from more mantissa bits, which help represent nearby values more precisely. Gradients can change much more during forward and backward passes. They can therefore benefit from more exponent bits and a larger dynamic range, which helps avoid overflow or underflow. The two encodings enable software to choose the right format for each tensor role. Use E4M3 when precision is more important and use E5M2 when dynamic range is more important. This is the key idea from FP8, and Arm reflects the same idea in the FPMR register. With FPMR, each source operand can independently select which FP8 format it uses. Supported data types E4M3 E5M2 Exponent bits 4 5 Mantissa bits 3 2 Bias 7 15 Max normal value 448 57344 Special values NaN only Inf and NaN E4M3 uses 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, and 3 mantissa bits, with a bias of 7. E4M3 uses most bit patterns for normal finite numbers instead of saving many of them for special values. This helps E4M3 extend dynamic range, which is more useful for deep learning workloads. E5M2 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 2 mantissa bits, with a bias of 15. E5M2 follows IEEE 754 conventions for the exponent field and special values, including infinities and NaNs. Because of this, it can be viewed as IEEE FP16 with fewer mantissa bits, like how bfloat16 and TF32 can be viewed as IEEE FP32 with fewer bits. This makes conversion between E5M2 and IEEE FP16 straightforward, while still providing a wider dynamic range than E4M3 FPMR: The Floating-Point Mode Register When hardware executes an FP8 instruction, it must know the format of each source operand, the format of the destination result, and the scale factors to apply. Because FP8 modes can change per tensor, software may need to update the format and scaling settings frequently inside performance-critical code. For this reason, Arm introduced a dedicated control register – FPMR. FPMR is separate from FPCR. Hardware can recognize and rename FPMR writes more efficiently, making per-tensor FP8 mode changes closer to a normal register write rather than a pipeline-serializing control update. FPMR contains the following fields: Field Bits Description F8S1 [2:0] Format of 1st FP8 source. 0b000 = E5M2, 0b001 = E4M3. F8S2 [5:3] Format of 2nd FP8 source. Same encoding as F8S1. F8D [8:6] Destination result Format for instructions that convert other floating-point formats to FP8. Same encoding as F8S1. OSM [14] Overflow Saturation for FP8 multiplication instructions. OSC [15] Overflow Saturation for FP8 convert instructions. LSCALE [22:16] Unsigned Log2 down-scaling factor. Result × 2^(−LSCALE). NSCALE [31:24] Unsigned Log2 up-scaling factor for widening FP8 sources. LSCALE2 [37:32] Second down-scaling value for dual-source convert instructions. FP8 instruction set on Arm The 2023 and 2024 architecture extensions add FP8 instructions across Advanced SIMD, SVE and SME. The following table summarizes the architectural features and the instructions they provide. Architectural features Supported category Instructions Description FEAT_FP8 Advanced SIMD/SVE/SME FCVTN, FCVT, F1CVT, F2CVT, BF1CVT, BF2CVT, FSCALE FP8 convert instructions; a floating-point scale instruction. FEAT_FP8FMA Advanced SIMD/SVE FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLBT, FMLALLTB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate. FEAT_FP8DOT4 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product. FEAT_FP8DOT2 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product. FEAT_SSVE_FP8FMA SME FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT4 SME FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT2 SME FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SME_F8F32 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOTB, FVDOTT, FMLALL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP32 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FEAT_SME_F8F16 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOT, FMLAL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP16 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP16 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP16 ZA array. FEAT_F8F32MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP32 FEAT_F8F16MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP16 All FP8 compute instructions read the source format from FPMR (F8S1/F8S2) and apply scaling via LSCALE/NSCALE. These widening instructions always use FP8 data as the input format. Accumulation uses a wider type, such as FP16 or FP32. This keeps the bandwidth advantage of FP8 inputs while preserving numerical stability during accumulation. Further reading For more detailed information about FP8, see the Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture and the FP8 Formats for Deep Learning paper . Part 2 will explore FP8 instructions, from conversion and scaling to dot products, matrix multiplication, and outer products in Advanced SIMD, SVE, and SME. events.title: RISC-V For AI: Breakthrough Or Bad Idea?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: RISC-V’s role in AI is contested. Its customization offers flexibility, but splitting inference workloads between CPUs and accelerators can introduce costly data movement and compiler complexity. Control may be RISC-V’s best option. Custom instructions can help orchestrate accelerators, reduce load/store latency, and handle limited mathematical tasks without taking on heavyweight inference. Correct instructions don’t guarantee a working chip. Custom AI systems also need observability and system-level verification to expose performance bottlenecks, cache-coherency problems, and interconnect deadlocks. Experts At The Table: Demand for parallelism and power efficiency is shifting chip design from general computing to AI, increasing the need for flexible, modular, and open hardware. This trend is bringing RISC-V into AI acceleration. Customizable hardware can implement AI computations directly instead of relying on fixed CPU designs. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Steve Roddy, chief marketing officer at Quadric ; Francisca Tan, director of product management and product engineering for Tessent at Siemens EDA ; Ewald Liess, senior vice president of sales and business development at SignatureIP ; and Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. L-R: Quadric’s Roddy; Siemens EDA’s Tan; SignatureIP’s Liess; Breker’s Kelf. SE: With AI models evolving rapidly, architects use RISC-V to design highly specialized extensions. From an IP provider standpoint, how would you balance delivering a standardized, reusable IP core with the extreme customization that customers are demanding for AI workloads? Leiss : We don’t think that we need to configure because we provide NoC and PCI Express and CXL CHI AMBA interfaces. Based on this, we don’t need to customize. Instead, it’s the NoC that will be configured. Because we have a pre-verified NoC, we can do that with our tools. We can configure customized RISC-Vs. Of course, the customers may modify the RISC-V core with new instructions, but they will stick to the interfaces like the AMBA bus, or CXL, PCI Express interfaces, because this enables them to access the external components that they need, like memory or going off-chip. And this is where we come in. So the RISC-V guys should feel free to do whatever they want. Tan : Custom verification and validation also become important, as does observability. For test and embedded analytics, engineers doing debug or silicon bring-up can monitor, introspect, and inspect internal signals, or calculate whether performance is being met. In my view, it’s also about hardware observability, as the industry moves into various challenges and complexity in the chip. Roddy : We’ll take the contrarian view in this particular area. We think that starting with RISC-V to do an AI accelerator is a flat-out bad idea, because you instantly create a problem. You now have a partition between some things running on a programmable processor with good ALU capacity, and some external accelerator where you’ve now had to partition the system. The minute you partition, the minute you create a problem, you need fancy compilers to go fix it and figure out how to move data from the accelerator or accelerators across a nice NoC over to a programmable core, and back and forth. That’s a problem that scales badly. The bigger the accelerator, the worse it gets. And so now you’re compounding the problem. If you have something that’s, say, 100 TOPS and you have to have, say, 16 RISC-V processors slave to a whole bunch of accelerator blocks, sure, you need great interconnect, and you need great verification, and all those things that go with it because you’re trying to solve the underlying fundamental problem, which is starting with a CPU. And CPUs are great for chasing pointers. That’s what CPUs do. CPUs have wonderful logic to handle the fact that you’ve got 40 threads running, and on the very next clock tick, you have no idea what you’ll be running. That’s not what you’re doing when you’re doing AI inference. You know for millions of cycles in advance what’s happening. You don’t need most of the CPU hardware. DSPs are a little closer to what you need, but DSPs are vector machines — vector-by-scalar or vector-by-vector. And most of what is challenging in AI is matrix-by-matrix. So we built a matrix-native machine. The only other one I know of that’s close to that is in the data center, and that’s the big giant TPUs from Google. Literally, everybody else has a partitioned problem, and then they struggle and spend billions of dollars trying to handle that partitioning problem and figure out how to make up for the fact that they started from, we think, a bad place. Kelf : I agree with Steve’s point, because what we’re seeing is large AI accelerators — which might be different architectures, SIMD, SIMT — are pretty common. These kinds of things basically are controlled, or have been controlled, by a complex state machine of some sort, and then there’ll be some kind of host processor driving several of these different things and telling the state machine what to do, and then driving the accelerator. What we’ve seen in four instances now, both big and small companies, is that the state machines are hopeless. So they’re taking a RISC-V processor, and they’re using that as the control function on top of these accelerators for a number of reasons. One is that they can, in fact, build in a bunch of mathematical engines — exactly what Steve was mentioning — vector type, using either the RISC-V vector instructions or those. And then they add in their own, as well, or some of the new matrix multiplication instructions. They’re also putting in their own instructions for very efficient load/store to reduce the latency that you see between partitions. So they’re trying to figure out how they can adjust these RISC-V processes to reduce that latency and to reduce that partitioning problem. We have a number of examples where some are successful, some are less so. They’re still working on this problem, but RISC-V is nice because they can add whatever custom instructions they want, still use a regular compiler, and create a mechanism to drive a very efficient load/store that they can’t with other processors. Then, of course, there are people like Arm and others who have built instructions into some of their processors, but they’re not variable. RISC-V is ideal for this, and pretty unique in its ability to create these powerful custom instructions. SE: Regarding those custom vector instructions, are EDA tools accounting for this and automating the verification? Roddy : I spent 17 years at Tensilica. We automated all that. events.title: Data centre industry butts up against community challenges
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre industry faces community challenges amid cancelled projects Data centre companies are reportedly grappling with how to get community engagement "right". ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) The industry body for data centre proponents says its members are battling community hesitancy and policy uncertainty. It comes amid calls by minor parties for SA to halt approvals for new centres. The state government is preparing legislation to regulate the industry. The peak body representing data centres in Australia say its members are still grappling with "getting community consultation right" after several AI companies have either dumped or paused their plans for building centres across the country. South Australia has today seen the first sign of data centre development in retreat , with Quantum DC announcing it will pause plans to build a 1200-megawatt AI data centre in Tungkillo, in the Adelaide Hills, following deep frustration, anger and protests from the surrounding community. In New South Wales, another AI data centre proposed for Sydney's south, on the Cooks River, was scrapped over the weekend, the latest in a series of proposed NSW data centres to be dumped following community opposition. Peak body Data Centres Australia does not represent Quantum DC. Speaking broadly, its CEO Belinda Dennett said the challenge with community engagement was choosing the right time. "Communities want early engagement, but they also want detailed answers, so there is a bit of a trade-off. "Often, early engagement means you don't have all those answers around design plans, around energy source, around how much water that may use." She said there was great potential and interest to build data centres in South Australia, but operators and investors wanted policy certainty. "That's the challenge for all the states at the moment, the challenge of not having federal rules in place … we don't have that policy certainty," she said. "The quicker we have certainty, the more viable I think Australia's going to be." Tungkillo's rolling hills won't have a data centre, for now. ( Supplied: Magdalene Lippett ) All sides of politics welcome pause On Thursday, political parties including the Liberals, One Nation and the Greens welcomed the pause on the Tungkillo development, while the SA government criticised the developer for its consultation process. The Greens went a step further, calling for a data centre moratorium. SA's minister for artificial intelligence (AI), Chris Picton, said the Tungkillo announcement highlighted why the state government was keen to get legislation through the parliament to enable proper regulatory control. "[It's] going to be critical to making sure that we can think through all these issues with data centres to make sure that can be managed in an appropriate way, whether that be issues about energy, or water, or land use," Mr Picton said. Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said it didn't make sense for a data centre at Tungkillo to be built on "prime agricultural land", but there was also a need to make sure the community understood why data centres are needed. "We believe that a vehicle to do that is including them in the royal commission," Ms Hurn said. When details of the state's Royal Commission into Artificial Intelligence were released in early October , its terms of reference did not include data centres. Mr Picton said it wasn't remiss of the government not to include them: "They are completely separate things. "Data centres have issues, but they're infrastructure issues … They're issues about energy use, water use and where the land is." Community protests against the Tungkillo data centre seem to have had an effect. ( ABC News: James Wakelin ) The Greens, One Nation and the Liberal Party united in the upper house on Wednesday to establish a parliamentary inquiry into data centres, which was not supported by Labor. One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said the party would like to see a pause on data centres until the inquiry is finished. "But we're also recognising that data centres per se are not bad," he said. "We have a data centre here in the metropolitan area of Adelaide that hasn't caused any fuss at all. "But what we want is a community licence for it.

events.title: Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists
events.summary: Island Energy said customers can contact its customer team for support Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses. The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026. It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran. Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter." Listen to the latest news for Jersey Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said. However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey." Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available. events.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
events.summary: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.” The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang faces second affair claim as Nvidia board considers his future
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is facing new allegations of a second affair, this time with a senior executive at the chipmaker, as the company's board meets to decide whether he should keep his job. The New York Times has reported that Mr Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and one of his about 60 direct reports, quoting five people who have worked at the company. Ms Powell has been with Nvidia for more than 18 years. Nvidia has declined to comment on the allegation and has not said whether its board inquiry, launched on Sunday into Mr Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, will be widened to cover it. The company's code of conduct addresses conflicts arising from personal relationships and requires reported misconduct to be investigated. The allegation came days after Mr Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife , following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China. Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation, while expressing confidence in his leadership. China has called the allegations “entirely groundless”. The Wall Street Journal reported late on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust Mr Huang. Directors have also hired an outside firm to identify possible replacements, according to reports. Under Nvidia's bylaws, a majority of its 11 directors, all of whom, except Mr Huang, are independent, can remove the chief executive “with or without cause”. Nvidia shares, which closed 2.9 per cent higher at $173.73 on Wednesday, fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading . The fallout extends well beyond the boardroom. Nvidia's chips underpin the global AI build-out, from US technology giants to sovereign projects in the Gulf, and the scandal has emboldened lawmakers seeking tighter controls on where those chips can be sold. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has estimated the company's value at $300 a share with Mr Huang as chief executive and $225 without him. Mr Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has no obvious successor. Analysts have suggested chief financial officer Colette Kress as a possible interim leader. Pressure is also building in Washington as House Republicans are pushing for Mr Huang to testify and have raised the possibility of a subpoena. Legislators from both parties are calling for tighter curbs on chip exports to China. US President Donald Trump has called Mr Huang “an honourable guy”. Mr Huang remains listed as the keynote speaker at Nvidia's GTC event in Washington from December 1 to 3.

events.title: AI won't transform your business unless you transform it first
events.summary: Organisations need to overhaul their processes to truly reap the benefits of artificial intelligence , according to experts. Bolting the technology to existing systems will not bring about the drastic changes that AI providers are touting. “It's a huge change and that's why the dynamic is not going to be as fast as people imagine,” said Denis Torii, vice president analyst at Gartner. “It's not an IT story for sure. It's not [the case of] only the business stakeholders who are pushing us to adopt more AI ,” he said. "It's actually an organisational story, where the organisation needs to adapt to it." AI is only working as an accessory today. “Right now [organisations] are doing the same stuff but with AI in the middle, and that probably is not going to bring that transformation that people are expecting,” he told The National on the sidelines of the recent Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas. Currently, organisations are using AI across the enterprise with a range of tools – from chatbots and software coding agents to agentic systems capable of acting autonomously across workflows, a McKinsey report in August found. However, enterprise-level financial impact remains limited. Only 37 per cent of respondents reported an AI contribution to their organisations' earnings before interest and tax (Ebit), unchanged from a year earlier, McKinsey's Global Survey on the State of AI found. To benefit from AI requires a shift in leadership mindset, according to Gabby Fredkin, head of analytics and insights at Adapt, a specialist IT research advisory. A fundamental change is needed to go from “we're just going to layer technology on, to we're actually going to think about the ethos of our organisation, what we do, the type of roles that we have”, he said. “So, it's a complicated process.” The organisations that generally succeed with AI tend to have a leadership that has a good conceptual understanding about it and encourages people to innovate, he added. The experience of a small group of high performers highlights the technology’s successful use, the McKinsey report said. “High performers pursue growth and/or innovation alongside efficiency; they fundamentally redesign workflows that are enabled by AI rather than insert AI into existing ones; and they back their deployments with the leadership commitment and operational rigor needed to achieve real gains," the report found. Mr Fredkin said companies must look into their operating models to see how they can go beyond traditional processes and capture new revenue streams. “If you're a bank and you've got data because you've got investments in different infrastructure, do you want to get into infrastructure as an investment? Do you want to start a real estate investment trust? How are you thinking about what you have and what you do, and what are the parallels outside of that?", he said. Such a shift would be harder for some organisations than others, he added. Cost factor AI-related operating costs are beginning to constrain its use for about one in five organisations, the McKinsey report said, even as most respondents expect their companies to increase AI investments in the year ahead. Companies are taking a cautious approach as they prepare their data and processes for AI integration, said analyst John Reed, co-founder of US-based tech platform diginomica. “If companies know that it's not going to be that expensive to use these technologies, I think they are going to find significant benefits,” he said. AI could prove particularly valuable in complex, mission-critical tasks that humans struggle to perform in real time, Mr Reed added. “For example, it's very difficult for a human to assess global supply chain impacts in real time … these [AI] systems actually are able to, if you provide them with the right data.” However, adoption will take time, as many companies grapple with fragmented data and legacy systems, he added. The trillion-dollar ROI challenge Investment in AI is soaring. Worldwide spending is forecast to total $2.7 trillion this year, up 49.5 per cent annually, Gartner said in a report in September. AI infrastructure, particularly data centres and specialised servers, remains the biggest spending driver, with Gartner describing the buildout as the “largest infrastructure project humanity has ever undertaken”. Goldman Sachs Research separately estimates $1 trillion in global AI-related investment this year, including $581 billion in the US. It expects AI capital expenditure to rise from 0.9 per cent of global GDP in 2026 to 1.4 per cent by 2028. But the spending boom is raising questions about the revenue needed to justify it. The AI industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed, a report by consultancy Bain in September found. “Return on investment is still one of the biggest issues [with AI],” said Mr Torii. “People are putting all this faith in AI, [with the assumption that] there's a lot of potential. “When you look at the broad picture, it's still lacking evidence that return on investment is there,” he said, adding, however, that vendors need to invest heavily upfront. “They need to help customers somehow to get to that journey. So there's a lot of friction and inertia that needs to be overcome.” He compared AI's trajectory to the early days of cloud computing, when heavy infrastructure investment preceded widespread adoption. The question, Mr Torii said, is how long it will take for AI to bridge the gap. Measuring returns is another challenge, Mr Fredkin said. “They [organisations] feel a productivity uplift. They feel better employee engagement. Putting an actual figure behind that is incredibly complex,” he said. “From the perspective of the CFO [chief financial officer], the calculations for how they look at ROI [return on investment] have changed significantly. It's not a line item any more; it's a meter.” He cited an emerging term “double T Ebitda”, which refers to earnings before interest, tax, tokens, depreciation, and amortisation. Unlike blockchain and metaverse technologies, AI is already gaining traction across businesses and is likely to see wider adoption, Mr Reed said. Looking ahead, he is slightly pessimistic about its broader implications. “I think we're in some significant trouble because we put a lot of eggs in the basket of a technology that, while it's good for business, I'm not convinced [about] the ultimate impact in terms of surveillance and disinformation and deep fakes and the inability to trust content and the displacement of humans from jobs,” he said. “But one of the things about technology is that it can be decentralised and changed and appropriated too. And there's a lot of very thoughtful people that are using some of these tools for really cool, worthwhile projects as well,” he added.

events.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
events.summary: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

events.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
events.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The other side: The White House didn't answer questions about the bill. In a statement, spokesperson Lauren Bis said President Trump has "been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee's subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein's Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein's victims than anyone before him." Speaker Mike Johnson's office did not respond to a request for comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January. Editor's note: This story has been updated to add the White House's comment.

events.title: Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss
events.summary: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services. Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach. On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility. Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

events.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
events.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

events.summary: China’s marriage rate fell to its lowest level in almost two decades , adding to worries about the country’s demographic crisis. Data this week showed 4.65 million couples tied the knot from January through September, while 2.08 million couples got divorced. Beijing has in recent years rolled out a series of measures aimed at increasing marriage rates and childbearing. But while some regions have seen results from such policies, fertility rates for the country as a whole continue to plummet, with women on average having fewer children than even during the era of the one-child policy . The demographic shift will have huge fiscal consequences for decades to come, with one prominent China academic urging Beijing to “formulate forward-looking plans for immigration .” — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: What it takes to bring an AI research assistant to thousands of medical experts
events.summary: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents What we learned rebuilding Novo’s clinical trials data agent on Microsoft Foundry: a simpler operating model, a stronger session isolation, and a direct path from tracing to evaluation and optimization. Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research. As part of a forward-deployed engineering engagement, a joint Microsoft and Novo Nordisk development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a Microsoft customer story . More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry . The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time. Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move. An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization. This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user. Our first production architecture ran the agent in Azure Container Apps . We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case. It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility. Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by Foundry Agent Service . We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it. At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure. For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways: Scaling became session-native. We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle. Isolation became the default unit of execution. Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data. Network isolation became part of the service architecture. Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary. The agent joined a broader development lifecycle. Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. Microsoft Agent 365 integration also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance. Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently. Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry: Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end. Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration. Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current networking guidance recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments. We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge. Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product. Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights.
