events.title: House Democrats lobby against China committee
events.summary: Some Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee are encouraging leaders to scrap the chamber’s Select Committee on China once their party takes over next year. “For a lot of what the China committee was doing — we’ve already got a Foreign Affairs Committee, we’ve already got the Subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific,” California’s Rep. Ami Bera, the top Democrat on that subcommittee, told Semafor. “We could do a lot of the work; I think Ways and Means [Committee] could do a lot of the trade policy stuff.” A spokesperson for New York’s Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs committee, told Semafor that “we will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy.” The committee’s current chair, Michigan Republican Rep. John Moolenaar, released a statement last week urging Democrats not to dismantle it. Other Democrats are pushing for the committee to broaden its focus beyond China if they opt to keep it next Congress. Still others in the party are worried about the politics of axing the committee for parochial committee leadership reasons, given recent China-related controversies . “Politically, they’re not smart, because they could use this against Trump, who’s being basically pro-China,” a person familiar with the jockeying told Semafor. “Maybe modify it [or] alter it in terms of scope — but to shut it down or make it part of the Foreign Affairs Committee is honestly dumb.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who as speaker would have the final say over the future makeup of select panels, said earlier this week he would discuss the issue with incoming committee leaders this morning. Some of them have also pushed back against the idea of forming a select panel on AI next year as Democratic committee leaders look to reserve their own turf on AI and other high-profile issues. Other observers have noted that the China panel’s jurisdiction extends across that of others, and it has collaborated with the House Oversight, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Homeland Security, Appropriations, and Natural Resources committees. At least five groups have sent letters, shared with Semafor, urging leaders to reauthorize the committee come January: the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, With Honor Action, the Alliance for Trade Enforcement NOW, the American Mold Builders Association, and the Forging Industry Association.

events.title: Miller’s promotion extinguishes hope for immigration deal
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s flirtation with a bipartisan immigration deal is running into a wall of skepticism in Washington. For one, Democrats scoffed at Trump’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policies, to chief of staff following the departure of Susie Wiles. There’s little indication that Miller has softened on immigration whatsoever. And while Trump acknowledged in a CBS interview that his deportation policy might “be too tough” and said a bipartisan deal could be “doable,” many in the White House agree there’s simply far too much daylight between Trump and newly-empowered Democrats. There’s “too big a margin” between the two sides “for it not to be a crazy bill,” one administration official told Semafor.“The Dems are going to overreach almost immediately, there will be no amnesty,” the official added. Still, Trump on Monday suggested that Miller would look to work with Democrats, while quickly drawing a clear line on what an immigration deal could include: “We’re not going to have amnesty or anything,” Trump said. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement that Trump’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” “The administration will continue removing the worst of the worst from our country,” Rogers said, blaming former President Joe Biden’s administration for creating an immigration crisis. “What the Democrats did to our country will not be forgotten, and the president is willing to work with anyone to ensure it never happens again.” The View From democrats Democrats have no interest in working with Miller given his record. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries dismissed the White House aide on Monday as “a stone-cold racist,” adding that he has “zero interest in working with that kind of individual.” Jeffries has talked up the “Dream and Promise Act” as a comprehensive immigration bill that Democrats want to move through both chambers, though it’s unlikely to break a filibuster in the Senate next year. Some lawmakers are also looking to the “Dignity Act” as one potential bipartisan compromise on border security and immigration reform, but that bill already fractured Republicans this Congress who balked at its pathways to legal residency for “Dreamers.” “The three things that Latinos expected Democrats to do is ICE accountability, pathway to citizenship, and to lower costs,” María Teresa Kumar, president and CEO of Voto Latino, said at a National Partnership for Women and Families Event Tuesday. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, said the “Dignity Act” would be reintroduced next Congress and could be rewritten to include more Democratic priorities now that they’d be in control of the House and Senate. She too, conceded that Miller would be “a problem” but added “the ultimate decision is Donald Trump’s, and he said he was open to making a deal. Let’s see if he’s a man of his word or not.” Room for Disagreement A Trump adviser echoed the president’s dismissal of any sort of deal on broad immigration amnesty, but suggested a longshot plan: “If [Trump] can get the Democrats on board with increased funding for ICE and law enforcement to specifically target murderers, rapists, drug dealers, and the most hardened criminals, I think that’d be a great deal for the country.” That adviser emphasized that Trump and Miller will be focused on doing “what’s best for the MAGA base.”

events.title: Republicans reckon with Iran war funding quagmire
events.summary: The News Senate Republicans spent this week wrestling through divisions, reelecting John Thune as their leader, and pledging to confirm conservative judges while avoiding a government shutdown during their last two months in the majority. They still haven’t figured out how to use their greatest power in the lame duck: another big party-line bill that would send billions to the Pentagon. Such a proposal could contain other GOP priorities; Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, dubbed it the “last supper” for the party’s reign. Republicans have just a few more weeks to use the blunt power of budget reconciliation, which allows them to evade a filibuster to send President Donald Trump funding viewed as crucial by many in the Republican Party for depleted military reserves and ammunition after nine months of war. Using the tool, which Republicans wielded last year to pass a party line tax bill and this year for immigration enforcement funding, represents a crucial calculation for Thune to make as Democrats weigh blocking a government funding bill if it includes money for the Iran conflict. But passing a party-line bill is not going to be easy: It requires 50 Senate votes, a majority in the House, and two unlimited Senate vote-a-ramas that defeated or retiring members may have little interest in enduring. And Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who would set the stage for another big party-line bill, said he’s worried the party isn’t moving quickly enough. “Right now, I’m not getting engagement from the White House, from either Senate or House leadership. So if that’s going to happen, it’s going to come from the pressure from members here,” Johnson told Semafor on Tuesday. Republicans are divided over whether they should shovel more money towards the Pentagon with the Iran war is ongoing, particularly since many in the GOP cite the conflict as one of the main reasons for the party’s brutal losses in this month’s midterm elections. Republicans are also growing more frustrated over the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who avoided a House impeachment on Tuesday but is facing sustained questions from congressional Republicans over Iran and his blocking of military promotions. And Republicans say there still isn’t a blueprint on how to move forward. “I think we’re going to have a plan,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., after a day of literally hours of internal GOP meetings. “If you’re asking me if we have a plan right now, I wouldn’t recognize it if it jumped up and yodeled and bit me in the butt.” When it comes to more Pentagon funding in a party-line bill, there are real divisions emerging behind the scenes already. On one side is Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., who said “we need to get reconciliation done.” Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Semafor the party needs to pass a “strong” reconciliation bill and that it’s not going to be aimed at Iran: “That has a lot more to do with funding our military and giving them what they need than it does the war.” But Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., argued it would be “tone-deaf” to pass such a bill and vowed to oppose it. He said passing anything “to further or enhance the Iran war, I think that’s not listening to the electorate.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said, “I can’t imagine why we would do that.” Both Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, are wary of using reconciliation. Republicans would not brand the effort as an Iran war funding bill, but they would have a difficult argument to make if the conflict continues. Many Republicans have wanted the war to end as soon as it started. unanswered questions Thune said repeatedly this week that he’s not sure he or House Speaker Mike Johnson can round up the votes to get another reconciliation bill done. He said Pentagon funding is a “major issue that has to be addressed” but that he doesn’t know if he has 50 Republicans ready to pass a budget resolution and endure those prolonged amendment votes. With a government funding deadline bearing down on Congress next month, putting a party-line funding bill on the table is “the only way we create some leverage with the Democrats,” argued Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a close Thune ally. “If we just sit and wait for them to come to the table, they’ll figure they have leverage because they’ll have the majority in the new Congress. So the thing they have to recognize is we can put a reconciliation bill together,” Hoeven said. There are competing priorities among Republicans of what that reconciliation bill would do. While Pentagon funding is the most obvious must for some Republicans, others would push to include measures to address the cost of living, elections, farm aid, and more. “What we’re trying to do is jam 18 things into a four-thing box,” said Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. “I may be a proponent of it. Because it’s very possible to try to get as much done as you can possibly get done before the other folks take over.” Room for Disagreement Justice said even Republican critics of the Iran war would have to come around eventually. “We’re there, like it or not like it. And if we’ve got folks there, and they need bullets and we can’t give them the bullets, shame on us,” he said. “However you feel about [the war], really, if we don’t fund the military, we’re sending the wrong signal for even the ones who want to settle out sooner,” Hoeven said. Burgess’s view Welcome to the first legislative battle after the midterms. Democrats are starting to line up against anything funding the Iran war, which could leave reconciliation as Republicans’ only play. But it’s still a risky one. There are logistical challenges: The Senate is only scheduled to be in session for four weeks the rest of the year, although Thune said he’s willing to add days and weeks to complete their agenda. If Republicans are going to move a big party-line bill, the earlier the better. If they wait until late in December to do it, lame-duck fatigue will have set in and outgoing Republicans will be itching to leave Washington. In other words, it’s already late.

events.title: Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year
events.summary: Japanese automaker Nissan has trimmed its losses over the first fiscal half, compared to the previous year, and reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year TOKYO -- Japanese automaker Nissan trimmed its losses over the first half of the fiscal year, compared to the previous year, and on Wednesday reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year. Losses at Nissan Motor Co. , based in the port city of Yokohama, for the April-September period totaled 39.7 billion yen ($250 million), smaller than the 221.9 billion yen red ink for the same period last year. Nissan’s six-month sales rose 8.8% to 6.07 trillion yen, helped by a favorable exchange rate and pricing. U.S. and Japanese markets did well as far as vehicle sales, while the situation remained challenging in China, where competition remains fierce . The unrest in the Middle East , which has raised the price of some raw materials, while blocking shipments, continues to hurt Nissan, as with other Japanese companies. Nissan stuck to its earlier projection to return to profit for the fiscal year through March 2027, at a net profit of 20 billion yen. That marks a recovery from the last two fiscal years, when Nissan has been in the red. “The second half offers real opportunities to make progress,” said Chief Executive Ivan Espinosa, stressing that model launches will build on the recovery “momentum, market by market.” “The next step is to build on that foundation,” he told reporters. Nissan’s new business plan is set to be announced in February next year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base: Sources China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments dismissed, saying agent lied to grand jury Nissan, which makes the Rogue sport utility vehicle, Z sports car and Infiniti luxury models, is allied with Renault SA of France and Mitsubishi Motors Corp. of Japan. It also has a partnership with Japanese rival Honda Motor Co., sharing technology and some parts. Nissan’s results were hurt by an earthquake that struck Kumamoto, southwestern Japan, earlier this year. Nissan’s plant there lost days of production, but no employee was injured. Nissan’s stocks, which have declined over the past year, slipped 1.5% in Wednesday trading, ahead of the earnings announcement. events.title: Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy She was building a career in Chinese finance before turning to tech with a leadership role at a data center company in Singapore. He is the high-profile CEO of Nvidia , the California-based company that makes computer chips relied upon by advanced artificial intelligence systems. An affair between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who reportedly was suspected of working as a spy for Beijing, has rocked the tech and political worlds . The Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to reports over the past month by the New York Times. The newspaper also reported that top policymakers were informed in a memo that intelligence indicated she was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China. In one widely shared photograph of the pair, Jensen Huang and people surrounding him are holding drinks in Taipei, while Alice Huang sits behind him, apparently watching him in conversation. The picture was posted in 2024 by software company NetThunder to its LinkedIn page. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. Publicly available information about Alice Huang is scant. She was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. In 2023, she became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which describes itself as an “NVIDIA cloud partner.” Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. over its alleged skirting of U.S. export restrictions and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips for Chinese users. Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 in Singapore with the name 7Road International, after being spun off as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, according to corporate registration records. Filings show that in March 2023, it renamed itself Megaspeed International, with all of the shares transferred to Huang Le Limited, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. That same month, Alice Huang became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security. But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan. While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations. What to know about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid espionage scandal Nvidia's Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged affair with reported spy 1 dead, 4 injured, in Washington, DC, after shooting Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database. Her roles at Hexi included deputy general manager, executive director and member of the investment committee, according to Hexi's social media posts, among possible other roles. Hexi's founder Kang Wei, who appeared on some records alongside Alice Huang, was fined in 2018 by China's securities regulator 400,000 yuan ($60,000) over financial misconduct behaviors while Hexi was fined 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million). Before that, Alice Huang worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her employment history. Beijing has refuted claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Its Foreign Ministry said this week that the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again under the spotlight. Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.” It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd. Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.

events.title: Democrats urge Rubio to act on Ethiopia
events.summary: Democratic senators are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene diplomatically to address the crisis in Ethiopia, warning that renewed fighting in Tigray and escalating tensions with Eritrea could spiral into a multi-front war destabilizing the region. In a letter shared first with Semafor , lawmakers led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s top Democrat, asked the State Department to back an immediate ceasefire and new mediation including groups left out of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. They also called for halting new arms sales to Ethiopia, reinstating Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopians in the US, and surging food aid as the fighting worsens the impact of drought on a deeply food insecure population. Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del. — expected to succeed the retiring Shaheen and chair the committee when Democrats take the Senate in January — also signed the letter, alongside the other three Democratic members of the committee’s Africa panel. “US diplomatic engagement has lacked the urgency, visibility, and coordination commensurate with the threat of another devastating civil war in Ethiopia and regional conflict,” the senators wrote. They warned against putting Eritrea’s Port of Assab — which Ethiopia wants to control — on the negotiating table. “Since the September 23 outbreak of fighting within Ethiopia, the United States has repeatedly called for Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors,” a State Department spokesperson said. “This message has been delivered by the highest levels of the US government to both sides privately and in our public statements over the last six months,” they said. Clashes in Tigray resumed in August, and in late September the Tigray People’s Liberation Front-led regional government launched an offensive after weeks of drone and artillery attacks from Ethiopia’s government. The TPLF was fighting alongside other armed opposition groups, but the campaign stalled within days and federal forces retook most of Tigray. Eritrean forces reportedly crossed the border to support the TPLF, though the country denies it. The Trump administration imposed visa restrictions on TPLF “hardliners” in June, but lifted its arms-export ban on Ethiopia in May and let the sanctions program targeting the conflict lapse in September. Rubio called for de-escalation during an October call with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed; a State Department statement described “peace through dialogue” as “the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity.”

events.title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
events.summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.” The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff. “The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli , Prada Group's chief group marketing officer. Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed. Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces. “We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli. Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway. And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo. Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988. The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport. “Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.” Microsoft Outlook outage updates: 'Progress toward recovery' Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition. Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission , targeted for 2028. Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution. Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment. Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises. The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.” “It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. events.title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
events.summary: As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s emphasis on zero waste puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, less than 7% of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over 2 billion tons of trash per year — a figure that could nearly double by 2050 . AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills. “A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.” See how four members of the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation. AIRECO Gives Plastic Waste New Life Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products. The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product. “The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.” The company uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%. In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%. EverestLabs AI Puts Robotics on the Recycling Line At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items. EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia. “Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.” EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on NVIDIA data center GPUs , optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries. Greyparrot Gives Recyclers a Clear View of the Waste Stream Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it. U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second. “Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.” Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six. Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of food-grade plastics by 12% . Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants. reverse.fashion Gives Discarded Garments a Second Look Europe generates nearly 7 million tons of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried. reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category. “Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.” As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with NVIDIA TensorRT software and running on NVIDIA Jetson modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud. The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe. events.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
events.summary: The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun. Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run. Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation. Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger. ‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won. Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes. Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios. "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios. 🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader." The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both. Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: " [T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change. 🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority. "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday. Some of his new members are signaling that they're not afraid to defy their new leaders. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker, "but Rome is burning." But other new members are on Jeffries' side, like Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.) and Cait Conley (D-N.Y.). 🤝 Jeffries also has high-profile progressive incumbents on board, such as Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race , Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising?" Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Between the lines: Thune and Jordan don't have much of a relationship; Thune had left the House for the Senate two years before Jordan arrived. What's next: Senators say they plan to be in the Capitol working on Veterans Day. Thune committed to working more days during the lame-duck session to ensure they leave no judge appointments behind, senators said.

events.title: "Rome is burning": Incoming House Democrats prove unusually willing to defy leaders
events.summary: House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare. Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger. "My class is huge not because of ... the Democratic Party and its brand but despite it," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "Many of us are outsiders who didn't come up through the machine, don't buy into the conventions." Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) told Axios: "Any members that are new and have just run their elections are going to be very close to where the voters are, and we know the voters are very upset." State of play: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is on track to become speaker, in part thanks to his rock-solid support among sitting House Democrats. His supporters include high-profile progressives such as Casar and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Things get more spotty when gauging Jeffries' support among incoming freshmen, some of whom have openly declined to commit to supporting his leadership. That includes members of the informal progressive "Bloc," including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Chris Rabb (D-Pa.). "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only one running," said progressive Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). "But ... I think we need to see some prioritization of some legislation, particularly around health care, foreign policy and immigration." Some incoming and sitting House Democrats have been flooded with calls and emails urging them not to elect Jeffries speaker, Axios previously reported . The intrigue: It's not just progressives hesitating to throw their full-throated support behind Jeffries. The list also includes some moderates in districts President Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Said Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-Nev.), a member of the center-left New Democrat Coalition: "I just won a district that went for Trump two years ago by 14%. … I've got to turn around and show that we're making change." "For anyone running for speaker, that's my message back to them," she added. "It's much more about, like, what can you do for Nevada?" "I'd like to see who's on the ballot," said Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), a member of both the New Dems and the centrist Blue Dogs. "Until I've had an opportunity to chat, until I've had an opportunity to see who's out there, I'm not making any decisions." Yes, but: Plenty of freshmen are supporting Jeffries as well. Well-represented in that contingent are incoming members who ran in marquee races with substantial backing from House Democrats' campaign apparatus, including Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Manny Rutinel (D-Colo.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.), Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) and Rebecca Bennett (D-N.J.). Rep.-elect Zack Mullock (D-N.J.), who didn't have support from the national party, told Axios he is "not making many big splashes" as a new member: "You're going to have pretty strong support for Hakeem, and I'll be part of that support." Zoom in: Several members, such as Leonard and Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.), have said they want to see Jeffries commit to a ban on corporate PACs as a prerequisite for voting for him. "We need a 28th Amendment in the year 2028 or before to shut down Elon Musk and corporate money and Israeli lobby money, for that matter," Leonard said. Said Ojeda: "I have hard lines: I want to make sure that we are making sure we are getting big money out of politics. It's time for us to stop allowing the billionaire class to buy our elections." The bottom line: Leonard said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker of the House, but that "Rome is burning." The Ohio Democrat said he needs to be able to tell his districts "the leader shares our sense of urgency for transformational change and is willing to take the size of his caucus and take it for a spin."

events.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
events.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities. Driving the news : Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times. The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's May 13–15 trip to China. Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday . On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips. Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers. Yes, but : It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals. Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets. What they're saying : Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me." The Commerce Department did not comment. Catch up quick : Nvidia has been rocked by the scandal , losing about $1 trillion in market value since the Times' first reported the relationship, although some of that decline also came after an overwhelming number of Democrats promising to slow an AI data-center buildout were elected in the midterms. Huang acknowledged an affair Sunday , and Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation. The board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security secrets were compromised. What to watch : New revelations continue to drop almost daily about the administration's handling of the Nvidia CEO's relationship. Lawmakers in both parties have promised investigations and demanded more information, including closed-door testimony from Jensen Huang next week. Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs committee have also demanded answers from Lutnick about the administration's chip approvals, "including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang."

events.title: Trump swung between war and diplomacy — then chose a third way
events.summary: When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios. Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants. "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said. This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them. Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris. "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room. Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date. "The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio said. The intrigue: U.S. officials say that Rubio was among the members of Trump's national security team who pushed for the strangulation strategy, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Jared Kushner, Trump's adviser and son-in-law. That group opposed the resumption of war, didn't believe Iran's current positions could lead to a deal that serves U.S. interests and lobbied for the third option. State of play: Rubio is deeply skeptical of a diplomatic breakthrough. " Iran would love a deal. The problem is the conditions they continue to place are absurd. Like, they're not even serious right now," he told reporters after the G7 meeting. That could change if the Iranians feel more economic pain, he said. "Eventually you have to eat," he said. "Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic. So I think as time goes on that will have an impact." Yes, but: Several U.S. allies — such as Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan — are concerned about Trump's intention to prolong the economic squeeze, a U.S. official said. The person said those allies worry that U.S. pressure on them to stop doing business with Iran — including by stopping flights and closing their borders — will create instability in their own countries. The other side: The course Trump has chosen is completely at odds with the directive Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave his government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Khamenei ordered an end to the "no war, no deal" status quo, demanding a clear conclusion to the war. Iran's civilian leadership interpreted this as a green light to negotiate a deal. But if the current stalemate continues and pressure on Iran intensifies, the IRGC could see it as a green light for more aggressive attacks in the region in an attempt to break the status quo. "Iran has no intention of simply accepting this situation indefinitely," said Danny Citrinowicz, an expert on Iran at the Atlantic Council. "Tehran may conclude that increasing the economic and security costs for Washington and its regional partners is the only way to force a change in American policy." He added: "The danger is obvious: Iran escalates, Washington responds, and both sides find themselves in another military confrontation that neither necessarily wanted." What to watch: Qatar's prime minister briefed the G7 meeting on mediation efforts and his conversation with Trump the previous day. Al Thani said he came away from his meeting with Trump believing there's more breathing room for diplomatic efforts. The sticking points remain which side will take the first step toward de-escalating and which confidence-building measures the parties will agree to take. The Qatari prime minister said he wants to bring in China and European countries as guarantors, to help ease deep Iranian suspicions that Trump will break the agreement and resume the war in a few months.

events.title: He took down Andrew Cuomo. Now Jensen Huang is in his crosshairs
events.summary: The Scene Joon Kim has taken down mobsters, pursued a congressman, and investigated sexual harassment claims that toppled a New York governor. His latest assignment will decide the fate of a $4 trillion dollar company the global economy depends on. The former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York was tapped to investigate whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, following Huang’s bombshell admission Sunday that the chief executive had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Kim, a 55-year-old prosecutor who joined Wachtell Lipton last month, will lead an internal probe overseen by a committee of independent directors, into whether Nvidia’s Huang compromised trade secrets — or, more pressingly, the US’ national security interests. The company has said it has confidence in its CEO and has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” A spokesperson for Wachtell declined to comment on the firm’s and Kim’s behalf. Shares in Nvidia have dropped 10% since Huang’s admission, knocking $500 billion off the company’s market value and stoking worries about the future of a company that underpins an AI financing buildout that has ensnared most of the global financial system. It comes against a fraught national security backdrop in which US officials have been warning for months of foreign influence campaigns and corporate espionage. A tangled web Huang, a close confidant of US President Donald Trump, has pushed Nvidia to take stakes in hundreds of companies across the AI boom it supplies. The company has also entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals up and down Wall Street. Even Kim’s own employer, Wachtell Lipton, is not immune: OpenAI is one of Wachtell’s highest-profile clients, and the law firm’s M&A advisors are working on the company’s pending IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. Nvidia is a major OpenAI investor and the primary supplier of the chips that underpin the data centers (which Nvidia also finances) that power OpenAI’s models. Corporate probes can range from window dressing to essentially prosecutorial in nature, and Nvidia has 4 trillion reasons to limit its damage. It’s unclear how far Nvidia’s board will let Kim roam, but the board has already drummed up corporate governance concerns: The unusually long-tenured board lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies as large as Nvidia’s and has let Huang run the company with no clear successor and more than 50 direct reports. Mob bosses Kim began his career at New York’s Southern District more than two decades ago, working in the organized crime unit before leaving for Cleary Gottlieb in 2006. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Kim traveled around the world, including in Jordan and the UK. In his first stint as a federal prosecutor, Kim took on mob boss John “Junior” Gotti in a federal racketeering trial, trying him for the kidnapping of future New York mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa. “His entire adult life, John Jr. has thought himself special, entitled to everything, accountable for nothing,” Kim said at the time. His former colleagues describe Kim as dogged, citing his time at the Southern District in 2013, under Attorney Preet Bharara, where Kim pursued a successful case against disgraced former Congressman Anthony Weiner and briefly ran the Southern District after Trump fired Bharara. Kim returned to Cleary in 2018, where he led a number of internal investigations into allegations of executive wrongdoing at large corporations, including Nissan Motors’ probe into former CEO Carlos Ghosn. But among his most defining cases was New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, which led to his 2021 resignation. Cuomo’s office was “rife with bullying, fear and intimidation,” Kim said when announcing his findings. A sensitive assignment Before Sunday, Huang and spokespeople for the company had publicly denied that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with Alice Huang. The company abruptly changed tack on Sunday, when Huang wrote a letter to employees admitting to the affair and announcing a plan to initiate an independent probe. The company had assembled an independent committee to oversee the investigation and was on Sunday leaning toward tapping former Cooley CEO Stephen Neal, the Financial Times reported and Semafor can confirm. Some Nvidia directors also suggested tapping Cooley to run the independent probe, other people familiar with the matter said. Cooley is Nvidia’s longtime outside counsel and would have exposed the company to criticism that the probe wasn’t independent, especially since Cooley is best known for its tech and IP practices, and isn’t considered by white-shoe lawyers to have a top-tier white-collar investigations practice. Nvidia declined to comment on either the nature of the independent committee or on whether directors considered tapping Cooley. Notable Neal has been involved in other high-profile misconduct cases , including representing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.

events.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
events.summary: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe , Apple , Google and Mozilla . Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969. November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device. This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes. According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194 , a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office . Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS , macOS , watchOS and visionOS . Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. Lee Neely , an instructor at the SANS Institute , noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18. “I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.” Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50 , which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350 , the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today ( Firefox 160 ) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity. Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited. Chris Goettl , vice president of product management at Ivanti , said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). “Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.” Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

events.title: A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.
events.summary: Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off. In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period. The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting . Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday . LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress . Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s. The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together. In NY-1, the people who funded the race and the people who voted in it were often different. Both campaigns were bankrolled mostly by donors outside the district, including major Wall Street, Hollywood and tech names. Even the men on the ballot live beyond its lines: both reside near Amityville, on Long Island’s South Shore, which means neither could vote for himself. A district with a summer address NY-1 runs from Suffolk County’s North Shore villages to the East End, with vineyards and farms on the North Fork and the Hamptons on the South Fork. In between lie Smithtown and Brookhaven, where suburban neighborhoods give way to woods and residents are largely commuters, law enforcement and small-business owners. Each summer, the South Fork fills with the people who run Wall Street and corporate America. That makes the district one of the country’s busiest political ATMs, where financiers and industry titans host fundraisers for both parties . Suffolk County donors gave more than $45 million to campaigns in the 2020 cycle alone, according to OpenSecrets data CNBC cited. In August, Vice President JD Vance raised more than $5 million from young Republican donors at the Southampton home of Omeed Malik , president of 1789 Capital and a prominent Trump donor. Two candidates, one shrinking margin LaLota, a Navy veteran and former Suffolk County elections commissioner, was first elected in 2022 to succeed Lee Zeldin and was re-elected in 2024, defeating former CNN anchor John Avlon by about 11 points. In that race, LaLota criticized Avlon for his dual residency in both Sag Harbor and Manhattan. Gallant, 37, is an Army National Guard Black Hawk pilot, a former FAA air traffic controller at JFK, a former union leader and a volunteer firefighter. He won the June primary with about 63% of the vote, defeating Lukas Ventouras , a 25-year-old law student and district resident who had raised about $124,000, mostly in unitemized small-dollar donations. Gallant later picked up endorsements from Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. After the Post story, Gallant’s attorney, Sara Azari, who previously represented former Rep. Eric Swalwell after misconduct allegations, confirmed the photos were authentic and consensual. Gallant told the New York Times he hoped it could be his “Kim Kardashian moment,” and the campaign began selling “Make Politics Sexy Again” merchandise . LaLota stuck to calling Gallant “weak and woke” and needling him for declining to debate . Asked by Fortune about the surge, Gallant answered through Slingshot Strategies , a consulting firm that promises “a proven track record of shifting the conversation” for candidates facing “overwhelming odds” and “difficult fights.” He said the Post story “backfired on them” and that the Times interview let voters see “a proud gay man who refused to be ashamed of his identity, and it resonated.” On LaLota’s outside money, he said, “I never had to rely on outside interests to try and buy this seat.” About a third of his own money from named donors came from inside the district. LaLota cast the surge as a product of the controversy itself. “On the same days my opponent was backing out of debates, he was monetizing his BDSM and pornographic modeling past,” he said in a statement to Fortune . “Instead of boasting how kinky he is, as he did to the Times , he owes Long Islanders an explanation for choosing vanity and fundraising over debates and accountability.” Where the money came from Fortune analyzed itemized contributions dated in 2026 in both campaigns’ raw FEC filings through Oct. 14, so the comparison covers the same stretch of the race for both candidates. Repeat donors were counted once, refunds subtracted and conduit entries adjusted so no gift was counted twice. The FEC does not require campaigns to name individuals who give $200 or less in a cycle, so those donors are excluded. Fortune placed donors inside or outside NY-1 based on the mailing city they listed, which may differ from where they vote. Individuals may give $3,500 per election this cycle, or $7,000 for the primary and general combined. Fortune tallied the filings by hand, then used Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, to clean the raw files and check the calculations. LaLota had the bigger war chest. Through Oct. 14, he had raised $4.5 million and had $2.31 million in cash on hand. Gallant had raised $1.7 million and had $426,000 on hand. The sharper contrast was where the money came from. Of the 785 named donors in LaLota’s 2026 filings, 29% listed mailing addresses in the district. Together they gave $207,161, only 16% of what he raised from named individuals. PACs and other committees supplied $1.18 million, about a quarter of his total for the cycle. Gallant’s support was more local, but not by much. Of his 1,031 named donors in the 2026 raw file, 390 (38%) listed addresses in NY-1 totaling nearly $300,000, about a third of the roughly $876,000 he raised from named individuals this year. Counting gifts from 2025, his itemized individual total for the cycle is $1.15 million . events.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
events.summary: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. events.title: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
events.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of New York ; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally. By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier. The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms. Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic. Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments. The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic. Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts. Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022. In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now $6,678, according to TransUnion's Q3 insights report. Borrowers under 30 had the highest rate of credit card debt newly becoming at least 90 days overdue, the Fed's report found. What we're watching: Democrats won the midterms promising to lower prices — but delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets will be difficult to fulfill.

events.title: Jim Jordan wins House GOP minority leader race
events.summary: House Republicans elected Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader Tuesday, handing the reins of the battered GOP conference to one of its most prominent conservative firebrands. Why it matters: Jordan's victory marks a major shake-up in House Republican leadership, elevating a founding member of the hardline Freedom Caucus who campaigned as an alternative to the leaders who presided over the GOP's crushing midterm defeat . Jordan bested Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), who had served as the No. 2 House Republican since 2014, in the conference-wide secret ballot for minority leader. Scalise trailed Jordan by 33 votes. Jordan's victory signals an appetite among House Republicans for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to enter the minority. State of play: Jordan and Scalise entered Tuesday's election locked in a tight race, with both camps expressing confidence in their chances of winning. Jordan drew public support from some of the conference's most conservative members, who argued Republicans needed a change in direction after their devastating midterm losses. Scalise leaned on his longstanding relationships across the conference and his decade-plus of experience in leadership. The big picture: Jordan's ascent represents a remarkable turnaround for a conservative agitator who spent much of his career challenging the Republican establishment before becoming one of President Trump's most vocal allies. He'll be tasked with uniting a fractured Republican conference and leading the party's efforts to reclaim the House majority in 2028. Zoom out: Beyond the top job, current whip Tom Emmer (Minn.) beat back a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (Texas) to stay on as minority whip. Conference Chair: Lisa McClain (Mich.) won a three-way race with Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.). NRCC Chair: Brian Jack (Ga.) beat out Rudy Yakym (Ind.) to lead House Republicans' campaign arm. Current NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson (N.C.) lost his own reelection bid last week. events.title: 3 charged with plotting terror attacks in U.S., Europe
events.summary: Three individuals were charged in connection with alleged Iranian-linked terror plots, including a September scheme against a British Royal Air Force Base that housed U.S. military personnel and aircraft, per an indictment unsealed Tuesday. The big picture: The indictment alleges that a leader of an Islamic terrorist group attempted to coordinate with his fellow defendants from jail by passing coded messages through third parties. The charges include conspiracy to provide material support to a Foreign Terrorist Organization, conspiracy to provide material support for acts of terrorism, attempted acts of terrorism across national boundaries and conspiracy to bomb a place of public use, among others. Driving the news: Since early in the year, the three men named in the indictment worked to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, the indictment alleges. The eight-count superseding indictment names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national. It highlights nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks, which included plots against Jewish institutions in Europe and the U.S. Al-Saadi was charged in May for working with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah, both of which the U.S. has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. What's inside: Even after al-Saadi was arrested and transferred to U.S. custody, he allegedly passed coded messages to his fellow defendants in the days leading up to an attempted plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in England. The U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities, elevating the base's position on the IRGC's radar . Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were in Iran at the time, but relied on a network of contacts in the U.K. whom Al-Hassani allegedly paid to prepare by acquiring vans and barrels of fuel and researching chemical accelerants in preparation for the Fairford attack, the indictment says. Catch up quick: British police arrested five men on suspicion of terrorism near the base back in September. Iran denied any involvement in the suspected plot at the time, Axios previously reported. What they're saying: "Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy," Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.
